Multiple enumeration: an IEnumerable from a query or yield runs again each time you enumerate it; materialise once with ToList when you need it twice.
In IRT the shipment list query stays IQueryable until paging and projection, so SQL Server returns only [50] rows of the DTO columns.
c:
IQueryable<Shipment> q = _db.Shipments.Where(s => s.StudyId == id);   // nothing executed yet
var page = await q.OrderBy(s => s.ShipmentDate).Skip(0).Take(50)
                  .Select(s => new ShipmentRow(s.Id, s.Status)).ToListAsync(ct); // one SQL query
var bad = _db.Shipments.AsEnumerable().Where(s => s.StudyId == id);   // loads the whole table!
f: What is an expression tree?
Code represented as data (Expression<T>) that a provider can inspect and translate, e.g. into SQL.
IEnumerable vs ICollection vs IList?
IEnumerable only iterates; ICollection adds Count/Add/Remove; IList adds index access.
p1-5.y: IEnumerable works on data in memory and filters it in C#. IQueryable builds an expression that the provider, like EF Core, turns into SQL, so filtering happens in the database. List is a concrete in-memory collection that is already loaded. So I keep queries as IQueryable until I have added filters and paging, and only then call ToListAsync, which avoids pulling whole tables into memory.
p1-5.k: linq, deferred execution, ef core, list
x: All three are about collections, but they differ in where the work happens.

IEnumerable works on data in memory. When you use LINQ on it, the filters run as C# code on the application server. IQueryable is different: it builds an expression tree, and a provider like EF Core translates that into SQL, so the filtering, sorting and paging run inside the database. A List is a concrete collection that's already loaded in memory, with indexing and a Count.

The important practical point is when the query actually executes. If you call ToList too early, or pass an IQueryable as IEnumerable, EF Core pulls the whole table into memory and then filters it in C#. That's a classic performance bug.

So in our APIs I keep the query as IQueryable while I add filters, sorting and paging, then I call ToListAsync once at the end. For example, on our shipment search screen, building the filters on IQueryable meant SQL Server returned only one page of rows instead of thousands.
I can explain deferred execution too, which is closely related.

p1-6.q: An abstract class is a partially implemented base type that can hold state, constructors and shared code, and a class can inherit only one; an interface is a contract that a class or struct can implement many of. Since C# 8 interfaces can have default implementations and static members, but still no instance fields or constructors.
i: Use an interface for capabilities and seams for DI and testing (ISftpClient, IClock); use an abstract class to share real code and enforce a template (SftpClientBase with retry and logging).
Template Method pattern: the abstract base defines the algorithm and calls abstract or virtual steps; that is how our SFTP base class wraps every provider call with retry, logging and error mapping.
Versioning: adding a member to an interface breaks implementers unless it has a default implementation; adding a virtual method to a base class does not.
Combine them: interface for consumers, abstract base for implementers (ISftpClient + SftpClientBase).
Static abstract interface members (C# 11) enable generic math and factory patterns.
f: Can an abstract class implement an interface?
Yes, and it may leave members abstract for subclasses to implement.
When do default interface methods make sense?
Evolving a public interface without breaking existing implementers.
p1-6.y: An interface is a contract that says what a class can do, and a class can implement many interfaces. An abstract class can hold shared code and state, but a class can inherit only one. I use interfaces for dependencies, so I can swap implementations and mock them in tests. For example, all our SFTP libraries sit behind one ISftpClient interface, and I used an abstract base class for the shared retry logic.
x: An interface is a contract. It says what a type can do, but not how, and a class can implement many interfaces. An abstract class is a partial base class. It can hold shared code, fields and constructors, but a class can inherit from only one.

So the way I decide is: if I need a capability or a dependency that I want to swap or mock, I use an interface. If several implementations share real code, I use an abstract base class. Since C# 8 interfaces can have default methods, but I still keep them mostly as pure contracts.

A real example is our SFTP integration. All three providers, ComponentPro, SSH.NET and Rebex, implement one ISftpClient interface, so the business code and the unit tests depend only on the interface, and the DI container or a factory picks the provider. Then they inherit from an abstract base class that holds the shared retry, timeout and logging logic, so I didn't repeat it three times.
So it's not either-or; they work well together. I can explain how that helped with testing.

p1-7.q: SOLID is five design principles that keep code easy to change: Single responsibility, Open/closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation and Dependency inversion. I can show each one in my SFTP integration and CSV import work.
i: S: the CSV import is split into parser, validator and importer classes, so a new validation rule never touches parsing code and each piece has focused unit tests.
O: adding Rebex meant one new ISftpClient class plus configuration; no caller or switch statement changed.

L: every provider honours the same contract (same exceptions mapped to SftpException, same behaviour on missing files), so swapping one for another cannot break callers; violating it would be a provider that silently ignores overwrite flags.
I: reporting code depends on a small IShipmentReader, not a large repository with write methods, so read services cannot write by accident.
D: high-level services depend on abstractions registered in ASP.NET Core DI; tests inject fakes and Moq mocks.
Balance: SOLID is a tool, not a goal; I avoid interfaces with exactly one implementation unless they are a test seam or a boundary.
f: Which principle is broken most often?
Single responsibility: services grow into god classes; I split by reason to change.
What is the difference between DI and DIP?
DIP is the design principle (depend on abstractions); DI is the technique that supplies those abstractions at runtime.
p1-7.y: SOLID is five principles that keep code easy to change. Single responsibility means one reason to change, open-closed means extend without editing, Liskov means a child class must work wherever the parent works, interface segregation means small focused interfaces, and dependency inversion means depending on abstractions. In my SFTP integration, each vendor library implements one interface, so adding a new library did not touch the business code.
p1-7.k: single responsibility, open closed, liskov, interface segregation, dependency inversion, design principles
x: SOLID is a set of five design principles that keep code easy to change and test. Let me explain each with an example from my work.

S is single responsibility: a class should have one reason to change. In our CSV import, the parser, the validator and the importer are separate classes. O is open-closed: open for extension, closed for modification. When we added Rebex as a new SFTP provider, I added a new class, I didn't edit the callers. L is Liskov substitution: any ISftpClient implementation can replace another without breaking the caller, so they all behave the same for errors and timeouts. I is interface segregation: small, focused interfaces, so a class that only reads files doesn't depend on write methods. And D is dependency inversion: high-level services depend on abstractions, which ASP.NET Core injects through DI, so I can mock them in unit tests.
I treat SOLID as guidance, not rules. Too many tiny interfaces can make code harder to follow. I can go deeper into any one of them.

p1-8.q: In production I have used Strategy and Adapter (SFTP providers behind one interface), Factory (choosing a provider by configuration), Decorator (adding retry and logging around clients), Repository/Unit of Work over EF Core in some services, Options and Singleton through DI, Observer/pub-sub via Kafka and RabbitMQ, plus Outbox and Retry for messaging.
i: Strategy: the algorithm (SFTP provider) is chosen at runtime; Adapter: each provider wraps a third-party API (Rebex, SSH.NET) into our ISftpClient.
Factory: SftpClientFactory reads the vendor's configured provider; with .NET 8 keyed services this is a one-liner.
Decorator: wrap an interface to add behaviour without changing it, e.g. a caching or retry decorator registered with Scrutor's Decorate.
Mediator (MediatR) and CQRS: separate commands and queries in larger services; useful but I avoid it in small ones to keep code simple.
Outbox: save the business change and the event in one transaction, then publish, so events are never lost when the broker is down.
I name patterns only when they clarify intent; the goal is simpler code, not pattern count.
f: Strategy vs Factory?
Strategy is the interchangeable behaviour; the factory decides which strategy instance to create.
A pattern you regret using?
Generic repositories on top of EF Core: they hid useful EF features and added code without value.
p1-8.y: In production I have used Strategy and Adapter to put different SFTP libraries behind one interface, and a Factory to pick the library from configuration. I used Decorator to add retry and logging around clients without changing them. With messaging I used the Outbox pattern so events are not lost, and publish-subscribe with Kafka and RabbitMQ. I pick a pattern only when it solves a real problem.
p1-8.k: design patterns, strategy, adapter, factory, decorator, outbox, singleton, repository
x: I use patterns only when they solve a real problem, and I've used several in production.

The one I use most is Strategy, together with Adapter. In our SFTP integration, three different libraries sit behind one ISftpClient interface, and each adapter hides its library's quirks. A Factory then picks the right provider for each vendor from configuration. I've used Decorator to add retry and logging around a client without changing the client itself, which is also how Polly handlers work in HttpClient.

For messaging, I've used the transactional Outbox pattern so events aren't lost when the database save succeeds but the publish fails, and publish-subscribe with Kafka and RabbitMQ. In some services we use Repository and Unit of Work over EF Core. And for configuration and shared clients we use the Options pattern and singletons, but through dependency injection, not a static Singleton class.
So for me the value of a pattern is the shared vocabulary and a proven solution. I can walk through the SFTP design in detail if you'd like.

p1-9.q: .NET uses a generational, compacting, tracing garbage collector: it finds objects no longer reachable from roots (statics, stack, registers, handles), frees them and compacts the heap. New objects go into generation 0, survivors are promoted to 1 and 2, and large objects of 85,000 bytes or more go to the Large Object Heap.
i: Generations work because most objects die young; gen 0 collections are cheap, gen 2 (full) collections are expensive.
Server GC (default in ASP.NET Core) uses a heap and GC thread per core for throughput; workstation GC suits desktop; concurrent/background GC reduces pauses.
LOH is not compacted by default, so repeated large allocations fragment memory; rent buffers from ArrayPool<T> instead.
Containers: the GC respects container memory limits; .NET 8 adds DATAS (dynamic adaptation of server GC heaps, default in .NET 9) for lower memory in small containers.
Finalizers delay collection by a cycle; implement IDisposable for deterministic cleanup and use SafeHandle instead of finalizers.
Diagnose with dotnet-counters (gc-heap-size, gen-2 count, % time in GC) and dotnet-gcdump; I used them for [a memory growth issue caused by an unbounded static cache].
f: What causes memory leaks in .NET?
Objects kept reachable: static collections, event handlers not unsubscribed, caches without limits, captured closures.
Should you call GC.Collect()?
Almost never; it disrupts the GC's tuning. Fix the allocation pattern instead.
p1-9.y: The garbage collector frees memory for objects that are no longer used. It divides objects into generations: new objects are in generation 0 and cleaned up often, while long-lived objects move to generation 1 and 2 and are checked less often. Large objects go on a separate heap. Most of the time I don't touch it, but I dispose resources properly, and once I fixed a memory leak caused by event handlers holding objects alive.
p1-9.k: gc, memory, generations, dispose, large object heap
x: Garbage collection in .NET automatically frees memory for objects that nothing references any more, so we don't free memory by hand.

It's generational, based on the idea that most objects die young. New objects go into generation 0, which is collected often and cheaply. Objects that survive move to generation 1, and long-lived ones move to generation 2, which is collected less often because it's more expensive. Objects larger than about 85 KB go to the Large Object Heap, which is collected with gen 2. ASP.NET Core uses server GC by default, with a heap per core, for throughput.
One important point: the GC only handles managed memory. Things like files, sockets, database connections and SFTP sessions are unmanaged resources, so they need IDisposable and a using statement.

In practice I don't tune the GC much, but I watch for leaks. For example, I once investigated a .NET service whose memory kept growing, and the cause was event handlers that were never unsubscribed, keeping objects alive. I can walk through how I diagnosed that.

p1-10.q: A delegate is a type-safe reference to a method; Func<> and Action<> are built-in generic delegates (Func returns a value, Action returns void); a lambda is concise syntax for creating a delegate or an expression tree; an event is a delegate wrapped so outsiders can only subscribe (+=) and unsubscribe (-=), not invoke or overwrite it.
i: Multicast: delegates can hold several methods; invoking runs them in order, and only the last return value is kept.
Closures: lambdas capture variables, not values; capturing a loop variable or a large object can surprise you or keep it alive longer.
Lambdas become Expression<Func<...>> when the target type asks for it; that is how EF Core reads your Where clause.
Event pattern: EventHandler<TEventArgs>, raise with `Handler?.Invoke(this, args)`; unsubscribe to avoid leaks when the publisher outlives the subscriber.
In ASP.NET Core, middleware is literally a chain of RequestDelegate instances, and Polly policies take Func<CancellationToken, Task> delegates.
f: Why use events instead of public delegates?
Events stop outside code from invoking the delegate or replacing all subscribers with =.
Func vs Predicate?
Predicate<T> is an older delegate equal to Func<T,bool>; LINQ uses Func.
p1-10.y: A delegate is a type-safe reference to a method. Func and Action are built-in delegates: Func returns a value and Action returns nothing. A lambda is a short way to write the method inline, and an event is a delegate that others can subscribe to but only the owner can raise. I use lambdas every day in LINQ and in minimal API endpoints.
p1-10.k: delegate, func, action, lambda, event, callback
x: A delegate is a type-safe reference to a method. You can store it in a variable, pass it to another method and call it later.

Func and Action are built-in generic delegates, so we rarely declare our own. Func returns a value; for example Func of int, string takes an int and returns a string. Action returns nothing. There's also Predicate, which returns a bool. A lambda is a short inline way to write the method, like x goes to x.IsActive. An event is a delegate with restricted access: other classes can subscribe and unsubscribe, but only the owning class can raise it.

One thing to be careful about is that lambdas can capture variables, which creates a closure. That's very useful, but it can keep objects alive longer than expected, and event handlers that are never unsubscribed are a common memory leak.

I use these every day: lambdas in LINQ queries, Func in minimal API endpoints, and Action delegates for options configuration, like services.AddOptions with a configure lambda. I can explain closures in more depth if useful.

p1-11.q: LINQ queries are not executed when you write them, only when you enumerate them (foreach, ToList, Count, First). The query is a recipe; each enumeration runs it again against the current data.
i: Deferred operators: Where, Select, OrderBy, Skip, Take; immediate operators: ToList, ToArray, Count, Sum, First, Any.
For IQueryable the whole chain is translated to one SQL statement at enumeration, so you can compose filters conditionally before executing.
Multiple enumeration pitfall: enumerating twice runs the database query or the yield iterator twice; analyzers warn about it.
Captured variables are read at execution time, not when the query was defined.
Exceptions inside the query appear at enumeration time, which can be far from the line that built it.
I use this for dynamic filters in IRT list endpoints: add Where clauses only for the parameters the user supplied, then page and execute once.
f: How do you force execution?
Call ToList/ToArray (or an aggregate) to materialise the results once.
Is deferred execution good or bad?
Good for composition and efficiency; risky when it causes repeated or late execution.
p1-11.y: Deferred execution means a LINQ query does not run when you write it. It runs only when you loop over it or call something like ToList or Count. The good part is you can keep adding filters before it runs. The risk is running the same query twice by accident, so when I need the result more than once, I call ToList once and reuse it.
x: Deferred execution means a LINQ query doesn't run when you write it. It only runs when you actually enumerate it, for example in a foreach loop, or when you call ToList, Count, First or Any.

That's useful, because you can build up a query step by step, adding filters and sorting based on conditions, and with EF Core it all becomes one SQL statement at the end. But there are two risks. First, every enumeration runs the query again, so if you loop over an IQueryable twice, you hit the database twice. Second, the data can change between definition and execution, because it reads the data at the time it runs.
So my rule is: if I need the results more than once, I materialise them once with ToList or ToArray and reuse that list. Operators like ToList, Count, Sum and First run immediately.

In our search APIs we build the query conditionally on IQueryable, and only call ToListAsync after paging, so SQL Server returns just one page. I can show the double-enumeration bug in code if you like.

p1-12.q: Code is thread-safe when concurrent callers cannot corrupt shared state. The best way is to avoid shared mutable state (immutability, local variables, scoped services); when sharing is needed, use the right primitive: lock, SemaphoreSlim for async code, Interlocked for counters, and concurrent collections.
i: lock (Monitor) for short synchronous critical sections; you cannot await inside a lock, so use SemaphoreSlim(1,1) with WaitAsync for async sections.
Interlocked.Increment and CompareExchange for lock-free counters and flags.
ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd can run the factory more than once; wrap the value in Lazy<T> if the factory must run exactly once.
Immutable records and ImmutableArray make sharing safe by design; .NET 8 adds FrozenDictionary for fast read-only lookups.
DI: singletons are shared by all requests, so they must be thread-safe; DbContext is not thread-safe, so never share it across concurrent tasks.
Across instances (several ECS tasks) in-process locks do nothing; use database locks, optimistic concurrency or a distributed lock. Our study transfer guard uses a lock row inside a transaction.
f: lock vs Monitor vs Mutex?
lock is syntax for Monitor (in-process, fast); Mutex can be cross-process and is slower. .NET 9 adds System.Threading.Lock as a dedicated lock type.
What is a race condition?
The result depends on timing between threads, e.g. two requests reading and writing the same counter.
p1-12.y: To make code thread-safe, first I avoid shared state where possible, by keeping services stateless and using immutable objects. When sharing is needed, I use concurrent collections like ConcurrentDictionary, the lock statement for small critical sections, and SemaphoreSlim for async code because you cannot await inside a lock. For example, our CSV import used a lock row in the database so two users could not import the same study at once.
p1-12.k: thread safety, lock, concurrency, race condition, semaphoreslim, concurrentdictionary
x: Code is thread-safe when it behaves correctly even if many threads run it at the same time.

My first approach is to avoid shared mutable state. I keep services stateless and use immutable objects, so there's nothing to protect. When I do need shared state, I pick the right tool. For simple counters I use Interlocked. For shared caches I use ConcurrentDictionary. For a short critical section I use the lock statement, and for async code I use SemaphoreSlim, because you can't await inside a lock. SemaphoreSlim is also handy to limit concurrency, for example to deploy to only a few nodes in parallel. For lazy initialisation I use Lazy of T instead of hand-written double-checked locking.
I'm also careful with singletons in DI, because a singleton that holds mutable state is shared by every request.

And thread safety can cross processes too. In our CSV import, we used a lock row in the database so two users couldn't import into the same study at the same time. I can go into that design if helpful.

p1-13.q: A class is a reference type with identity; a struct is a value type copied by value; a record is a type (record class by default, or record struct) with compiler-generated value-based equality, ToString, deconstruction and non-destructive mutation through `with`.
i: Records are ideal for DTOs, messages and value objects: two ShipmentCreated events with the same data are equal.
Positional records (`record Kit(string Number, int SiteId)`) create init-only properties; `with` makes a copy with changes.
Equality includes the runtime type (EqualityContract), so a derived record never equals its base record.
record struct (C# 10) gives value-type records; readonly record struct makes them immutable.
EF Core entities should usually be classes with identity, not records, because value equality confuses change tracking.
Structs: small, short-lived, immutable values (coordinates, money); large or mutable structs cause copying bugs and costs.
f: Are records immutable?
Positional records have init-only properties, but you can add mutable properties, and referenced objects (lists) can still change.
Why not records for EF entities?
Entities need stable identity and tracked mutation; value equality and with-copies fight that.
p1-13.y: A class is a reference type with identity, so two objects with the same values are still different. A record is mainly for data: it compares by value, is easy to make immutable, and has a nice ToString and the with-expression for copies. A struct is a value type that is copied, best for small values. I use records for DTOs and events, and classes for services and entities.
p1-13.k: record, class, struct, immutable, value equality, dto
x: All three define types, but they behave differently.

A class is a reference type with identity. Two objects with exactly the same values are still different objects, because equality compares references by default. A record is designed for data. It's still a reference type by default, but it compares by value, so two records with the same values are equal. It also gives you concise immutable syntax, a readable ToString, and with-expressions to create a modified copy. A struct is a value type, so it's copied on assignment, and it's best for small values. There's also record struct, which is a value type with value equality.

In my services I use records for DTOs, API contracts and messages we publish to Kafka or RabbitMQ, because those are pure data and should be immutable. I use classes for services and EF Core entities, because entities have identity and change over time. Structs I use rarely, only for small values.
I can explain why EF entities shouldn't be records, if that's useful.

p1-14.q: Catch exceptions only where you can handle them meaningfully, let the rest bubble to one global handler that logs and returns ProblemDetails, and never swallow them silently. Use specific exception types, preserve stack traces with `throw;`, and do not use exceptions for normal control flow.
i: `throw;` keeps the original stack trace, `throw ex;` resets it; wrap with an inner exception when adding context.
Exception filters (`catch (SqlException ex) when (ex.Number == 1205)`) catch only matching cases without unwinding the stack first, which helps debugging.
Use finally or using/await using for cleanup; IAsyncDisposable for async resources.
Expected outcomes (validation, not found) are often clearer as results or specific domain exceptions mapped to 400/404/409 centrally.
Cancellation: let OperationCanceledException flow when the request is aborted; do not log it as an error.
Logging: log once, at the boundary, with structured context (ids), not at every layer; never expose stack traces to clients.
f: Why not catch (Exception) everywhere?
It hides bugs and leaves state inconsistent; only boundaries (global handler, background loops) should catch everything.
Exceptions vs error codes?
Exceptions for exceptional failures; results for expected business outcomes.
p1-14.y: My rules are simple: catch an exception only where I can actually handle it, otherwise let it bubble up to one global handler. I never swallow exceptions, I log them once with context, and I return a clean ProblemDetails response without exposing stack traces. I use specific exception types and avoid using exceptions for normal flow. In our APIs, one exception handler converts all errors into consistent responses.
p1-14.k: exception handling, try catch, problemdetails, global error handler, logging
x: My main rule is: catch an exception only where I can actually do something about it, and let everything else bubble up to one global handler.

In practice that means a few things. I never swallow exceptions with an empty catch. When I rethrow, I use throw on its own, not throw ex, so the stack trace is kept. I log an exception once, with context like the correlation id and the study id, instead of logging it at every layer. I create specific domain exceptions for business rules, for example a StudyTransferNotAllowedException, but I don't use exceptions for normal flow like validation, because they're slow and hide intent. And I use using or finally to clean up resources.

In our ASP.NET Core APIs, one global exception handler catches anything unhandled, logs it, and returns a consistent ProblemDetails response with the right status code, without leaking stack traces to the client.
That gives us consistent errors and clean logs during an incident. I can show how we set up IExceptionHandler in .NET 8.

p1-15.q: Generics let you write type-safe, reusable code parameterised by type, such as List<T> or Result<T>, without casting or boxing. Constraints (`where T : class, new(), IEntity`) tell the compiler what T can do, so you can call members on it safely.
i: Performance: generics over value types get specialised code, so List<int> does not box like ArrayList.
Constraints: class, struct, notnull, unmanaged, new(), base class, interface, and in C# 11 static abstract interface members for generic math.
Variance: `out T` (covariance) on IEnumerable<out T> lets IEnumerable<string> be used as IEnumerable<object>; `in T` (contravariance) on Action<in T>.
Generic methods with inference keep call sites clean: `Map<TSource, TDest>()`.
Open generic DI registration: `services.AddScoped(typeof(IRepository<>), typeof(EfRepository<>));`.
Used in IRT for [a Result<T> type returned by validation services and a generic paged response PagedResult<T>].
f: What is covariance?
Using a more derived type argument where a less derived one is expected, allowed for out-only positions.
Generics in C# vs Java?
C# generics are reified at runtime (real types per instantiation); Java uses type erasure.
p1-15.y: Generics let me write code once and use it with any type while keeping type safety, so no casting and no boxing. Constraints like where T is a class or has a parameterless constructor tell the compiler what the type can do. For example, I wrote a generic paged result type and a generic repository method, so every list API returns pages in the same way.
p1-15.k: generics, constraints, type safety, where t
x: Generics let me write code once and use it with many types, while keeping full type safety.

Without generics, you'd use object and cast everywhere, which is error-prone, and value types would get boxed. With List of T or Dictionary of K and V, the compiler knows the exact type, so there's no casting and no boxing. Constraints tell the compiler what a type parameter can do. For example, where T is a class, where T implements an IEntity interface, or where T has a parameterless constructor. Then I can safely call those members inside the generic code. There's also variance: IEnumerable of a derived type can be used as IEnumerable of the base type.

In my work, I wrote a generic paged result type, so every list API returns items, total count and page info in the same shape. I've also used a generic Result of T wrapper for success or error responses, and generic repository methods constrained to our entity base class.
So generics reduce duplication and catch mistakes at compile time. I can explain covariance in more detail if you want.

p1-16.q: For backend services, .NET 8 (LTS) brought big performance gains, native AOT for ASP.NET Core, TimeProvider, keyed DI services, IExceptionHandler, built-in Identity API endpoints, better metrics and the resilience libraries. .NET 10 (LTS, November 2025) adds C# 14, further JIT and GC improvements, built-in minimal API validation, OpenAPI 3.1 and more AOT work.
i: Performance: Dynamic PGO on by default in .NET 8, faster JSON, Kestrel and LINQ; most services get faster just by upgrading.
Native AOT: small, fast-starting binaries for minimal APIs and Lambda; limits on reflection and EF Core.
Developer productivity: primary constructors (C# 12), collection expressions, keyed services, FrozenDictionary, TimeProvider for testable time.
Observability: built-in metrics with System.Diagnostics.Metrics and OpenTelemetry-friendly meters; .NET Aspire for local orchestration and dashboards.
.NET 9 (STS) in between: HybridCache, built-in OpenAPI document generation (Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi), DATAS GC by default.
In IRT we moved from .NET 8 to 10 before .NET 8 support ends (November 2026) and saw [10 to 15 percent] lower p95 latency.
f: Which C# 14 feature do you like?
Extension members (extension properties and static extension members) and the field keyword for properties.
Why stay on LTS?
Longer support and fewer upgrades, which matters when every upgrade needs validation in a regulated product.
p1-16.y: For backend services, .NET 8 brought Native AOT for APIs, keyed services in dependency injection, TimeProvider for testable time, built-in resilience handlers, and IExceptionHandler. .NET 10 is the next LTS with C# 14 and more performance improvements. When I upgraded [3] services to .NET 10 in [early 2026], we saw about [10 to 15 percent] lower p95 latency without code changes.
p1-16.k: .net 8, .net 10, new features, keyed services, native aot, timeprovider, c# 14
x: For backend services, each recent release brought real, practical improvements.

.NET 8, which is an LTS, gave us a lot: keyed services in dependency injection, TimeProvider so time is testable, built-in resilience handlers on HttpClient based on Polly, IExceptionHandler for global errors, native AOT for minimal APIs, and built-in rate limiting. It also kept improving System.Text.Json, and the runtime got faster with things like dynamic PGO. .NET 10 is the next LTS, with C# 14, better OpenAPI support and more performance work, so you often get speed-ups just by upgrading.

In a regulated product, the LTS support window drives our upgrade plan. In [early 2026] I upgraded [3] of our IRT services from .NET 8 to .NET 10. It was mostly package updates and a few breaking changes, and we saw about [10-15%] lower p95 latency without touching business logic.

I planned it service by service over [about six weeks]: first update the target framework and packages on a branch, fix the breaking changes, run the full unit and integration test suites, then compare performance in a test environment before the normal FV and UAT validation. We also added [Trivy] image scanning to the pipeline at the same time.

p1-17.q: The pipeline is the ordered chain of middleware that every HTTP request passes through in ASP.NET Core: Kestrel receives the request, builds an HttpContext, and each middleware can act before and after calling the next one until an endpoint produces the response, which then flows back out in reverse. See Part 10 for standalone deep answers on middleware and custom middleware.
i: Recommended order: exception handler, HSTS, HTTPS redirection, static files, routing, CORS, authentication, authorization, custom middleware (rate limiting, correlation id), endpoints.
Routing is split in two: UseRouting selects the endpoint early so later middleware (CORS, auth) can read its metadata; the endpoint executes at the end.
Branching: Map (by path), MapWhen (by predicate, separate branch), UseWhen (conditional middleware that rejoins).
Short-circuit: any middleware can end the request; .NET 8 adds `.ShortCircuit()` on endpoints such as /health to skip the rest of the pipeline.
Cost: every middleware runs for every request, so keep them fast and async.
In IRT the order is exception handler, correlation id, routing, CORS, authentication, authorization, rate limiting, controllers.
f: Where does Kestrel fit?
Kestrel is the server underneath; it accepts connections and hands each request to the pipeline.
What does app.Run do at the end of Program.cs?
Starts the host and blocks until shutdown; Run(delegate) in the pipeline is different: a terminal middleware.
p1-17.y: The middleware pipeline is a chain of components that every HTTP request passes through, in the order they are registered in Program.cs. Each middleware can do something before calling the next one and something after, or stop the request early. The order matters a lot: exception handling first, then HTTPS, routing, CORS, authentication, authorization, and finally the endpoints. In my project I added a correlation-id middleware so every log line could be traced across services.
p1-17.k: middleware, request pipeline, request delegate, use, run, ordering
x: The middleware pipeline is the chain of components that every HTTP request passes through in ASP.NET Core, from the moment Kestrel receives it until the response goes back.

Each middleware gets the HttpContext and a next delegate. It can do work, call next to pass the request along, and then do more work as the response comes back through it, in reverse order. Or it can short-circuit, like the static files middleware returning a file, or authorization returning 403. The pipeline is built in Program.cs with app.Use calls, and order matters a lot. A typical order is: exception handler first, so it catches everything, then HSTS and HTTPS redirection, static files, routing, CORS, authentication, authorization, rate limiting, custom middleware like logging and correlation ids, and finally the endpoints.
A good mental picture is Russian dolls: each layer wraps the next.

In our services, the first custom piece is our correlation-id middleware, placed near the top so even errors from later middleware are logged with the id. That lets us trace one request across [4] services. I can explain what goes wrong when the order is wrong.

p1-18.q: DI lifetimes define how long a service instance lives: Singleton is one instance for the whole application, Scoped is one per request (per DI scope), Transient is a new instance every time it is resolved. Choose by state and thread safety: stateless or thread-safe shared things as singletons, per-request things like DbContext as scoped, lightweight stateless helpers as transient.
i: Captive dependency: a singleton must not depend on scoped or transient services that hold state, or it keeps them forever; ValidateScopes catches this in Development.
Background code has no request scope: create one with IServiceScopeFactory.CreateScope() (or CreateAsyncScope) per unit of work.
Disposal: the container disposes services it created when their scope ends; do not dispose injected services yourself.
Transient IDisposable services resolved from the root provider are kept until app shutdown, a hidden leak.
.NET 8 keyed services let one interface have several named registrations.
In IRT: DbContext scoped, HttpClient typed clients transient via IHttpClientFactory, SFTP provider factory and caches singleton.
f: What is ValidateOnBuild?
It checks at startup that every registered service can be constructed, catching missing registrations early.
Is HttpClient a singleton?
Use IHttpClientFactory or one long-lived client with PooledConnectionLifetime, not new HttpClient per call.
p1-18.y: Singleton means one instance for the whole application. Scoped means one instance per HTTP request, which is right for DbContext. Transient means a new instance every time it is asked for. The key rule is that a longer-lived service must not depend on a shorter-lived one, for example a singleton holding a scoped DbContext, because that causes threading bugs. In our services, DbContext and repositories are scoped and stateless helpers are singletons.
p1-18.k: di, dependency injection, lifetimes, singleton, scoped, transient, captive dependency
x: Service lifetimes decide how long an object created by the DI container lives, and who shares it.

Singleton means one instance for the whole application. Everyone gets the same object, so it must be thread-safe. It's good for configuration, caches, IHttpClientFactory or a RabbitMQ connection. Scoped means one instance per scope, which in a web app is one per HTTP request. Everything in that request shares it, and it's disposed at the end. DbContext is the classic example, because it's a unit of work. Transient means a new instance every time it's requested. It's good for lightweight, stateless helpers like validators or mappers.

The most important rule is about dependencies: a service shouldn't depend on something with a shorter lifetime. If a singleton takes a scoped DbContext, that DbContext gets captured forever, shared across threads and requests. That's called a captive dependency, and ASP.NET Core's scope validation catches it in development.
In our services, DbContext is scoped, the RabbitMQ connection is a singleton, and validators are transient. Our background services create a scope per message. I can explain that pattern if useful.

p1-19.q: Controllers group actions in classes with attributes, filters, model binding conventions and [ApiController] behaviour; Minimal APIs map routes directly to lambdas or methods with less ceremony and slightly better performance. Both share routing, DI, auth and OpenAPI, so the choice is about structure and team preference.
i: Controllers: mature conventions, action filters, model validation automatically, great for large APIs and teams used to MVC.
Minimal APIs: route groups, endpoint filters, TypedResults, native AOT support; ideal for small services, Lambda and new code.
Validation: automatic in controllers with [ApiController]; .NET 10 adds built-in validation to minimal APIs (AddValidation).
Testing: both via WebApplicationFactory; minimal handlers can be unit-tested as static methods.
Mixing is fine: one app can have controllers and minimal endpoints.
IRT uses controllers; for [the Node log summariser's .NET replacement prototype] I would use minimal APIs.
f: Which is faster?
Minimal APIs have less overhead, but the difference rarely matters compared with database calls.
How do you organise many minimal endpoints?
MapGroup per feature and one extension method per feature file.
p1-19.y: Controllers are the classic MVC way: classes with actions, filters and attribute routing, good for large APIs. Minimal APIs map endpoints directly in Program.cs with lambdas, with less ceremony and slightly better performance. Both share the same routing, DI and middleware. I use controllers for our larger domain APIs and minimal APIs for small services and health or internal endpoints.
p1-19.k: minimal api, controllers, mvc, endpoints, routing
x: Both build HTTP APIs on the same foundation, the same routing, DI, middleware and authentication. The difference is style and structure.

Controllers are classes that inherit ControllerBase, with actions marked by attributes like HttpGet. They give you a mature, conventional structure, the full filter pipeline, ApiController behaviours like automatic validation, and they're familiar to every .NET developer. That suits large APIs with many endpoints and teams. Minimal APIs map routes directly to lambdas or methods with MapGet and MapPost. There's less ceremony, startup is faster, performance is slightly better, and they work well with native AOT. Route groups, endpoint filters, TypedResults and, since .NET 10, built-in validation have closed most of the gaps.

So my choice is practical, not religious. For a large existing service with many controllers, I stay with controllers, for consistency. For a new small service, or a few endpoints, minimal APIs are cleaner.

In our team, the main IRT APIs use controllers, and newer small internal services use minimal APIs organised into feature-based extension methods. I can show how a minimal API is structured for a larger service.

p1-20.q: Program.cs builds and runs the app with the minimal hosting model: WebApplication.CreateBuilder sets up configuration (appsettings, environment variables, secrets), logging and the DI container; you register services; builder.Build() creates the app; then you configure the middleware pipeline and endpoints; app.Run() starts Kestrel and blocks until shutdown.
i: Configuration sources load in order, later ones override: appsettings.json, appsettings.{Environment}.json, user secrets (Development), environment variables, command line.
Services must be registered before Build(); after Build the container is read-only.
Hosted services start before Kestrel starts listening (in registration order); .NET 8 adds IHostedLifecycleService hooks.
Startup validation: ValidateOnStart for options and ValidateOnBuild for DI make misconfiguration fail fast at deployment.
Graceful shutdown: SIGTERM triggers IHostApplicationLifetime.ApplicationStopping, then hosted services' StopAsync within ShutdownTimeout.
Startup.cs (ConfigureServices/Configure) still works but is no longer the template.
f: Where would you put startup tasks like migrations?
Not in app startup for regulated releases; we run migration scripts as a controlled release step.
What happens if configuration is invalid?
With ValidateOnStart the app fails to start and the health check fails the deployment instead of failing at runtime.
p1-20.y: In Program.cs, first the builder is created, which loads configuration from appsettings, environment variables and secrets, and sets up logging. Then I register services in the DI container. Then app is built, and I add middleware in the right order and map the endpoints. Finally app.Run starts the Kestrel server. Since .NET 6 there is no separate Startup class, everything is in this one file.
p1-20.k: program.cs, startup, host, builder, configuration, kestrel
x: Program.cs is where the application is assembled. It has two phases: building the services, and building the pipeline.

First, WebApplication.CreateBuilder sets up the basics: configuration from appsettings.json, the environment-specific appsettings file, environment variables and user secrets; logging providers; and the DI container. Then I register services on builder.Services, things like controllers, DbContext, authentication, health checks, options and my own services. Calling builder.Build creates the app and the root service provider. Second phase: I configure the middleware pipeline in order, with app.Use calls, and map the endpoints. Finally app.Run starts Kestrel, which begins listening for requests, and hosted services start too.
I also make startup fail fast. With ValidateOnStart on options and ValidateOnBuild for DI, a missing setting or registration fails the deployment, not the first user request.

In CIRT, environment settings come from Azure DevOps variable groups, and in our AWS services, from Parameter Store and Secrets Manager, and we group registrations into extension methods like AddMessaging and AddPersistence, so Program.cs reads like a table of contents. I can walk through a real example.

p1-21.q: Middleware runs for every request at the HTTP level and knows nothing about MVC; filters run only inside the MVC (or endpoint) pipeline around a selected action, so they can see action arguments, model state and the action result. Use middleware for cross-cutting HTTP concerns and filters for action-specific concerns.
i: Middleware examples: exception handling, correlation id, CORS, authentication, rate limiting, response compression.
Filter examples: validation, auditing an action's arguments, a "study not locked" rule, caching a result, transforming results.
Ordering: middleware order is Program.cs order; filters run authorization, resource, action, exception, result, ordered by scope and Order.
Global exception handling belongs in middleware, because exception filters miss errors from other middleware and result execution.
Minimal APIs use endpoint filters, the filter equivalent.
Detailed filter answer and code: see Part 10 "MVC filter types".
f: Can middleware read the selected endpoint?
Yes, after UseRouting via context.GetEndpoint(), including its metadata (attributes).
Can a filter short-circuit?
Yes, by setting context.Result in an authorization, resource or action filter.
p1-21.y: Middleware runs for every request, early in the pipeline, and only knows about the HTTP context. Filters run inside MVC, around a specific controller action, so they know which action is being called and can see the model binding results. So I use middleware for cross-cutting things like correlation ids, logging and exception handling, and filters for action-specific things like validation or an audit attribute on certain endpoints.
p1-21.k: filters, middleware, action filter, mvc pipeline, cross-cutting
x: Middleware and filters can both run code before and after a request, but they work at different levels.

Middleware sits in the ASP.NET Core pipeline and runs for every request, including static files, health checks and requests that never reach a controller. It only knows about the HttpContext: the request, the response and the user. Filters run inside MVC, around a specific controller action. They know the action context: which controller and action is running, the bound arguments, model state and the result. They also run in a defined order: authorization, resource, then model binding, action, exception and result filters.

So my rule is simple. If the concern is about HTTP in general and applies everywhere, I use middleware, for example correlation ids, request logging, security headers or global exception handling. If it needs to know about the action, its arguments or its result, I use a filter, for example validating a model, auditing which study an action changed, or caching an action's result.

In our project, the correlation-id is middleware because it must cover every request across [4] services, while study-level audit logging is an action filter because it reads the action's arguments. I can show both in code.

p1-22.q: Model binding converts HTTP data (route values, query string, headers, form, JSON body) into action parameters and objects; validation then checks them against rules (DataAnnotations or FluentValidation) and fills ModelState. With [ApiController], invalid models automatically return a 400 ValidationProblemDetails before your action runs.
i: Sources: [FromRoute], [FromQuery], [FromBody] (one per action, read by System.Text.Json input formatter), [FromHeader], [FromForm], [FromServices]; [ApiController] infers most of them.
Complex types from the body are deserialised once; the body stream is not rewindable by default (EnableBuffering if middleware must read it).
Validation attributes: [Required], [Range], [StringLength], [RegularExpression]; IValidatableObject for cross-field rules; FluentValidation for complex rules and better testability.
Over-posting: bind to request DTOs, never directly to EF entities.
Custom binders (IModelBinder) for special formats; TypeConverter or TryParse for simple custom types in minimal APIs.
In IRT request DTOs validate format, while business rules (site active, depot valid) run in the service layer and return 409/422.
f: Why is required validation on a non-nullable value type tricky?
A missing Guid binds to Guid.Empty; use Guid? with [Required] or validate explicitly.
FluentValidation vs DataAnnotations?
FluentValidation keeps rules in testable classes and handles complex conditional rules better.
p1-22.y: Model binding takes data from the route, query string, headers and body and converts it into my action parameters. Then validation runs using data annotations or FluentValidation. With the ApiController attribute, if the model is invalid, ASP.NET Core automatically returns a 400 with the errors. In our CSV import API, I validated each row and returned errors with row and column numbers so users could fix the file easily.
p1-22.k: model binding, validation, data annotations, fluentvalidation, apicontroller, 400
x: Model binding is how ASP.NET Core turns the raw HTTP request into typed parameters for my action, and validation then checks those values before my code runs.

Binding reads values from different sources: the route, the query string, headers, form fields and the JSON body. I can be explicit with attributes like FromRoute, FromQuery and FromBody, and with ApiController, complex types come from the body by default. If a value can't be converted, like text for an integer, it's recorded as a model state error. Then validation runs, using data annotations like Required and Range, or FluentValidation for richer rules. With ApiController, an invalid model automatically returns a 400 with ValidationProblemDetails, listing each field and its error.
That checks the shape of the data. Business rules, like "this site must belong to an active depot", still belong in the service layer, because they need data and context.

For our CSV bulk import, a single request can contain [around 10,000] rows. So we validated every row and returned a per-row error report with line numbers, instead of failing on the first error. Users fixed everything in one go. I can explain that design.

p1-23.q: Global exception handling catches every unhandled exception in one place, logs it with context, and returns a consistent error response (ProblemDetails) instead of leaking stack traces. In .NET 8 I use UseExceptionHandler with IExceptionHandler implementations and AddProblemDetails; Part 10 has the detailed IExceptionHandler answer with code.
i: Map exception types to status codes centrally: validation 400, not found 404, conflict 409, everything else 500.
Include a traceId or correlation id in the response so users can quote it to support.
Register the handler first in the pipeline; it only catches exceptions from later components.
Development shows the developer exception page; production shows a generic message.
Background services and message consumers need their own try/catch, the HTTP handler does not cover them.
Exceptions after the response has started cannot change the status code; the connection is aborted instead.
f: Why not try/catch in every controller?
Duplication and inconsistency; one handler gives one format and one logging policy.
How do you test it?
Integration test an endpoint that throws and assert the status and ProblemDetails body.
p1-23.y: I handle exceptions globally in one place instead of try-catch in every controller. In .NET 8 I use UseExceptionHandler with an IExceptionHandler class that logs the error with the correlation id and returns a standard ProblemDetails response. Known errors, like not found or validation, map to the right status code, and unknown errors return a 500 without internal details. This keeps every service's errors consistent.
p1-23.k: global exception handling, iexceptionhandler, problemdetails, useexceptionhandler, error handling
x: Global exception handling means one central place catches every unhandled exception and turns it into a consistent, safe error response, instead of try-catch blocks in every controller.

In ASP.NET Core, I put UseExceptionHandler at the top of the pipeline, so it wraps everything after it. Since .NET 8, I write IExceptionHandler classes that map known exceptions to the right status code. For example, a validation exception becomes 400, not found becomes 404, a concurrency conflict becomes 409, and anything unknown becomes 500. With AddProblemDetails, every error follows the standard ProblemDetails format, with a type, title, status and trace id.

Two rules matter. Log the full exception server-side, with the stack trace and correlation id. But never return internal details to the client in production, just a clear message and the id. Also, I don't use exceptions for normal flow; expected outcomes like "not found" can just return a result.

This kept our controllers clean and our errors consistent across services. When a user reports an error, they give support the correlation id from the response, and we find the exact exception in Splunk in seconds. I can show a sample handler.

p1-24.q: REST models the API as resources identified by URLs, manipulated with standard HTTP methods, stateless requests and representations such as JSON. GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, DELETE removes; GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, POST and PATCH are not (by default).
i: Idempotent means repeating the same request leaves the server in the same state; safe means no state change at all (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS).
Status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created with Location, 202 Accepted for async jobs, 204 No Content, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409 Conflict, 422, 429, 500, 503.
Make POST safe to retry with an Idempotency-Key header stored with the result.
Resource naming: plural nouns (/studies/{id}/sites), no verbs, filtering and paging with query parameters.
HATEOAS and Richardson maturity level 3 are rarely used in practice; consistent conventions and OpenAPI matter more.
Concurrency: ETags with If-Match return 412 on conflicting updates.
f: PUT vs PATCH?
PUT replaces the whole resource; PATCH changes some fields (JSON Patch or merge patch).
Is DELETE idempotent if the second call returns 404?
Yes; the state is the same (resource gone), even though the response differs.
p1-24.y: REST means treating things as resources with URLs and using HTTP verbs for actions: GET to read, POST to create, PUT to replace, PATCH to update part, and DELETE to remove. Idempotent means calling it many times gives the same result: GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, POST is not. For POSTs that must not repeat, like creating a shipment, we use an idempotency key so a retry does not create duplicates.
p1-24.k: rest, http verbs, idempotency, get, post, put, patch, delete
x: REST is an architectural style for APIs built on HTTP. Everything is a resource, identified by a URL, like /studies/12/shipments. Clients use standard HTTP verbs to act on them, exchange representations, usually JSON, and every request is stateless, meaning it carries everything the server needs, like the token. Responses can also be cacheable.

The verbs have clear meanings. GET reads data, and it's safe, it changes nothing. POST creates, and it's not idempotent: sending it twice creates two things. PUT replaces a resource, and it's idempotent: sending it twice gives the same result. PATCH partially updates. DELETE removes, and it's idempotent too. Idempotent means repeating the request has the same effect as doing it once, which is what makes retries safe.
Status codes complete the picture: 200, 201 with a Location header, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409 and so on.

The idempotency part matters in real systems, because networks fail and clients retry. For POST operations that create important things, like a shipment, we accept an idempotency key, so a retry returns the original result instead of creating a duplicate. I can explain that pattern.

p1-25.q: API versioning lets you evolve an API without breaking existing clients. Common approaches are URL segment (/api/v2/...), query string (?api-version=2.0), header (api-version or a media type); in ASP.NET Core the Asp.Versioning package handles routing, reporting and deprecation.
i: Prefer additive, backward-compatible changes (new optional fields) so most changes need no new version.
Breaking changes (renamed fields, changed semantics, removed endpoints) get a new major version, with the old one supported for an agreed period.
Report supported and deprecated versions in response headers (api-supported-versions) and announce sunset dates.
Keep versions in OpenAPI documents per version so clients see exactly what they get.
Version message contracts too (events on Kafka) with a schema version field.
In IRT vendor-facing APIs use URL versions because vendors' tools handle them easily.
f: Which approach do you prefer?
URL versioning for external clients (visible, cache-friendly); headers for internal APIs if the team prefers clean URLs.
How long do you keep old versions?
As long as agreed with clients, with usage metrics to see when traffic drops to zero.
p1-25.y: I version APIs so existing clients don't break when the contract changes. The common options are a version in the URL like /v1, a query string, or a header. I prefer URL versioning because it is clear and easy to test. Mostly I avoid new versions by making only backward-compatible changes, like adding optional fields, and I create v2 only for breaking changes, with a deprecation period for v1.
p1-25.k: api versioning, v1, v2, backward compatibility, breaking change
x: API versioning lets an API evolve without breaking existing clients.

There are four common ways to put the version in a request: in the URL, like /api/v2/shipments; in a query string, like api-version=2; in a header; or in the media type. I prefer the URL segment, because it's explicit, easy to see in logs, and easy to route at the load balancer. In .NET, the Asp.Versioning library handles this, including reporting supported and deprecated versions in response headers, and it works with OpenAPI, so each version gets its own document.

But the best strategy is to avoid needing new versions. Additive changes, like adding an optional field or a new endpoint, are not breaking. Renaming or removing fields, or changing types or meanings, are breaking, and only those need a new version. When we do release one, the old version is deprecated with a clear timeline, and we watch the logs until no one calls it.
Because external vendors integrate with our APIs, we're strict about this. We also compare OpenAPI documents in the pipeline to catch accidental breaking changes. I can explain that check.

p1-26.q: ASP.NET Core configuration merges key-value pairs from providers (appsettings.json, environment-specific files, environment variables, user secrets, command line, Azure App Configuration, AWS Parameter Store) with later sources overriding earlier ones. The Options pattern binds sections to typed classes (IOptions<T>, IOptionsSnapshot<T>, IOptionsMonitor<T>) with validation; Part 10 compares the three in depth.
i: Hierarchical keys use ":" in JSON and "__" in environment variables (Sftp__Vendors__DepotA__Host).
Secrets: user secrets locally, AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store in deployed environments; never commit them.
Validate with ValidateDataAnnotations and ValidateOnStart so bad config stops the deployment.
Reloading works only with providers that support it (JSON files with reloadOnChange, App Configuration); use IOptionsMonitor to react.
Keep configuration per environment in IaC or variable groups, so environments differ by data, not by code.
f: Why bind to classes instead of IConfiguration["key"]?
Types, validation, IntelliSense and easy testing, with no magic strings scattered around.
How does ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT affect config?
It selects appsettings.{Environment}.json and enables Development-only features such as user secrets.
p1-26.y: Configuration in ASP.NET Core comes from layers: appsettings.json, environment-specific files, environment variables and secret stores, where later sources override earlier ones. The Options pattern binds a section to a strongly typed class, so I inject IOptions of that class instead of reading strings. I also validate options at startup, so a missing setting fails the deployment immediately instead of failing later in production.
p1-26.k: configuration, options pattern, ioptions, appsettings, environment variables, validateonstart
x: Configuration in ASP.NET Core comes from layered providers, and the Options pattern turns it into strongly-typed, validated classes.

The providers are layered, and later ones override earlier ones: appsettings.json, then appsettings for the environment, like Production, then user secrets in development, environment variables, and command-line arguments. For our services on AWS, we add Systems Manager Parameter Store and Secrets Manager. With the Options pattern, I bind a section to a class, for example builder.Services.Configure of SftpOptions, and then inject IOptions of SftpOptions instead of reading strings. I add ValidateDataAnnotations and ValidateOnStart, so a missing or invalid setting stops the app at startup.
For changing values, IOptionsSnapshot re-reads per request, and IOptionsMonitor gives live updates to singletons.

In our services, vendor SFTP settings are named options, secrets like passwords and keys come from Secrets Manager, never from appsettings, and the same container image runs in every environment with different configuration. I also validate options at startup with ValidateDataAnnotations and ValidateOnStart, so a missing or wrong setting stops the service immediately with a clear message, instead of failing later on the first real request.

p1-27.q: I log with ILogger<T> using structured message templates, enrich every entry with a correlation id through logging scopes, and send JSON logs to a central store (CloudWatch Logs); for tracing I propagate the id (or W3C traceparent) across HTTP and messages so one request can be followed across services. Part 10 covers ILogger and structured logging in depth.
i: Three pillars: logs for details, metrics for trends and alerts, traces for the path and timing of a request across services.
OpenTelemetry in .NET: ActivitySource and Activity give spans; exporters send traces to X-Ray, Jaeger or Tempo; ASP.NET Core and HttpClient are instrumented automatically.
Log levels per category in configuration; avoid Information-level noise from framework namespaces.
Use LoggerMessage source generators on hot paths; never log secrets or patient data.
Metrics: request rate, errors, latency (p95/p99), queue depth; alert on SLOs, not on single errors.
In IRT: correlation-id middleware and a DelegatingHandler, JSON logs to CloudWatch, Grafana dashboards and alarms.
f: Logging vs tracing?
Logs record events; traces connect timed spans of one request across services.
What should every log entry contain?
Timestamp, level, service, environment, version, correlation id and the relevant business ids.
p1-27.y: I use structured logging with ILogger, so logs are key-value data, not just text, and they go to CloudWatch where we can query them. Every request gets a correlation id that is added to all logs and passed to other services, so I can follow one request end to end. For tracing and metrics we use OpenTelemetry and Grafana dashboards. This is how we find production issues quickly.
p1-27.k: logging, tracing, ilogger, structured logging, correlation id, opentelemetry, observability
x: Good logging and tracing means that when something fails, I can find exactly what happened to one request across every service.

I use ILogger with structured logging, which means message templates with named placeholders, like "Shipment {ShipmentId} failed", so values are stored as searchable fields, not text. Levels matter: Debug only in development, Information for meaningful business events, Warning and Error for problems. And I never log secrets or patient data, which is critical in a clinical system. For tracing, every request gets a correlation id from middleware. It goes into a logging scope, so every log line carries it, and it's passed on to downstream HTTP calls and messages. OpenTelemetry adds distributed traces and spans for timing.
Logs go to Splunk as JSON through Serilog, and we have dashboards and alerts in Grafana on error rates and latency.

The correlation-id work I did in [2024] changed our support process. Tracing a failed shipment across [4] services used to take [about an hour]. Now one Logs Insights query shows the whole journey in [a few minutes]. I can walk through that implementation.

p1-28.q: Measure first (Application Insights, CloudWatch, dotnet-counters, a profiler), then fix the biggest bottleneck, which is usually the database: efficient queries, indexes, projections, no N+1. Then use async I/O end to end, caching, response compression, pagination, pooling, and offload long work to background jobs.
i: EF Core: AsNoTracking, Select projections, split queries, compiled queries for hot paths, DbContext pooling.
Avoid sync-over-async and thread-pool starvation; pass CancellationToken.
Caching: output caching or HybridCache for reference data; HTTP caching headers for public data.
Payloads: pagination, smaller DTOs, System.Text.Json source generation, response compression (Brotli/Gzip) where CPU allows.
Platform: upgrading to .NET 8/10 gives free wins (Dynamic PGO); right-size containers and autoscale on latency or CPU.
Prove it: load test with k6 or JMeter before and after; my shipment list fix took [9 seconds to under 300 ms].
f: What is your first step with a slow endpoint?
Find where the time goes: trace spans or logs with durations, then the SQL plan if it is the database.
When does caching hurt?
When data must be consistent (kit allocation) or invalidation is unclear.
p1-28.y: First I measure, because guessing wastes time. Then I fix the biggest problems, which are usually in the database: missing indexes, N+1 queries, or loading too much data. I make calls async, add paging, use AsNoTracking for read-only queries, and cache data that rarely changes. For example, one shipment list query went from about [9 seconds to under 300 milliseconds] just by fixing the query and adding a covering index.
p1-28.k: performance, optimization, caching, async, asnotracking, paging, profiling
x: My approach to performance is always measure first, then fix the biggest bottleneck, and then measure again.

I start with data: Splunk logs and Grafana metrics for latency percentiles and error rates, traces to see where time goes, and profiling or slow query logs. Most of the time, the database is the problem. So I fix queries first: proper indexes, AsNoTracking for reads, projecting into DTOs so we only fetch needed columns, paging, and removing N+1 queries. Then the code: async I/O all the way, IHttpClientFactory for outgoing calls, avoiding unnecessary allocations in hot paths. Then caching: in-memory or Redis for reference data, and output caching for expensive responses. Response compression helps for large payloads. Only once the code is efficient do I scale horizontally behind the load balancer.

A real example: one shipment search query took [about 9 seconds]. The execution plan showed a scan with [400,000] logical reads. With a covering index and a rewritten predicate, it dropped to [under 300 ms] and [about 2,000] reads.
Upgrading the runtime also helped: moving to .NET 10 gave about [10-15%] better p95. I can go into the SQL fix in detail.

p1-29.q: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser mechanism that lets a server say which other origins may call it from JavaScript. The browser sends an Origin header (and a preflight OPTIONS request for non-simple calls), and the server answers with Access-Control-Allow-* headers; in ASP.NET Core you define named policies with AddCors and apply UseCors after UseRouting.
i: CORS is not security for your API: it only restricts browsers; curl, Postman and servers ignore it. Authentication and authorization protect the API.
Preflight happens for methods other than GET/POST/HEAD, custom headers (Authorization) or JSON content type; cache it with SetPreflightMaxAge.
AllowCredentials cannot be combined with AllowAnyOrigin; list exact origins.
Order: UseCors after UseRouting and before UseAuthentication/UseAuthorization so preflights are answered before auth rejects them.
In IRT the API allows only [the IRT UI origins per environment] from configuration.
f: Does CORS stop CSRF?
No; CSRF uses simple requests that may not need preflight. Use SameSite cookies and anti-forgery tokens.
Why does a preflight fail with 401?
The auth middleware ran before CORS or the OPTIONS request was not allowed; fix the order.
p1-29.y: CORS is a browser security rule that blocks a web page from calling an API on a different domain unless the API allows it. In ASP.NET Core I add a named policy with the exact allowed origins, methods and headers, and call UseCors in the right place in the pipeline. I never use allow-any-origin together with credentials. Our React app calls the APIs with a specific allowed origin per environment.
p1-29.k: cors, cross-origin, preflight, browser security, usecors
x: CORS stands for Cross-Origin Resource Sharing. Browsers enforce the same-origin policy, which blocks a page from one origin, like our front-end domain, from reading responses from a different origin, like our API domain. CORS is how the server tells the browser which other origins are allowed.

For simple requests, the browser sends the request with an Origin header and checks the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header in the response. For other requests, like ones with a JSON content type or an Authorization header, the browser first sends a preflight OPTIONS request, asking which origins, methods and headers are allowed, and only sends the real request if the answer allows it.

In ASP.NET Core, I call AddCors with a named policy that lists the exact allowed origins, methods and headers, and add UseCors in the pipeline after routing and before authentication, so preflight requests aren't rejected for having no token. I never combine AllowAnyOrigin with credentials, and I avoid wildcards in production.
Also, CORS isn't API security, it only affects browsers. In our services, origins come from configuration per environment. I can explain how to debug a CORS error.

p1-30.q: I make service-to-service calls resilient with timeouts on every call, retries with exponential backoff and jitter only for transient failures, circuit breakers to fail fast when a dependency is down, idempotent operations so retries are safe, and fallbacks or asynchronous messaging where an immediate answer is not required. In .NET 8 this is Polly v8 through AddStandardResilienceHandler (Part 10 has the deep answer).
i: Timeouts: without them a slow dependency ties up threads and connections; set per-attempt and total timeouts.
Transient = timeouts, 5xx, 408, 429, connection resets; respect Retry-After.
Circuit breaker states: closed, open (fail fast), half-open (trial calls).
Bulkheads and concurrency limits isolate one slow dependency.
Idempotency keys make POST retries safe; consumers dedupe messages by id.
Observe it: metrics on retries and breaker state, alerts when a breaker opens.
f: What is a retry storm?
Many clients retrying aggressively at once, multiplying load on a struggling service; backoff, jitter and breakers prevent it.
Sync call or message?
If the caller does not need the answer now, publish a message and let the consumer retry independently.
p1-30.y: Network calls between services will fail sometimes, so I plan for it. I use IHttpClientFactory with resilience policies: a timeout on every call, retries with backoff for temporary errors, and a circuit breaker so we stop calling a service that is down. In .NET 8, AddStandardResilienceHandler gives this in one line. For work that doesn't need an immediate answer, I use messaging instead of HTTP.
p1-30.k: resilience, polly, retry, circuit breaker, timeout, httpclientfactory
x: In microservices, calls to other services will fail sometimes, so resilience is about making sure a temporary problem in one service doesn't become an outage for everyone.

I use several patterns together. Timeouts on every call, because a hanging call is worse than a failed one. Retries with exponential backoff and jitter, but only for transient errors, like timeouts, 503s and 429s, and only for idempotent operations. A circuit breaker: after repeated failures it opens and stops calling the failing service for a while, then tests it with a single call in the half-open state before closing again. Bulkheads to limit how many concurrent calls one dependency can use, and fallbacks, like cached data, where that makes sense. In .NET, I configure this on IHttpClientFactory with Polly, usually with AddStandardResilienceHandler.

And often the best resilience is not calling synchronously at all. For work that doesn't need an immediate answer, we publish a message to RabbitMQ, so if the other service is down, the work just waits in the queue.
Our vendor API calls use the standard resilience handler, and most short vendor outages now recover without anyone noticing. I can explain how the circuit breaker states work.

p1-31.q: REST uses HTTP resources and JSON, simple and universal; SOAP (WCF) uses XML envelopes and a strict WSDL contract with WS-* standards; gRPC uses HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers for fast, strongly typed service-to-service calls and streaming; GraphQL lets clients ask for exactly the fields they need from one endpoint.
i: REST: best for public and browser APIs, caching, broad tooling; risk of over- or under-fetching.
SOAP: legacy enterprise integrations, WS-Security, transactions; heavy and verbose; CoreWCF helps migrate.
gRPC: binary, compact, contract-first .proto, bidirectional streaming, deadlines; limited browser support (gRPC-Web), harder to debug by hand.
GraphQL: flexible queries for many front ends, one round trip; needs care with N+1 resolvers (DataLoader), caching and query cost limits.
In IRT: REST for UI and vendors, legacy WCF endpoints in older areas, Kafka and RabbitMQ for async.
f: When would you pick gRPC?
Internal high-throughput service calls or streaming between services you control.
Why not GraphQL everywhere?
Extra complexity in caching, security and performance control that simple REST APIs do not need.
p1-31.y: REST uses HTTP and JSON and is the default for public and web APIs. SOAP, which WCF used, is XML with strict contracts, still found in older enterprise systems. gRPC uses HTTP/2 and binary Protobuf, so it is very fast for service-to-service calls. GraphQL lets the client ask for exactly the fields it needs. In my work we use REST, and I also maintained older WCF services.
p1-31.k: rest, soap, wcf, grpc, graphql, protocols
x: These are four styles of API communication, each good at different things.

REST is resource-based HTTP with JSON. It's simple, universal, cacheable, and every client and tool understands it, so it's my default for public and front-end APIs. SOAP, which in .NET usually meant WCF, uses XML envelopes with strict contracts defined in WSDL, plus standards like WS-Security and transactions. It's heavy, but still common in older enterprise systems. gRPC uses binary Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2. It's very fast, strongly typed from a shared contract, and supports streaming in both directions. That makes it great for internal service-to-service calls, but browser support is limited. GraphQL exposes one endpoint where the client asks for exactly the fields it needs. That's great when many different front ends need different shapes of data, but caching and authorization per field are harder.
So the choice depends on the consumer. Public or browser APIs get REST. High-performance internal calls can use gRPC. Varied front-end needs suggest GraphQL.
In our IRT platform, the APIs are REST, and some older integrations still expose WCF SOAP endpoints, which we're gradually modernising. I can explain how I'd migrate those.

p1-32.q: Short background work uses hosted services (BackgroundService) with queues such as Channels; durable or scheduled work uses a message broker (RabbitMQ, SQS) or a scheduler (Hangfire, Quartz); long-running or heavy jobs run in separate worker services or Lambda. Never use fire-and-forget Task.Run inside a request. Part 10 covers BackgroundService in depth.
i: Request returns 202 Accepted with a job id, a worker processes it, and the client polls or gets notified.
Hosted services are singletons; create scopes for DbContext.
Graceful shutdown: honour the stopping token and finish or checkpoint work within the shutdown timeout.
Multiple instances run every hosted service; avoid duplicate work with queues or distributed locks.
In IRT: RabbitMQ consumers as BackgroundServices in worker containers, [an SFTP poller], and Ansible-driven deployment jobs outside the app.
f: Why not Task.Run in a controller?
The work is lost on shutdown or crash, exceptions vanish, and it has no retries or visibility.
Hangfire vs hosted service?
Hangfire adds persistence, retries, cron and a dashboard; a hosted service is a simple in-process loop.
p1-32.y: For background work I use a BackgroundService, which is a hosted service that runs a loop alongside the web app, using a scoped service for each unit of work. For queued work I use Channels or a message queue. For example, our SFTP poller runs [every 5 minutes] to pick up vendor files. For heavy or scheduled jobs that must survive restarts, a separate worker or a scheduler is better.
p1-32.k: background work, hosted service, backgroundservice, worker, channels, scheduler
x: Background work in ASP.NET Core means work that runs outside the request, either long-running, like consuming a queue, or scheduled, like a nightly cleanup.
