For timing, I rely on Playwright's auto-waiting and web-first assertions, like expect locator toBeVisible, which retry until they pass or time out. I never use fixed sleeps. For isolation, each test gets a fresh browser context and its own seeded data, so tests can run in parallel without affecting each other. I log in once and reuse the saved storage state, which saves a lot of time.
When a test fails in CI, traces, screenshots and videos show exactly what happened, step by step. I also use the page object pattern to keep tests readable.

In our IRT suite, the biggest improvement came from replacing sleeps with web-first assertions and seeding data through the API instead of the UI. Flaky failures dropped a lot, and the suite got faster. I can explain how we run them in the pipeline.

p1-61.q: BDD (Behaviour-Driven Development) describes behaviour as examples in business language before coding; Cucumber runs those examples written in Gherkin (Feature, Scenario, Given/When/Then) by binding each step to code, such as Playwright actions. It creates living documentation that BAs, QA and developers can all read.
i: Write scenarios with the BA and QA in refinement (three amigos), then automate them.
Keep steps declarative (business intent) rather than UI clicks, so scenarios survive UI changes.
Scenario Outline with Examples tables covers many data cases.
In regulated work, Gherkin scenarios map nicely to requirements for traceability.
Downside: the step layer adds maintenance; use BDD for key behaviours, plain tests elsewhere.
c:
Scenario: Block transfer to a live study
  Given the target study "ABC-301" has randomized subjects
  When a study manager requests a configuration transfer to "ABC-301"
  Then the transfer is blocked with reason "Target study is live"
f: Cucumber vs SpecFlow/Reqnroll?
Same idea; Reqnroll is the .NET successor of SpecFlow, Cucumber is the JS/Java family.
Who writes the scenarios?
Together in refinement; QA or BA usually drafts, developers automate.
p1-61.y: BDD means describing behaviour in plain language that business people can read, using Given, When, Then scenarios. Cucumber, or SpecFlow and Reqnroll in .NET, connects each line of the scenario to test code. The main value is shared understanding between the business, QA and developers. In a regulated product, these readable scenarios can also link nicely to requirements.
p1-61.k: bdd, cucumber, gherkin, given when then, specflow, reqnroll
x: BDD, Behaviour-Driven Development, is an approach where we describe how the system should behave in plain language, agreed between business, QA and developers, and then automate those descriptions as tests. Cucumber is a popular tool for it.

The scenarios are written in Gherkin, using Given, When, Then. Given sets the context, When is the action, and Then is the expected outcome. For example: Given a study with two sites and stock at the depot, When a subject is randomised at site one, Then a kit from the correct depot is assigned. Each line is connected to code through step definitions, which do the actual work, like calling the API or driving the UI with Playwright.

The big value is shared understanding. Business analysts and QA can read and review the scenarios, and the scenarios become living documentation. In a GxP product, that's especially useful, because each scenario traces back to a requirement, and the test run produces evidence for validation.
The risk is writing scenarios that are too technical or too detailed. I keep them focused on behaviour, not clicks. I can show how we structure step definitions.

p1-62.q: A quality gate is a set of pass/fail conditions SonarQube applies to new code in each analysis, for example no new bugs or vulnerabilities, all security hotspots reviewed, coverage on new code at least [80 percent] and duplication under [3 percent]. The pipeline fails the build (or blocks the pull request) when the gate fails.
i: "Clean as you code": the gate focuses on new code, so legacy debt does not block delivery while new code stays clean.
Quality profiles define the rules; gates define the thresholds.
PR decoration shows issues inline in Azure DevOps pull requests.
Do not chase the coverage number with assertion-free tests; review what is covered.
Security hotspots need human review; vulnerabilities must be fixed or justified.
Part 3 has a scenario about a failing gate right before a release.
f: What if a rule is wrong for your code?
Mark the issue as won't fix with a reason, or adjust the profile through the team, never silently.
Gate on overall or new code?
New code; overall metrics improve as you touch old code.
p1-62.y: A SonarQube quality gate is a set of conditions that new code must pass, like no new bugs or vulnerabilities, enough test coverage on new code, and limited duplication. It runs in the CI pipeline, and if the gate fails, the pull request can't be merged. It keeps code quality from slowly getting worse without arguing about it in every review.
p1-62.k: sonarqube, quality gate, static analysis, code coverage, ci
x: A SonarQube quality gate is a set of pass or fail conditions that code must meet before it can be merged or released.

SonarQube analyses the code in the CI pipeline. It finds bugs, vulnerabilities, security hotspots, code smells and duplication, and it reads test coverage reports. The quality gate then checks conditions, usually focused on new code: for example, coverage on new code above 80 percent, no new bugs or vulnerabilities, all security hotspots reviewed, and duplication below a limit. If any condition fails, the gate fails, and the pipeline blocks the pull request or release.
Focusing on new code is clever, because you don't have to fix a whole legacy codebase at once. Quality improves gradually with every change, and it can never get worse.

In our regulated environment, it also gives auditors objective evidence that every release met defined quality standards. My approach is to fix issues at the source, not suppress them. If a rule genuinely doesn't apply, we mark it with a documented reason. I can explain how we keep coverage meaningful rather than just hitting a number.

p1-63.q: Jest runs JavaScript/TypeScript tests with describe/it, expect matchers, mocking (jest.fn, jest.mock) and snapshot support; for React I use React Testing Library to render components and interact with them the way a user would (getByRole, userEvent), and for Node I test services directly and APIs with supertest.
i: Test behaviour, not implementation: avoid testing internal state or component internals.
Mock network calls with MSW (Mock Service Worker) for realistic API responses.
Fake timers (jest.useFakeTimers) for debounce and retry logic.
Async: await findBy* queries and waitFor; always return or await promises.
Vitest is a faster, Vite-based alternative with the same API.
f: Are snapshot tests useful?
Only small, stable ones; big snapshots get approved blindly.
How do you test a custom hook?
renderHook from React Testing Library.
p1-63.y: For Node.js I use Jest to unit test functions and services, mocking things like the database or HTTP calls, and Supertest to test API routes. For React I use Jest with React Testing Library, which tests components the way a user uses them, by finding buttons and text instead of internal details. I keep tests focused on behaviour, so refactoring doesn't break them.
p1-63.k: jest, react testing library, node testing, supertest, unit test
x: Jest is a JavaScript testing framework. It runs tests, provides assertions and mocking, and measures coverage, all in one tool.

For Node.js code, I write tests with describe and it blocks, and expect for assertions. For dependencies, jest.fn creates mock functions, and jest.mock replaces whole modules, for example a database client or an HTTP library, so the logic is tested in isolation. Async code is easy to test with async and await. For React components, I combine Jest with React Testing Library. I render the component, query elements the way a user would, by role or label text, simulate user events like typing and clicking with user-event, and assert what appears on screen. That tests behaviour, not implementation details like internal state.
I use snapshot tests sparingly, because large snapshots get approved without anyone reading them. And for API calls in components, Mock Service Worker gives realistic network mocks.
In our React work, every new component came with Testing Library tests for its key states: loading, error, empty and data. Tests run with coverage in CI. I can show a sample component test.

p1-64.q: I check correctness first (does it meet the requirement and edge cases), then security, tests, readability and design, performance risks, and operability (logging, errors, configuration). I keep comments specific, explain the why, separate must-fix from suggestions, and prefer small pull requests.
i: Correctness: null handling, time zones (my own lesson), concurrency, idempotency, transaction boundaries.
Security: input validation, authorisation on every endpoint, SQL injection, secrets, PHI in logs.
Tests: do they fail if the code is wrong; are integration paths covered.
Data: migrations backward compatible; indexes for new queries.
Automation first: formatting, analyzers and SonarQube handle style, so humans focus on logic.
Tone: questions instead of orders ("what happens if the file is empty?"), and praise good solutions.
f: How long should a review take?
Small PRs within hours; large ones get split or walked through together.
What do you do with a huge PR?
Ask to split it, or review it in a call with the author.
p1-64.y: In a code review I first check that the change does what the story needs and is correct, including edge cases and error handling. Then security, like input validation and secrets, then performance, like N+1 queries, then tests and readability. I keep comments respectful and explain the why. I also review small pull requests faster, so I encourage the team to keep them small.
p1-64.k: code review, pull request, best practices, review checklist
x: In a code review, I look at the change from a few angles, roughly in order of risk.

First, correctness: does it do what the story says, and does it handle edge cases like null, empty lists, concurrency and failure paths? Second, security: input validation, authorization checks, especially study-level access in our system, no secrets in code, no injection risks, and no sensitive or patient data in logs. Third, design and readability: clear naming, single responsibility, no duplication, and code that the next person can understand. Fourth, tests: are there tests for the change, and do they test behaviour, not implementation? Fifth, performance and operability: N+1 queries, missing async, missing indexes, and whether there are useful logs and metrics if it fails in production.
Style issues are for linters and analysers, not people, so I don't spend review time on formatting.

And how I review matters too. I ask questions instead of giving orders, explain the why, mark minor points as optional, and praise good solutions. When I mentored [two graduate developers in 2024], code reviews were one of the best teaching tools. I can give an example of a bug I caught in review.

p1-65.q: In GxP, testing is not just a developer activity but documented evidence: requirements trace to test cases, formal validation (FV) runs scripted tests with recorded results and sign-off, defects follow controlled processes, and only validated, change-controlled builds reach production. Automated tests support this but the evidence and traceability are what auditors check.
i: Traceability matrix: requirement, design, code change, unit/integration tests, FV test case, result.
Computer System Validation (CSV) and GAMP 5 risk-based approach: test more where patient risk is higher (randomisation, dosing, blinding).
Test environments are controlled and qualified; no ad-hoc changes during FV.
Regression evidence for every release; deviations documented and assessed.
Automated test results are archived as evidence.
Developers still write unit, integration and Playwright tests, but FV is independent.
f: What is GAMP 5?
Industry guidance for risk-based validation of computerised systems in regulated life sciences.
How do you speed up testing without losing compliance?
More automation with archived evidence and risk-based focus on critical functions.
p1-65.y: In GxP, testing is also documented evidence, not just something developers do. Requirements are traced to test cases, formal validation runs scripted tests with recorded results and sign-off, defects follow a controlled process, and only validated builds reach production. Automated tests help a lot, but what auditors check is the evidence and traceability. That's how we work on our IRT product.
p1-65.k: gxp, regulated testing, validation, traceability, fv, audit
x: In a GxP regulated product, like our clinical trial IRT system, testing isn't just about finding bugs. It's about proving, with documented evidence, that the system does what it's supposed to do, because errors can affect patient safety and trial data integrity.

That changes a few things. Every requirement must trace to tests and their results, through a traceability matrix. Validation phases, like formal verification, FV, and user acceptance, UAT, are formal, with documented test scripts, results, and sign-offs. Every change needs an impact assessment, to decide what must be retested, plus regression testing. And releases follow a quality process with audit trails, so you can show who approved what and when.

Automation helps a lot. Our Playwright and Cucumber suites make regression fast and repeatable, and they generate evidence automatically. But the evidence must still be reviewed and stored properly, and automated tools themselves may need validation.

For developers, this means writing testable code, documenting changes clearly, and never making untracked changes. I've seen how this discipline catches problems early, especially before anything reaches a validated environment.

p1-66.q: Hooks give function components state and lifecycle behaviour: useState replaces this.state, useEffect replaces componentDidMount, componentDidUpdate and componentWillUnmount (via its cleanup function), useRef replaces instance fields, and useMemo/useCallback replace manual shouldComponentUpdate optimisations.
i: Think in synchronisation, not lifecycle: an effect keeps something outside React in sync with props/state.
Cleanup runs before the next effect and on unmount: cancel fetches with AbortController, clear timers, unsubscribe.
StrictMode in development mounts, unmounts and remounts to reveal missing cleanups.
Rules of hooks: call them at the top level, in the same order, only from components or custom hooks.
Many effects are unnecessary: derive values during render, handle events in handlers, fetch with React Query.
f: What is getDerivedStateFromError's hook equivalent?
None; error boundaries still need class components (or a library like react-error-boundary).
useEffect vs useLayoutEffect?
useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM changes before paint, for measuring layout.
p1-66.y: Hooks let function components do what class lifecycle methods did. useState holds state, and useEffect runs side effects: with an empty dependency list it runs once like componentDidMount, with dependencies it runs when they change, and its cleanup function works like componentWillUnmount. It keeps related logic together instead of splitting it across lifecycle methods, and custom hooks make it reusable.
p1-66.k: react hooks, useeffect, usestate, lifecycle methods, custom hooks
x: Hooks let function components do everything class components used to do with lifecycle methods, but organised by concern instead of by lifecycle.

useState holds local state. useEffect runs side effects after render, and it covers the three main lifecycle methods. With an empty dependency array, it runs once after the first render, like componentDidMount. With dependencies, it runs again whenever they change, like componentDidUpdate for those values. And the cleanup function you return runs before the next effect and when the component unmounts, like componentWillUnmount, which is where I cancel requests or remove listeners. useRef keeps a mutable value or a DOM reference without causing re-renders, useContext reads shared context, and useMemo and useCallback help with performance.

The big advantage is custom hooks. Logic like fetching data, with loading and error state, can be extracted into a hook like useShipments, and reused across components, which was awkward with classes.

In our React screens, we have custom hooks for API calls with cancellation, so leaving a page aborts the request. A common bug I watch for is a missing dependency, which causes stale values. I can explain that.

p1-67.q: Redux Toolkit (RTK) is the official way to use Redux: configureStore sets up the store with good defaults, createSlice defines state, reducers and actions together (with Immer so you can write "mutating" code safely), createAsyncThunk handles async logic, and RTK Query adds data fetching and caching.
i: Single store, actions describe what happened, reducers are pure functions, selectors read state; components subscribe with useSelector and send actions with useDispatch.
Immer produces immutable updates from mutable-looking code.
RTK Query generates hooks (useGetSitesQuery) with caching, invalidation tags and loading states, replacing hand-written thunks.
Use Redux for complex shared client state; server data often fits RTK Query or React Query better.
Redux DevTools give time-travel debugging.
f: Why are reducers pure?
Predictable state, easy tests and time-travel debugging.
RTK Query vs React Query?
Similar features; RTK Query integrates with the Redux store, React Query is standalone.
p1-67.y: Redux Toolkit is the official, simpler way to write Redux. I create a store with configureStore and define slices with createSlice, which gives the reducers and actions together, and I can write updates that look like mutations because Immer handles immutability. For server data, RTK Query or React Query handles fetching and caching. I use it when shared state is complex, otherwise local state or context is enough.
p1-67.k: redux toolkit, createslice, store, rtk query, state management, react
x: Redux is a pattern for managing shared application state in one predictable place, and Redux Toolkit is the official, modern way to write it with much less boilerplate.

The core flow is: a single store holds the state. Components dispatch actions, which describe what happened. Reducers, which are pure functions, take the current state and an action and return the next state. Components subscribed to that part of the state re-render. Redux Toolkit simplifies this. createSlice defines the state, reducers and action creators together, and uses Immer, so you can write code that looks like it mutates state, while it actually produces a new immutable state. configureStore sets up the store with good defaults and dev tools. For API calls, createAsyncThunk handles async logic, and RTK Query goes further, handling fetching, caching and invalidation for you.
An important design choice is not putting everything in Redux. Server data is best handled by RTK Query or a similar data-fetching library, and local UI state stays in components.
In our React work, we used slices for things like the selected study and user preferences, and RTK Query for API data. I can explain cache invalidation with tags.

p1-68.q: Reusable components have a small, typed props API, are composable (children, slots, render props) rather than configured with dozens of flags, own no business logic or data fetching, are accessible by default, and come with documentation and tests. I build them as controlled components with sensible defaults.
i:
Composition over configuration: `...
` scales better than 30 boolean props.
Accessibility: semantic elements, labels, keyboard support, focus management, aria attributes.
Styling via design tokens or CSS variables so themes (dark mode) work.
Storybook documents states (loading, empty, error) and enables visual tests.
Stable APIs: deprecate props before removing them, version a shared component library.
In IRT: [the configurable data table] reused on several screens; Part 9 has the resume-verification answer.
f: Controlled vs uncontrolled for library components?
Support controlled use (value + onChange) with an uncontrolled default for simple cases.
How do you stop a component from growing too many props?
Split it, use composition, and push variations into wrappers.
p1-68.y: A reusable component should do one job, take clear typed props, and not know about where its data comes from. I keep it flexible with props and children, handle loading, empty and error states, and make it accessible. For example, I built a data table component used across our IRT screens, with sorting, paging and row actions, so every screen looks and behaves the same.
p1-68.k: reusable components, react, props, design system, typescript
x: Reusable UI components are about making something easy to use correctly in many places, without it becoming a mess of special cases.

I keep components small and focused, with clearly typed props through TypeScript interfaces, so the contract is obvious. I prefer composition over configuration: accepting children or slots instead of adding a new boolean flag for every variation, because twenty flags usually means the component is doing too much. I keep them presentational, so they get data through props, and data fetching lives in container components or custom hooks. They should be accessible by default, with proper labels, keyboard support and focus handling, and use theme tokens for colours and spacing instead of hard-coded values. Finally, they're documented, for example in Storybook, and tested with Testing Library.
A good test of reusability is whether another developer can use it correctly just by reading the props.

In our React UI, I built a reusable data table component, with sorting, paging, empty and loading states, and accessible headers. It replaced several slightly different tables across screens, and fixes now happen in one place. I can explain how I decided its API.

p1-69.q: Measure first with the React Profiler and browser performance tools, then reduce unnecessary renders (move state down, split context, React.memo, useMemo/useCallback for expensive work or stable props), virtualise long lists, code-split routes with lazy and Suspense, and avoid large bundles and request waterfalls.
i: Virtualisation (react-window, TanStack Virtual) renders only visible rows for tables with thousands of rows.
Keys: stable unique keys for lists; index keys cause wrong state and extra work when items move.
Expensive calculations in useMemo; debounced inputs for search.
Data: cache server data (React Query), prefetch, avoid fetching in deeply nested effects.
React 18 concurrent features: useTransition and useDeferredValue keep typing responsive; React Compiler (React 19 era) auto-memoises.
Bundle: analyse with a bundle analyser, tree-shake, lazy-load heavy libraries.
f: Should you wrap everything in React.memo?
No; it adds comparison cost and complexity. Use it where profiling shows waste.
What is a waterfall?
Sequential requests where one fetch waits for another, often caused by fetching inside nested components.
p1-69.y: First I measure with the React Profiler to see what re-renders. Then I fix the cause: keep state close to where it is used, avoid creating new objects and functions on every render, and use memo, useMemo and useCallback where it actually helps. For long lists I use virtualization and paging, and I split code with lazy loading so the first page loads fast.
p1-69.k: react performance, memo, usememo, usecallback, re-render, virtualization, lazy loading
x: React performance work starts with measuring. I use the React DevTools Profiler to see which components re-render and how long they take, before changing anything.

The most common problem is unnecessary re-renders. When a parent re-renders, all children re-render by default. React.memo lets a component skip rendering when its props haven't changed. useMemo caches expensive calculations, and useCallback keeps function references stable, so memoised children aren't re-rendered just because a new function was created. I keep state as local as possible, because state high up the tree re-renders everything below it. For lists, I use stable unique keys, not array indexes, and for long lists or big tables, virtualisation, which only renders visible rows. For load time, I split code with React.lazy and Suspense, so each screen loads only its own code.
I don't wrap everything in memo by default, because memoisation has its own cost. I use it where the profiler shows a real problem.
In our IRT UI, a site inventory table with thousands of rows was slow. Virtualising the rows and memoising the row component made scrolling smooth again. I can explain the new React compiler too.

p1-70.q: TypeScript adds static types to JavaScript, catching errors at compile time, enabling refactoring and IntelliSense, and documenting contracts between front end and API. interface and type both describe object shapes; interface can be extended and declaration-merged and is preferred for object contracts, while type aliases can express unions, intersections, tuples, mapped and conditional types.
i: Interfaces merge when declared twice (useful for augmenting libraries); types cannot be reopened.
Unions (`type Status = 'Pending' | 'Shipped'`) and discriminated unions model API states precisely.
Utility types: Partial, Pick, Omit, Record, ReturnType help reuse types.
Generate API types from OpenAPI (openapi-typescript, NSwag) so front end and .NET back end stay in sync.
strict mode on; avoid any, prefer unknown with narrowing.
f: Types disappear at runtime: how do you validate API data?
With a runtime schema such as Zod, generating the TS type from the schema.
interface or type for React props?
Either; teams pick one convention. I use type for props with unions, interface for public object contracts.
p1-70.y: TypeScript catches mistakes at compile time, gives great auto-complete, and makes large code bases safer to change. Interface and type are similar: interface is good for object shapes and can be extended or merged, while type can also describe unions, intersections and other combinations. I use interface for props and API models, and type for unions like status values.
p1-70.k: typescript, interface vs type, type safety, union types
x: TypeScript adds static types on top of JavaScript. The code compiles to normal JavaScript, but type errors are caught while you write code, instead of in production.

The benefits are real: errors like misspelled properties or passing the wrong type are caught at compile time, the editor gives accurate autocompletion, and refactoring is much safer, because renaming something shows every place it breaks. Types also document the code, especially API contracts. I always use strict mode and avoid any, which switches the checks off.

On interface versus type: both can describe object shapes, and for most cases either works. Interfaces can be extended and can be declaration-merged, meaning two declarations with the same name combine. That makes them good for object shapes and public contracts. Type aliases are more flexible: they can describe unions, like "Pending" or "Shipped", intersections, tuples, and advanced mapped and conditional types. My usual rule is interface for object shapes and props, and type for unions and compositions.
In our front end, we generate TypeScript types from our OpenAPI documents, so the front end and API stay in sync, and a backend contract change shows up as a compile error. I can show how that works.

p1-71.q: Angular is a complete, opinionated framework (TypeScript, DI, router, forms, HttpClient, RxJS, CLI) suited to large teams that want one standard way; React is a UI library focused on components, where you choose routing, state and data libraries yourself, giving flexibility and a huge ecosystem. IRT has both: Angular modules in older areas and React for newer reusable components.
i: Angular: two-way binding options, modules (now standalone components), signals for fine-grained reactivity (Angular 16+), strong conventions.
React: one-way data flow, JSX, hooks, many meta-frameworks (Next.js).
Learning curve: Angular steeper (RxJS, DI); React simpler core but more choices.
Change detection: Angular zone.js or signals; React re-renders and reconciles a virtual DOM.
Choose by team skills, existing codebase and the need for built-in structure.
f: Can they coexist?
Yes, through micro-frontends or by mounting components in separate parts of the app, as in IRT.
What are Angular signals?
Reactive values that notify dependents precisely, reducing reliance on zone.js change detection.
p1-71.y: Angular is a full framework with everything built in, like routing, forms and dependency injection, and a strong structure, which suits large teams that want conventions. React is a library focused on the UI, more flexible, where you choose your own libraries. Both are good. Our team used React because of its ecosystem and the team's experience.
x: Angular and React can build the same applications, but they're different kinds of tools.

Angular is a complete, opinionated framework from Google. It includes modules or standalone components, dependency injection, a router, forms, an HTTP client and RxJS for async streams, all built in, and it's TypeScript-first. Teams get one consistent way of doing things, which suits large enterprise apps. React is a UI library from Meta. It focuses on rendering components with JSX and hooks, and you choose the rest yourself, like the router, state management with Redux Toolkit, and data fetching. That gives flexibility, but needs more decisions. On rendering, Angular uses change detection, traditionally with zone.js and now with signals for fine-grained updates. React re-renders components and reconciles a virtual DOM.
My view is that either works well. Angular for large teams that want structure out of the box, React for flexibility and its huge ecosystem.

I've worked with both on IRT. Our legacy portal is ASP.NET MVC with Angular 8 and 12 sub-applications, and we're moving to React with TypeScript, module by module, using IQVIA's MUI-based design system. Both are component-based, and our newer study builder is on Angular 17. So I maintain Angular modules and build new React screens.

p1-72.q: JavaScript runs on one thread with a call stack; asynchronous work (timers, I/O, fetch) is handled by the browser or Node, and when it completes its callback is queued. The event loop takes the next task when the stack is empty, but first drains all microtasks (Promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) after each task, then the browser may render.
i: Order: synchronous code, then microtasks (promises), then the next macrotask (setTimeout, I/O, events).
Long synchronous work blocks everything, including rendering and clicks; split it or use Web Workers.
Node has phases (timers, poll for I/O, check for setImmediate) and process.nextTick, which runs before promise microtasks.
await is syntax over promises, so code after await runs as a microtask.
f: Can a microtask loop starve rendering?
Yes; endlessly queuing microtasks blocks the next task and paint.
setTimeout(fn, 0) runs immediately?
No; at least after the current task and all microtasks, and browsers clamp nested timers.
p1-72.y: JavaScript runs on one thread with a call stack. When something async happens, like a timer or a network call, the callback waits in a queue. The event loop takes the next item from the queue when the stack is empty. Promise callbacks are microtasks and run before timers, which are macrotasks. That's why a long synchronous loop freezes the page.
p1-72.k: event loop, call stack, microtask, macrotask, javascript, async
x: The event loop is how JavaScript handles asynchronous work, even though it runs your code on a single thread.

There's one call stack, where your code runs. When you start async work, like a timer, a network request or file I/O, it's handed off to the browser or, in Node, to libuv, which does it in the background. When it finishes, its callback is put in a queue. The event loop's job is simple: whenever the call stack is empty, take the next task and run it. There are two kinds of queues. Microtasks, which are promise callbacks and awaits, and macrotasks, like setTimeout and I/O callbacks. After each task, the loop runs all pending microtasks first, then takes the next macrotask. That's why a resolved promise's then runs before a setTimeout with zero delay.

The practical lesson: long synchronous code blocks everything, because nothing else can run while the stack is busy. In the browser the UI freezes, and in Node every request waits. So heavy CPU work goes to Web Workers or worker threads.
I can walk through a small code example that shows the ordering.

p1-73.q: I watch for XSS (never inject unsanitised HTML; React escapes by default), reverse tabnabbing (rel="noopener noreferrer"), token storage (prefer HttpOnly secure cookies or in-memory tokens over localStorage), CSRF with cookie auth (SameSite plus anti-forgery tokens), a strict Content Security Policy, dependency vulnerabilities, and sensitive data exposed in the browser.
i: dangerouslySetInnerHTML only with DOMPurify; avoid href with user-controlled "javascript:" URLs.
CSP with nonces or hashes blocks injected scripts; add frame-ancestors to stop clickjacking.
Never trust the UI for authorisation: hidden buttons are not security.
Keep secrets out of front-end bundles; anything in JS is public.
npm audit, Dependabot/Snyk and lockfiles for supply-chain risk.
I fixed reverse tabnabbing in IRT on [about 40] links and added the ESLint rule so it cannot return.
f: Why is localStorage risky for tokens?
Any XSS can read it; HttpOnly cookies are not readable by scripts.
What does CSP do?
Tells the browser which sources of scripts, styles and frames are allowed, limiting XSS impact.
p1-73.y: The main ones are XSS, so I never insert raw HTML and let React escape output, and I add a Content Security Policy. Then token storage: I prefer secure HttpOnly cookies over local storage. Also CSRF protection, dependency vulnerabilities, and tabnabbing on links that open in a new tab. I actually fixed a tabnabbing issue across about [40] links by adding rel noopener noreferrer.
p1-73.k: frontend security, xss, csrf, csp, tabnabbing, owasp
x: On the front end, I watch for a few main categories of security issues.

First, cross-site scripting, XSS. React escapes values by default, which protects us, but dangerouslySetInnerHTML, or putting user input into URLs like javascript links, bypasses that, so I avoid it or sanitise with DOMPurify. A Content Security Policy adds another layer. Second, token storage. Tokens in localStorage can be stolen by any XSS, so I prefer HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies, or keeping tokens in memory. Third, reverse tabnabbing. Links with target blank used to give the new page access to window.opener, so it could redirect our original tab to a phishing page. The fix is rel noopener noreferrer. Fourth, never trusting the front end for security. Hiding a button isn't authorization; the API must check everything. And fifth, dependency vulnerabilities, checked with npm audit in the pipeline.

The tabnabbing one is a real fix I did in IRT. A security scan flagged it, and I updated [about 40] external links, added a shared link component that sets rel by default, and a lint rule so it can't come back. I can explain how CSP helps.

p1-74.q: Node.js runs JavaScript on one main thread with an event loop and non-blocking I/O handled by libuv (thread pool for file system, DNS and crypto); one process can serve thousands of concurrent connections as long as no request does heavy CPU work. It fits I/O-heavy APIs, gateways, real-time and glue services, not CPU-heavy computation.
i: CPU work blocks every request; move it to worker_threads, a separate service or another language.
Scale across cores with multiple processes (cluster, PM2) or containers.
Streams handle large files and responses with backpressure and low memory.
Event loop lag is the key health metric; monitor it.
My Node service was [the build-log summariser]: fetch logs, parse text, return JSON, a perfect I/O-bound fit.
f: Is Node single-threaded?
JavaScript execution is, but libuv uses a thread pool and the OS handles network I/O asynchronously.
What blocks the event loop?
Synchronous fs calls, big JSON.parse, heavy regex or loops, and crypto without async APIs.
p1-74.y: Node.js runs JavaScript on one main thread with an event loop, and all input and output, like network and files, is non-blocking. So one process can handle many concurrent connections well. It is a good fit for I/O-heavy services, like APIs that call other services or process text. It is a poor fit for heavy CPU work, unless you move it to worker threads.
p1-74.k: node.js, concurrency, event loop, non-blocking, libuv
x: Node.js runs JavaScript on a single main thread with an event loop, and uses non-blocking I/O through a library called libuv.

When a request needs a database query or an HTTP call, Node doesn't wait. It starts the operation, moves on to other requests, and runs the callback when the result arrives. So one process can handle thousands of concurrent connections with very little memory, because there's no thread per request. Things like file system operations and DNS run on a small libuv thread pool behind the scenes.

That makes Node a great fit for I/O-heavy work: APIs that mostly call databases and other services, backend-for-frontend layers, real-time apps with WebSockets, and developer tooling. Sharing TypeScript with the front end is also a productivity win. It's a weak fit for CPU-heavy work, like large calculations or image processing, because that blocks the event loop and every request waits. For those, worker threads or a different service are better. And in production, you run several processes or containers to use all CPU cores.
In my work, I've used Node and TypeScript for internal tooling and integration services, while the core domain logic stays in .NET. I can explain the event loop phases.

p1-75.q: I structure a Node/TypeScript microservice by feature with clear layers: routes/controllers for HTTP, services for business logic, repositories or clients for data and external APIs, schemas (Zod) for validation, central config and logging, and one error-handling middleware; plus health endpoints, tests and a Dockerfile, using the same pipeline template as our .NET services.
i: Config validated at startup (Zod over process.env), failing fast on missing values.
Logging with pino (JSON) including correlation ids, shipped to CloudWatch.
Graceful shutdown on SIGTERM: stop accepting, finish in-flight requests, close connections.
Dependency injection by constructor parameters or a small container, so tests can pass fakes.
strict TypeScript, ESLint, Prettier, Jest/Vitest, supertest for API tests.
c:
const Config = z.object({ PORT: z.coerce.number().default(8080), ADO_URL: z.string().url() });
export const config = Config.parse(process.env);
f: Express or Fastify?
Fastify for performance and built-in schema validation; Express for familiarity and ecosystem.
How do you share types with the front end?
A shared package or types generated from OpenAPI.
p1-75.y: I structure a Node TypeScript service in layers: routes or controllers for HTTP, services for business logic, and a data layer for the database or external calls. Configuration comes from environment variables and is validated at startup, inputs are validated with a schema library like Zod, and errors go through one error middleware. It has the same logging, health checks and Docker setup as our .NET services.
p1-75.k: node.js, typescript, microservice structure, express, layers
x: I structure a Node.js TypeScript microservice much like a .NET one: clear layers, typed contracts, and the same operational basics.

The layers are: routes or controllers that handle HTTP, services that hold the business logic, and repositories or clients that talk to databases and other services. Request and response shapes are typed, and inputs are validated at the edge with something like zod, so the rest of the code can trust the types. I use Express for simple services, or NestJS when I want more structure, since NestJS has modules and dependency injection very similar to ASP.NET Core. Errors go through a central error-handling middleware that returns a consistent error format, and async errors are captured properly.

Operationally: configuration from environment variables, validated at startup; structured JSON logging with pino, including a correlation id; a health endpoint; and graceful shutdown on SIGTERM. Then Jest tests, ESLint, a Dockerfile with a small base image, and the same CI/CD pipeline template as our .NET services.
Keeping that consistency means any engineer can work on any service, whatever the language. I can compare NestJS with ASP.NET Core in more detail.

p1-76.q: FastAPI is a modern async Python framework built on Starlette and Pydantic: type hints drive request validation, serialisation and automatic OpenAPI docs, and it is very fast for Python. Flask is a minimal, synchronous-first micro-framework where you add validation, docs and structure yourself; simple and flexible with a huge ecosystem.
i: FastAPI: dependency injection with Depends, async endpoints, automatic /docs, Pydantic v2 performance.
Flask: great for small internal tools and templates; async support exists but the ecosystem is mostly sync.
Both run in containers behind a reverse proxy (uvicorn/gunicorn).
I used FastAPI for [the vendor file pre-validation service] and Flask for [a small release-status endpoint].
f: Why is FastAPI fast?
Async I/O on Starlette/uvicorn and Pydantic's Rust-based validation core in v2.
When would you still pick Flask?
Very small apps, server-rendered pages, or teams already on Flask.
p1-76.y: Flask is a small, simple framework where you add what you need, and it is synchronous by default. FastAPI is newer and async-first, uses Python type hints with Pydantic for automatic validation, and generates OpenAPI documentation for free. For a new API I would choose FastAPI. We used it for a [vendor file validation service].
x: FastAPI and Flask are both popular Python web frameworks, but they're built for different eras of Python.

Flask is a minimal micro-framework, built on WSGI, and synchronous by default. It's simple, very flexible, and has a huge ecosystem, but you add things like request validation and API documentation yourself with extensions. FastAPI is newer and async-first, built on ASGI. It uses Python type hints with Pydantic models, so request bodies are validated and converted automatically, and invalid input returns a clear 422 error. It generates OpenAPI documentation and Swagger UI from the code, it has built-in dependency injection with Depends, and it's one of the fastest Python frameworks.

So for a new typed REST service, I choose FastAPI. It feels quite close to ASP.NET Core minimal APIs, with typed models and automatic docs. Flask still makes sense for very simple apps, or existing Flask codebases where there's no reason to rewrite.

I've built REST services with both. In practice, the type-driven validation in FastAPI removed a lot of hand-written checking code, and the automatic docs made integration with other teams easier. I can explain how async works in FastAPI.

p1-77.q: FastAPI endpoints declared with async def run on the event loop, so they must await I/O and avoid blocking calls; plain def endpoints run in a thread pool automatically. Validation comes from Pydantic models and type hints: FastAPI parses the request into models, returns 422 with detailed errors when validation fails, and uses the same models to generate OpenAPI.
i: Blocking libraries inside async def (requests, sync DB drivers) block the whole loop; use httpx or async drivers, or a plain def endpoint.
Pydantic validators (field_validator, model_validator) express business rules such as "site code must match pattern".
response_model filters output and documents it.
Background tasks for small post-response work; Celery or queues for heavy work.
f: What status does FastAPI return for invalid input?
422 Unprocessable Entity with a list of field errors.
def vs async def?
async def for non-blocking async I/O; def for blocking code, which FastAPI runs in a thread pool.
p1-77.y: In FastAPI, I declare endpoints with async def, so slow input and output, like database or HTTP calls, don't block the server. For validation, I describe the request as a Pydantic model with type hints, and FastAPI checks every request automatically and returns a 422 with the exact field errors if something is wrong. The same models also produce the API documentation.
x: FastAPI is built on ASGI, so it supports async natively, and it uses Pydantic for validation.

For async: if I declare an endpoint with async def, it runs on the event loop. That's efficient for I/O, but only if everything inside is also async, using libraries like httpx for HTTP calls and asyncpg or async SQLAlchemy for databases. If I call blocking code inside an async def, it blocks the whole event loop and every request waits. If I have to use blocking libraries, I declare the endpoint with plain def, and FastAPI runs it in a thread pool instead. That's a common mistake to watch for.

For validation, I define Pydantic models with type hints and constraints. FastAPI automatically parses and validates the request body, query and path parameters against them, and returns a 422 with detailed errors if they're invalid. Response models filter and serialise the output, so internal fields aren't leaked. Depends provides dependency injection for database sessions, authentication and configuration.
In production, I run it with uvicorn workers, behind a load balancer, in a container. It's conceptually very similar to ASP.NET Core model binding plus DI. I can show a short example.

p1-78.q: Spring Boot and ASP.NET Core solve the same problems with similar concepts: DI containers, middleware/filter chains, controllers with attribute routing, configuration with profiles/environments, ORMs (JPA/Hibernate vs EF Core), and production features (Actuator vs health checks and metrics). Differences are mostly ecosystem and language: Java/JVM with Spring's annotations and auto-configuration vs C#/.NET with explicit Program.cs setup.
i: Startup: Spring auto-configures from the classpath; ASP.NET Core registers explicitly in Program.cs.
Performance: both are fast; .NET often leads TechEmpower benchmarks, Java has GraalVM native images, .NET has native AOT.
Concurrency: Java 21 virtual threads vs .NET async/await.
I can work in Spring Boot by mapping concepts, as in Part 9's comparison table.
f: What is Spring's equivalent of middleware?
Servlet filters and Spring Security's filter chain; interceptors for MVC-level concerns.
Biggest mindset change?
Annotation-driven magic in Spring vs explicit configuration in modern .NET.
p1-78.y: Spring Boot and ASP.NET Core are very similar. Both have dependency injection built in, controllers, middleware or filters, configuration by environment, and good ORMs: JPA with Hibernate on Java, and EF Core on .NET. The main differences are the language and ecosystem. Since the ideas map almost one to one, I can pick up Spring Boot quickly with my ASP.NET Core background.
p1-78.k: spring boot, asp.net core, java, comparison
x: Spring Boot and ASP.NET Core are very similar in concept, so moving between them is mostly learning new names.

Both have a built-in dependency injection container with constructor injection, use annotations or attributes to declare routes, run on an embedded web server, support configuration profiles per environment, and have a mature ORM. The mapping is quite direct. RestController in Spring is like a controller with ApiController. Constructor injection works the same way. JPA with Hibernate is like EF Core. application.yml is like appsettings.json, Spring profiles are like ASP.NET Core environments, and Maven or Gradle play the role of NuGet and the dotnet CLI. Spring filters and interceptors are similar to middleware and filters.

The differences are more about ecosystem and style. Spring has a very large ecosystem, like Spring Security, Spring Cloud and Spring Data, and relies heavily on annotations and auto-configuration, which can feel magical. ASP.NET Core is a bit more explicit, with configuration in Program.cs, and it's very fast in benchmarks.
Because the concepts transfer, I'm comfortable reading and contributing to Spring Boot services, and the design principles I use in .NET apply directly. I can compare their security models too.

p1-79.q: I keep services consistent across .NET, Node.js and Python with shared standards rather than shared code: REST and event contracts defined in OpenAPI and schemas, the same structured logging fields and correlation ids, the same health endpoints, Docker conventions, one Azure DevOps pipeline template, and the same security and testing rules.
i: Contracts first: OpenAPI and JSON Schema reviewed before implementation; generated clients.
Observability: same log fields (service, env, version, correlationId) and OpenTelemetry in every language.
Pipeline template: build, test, scan (SonarQube, dependency scan), image build, deploy, identical stages.
Templates/scaffolds per language so new services start compliant.
Security: same auth library patterns, secrets from AWS Secrets Manager, no secrets in env files.
f: Do you share code libraries across languages?
No; share contracts and conventions, and keep per-language libraries small.
How do you enforce it?
Templates, pipeline gates and review checklists, not documents alone.
p1-79.y: I keep services consistent with shared standards rather than shared code. Every service, whether .NET, Node or Python, follows the same API and event contracts, the same structured logging fields and correlation ids, the same health endpoints, the same Docker conventions, and one pipeline template in Azure DevOps. So any engineer can operate any service, whatever the language.
x: When a team uses several languages, consistency comes from shared contracts and conventions, not from the language.

First, contracts. Every API is designed contract-first with OpenAPI, uses the same error format, based on ProblemDetails, and follows the same versioning rules. So a consumer can't tell which language a service is written in. Second, operational conventions. Every service uses correlation ids, structured JSON logs to CloudWatch, health endpoints, and metrics to Grafana, so support works the same way everywhere. Third, the delivery pipeline. The same CI/CD template builds, tests, runs a SonarQube quality gate, builds a container image, and deploys with infrastructure as code, whatever the language. Each language has a service template with all of this ready, so a new service starts consistent.
And I choose the language by fit, not taste. .NET for core domain services, Node and TypeScript for I/O glue and tooling, and Python for data and AI scripting.

The correlation-id work is a good example. I wrote it for .NET first, then we added the same header convention in Node and Python, so one query traces a request across all of them. I can explain how we keep the templates updated.

p1-80.q: Node uses npm/pnpm with package.json and a committed lockfile (package-lock.json or pnpm-lock.yaml) and `npm ci` in pipelines for reproducible installs; Python uses virtual environments with pinned dependencies (requirements.txt with hashes, or Poetry/uv with a lock file). In both I scan for vulnerabilities, update regularly with Dependabot or Renovate, and use internal feeds (Azure Artifacts) as a proxy.
i: Semantic versioning ranges (^, ~) are resolved once into the lockfile; builds use the lockfile only.
Separate dev and prod dependencies to keep images small.
npm audit, pip-audit, Snyk or Mend in CI; fail on criticals.
Supply chain: verify package names (typosquatting), restrict install scripts, use upstream proxy feeds.
.NET equivalent: central package management with Directory.Packages.props and packages.lock.json.
f: npm install vs npm ci?
npm ci installs exactly from the lockfile, fails if it is out of sync, and is faster for CI.
Why pin Python dependencies?
Unpinned installs can pull new versions and break builds unexpectedly.
p1-80.y: In Node I use npm with a committed package-lock file and npm ci in pipelines, so builds are repeatable. In Python I use a virtual environment with pinned versions in requirements or a Poetry lock file. In both, I scan for vulnerabilities in the pipeline and update dependencies regularly, a few at a time, with tests running.
p1-80.k: dependency management, npm, package-lock, pip, poetry, vulnerabilities
x: In both ecosystems, the goal is the same: reproducible builds, controlled updates, and catching vulnerable packages early.

In Node, package.json declares dependencies with version ranges, and the lock file, package-lock.json, records the exact versions of everything, including transitive dependencies. The lock file is always committed. In CI, I use npm ci instead of npm install, which installs exactly what's in the lock file and fails if it's out of sync. npm audit, or a tool like Dependabot, checks for known vulnerabilities. In Python, I use a virtual environment per project, so dependencies don't clash, and pin exact versions, either in requirements.txt or with a lock file from Poetry or uv. pip-audit checks for vulnerabilities.
For both, Docker images pin versions too, including the base image, and updates happen regularly through small pull requests, so we never face one huge risky upgrade.

It's the same idea as NuGet with central package management in .NET, which I introduced during our .NET 10 upgrade after a version conflict. I can explain how we handle a vulnerable transitive dependency.

p1-81.q: I choose by fit for the job, team skills and operability: .NET for core domain services with complex logic, transactions and performance; Node.js for I/O-bound glue, real-time and front-end-adjacent services; Python for data processing, validation and scripting or ML libraries. A new language must justify the extra cost of tooling, support and on-call knowledge.
i: Default to the team's main stack (.NET in IRT) unless there is a clear benefit.
Consider libraries available (Pydantic for validation, Azure DevOps SDKs in C#), performance needs and hosting (Lambda cold starts).
Operational cost: pipelines, monitoring, security patching and who can support it at 2 a.m.
Document the decision in an ADR (architecture decision record).
f: Have you said no to a language choice?
[Yes, a proposal to write a small service in Go]; nobody else could support it, so we used .NET.
What is an ADR?
A short document recording a decision, its context, options and consequences.
p1-81.y: I choose based on the team and the job, not personal taste. For core business services I default to .NET, because the team knows it, it is fast and our tooling is built around it. I'd choose Node for small input-output heavy tools, and Python for data handling or scripts. The service must fit our standards for logging, testing and deployment, whatever the language.
p1-81.k: language choice, technology choice, .net, node, python
x: I choose the language for a new microservice based on fit and on what the team can support, not on personal preference.

First, team skills and the existing ecosystem in that domain. If the team and all neighbouring services are .NET, there needs to be a strong reason to introduce something else, because every new language adds maintenance, hiring and support cost. Second, the workload. Complex domain logic or CPU-heavy work suits .NET or Java. I/O-heavy glue, backend-for-frontend layers and tooling suit Node and TypeScript. Data processing, machine learning and AI scripting suit Python. Third, libraries. Sometimes the best library decides, for example mature commercial SFTP providers in .NET, or the newest LLM SDKs often appearing first in Python and TypeScript. Fourth, operations: can we monitor, secure, test and deploy it with our existing templates and pipelines?
So in practice, our core IRT services are .NET, and other languages appear where they clearly fit better.
The decision should be written down, for example in an architecture decision record, so the next person knows why. I can give an example of a decision like that.

p2-1.q: I use ECS (on Fargate or EC2) for long-running containerised services and workers with steady traffic, Lambda for short, event-driven or spiky work (S3 events, queue triggers, schedules) where pay-per-use and zero servers win, and plain EC2 when I need full control of the OS, special software, or licensing that containers or Lambda cannot handle.
i: Lambda limits: 15-minute max duration, up to 10 GB memory, cold starts, concurrency limits; costly at high steady load.
ECS Fargate: no servers to patch, per-task CPU/memory billing; ECS on EC2 is cheaper at scale and allows GPUs or daemon tasks.
EC2: legacy apps, Windows services with installers, custom agents; you own patching, scaling and AMIs.
Cost rule of thumb: spiky or low traffic favours Lambda; constant high traffic favours containers.
In IRT: .NET APIs and RabbitMQ workers on ECS, Lambda for [event-driven pieces such as S3 file arrival notifications], EC2 for [the on-prem-like deployment nodes and tooling servers].
f: Can Lambda run a full ASP.NET Core API?
Yes, with the Lambda ASP.NET Core hosting adapter, but cold starts and per-request cost need checking.
Fargate vs ECS on EC2?
Fargate for simplicity; EC2 capacity providers for cost control at scale or special hardware.
p2-1.y: I use ECS with Fargate for long-running services like our APIs, because containers run all the time with no servers to manage. I use Lambda for short, event-driven tasks, like reacting to a file landing in S3, where I pay only when it runs. I use EC2 when I need full control of the machine, special software, or very steady heavy load. [Those services run on ECS.]
p2-1.k: ecs, lambda, ec2, fargate, compute choice, aws
x: EC2, ECS and Lambda are three levels of compute on AWS, from most control to least management.

EC2 gives you virtual machines. You choose the instance type and operating system and manage everything on it: patching, scaling, software. It's the right choice for legacy applications, special software that needs OS-level access, or workloads that don't fit containers. ECS runs Docker containers as long-running services, either on EC2 instances or on Fargate, where you don't manage servers at all. It's a great fit for web APIs and background workers with steady traffic, because containers are always running, start consistently, and you control the runtime. Lambda runs functions in response to events, like an HTTP request, a file in S3, or a message in a queue. You pay only per invocation and duration, and it scales automatically, even to zero. But each run is limited to 15 minutes, and cold starts add latency.
So my rule: Lambda for event-driven glue, scheduled jobs and spiky or low traffic. ECS for core APIs and workers with steady load. EC2 only when I need that level of control.

[The newer IQVIA services I've worked on] follow exactly that: the .NET services and consumers run on ECS, and Lambda handles event-driven pieces like reacting to files in S3. I can explain the cost trade-offs.

p2-2.q: An ECS cluster is a logical group of capacity (Fargate or EC2 instances); a task definition is the versioned blueprint (images, CPU, memory, ports, environment, secrets, IAM roles, logging); a task is a running copy of it; a service keeps the desired number of tasks running, replaces failed ones, registers them with a load balancer and performs rolling or blue/green deployments.
i: Two IAM roles: the task execution role (pull images from ECR, write logs, read secrets at start) and the task role (what your code may call, e.g. S3, SQS).
Networking: awsvpc mode gives each task its own ENI and security group.
Deployments: rolling with minimumHealthyPercent/maximumPercent and the deployment circuit breaker with automatic rollback, or CodeDeploy blue/green.
Service auto scaling with target tracking on CPU, memory or ALB request count per target.
Service Connect or Cloud Map for service discovery between services.
Logs via the awslogs driver to CloudWatch Logs, or FireLens.
f: Task role vs execution role?
Execution role is used by ECS to start the task; the task role is assumed by your application code at runtime.
What happens when a task fails its health check?
The service stops it and starts a replacement, and the ALB stops routing to it.
p2-2.y: In ECS, a cluster is the logical group where things run. A task definition is like a blueprint: the image, CPU, memory, environment variables, secrets and IAM role. A task is one running copy of it, and a service keeps the desired number of tasks running, replaces failed ones and connects them to the load balancer. With Fargate, AWS runs the servers for us.
p2-2.k: ecs, cluster, task definition, task, service, fargate
x: ECS has a small set of building blocks, and once you know them, the rest is straightforward.

A cluster is a logical group of capacity where tasks run, either EC2 instances you manage, or Fargate, where AWS manages it. A task definition is the blueprint, a bit like a docker-compose file. It specifies the container image, CPU and memory, environment variables and secrets, port mappings, the IAM task role the app uses to call AWS services, the execution role ECS uses to pull images and secrets, and the logging configuration. A task is a running instance of that definition, one or more containers running together. A service keeps a desired number of tasks running, for example three. It replaces unhealthy or stopped tasks, registers them with a load balancer target group, handles rolling deployments when you update the task definition, and integrates with autoscaling.
There are also capacity providers, which decide where tasks run, like Fargate or Fargate Spot.

In the newer IQVIA services on AWS, each .NET service has its own task definition and ECS service, behind an ALB target group, with a task role scoped to just what it needs. Deployments simply register a new task definition revision. I can explain how a rolling deployment works step by step.

p2-3.q: API Gateway is a managed front door for APIs: it receives requests, authenticates and authorises them (JWT, Cognito, Lambda authorizers, IAM), throttles and applies usage plans, validates and transforms requests, and routes them to Lambda, HTTP backends or AWS services, with logging and metrics built in.
i: REST APIs (v1) have more features (usage plans, API keys, request validation, caching, WAF); HTTP APIs (v2) are cheaper and faster with JWT authorizers.
Private integrations reach services in a VPC through VPC Link to an NLB or ALB.
Limits: 29-second default integration timeout (raisable for some APIs), 10 MB payload.
Throttling is token-bucket based per account, stage and method; returns 429.
Custom domains, stages (dev, uat, prod), canary releases per stage.
f: API Gateway or ALB?
API Gateway for API management and serverless; ALB for container services with high steady traffic (Part 5 has the table).
How do you secure it?
JWT/OAuth authorizers, WAF, resource policies, throttling and mutual TLS where needed.
p2-3.y: API Gateway is the front door for APIs. It handles routing to backends like Lambda or HTTP services, authentication with JWT or IAM, throttling, request validation, usage plans and API keys. So the services behind it can focus on business logic. For containers with heavy traffic, an Application Load Balancer is often cheaper, so the choice depends on what features we need.
p2-3.k: api gateway, throttling, routing, authentication, aws
x: API Gateway is a managed front door for APIs. Clients call it, and it routes requests to the backend, like Lambda functions, HTTP services on ECS, or directly to other AWS services.

Its value is everything it handles before the request reaches your code. Authentication: JWT and Cognito authorisers, custom Lambda authorisers, or IAM. Throttling and quotas, including usage plans with API keys per client, so one partner can't overload the system. Request validation against a schema, CORS, and request and response transformation. It also supports stages, like dev and prod, custom domains, caching, and logging and metrics in CloudWatch. There are three types: REST APIs, the most feature-rich; HTTP APIs, which are simpler, faster and cheaper; and WebSocket APIs for real-time two-way communication.
Limits to remember: a default 29-second integration timeout, and payload size limits, so it's not for long-running or large requests.

In the newer IQVIA services on AWS, partner-facing APIs go through API Gateway, which gives us per-partner throttling and keys, while internal UI traffic goes through the ALB directly to ECS. I can compare it with an ALB in more detail.

p2-4.q: A cold start is the extra latency when Lambda creates a new execution environment: download code, start the runtime, run initialisation, then the handler. It happens on the first request, after idle periods and when scaling out. Reduce it with smaller packages, less work at init, more memory (more CPU), Provisioned Concurrency, SnapStart and, for .NET, native AOT.
i: .NET options: ReadyToRun or native AOT (`PublishAot`) cut startup a lot; avoid heavy reflection and DI scanning at init.
SnapStart (Java, Python and .NET 8 managed runtime) snapshots the initialised environment and restores it.
Provisioned Concurrency keeps environments warm (costs money); schedule it for business hours.
VPC cold-start penalty was largely fixed by Hyperplane ENIs, but still keep dependencies light.
Initialise SDK clients outside the handler so warm invocations reuse them.
f: Does memory affect cold start?
Yes; CPU scales with memory, so more memory often means faster init and can even reduce cost.
How do you measure it?
The Init Duration field in REPORT log lines, or X-Ray traces.
p2-4.y: A cold start is the extra delay when Lambda has to create a new environment and load my code before the first request. For .NET it can be noticeable. I reduce it with more memory, which also gives more CPU, smaller packages, Native AOT or SnapStart, and provisioned concurrency to keep instances warm for critical functions. For steady traffic, a container on ECS avoids cold starts completely.
p2-4.k: lambda, cold start, provisioned concurrency, snapstart, native aot
x: A cold start happens when Lambda has to create a new execution environment to handle a request. That means downloading the code, starting the runtime, and running your initialisation code, before the function itself runs. Later requests reuse the warm environment and are fast.

Cold starts happen on the first request, after a period of inactivity, and when scaling up, because each new concurrent execution needs its own environment. For .NET, cold starts have traditionally been longer than for Node or Python, because of runtime startup and JIT compilation, sometimes over a second.

To reduce them: keep the deployment package small and trim dependencies. Use native AOT compilation, which removes JIT and makes .NET start much faster, or ReadyToRun as a lighter option. Use SnapStart where supported, which restores a snapshot of an initialised environment. Keep initialisation code light, and lazily create heavy clients. Allocating more memory also gives more CPU, which speeds up startup. And for latency-critical functions, provisioned concurrency keeps environments warm, at an extra cost.

Often the simplest answer is architecture: if a path is latency-critical and constant, a container on ECS may suit it better. Our Lambdas are event-driven background tasks, where a cold start doesn't hurt users. I can explain native AOT trade-offs.

p2-5.q: DynamoDB modelling starts from access patterns, not entities: list every query, choose a partition key with high cardinality and even traffic, a sort key for ranges and ordering, and add GSIs for other patterns. Often several entity types share one table (single-table design) with generic keys like PK = STUDY#42, SK = SITE#7.
i: Item collections: items sharing a partition key can be fetched together with one Query.
Avoid scans; every request should be GetItem or Query by key.
Hot partitions: spread writes with sharded keys if one key gets most traffic.
Item limit 400 KB; large payloads go to S3 with a pointer.
Use conditional writes for idempotency and optimistic locking (version attribute), TTL for expiry, Streams for change events.
c:
PK            SK                  Attributes
IDEMP#a1b2    REQ                 status=Done, response=..., ttl=1718000000
STUDY#42      SITE#007            name, country
STUDY#42      SHIPMENT#2024-06-01#881   status, kitCount
f: Single-table design always?
No; it optimises known patterns but is hard to evolve; separate tables are fine for simple cases.
Query vs Scan?
Query reads one partition by key; Scan reads the whole table and is slow and expensive.
p2-5.y: In DynamoDB I start from the access patterns, not from tables and joins. I choose a partition key that spreads load evenly and a sort key for ranges, like customer id and order date. Often several entity types live in one table. For other query patterns I add global secondary indexes. Getting the keys wrong is expensive to change later, so I design them carefully up front.
p2-5.k: dynamodb, partition key, sort key, gsi, single table design, nosql
x: DynamoDB modelling is the opposite of relational modelling. Instead of starting from entities and normalising, you start from the access patterns.

First, I list every query the application needs, like "get a shipment by id", "list shipments for a site by date", or "get all events for a shipment". Then I design keys to serve them. The partition key must have high cardinality, like a shipment id rather than a status, so data and traffic spread evenly and we avoid hot partitions. The sort key allows range queries within a partition, with conditions like begins_with or between, for example a sort key of "EVENT#" plus a timestamp. Extra access patterns are served with global secondary indexes. Single-table design goes further, storing related item types in one table with generic key names, so one query can fetch a shipment and its events together.
Other tools I use: conditional writes for optimistic concurrency and uniqueness, TTL to expire old items automatically, and Streams to react to changes.

The trade-off is that unplanned queries are expensive, so this works best when access patterns are stable. In the newer IQVIA services on AWS, DynamoDB holds simpler, high-volume status and event data, designed exactly this way. I can sketch a key design.

p2-6.q: The main patterns are cache-aside (app reads cache, on miss loads from DB and stores it), read-through, write-through (write cache and DB together), write-behind (write cache, persist later) and refresh-ahead. ElastiCache (Redis or Valkey) is AWS's managed in-memory cache, used for shared caches, sessions, rate limits, distributed locks and token denylists.
i: Cache-aside is the most common and simplest; set TTLs and invalidate on writes.
Stampede protection: locks or HybridCache, jittered TTLs, early refresh.
Eviction policies (allkeys-lru, volatile-ttl) and memory limits must be set deliberately.
Redis replication with Multi-AZ failover; cluster mode for sharding.
Never cache without a plan for invalidation and consistency.
In IRT: [study configuration and reference data] cached; the logout fix used ElastiCache for the jti denylist with TTLs.
f: Redis vs Memcached?
Redis has data structures, persistence options, replication and pub/sub; Memcached is simpler, multithreaded, cache-only.
What is a hit ratio?
The share of reads served from cache; monitor it to judge if caching works.
p2-6.y: The most common is cache-aside: the app checks the cache, and on a miss reads the database and stores the result with an expiry time. Write-through updates the cache when writing the database. I always set TTLs and invalidate on changes. We used ElastiCache Redis for reference data, and also for our token logout denylist, where lookups take about [1 millisecond].
p2-6.k: caching, elasticache, redis, cache-aside, write-through, ttl
x: Caching strategies differ mainly in when the cache and the database are written, and which one you read first.

Cache-aside, or lazy loading, is the most common. The application reads from the cache; on a miss, it reads from the database and stores the result in the cache with an expiry. It only caches data that's actually requested, and the cache can fail without breaking anything, but the first read is slower and data can be stale until it expires. Write-through writes to the cache and the database together, so the cache is always up to date for reads, at the cost of slower writes and caching data that may never be read. Write-behind writes to the cache first and flushes to the database later. It's very fast, but risky, because data can be lost if the cache fails.

Whatever the strategy, a few rules apply: set TTLs, invalidate or update the cache when data changes, add jitter to expiries, and protect against cache stampedes, where many requests miss at once, with locking or HybridCache. And never treat the cache as the source of truth.

In the newer IQVIA services on AWS, ElastiCache Redis uses cache-aside for reference data, like depots and country rules, with short TTLs and eviction on change. I can explain how we handle invalidation.

p2-7.q: ALB (Application Load Balancer) works at layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS/gRPC): routing by path, host, headers and query, TLS termination, redirects, OIDC authentication and WebSockets. NLB (Network Load Balancer) works at layer 4 (TCP/UDP/TLS): extreme throughput, very low latency, static IPs/Elastic IPs and source IP preservation.
i: ALB targets: instances, IPs, Lambda; NLB targets: instances, IPs and even an ALB.
Use NLB for non-HTTP protocols, PrivateLink services, or when clients need fixed IPs.
API Gateway private integrations (REST APIs) need an NLB via VPC Link.
Health checks: ALB uses HTTP paths; NLB can use TCP or HTTP.
Gateway Load Balancer is the third type, for inline appliances (firewalls).
f: Which one for your .NET APIs?
ALB, for path routing to several ECS services and HTTP health checks.
Can ALB give static IPs?
Not directly; put an NLB or Global Accelerator in front.
p2-7.y: An Application Load Balancer works at layer 7, so it understands HTTP: it can route by path or host name, terminate TLS, and do health checks on HTTP endpoints. A Network Load Balancer works at layer 4 with TCP and UDP, so it is extremely fast, keeps static IPs, and suits non-HTTP traffic. For our web APIs on ECS we use an ALB.
p2-7.k: alb, nlb, load balancer, layer 7, layer 4, aws
x: Both distribute traffic across targets, but they work at different network layers.

The Application Load Balancer works at layer 7, the HTTP level. It understands HTTP and HTTPS, so it can route based on the URL path, the host name, headers or query strings. For example, /api/shipments goes to one service and /api/sites to another. It terminates TLS, integrates with AWS WAF for web protection, supports WebSockets and HTTP/2, can authenticate users with OIDC, and works directly with ECS target groups. The Network Load Balancer works at layer 4, TCP and UDP. It doesn't look inside the request, so it's extremely fast, with very low latency, handles millions of requests per second, and provides static IP addresses, which some partners need for firewall allow-lists. It also supports non-HTTP protocols.
Both perform health checks and spread traffic across availability zones.

So for web APIs and microservices, the ALB is the default. I use an NLB when I need static IPs, extreme performance, or non-HTTP traffic, like an SFTP endpoint or a TCP service. In the newer IQVIA services on AWS, the ALB fronts all our ECS services, with path-based routing to each service. I can explain how target group health checks work.

p2-8.q: S3 is durable object storage (eleven nines durability) used for files, backups, data lakes, static websites, logs and artifacts. A presigned URL grants temporary access to one object operation (GET or PUT) using the signer's permissions, so clients can download or upload directly to S3 without AWS credentials and without passing through your API.
i: Presigned URLs expire (up to 7 days with IAM user credentials, shorter with temporary credentials); keep them short (minutes).
Uploads: presigned PUT or POST (POST policies can restrict size and content type); multipart for large files.
Storage classes and lifecycle rules (Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Glacier) cut cost.
Security: Block Public Access, bucket policies, SSE-KMS, versioning, Object Lock for WORM retention (useful for GxP evidence).
Events: S3 notifications to Lambda, SQS or EventBridge trigger processing.
f: Who can use a presigned URL?
Anyone who has it until it expires, so treat it like a short-lived secret.
Why upload directly to S3?
It offloads large transfers from your API, avoiding timeouts and memory pressure.
p2-8.y: S3 is object storage for files: uploads, exports, backups, logs and static websites. It is very durable and cheap. A presigned URL is a temporary link, signed with our credentials, that lets a client upload or download one specific object directly, without going through our API and without AWS credentials. It is great for large file uploads, like CSV imports.
p2-8.k: s3, presigned url, object storage, file upload, aws
x: S3 is AWS's object storage. It stores files, called objects, in buckets, with extremely high durability, eleven nines, and practically unlimited capacity.

It's used for all kinds of things: uploaded files and exports, backups, static websites, build artifacts, data lakes and logs. Storage classes trade cost against access speed, from S3 Standard for frequently accessed data, to Infrequent Access, to Glacier for archives. Lifecycle rules automatically move objects to cheaper classes or delete them after a period.

A presigned URL gives temporary access to one specific object, for upload or download, without giving the client any AWS credentials. Our backend, which has permission, generates a URL signed with its credentials, valid for a short time, like five minutes. The client uses that URL directly with S3. This is very useful for large files, because the upload goes straight to S3 instead of through our API, which saves bandwidth and memory, and avoids API Gateway size limits.

Security basics always apply: Block Public Access, encryption, least-privilege policies. In our platform, CSV imports and exports use presigned URLs, and our API only receives the object key after the upload completes. I can walk through that flow.

p2-9.q: Least privilege means every identity gets only the actions on the specific resources it needs, nothing more.
