It has very flexible routing, per-message acknowledgements, priorities, and dead-letter queues, so it's excellent for task queues, commands, and work distribution, where each message should be processed once by one worker. Kafka is a distributed, partitioned, append-only log. Producers write events to topics, and the events are kept for a retention period, whether they've been read or not. Consumers track their own position, called the offset, so many independent consumer groups can read the same events, and you can replay history. It provides ordering within a partition and very high throughput.
So I choose RabbitMQ for commands and work queues with complex routing, and Kafka for event streaming, when several services need the same events, or replay, retention and high volume matter.
In our platform, RabbitMQ handles service-to-service workflows like shipment processing. I can explain how we made publishing reliable after our [mid-2024] incident, which applies to both.

p2-38.q: A topic is a named stream of events split into partitions; each partition is an ordered, append-only log stored on brokers and replicated. Producers choose the partition by key (same key, same partition, same order); a consumer group shares the partitions among its consumers so each partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group, while different groups read independently.
i: Parallelism is capped by partition count within a group.
Offsets are committed per group and partition; consumers resume from them after restarts.
Rebalancing reassigns partitions when consumers join or leave; cooperative rebalancing reduces pauses.
Choose keys for ordering needs (ShipmentId) and even distribution.
Retention by time or size, independent of consumption.
f: Can you reduce partitions?
No; you can only add them, and adding changes key-to-partition mapping for new messages.
What happens with two groups on one topic?
Each group gets every message, so different services can process the same events.
p2-38.y: A topic is a named stream of events, like shipment-status. Each topic is split into partitions, which allow parallel processing, and order is kept only inside a partition. A consumer group is a set of consumers sharing the work: each partition is read by one consumer in the group. So more partitions mean more parallelism, and we use the shipment id as the key to keep its events in order.
p2-38.k: kafka, topic, partition, consumer group, offset, ordering
x: These are the three core concepts that give Kafka its scalability and ordering.

A topic is a named stream of events, like "shipment-events". Each topic is split into partitions. A partition is an ordered, append-only log, where each event gets a sequential offset. Partitions are spread across brokers, which is how Kafka scales. When producing, the producer chooses the partition, usually by hashing the message key. So all events with the same key, like the same study id or shipment id, always go to the same partition, and stay in order. Ordering is only guaranteed within a partition, not across the whole topic.

A consumer group is a set of consumers that share the work of reading a topic. Each partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group at a time. So if a topic has six partitions, up to six consumers in a group can work in parallel; a seventh would sit idle. The partition count therefore limits parallelism. Different consumer groups read the same topic independently, each with its own offsets. When consumers join or leave, Kafka rebalances partitions among them.
Consumers commit offsets after processing, so after a restart they continue where they left off. I can explain how to choose a good partition key.

p2-39.q: RabbitMQ has four main exchange types: direct (routes to queues whose binding key equals the routing key), topic (pattern matching with * for one word and # for zero or more, like shipment.*.delivered), fanout (broadcasts to all bound queues, ignoring keys) and headers (routes on message header values). The default exchange routes directly to the queue named by the routing key.
i: Direct for commands to specific workers; topic for event categories; fanout for broadcast notifications.
Alternate exchanges catch unroutable messages; mandatory flag returns them to the publisher.
Dead-letter exchanges route rejected or expired messages.
Consistent-hash exchange (plugin) spreads by key for sharding.
c:
await channel.ExchangeDeclareAsync("shipments", ExchangeType.Topic, durable: true);
await channel.QueueBindAsync("notify-sites", "shipments", "shipment.*.delivered");
f: Which exchange for "every service gets every event"?
Fanout, or topic with # binding.
What happens to messages with no matching binding?
They are dropped, unless mandatory or an alternate exchange is used.
p2-39.y: RabbitMQ has four exchange types. Direct sends a message to queues whose binding key exactly matches the routing key. Topic matches patterns with wildcards, like shipment dot star. Fanout sends to all bound queues, ignoring the key. Headers routes based on message headers. We mostly use topic exchanges, with dead-letter queues for failures.
p2-39.k: rabbitmq, exchange, direct, topic, fanout, headers, routing key
x: In RabbitMQ, producers never publish directly to a queue. They publish to an exchange, and the exchange type decides how messages are routed to the queues bound to it.

A direct exchange routes by exact match. A message with routing key "shipment.created" goes to queues bound with exactly that key. It's good for commands and simple point-to-point routing. A topic exchange routes by pattern. Routing keys are dot-separated words, and bindings can use wildcards: a star matches exactly one word, and a hash matches zero or more. For example, a queue bound with "shipment.*.created" gets created events from any region. It's the most flexible and the one I use most. A fanout exchange ignores the routing key and copies every message to all bound queues, which is a simple broadcast, like notifying several services that reference data changed. A headers exchange routes based on message header values instead of the routing key, which is rarely needed.
There's also the default exchange, which routes to a queue with the same name as the routing key.

In our platform, we use topic exchanges for domain events, like shipment status changes, so each consuming service binds only to the event patterns it cares about. I can explain how dead-letter exchanges fit in.

p2-40.q: Publisher confirms make RabbitMQ acknowledge each published message once it is safely stored (or nack it), so the publisher knows about failures instead of losing messages silently. In [mid-2024] a memory alarm blocked publishers and dropped connections, and for [about 40 minutes] shipment-status updates vanished without errors because we published without confirms; I recovered by replaying the vendor files (consumers upsert, so it was safe) and fixed it permanently with confirms, retries, alerts and memory tuning.
i: How confirms work: channel in confirm mode, each message gets a delivery tag, broker sends basic.ack or basic.nack; with persistent messages to durable or quorum queues the ack comes after writing to disk.
In RabbitMQ.Client 7, `CreateChannelOptions(publisherConfirmationsEnabled: true, publisherConfirmationTrackingEnabled: true)` makes BasicPublishAsync wait for the confirm and throw on nack.
Track asynchronously in batches to keep throughput; we saw about [5 percent] cost.
Full guarantee chain: durable queues, persistent messages, confirms, manual consumer acks, DLQ, idempotent consumers; plus an outbox for publish-after-commit.
Monitoring added: memory and disk alarms, blocked connections, publish vs deliver rates, and an alert when the incoming rate drops to zero during business hours.
f: What does the memory high watermark do?
When RabbitMQ memory exceeds it (default 40 percent of RAM, or a set value), the broker blocks publishing connections until memory drops.
Confirms vs transactions?
AMQP transactions also give safety but are much slower; confirms are the recommended approach.
w: I take ownership on support duty: restore service first, then fix the root cause.
I turn an incident into lasting guarantees and monitoring, not just a one-off fix.
p2-40.y: In [mid-2024], RabbitMQ hit a memory alarm, blocked publishers and dropped connections. Because we published without confirms, shipment status updates were lost silently for [about 40 minutes]. I recovered by replaying the vendor files, which was safe because consumers upsert. Then I fixed it properly with publisher confirms, so RabbitMQ acknowledges each message once stored, plus retries, alerts and memory tuning. Since then we haven't lost a message.
p2-40.k: publisher confirms, rabbitmq outage, message loss, story, reliability
x: Situation: In [mid-2024], our RabbitMQ broker hit its memory high watermark during a busy period. When that happens, RabbitMQ blocks publishing connections, and some connections were dropped. The problem was that our services published shipment status updates without publisher confirms, which is fire-and-forget. So for [about 40 minutes], [about 1,200] status updates simply vanished, with no errors in our logs. We found out when study teams reported shipments stuck in the wrong status.
Task: I was on support duty, so my job was to restore the missing data first, and then make sure messages could never be lost silently again.

Action: For recovery, I replayed the vendor status files for that window. That was safe because our consumers upsert, so reprocessing was idempotent. For the permanent fix, I enabled publisher confirms. The channel is put into confirm mode, and the broker acknowledges each message once it's safely stored, or sends a negative acknowledgement. In RabbitMQ.Client 7, BasicPublishAsync then waits for the confirm and throws on failure, so we can retry. Messages are persistent, queues are durable, and consumers use manual acks with dead-letter queues. We also tuned memory, and added alerts on memory, blocked connections, and the incoming update rate dropping to zero during business hours.
Result: Throughput cost was about [5 percent], and since then we haven't lost a message. I can show the code.

p2-41.q: At-most-once means a message is delivered zero or one time (may be lost, never duplicated: ack before processing); at-least-once means it is never lost but may be duplicated (ack after processing, retry on failure); exactly-once means each message affects the system once, which in practice is achieved as effectively-once: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing.
i: Most real systems choose at-least-once with idempotent consumers.
Kafka offers exactly-once semantics inside Kafka (idempotent producer plus transactions for read-process-write).
Across systems (Kafka to database) you need idempotency or storing offsets with the data in one transaction.
At-most-once fits metrics or telemetry where loss is acceptable.
f: Where can duplicates come from?
Producer retries, consumer crashes before committing, redelivery after timeouts.
How do you test idempotency?
Deliver the same message twice in an integration test and assert the state is unchanged.
p2-41.y: At-most-once means a message is delivered zero or one time, so it can be lost but never duplicated. At-least-once means it is never lost but can arrive more than once, which is the most common choice. Exactly-once is hard across systems, so in practice we use at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers, which gives exactly-once effect.
p2-41.k: delivery guarantees, at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once, messaging
x: These are the three delivery guarantees a messaging system can offer, and each is a trade-off between losing messages and duplicating them.

At-most-once means a message is delivered once or not at all. There are no retries, so if something fails along the way, the message is lost. It's only acceptable for data where loss doesn't matter, like some metrics. At-least-once means the system keeps retrying until the message is acknowledged, so nothing is lost. But if a consumer processes a message and crashes before acknowledging, it will receive it again, so duplicates are possible. That's why consumers must be idempotent. Exactly-once means no loss and no duplicates. It's only truly available within limits, like Kafka transactions for read-process-write inside Kafka. Across different systems, like a broker and a database, it's achieved "effectively" through at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing.
In practice, at-least-once with idempotent consumers is the standard choice for business data.

That's how our platform works. Publishing uses confirms, so the broker definitely has the message, consumers acknowledge only after successful processing, and every message has an id, which consumers use to skip duplicates. I can explain how to make a consumer idempotent.

p2-42.q: An idempotent consumer produces the same result if it processes the same message twice. I give every message a unique id and either record processed ids in a table (inbox pattern) in the same transaction as the business change, or design the change itself as an upsert or conditional update (set status where version is older) so repeats are harmless.
i: Inbox table: unique constraint on MessageId; insert fails for duplicates, so skip them.
Natural idempotency: "set shipment 881 to Delivered" is idempotent; "add 10 kits" is not, so carry the target state or a version.
Keep processed-id records for longer than the maximum redelivery window, then clean up.
External side effects (emails, API calls) need their own idempotency keys.
Our shipment consumers upsert status by shipment id, which is why replaying vendor files after the outage was safe.
c:
INSERT INTO dbo.InboxMessages (MessageId, ProcessedAt) VALUES (@MessageId, SYSUTCDATETIME()); -- unique key
UPDATE dbo.Shipments SET Status = @Status, StatusAt = @At
WHERE ShipmentId = @ShipmentId AND (StatusAt IS NULL OR StatusAt < @At);  -- ignore older/duplicate events
f: Why do this in one transaction?
So the business change and the processed marker succeed or fail together.
What about out-of-order messages?
Compare timestamps or versions and ignore stale updates, as in the WHERE clause.
p2-42.y: An idempotent consumer gives the same result even if it gets the same message twice. I do it by giving each message a unique id and storing processed ids in a table with a unique key, in the same transaction as the business change, so a duplicate is simply skipped. Another way is using upserts or checking the current state, for example ignore a status update older than what we already have.
p2-42.k: idempotent consumer, deduplication, message id, upsert, at-least-once
x: An idempotent consumer produces the same result whether it processes a message once or several times. With at-least-once delivery, duplicates will happen, so this is essential.

There are a few techniques, and I often combine them. First, every message carries a unique message id. The consumer keeps an inbox table of processed ids, and skips any message it has already seen. The key detail is that the insert into the inbox table and the business update happen in the same database transaction, so either both are saved or neither is. Second, natural idempotency: design operations so repeating them is harmless. "Set shipment status to Delivered" is idempotent, while "increment delivered count" isn't. Upserts instead of inserts, and unique constraints, help too. Third, for ordering problems, a version or timestamp check, so an older event can't overwrite newer data.
Then the failure path: retry transient errors with backoff, and after a few attempts move the message to a dead-letter queue, instead of retrying forever.
This property saved us in our RabbitMQ incident in [mid-2024]. Because consumers upsert, I could safely replay a whole window of vendor files without creating duplicates. I can explain that recovery.

p2-43.q: A dead-letter queue holds messages that could not be processed after retries (or that expired or were rejected), so they do not block the main queue or get lost. Operators inspect them, fix the cause and replay them; alerts fire when the DLQ is not empty.
i: RabbitMQ: queue argument x-dead-letter-exchange; messages rejected with requeue=false, expired by TTL or over a length limit go there; quorum queues add delivery limits.
SQS: redrive policy with maxReceiveCount and DLQ redrive back to the source.
Kafka: dead-letter topic written by the consumer code or the framework.
Store failure reason and attempt count in headers for diagnosis.
Poison messages (always failing) must go to the DLQ quickly instead of retrying forever.
f: What do you do with DLQ messages?
Investigate, fix code or data, then replay them with a tool or script, and document it.
Can retries cause DLQ storms?
Yes, if a dependency is down; use backoff and circuit breakers so transient outages do not dead-letter everything.
p2-43.y: A dead-letter queue is where messages go when they can't be processed, for example after several retries or if the message is invalid. This keeps one bad message from blocking the queue or being retried forever. We monitor the dead-letter queue with alerts, look at why the message failed, fix the issue and then replay it.
p2-43.k: dead letter queue, dlq, poison message, retries, rabbitmq, kafka
x: A dead-letter queue, or DLQ, is a separate queue where messages go when they can't be processed successfully, so they don't block the main queue or get lost.

Messages typically end up there for three reasons: processing keeps failing after a set number of retries, for example because of bad data or a bug; the message is explicitly rejected; or it expires. Without a DLQ, a "poison message" that always fails can be retried forever, blocking other messages or burning resources. With a DLQ, it's moved aside, and normal processing continues.

In RabbitMQ, you configure a dead-letter exchange on the queue, and rejected or expired messages are routed there. With quorum queues, you can also set a delivery limit. In Kafka, there's no built-in DLQ, so the consumer publishes failed messages to a retry topic or a dead-letter topic itself. In AWS SQS, you configure a redrive policy with a maximum receive count.

The most important rule is that a DLQ must never be silent. We alert on any message in a DLQ, someone inspects it, fixes the cause, and then replays the messages back to the main queue. Our consumers are idempotent, so replaying is safe. I can explain our replay process.

p2-44.q: The transactional outbox pattern saves the business change and the event to publish in the same database transaction (into an Outbox table); a separate relay then reads unpublished outbox rows and publishes them to the broker, marking them sent. This guarantees an event is published if and only if the change committed, without distributed transactions.
i: Delivery is at-least-once (the relay may publish twice after a crash), so consumers must be idempotent.
Relay options: polling background service, CDC (Debezium reading the transaction log), or libraries (MassTransit, NServiceBus, Wolverine outbox).
Keep ordering per aggregate by publishing in sequence per key.
Clean up old published rows.
Inbox pattern is the consumer-side mirror for deduplication.
f: Why not publish right after SaveChanges?
If publishing fails or the process crashes between the two, the event is lost while the data changed.
Polling vs CDC?
Polling is simple; CDC has lower latency and no polling load but needs more infrastructure.
p2-44.y: The outbox pattern solves the problem of saving to the database and publishing an event reliably. In the same transaction as the business change, I insert the event into an outbox table. A background process then reads the outbox and publishes to the broker, marking rows as sent. So if the broker is down, events wait safely in the database and nothing is lost.
p2-44.k: outbox pattern, transactional outbox, reliable messaging, events, dual write
x: The transactional outbox pattern solves a very common reliability problem in microservices: updating your database and publishing an event as one reliable step.

The problem is that the database and the message broker can't share one transaction. If you save the change and then publish, the publish might fail after the commit, and other services never hear about it. If you publish first and then the save fails, other services react to something that never happened. Either way, systems disagree.

The outbox pattern fixes this. In the same database transaction as the business change, you also insert a row into an outbox table, containing the event. Because it's one local transaction, either both are saved or neither is. Then a separate background relay reads unpublished rows from the outbox, publishes them to RabbitMQ or Kafka, and marks them as published. If publishing fails, it simply retries later. This gives at-least-once publishing, so consumers must be idempotent. The relay can poll the table, or use change data capture with a tool like Debezium.

In our shipment flow, the shipment update and its outbox event are saved together, and a background service publishes them with publisher confirms. If the broker is down, events just wait. I can show the table design.

p2-45.q: Authentication answers "who are you?" by verifying identity (password, SSO, token, certificate); authorization answers "what are you allowed to do?" by checking permissions for that identity on a resource or action. In ASP.NET Core, UseAuthentication builds HttpContext.User and UseAuthorization enforces policies; failures return 401 and 403 respectively.
i: Role-based (RequireRole), claims-based and policy-based authorization; resource-based for "this user on this study".
Authorization must happen on the server for every request; UI hiding is not security.
Least privilege and separation of duties (e.g. unblinded vs blinded roles in clinical trials).
OAuth 2.0 is about delegated authorization; OpenID Connect adds authentication.
f: 401 Unauthorized actually means unauthenticated; 403 Forbidden means authenticated but not permitted.
Where do you check "user can access this study"?
In a resource-based authorization handler, using the study id from the request.
p2-45.y: Authentication answers who you are, for example by validating a login or a token. Authorization answers what you are allowed to do, like checking roles, policies or whether you have access to a specific study. Authentication always comes first. In ASP.NET Core they are separate middleware, and a failed authentication returns 401, while a failed authorization returns 403.
x: Authentication and authorization are two separate questions, and they always happen in that order.

Authentication answers "who are you?" It's proving identity, like logging in with single sign-on, or an API validating a token's signature, issuer, audience and expiry, and then knowing the user's identity and claims. Authorization answers "what are you allowed to do?" It's checking permissions, through roles, claims, policies, and resource-level checks, like "can this user see this specific study?"

In ASP.NET Core, they're two middleware: UseAuthentication runs first and sets HttpContext.User, then UseAuthorization evaluates the Authorize attributes and policies on the endpoint. The status codes reflect the difference too. 401 Unauthorized actually means not authenticated: no valid token. 403 Forbidden means authenticated, but not allowed.

In our clinical system, authorization is the harder and more important part. A user with a valid login and the right role still mustn't see data from a study they're not assigned to. So beyond roles, we have resource-based checks on every request that touches study data. Missing that kind of check is the number one API risk in the OWASP list. I can show how our study access policy works.

p2-46.q: A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a compact, signed token with three Base64URL parts: header (algorithm, key id), payload (claims such as sub, iss, aud, exp, roles) and signature. The API validates it by checking the signature with the issuer's public key (from JWKS), then issuer, audience, expiry and not-before, and only then trusts the claims.
i: Signed is not encrypted: anyone can read the payload, so never put secrets or PHI in it (JWE exists for encryption).
Reject alg "none" and enforce expected algorithms (RS256/ES256); never let the token choose a symmetric key.
Short lifetimes plus refresh tokens; revocation needs extra measures (our jti denylist).
Key rotation via kid and JWKS caching.
ASP.NET Core JwtBearer does all this; Part 10 shows the pipeline.
f: Access token vs ID token?
The access token is for APIs; the ID token tells the client app who logged in and must not be sent to APIs.
Where should a SPA store tokens?
In memory with a BFF or HttpOnly cookies, not localStorage.
p2-46.y: A JWT is a signed token with three parts: a header, a payload with claims like user id, roles and expiry, and a signature. It is only encoded, not encrypted, so no secrets go inside. The API validates the signature with the identity provider's public key, then checks the issuer, audience and expiry. If all are good, it trusts the claims without calling the server.
p2-46.k: jwt, json web token, claims, signature, token validation, bearer
x: A JWT, or JSON Web Token, is a compact, signed token that carries claims about a user. It has three parts, separated by dots, each base64url-encoded.

The header says which algorithm was used to sign it, like RS256, and which key. The payload contains the claims: sub for the user id, roles or scopes, iss for who issued it, aud for which API it's meant for, exp for when it expires, and so on. The signature is created by the identity provider with its private key, over the header and payload.

To validate it, the API checks the signature using the issuer's public key, usually downloaded from its JWKS endpoint, which proves the token wasn't tampered with and came from the trusted issuer. Then it checks the issuer and audience match what's expected, and that the token isn't expired or used before its not-before time, allowing small clock skew. Only then are the claims trusted.

Two important points. A JWT is signed, not encrypted, so anyone can read the payload; never put secrets or personal data in it. And because it's validated without a server call, it can't be revoked easily. That's why we keep access tokens short, [15 minutes], and added a denylist for logout. I can explain that fix.

p2-47.q: In the authorization code flow with PKCE, the app redirects the user to the identity provider with a code_challenge (a hash of a random code_verifier); the user logs in; the provider redirects back with a short-lived authorization code; the app exchanges the code plus the code_verifier at the token endpoint for tokens (ID token with OpenID Connect, access token, refresh token). PKCE proves the same app that started the flow is finishing it, so stolen codes are useless.
i: PKCE is recommended for all clients, including confidential ones (OAuth 2.1 makes it mandatory).
state parameter prevents CSRF; nonce protects the ID token from replay.
The implicit flow is deprecated; SPAs use code + PKCE or a backend-for-frontend.
Refresh token rotation detects token theft.
Machine-to-machine uses client credentials instead.
f: Why is the code exchanged on a back channel?
Tokens are not exposed in browser URLs or history.
What does the BFF pattern do?
A server-side component handles tokens and gives the SPA only a secure session cookie.
p2-47.y: The app redirects the user to the identity provider with a code challenge, which is a hash of a random secret. The user logs in there, and the provider redirects back with a short-lived authorization code. The app exchanges the code plus the original secret for tokens. PKCE makes sure a stolen code is useless. OpenID Connect adds an ID token that tells the app who the user is.
p2-47.k: oauth, openid connect, oidc, authorization code flow, pkce, sso
x: The authorization code flow with PKCE is the recommended way for apps to log users in with OpenID Connect and get tokens to call APIs.

First, the app creates a random secret called the code verifier, and sends a hashed version of it, the code challenge, when it redirects the user to the identity provider's login page. The user logs in there, through single sign-on, and the app never sees their password. The identity provider then redirects back to the app with a short-lived, one-time authorization code. The app exchanges that code at the token endpoint, sending the original code verifier. The provider checks that the verifier matches the challenge, which proves the same app that started the login is finishing it, so a stolen code is useless. It then returns tokens: an access token, which is the OAuth part, for calling APIs; an ID token, which is the OpenID Connect part, saying who the user is; and often a refresh token.
PKCE was originally for mobile and single-page apps that can't keep a client secret, but it's now recommended for all clients, and it replaces the old implicit flow.
Our web apps use this flow with Keycloak, our single sign-on identity provider, and our APIs validate the access tokens. I can explain how refresh tokens fit in.

p2-48.q: JWTs stay valid until expiry even after logout because the API validates them statelessly. In [2024] a security review found tokens in one IRT module still worked [60 minutes] after logout; I cut access-token lifetime to [15 minutes], revoked refresh tokens server-side, added a jti denylist in ElastiCache with TTL equal to the remaining lifetime checked in OnTokenValidated, cleared cookies and ended the IdP session. Old tokens were rejected immediately, at about [1 ms] per request.
i: Denylist only stores logged-out tokens, so it stays tiny and keeps APIs mostly stateless.
Fail closed if Redis is unavailable (401 and re-login), with alerting.
Also revoke on password change, role removal or account disable.
Tests: unit test for the event handler, Playwright test replaying an old token after logout expecting 401.
Alternatives: reference tokens with introspection, or server-side sessions; heavier for many services.
f: Why not just shorten tokens to 1 minute?
Constant refreshes add load and complexity; short tokens plus a denylist is a better balance.
What is the end-session endpoint?
The OpenID Connect logout endpoint that ends the SSO session at the identity provider.
w: I balance security with performance and choose the smallest safe change.
I prove a security fix with automated tests, not just manual retest.
p2-48.y: JWTs are checked without calling a server, so a token keeps working after logout until it expires. In [2024] a security review found tokens in one module still working [60 minutes] after logout. I reduced access tokens to [15 minutes], revoked refresh tokens on the server, and added a denylist of token ids in ElastiCache that is checked on every request, which costs about [1 millisecond]. Old tokens were rejected immediately.
p2-48.k: jwt logout, token revocation, denylist, jti, elasticache, story
x: Situation: In [2024], a security review found that in one of our IRT modules, a user's token still worked for up to [60 minutes] after they clicked logout. That's because JWTs are validated statelessly: the API checks the signature and expiry, but never asks a server whether the user has logged out. In a clinical system, a stolen or shared token staying valid after logout was not acceptable.
Task: I was asked to make logout effective immediately, without making every API call a heavy round trip to the identity provider.

Action: I did it in layers. First, I reduced the access token lifetime to [15 minutes], so any leaked token has a small window. Second, on logout, we revoke the refresh token on the server, clear the cookies, and end the identity provider session. Third, for the remaining minutes, I added a denylist. When a user logs out, the token's unique id, the jti claim, goes into ElastiCache Redis, with a time-to-live equal to the token's remaining lifetime, so the list stays tiny. In the JWT bearer OnTokenValidated event, every API checks that list. If Redis is unavailable, we fail closed. We also revoke on password change or role removal. I added a Playwright test that replays an old token after logout and expects a 401.
Result: Old tokens are now rejected immediately, the check adds only about [1 ms] per request, and the APIs stay essentially stateless. I can show the event handler.

p2-49.q: Browsers send all cookies for a domain on every request, and servers cap total header size (IIS/http.sys around 16 KB in our setup); SSO auth cookies holding many role and group claims are chunked into several cookies and can exceed it, giving 400 "request header too long" for users in many groups. I fixed it by moving the auth ticket server-side with ITicketStore (cookie holds only a key), loading study permissions per request with cached claims transformation, and narrowing cookie domain and path, so the cookie dropped from [about 13 KB to under 1 KB].
i: Diagnosis: the pattern (only users with many studies) pointed to claim volume; a test user with many groups reproduced it.
Why not raise limits: the next user with more groups fails again, and every request carries kilobytes of cookie.
ITicketStore backed by [Redis/ElastiCache] with sliding expiry matching the session.
Claims transformation (IClaimsTransformation) adds permissions per request from a cache.
Result: tickets stopped, no user-visible change, released through the regulated process.
f: What is cookie chunking?
ASP.NET Core splits a large auth cookie into several cookies (.AspNetCore.CookiesC1, C2...) to stay under per-cookie size limits.
How did you verify the fix?
Test users with many groups in validation, header size measurements, and no new tickets after release.
w: I look for the pattern behind "random" user problems before changing configuration.
I prefer fixing the root cause over raising a limit.
p2-49.y: Browsers send all cookies with every request, and servers limit header size, about [16 KB] in our setup. Our SSO cookie had many group and role claims, so users in many groups got a 400 "request header too long" error. I moved the auth ticket to the server side with ITicketStore, so the cookie only holds a key, and loaded study permissions per request with caching. The cookie went from about [13 KB to under 1 KB].
p2-49.k: sso cookie, request header too long, iticketstore, cookie size, story
x: Situation: Some users of our IRT system started getting a 400 error, "request header too long", and couldn't use the application at all. We had [about 30] support tickets, and the pattern was clear: it only affected users assigned to many studies.
Task: I picked up the investigation, with the goal of fixing it properly, not just for the current users.

Action: I reproduced it with a test user in many groups. Browsers send all cookies for a domain on every request, and servers cap the total header size, about [16 KB] in our setup. Our SSO authentication cookie stored every role and group claim, so for these users it was split into several chunked cookies totalling [about 13 KB], and with other cookies on the domain, it went over the limit. Raising the server limit would only postpone the problem, and every request would still carry kilobytes of cookie. So I moved the authentication ticket to the server side with ITicketStore, backed by [Redis], so the cookie only holds a small session key. Study permissions are now loaded per request through a cached claims transformation. I also narrowed the cookie domain and path. It went through our regulated release process.
Result: The cookie dropped from [about 13 KB to under 1 KB], the tickets stopped, and users noticed nothing except that it worked. I can explain ITicketStore in more detail.

p2-50.q: Reverse tabnabbing is when a page opened with target="_blank" uses window.opener to navigate the original tab, for example to a fake login page, while the user is looking at the new tab. The fix is rel="noopener noreferrer" on links and the noopener feature in window.open, plus Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy; modern browsers default to noopener for target="_blank", but explicit is safer.
i: noopener sets window.opener to null; noreferrer also hides the Referer header.
COOP: same-origin isolates your browsing context group from cross-origin popups.
ESLint react/jsx-no-target-blank prevents regressions in React code.
I fixed [about 40] links in IRT in [2024] and enabled the lint rule (full story in Part 6).
f: Why does it matter in a clinical app?
A phishing redirect of a logged-in study manager's tab could steal credentials.
Do modern browsers fix it?
Most default _blank links to noopener, but window.open and older browsers still need explicit protection.
p2-50.y: Reverse tabnabbing happens when a link opens a new tab with target blank, and the new page uses window.opener to change the original tab to a fake login page. The fix is adding rel noopener noreferrer to those links, which modern browsers also do by default now. I fixed this on about [40] links in our application after a security scan.
p2-50.k: reverse tabnabbing, noopener, noreferrer, target blank, security
x: Reverse tabnabbing is a phishing attack that abuses links opening in a new tab.

When a page opens a link with target equals blank, historically the new page got a reference back to the original page through window.opener. A malicious or compromised external site could then use window.opener.location to silently redirect the original tab, for example to a fake login page that looks exactly like ours. The user finishes reading the new tab, goes back to what they think is our app, sees "your session expired, please log in", and enters their credentials into the attacker's page.

The fix is to add rel equals noopener noreferrer to links with target blank. noopener removes the window.opener reference, and noreferrer also stops the referrer header from leaking our URL. For links opened in JavaScript, use window.open with the noopener feature. Modern browsers now treat target blank as noopener by default, but being explicit is still best practice, and security scanners flag it. A Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy header adds another layer.

I fixed this in IRT. A security scan flagged it, and I updated [about 40] external links, created a shared link component that sets rel by default, and added a lint rule so it can't come back. I can show the lint rule.

p2-51.q: For APIs the most important risks (OWASP API Security Top 10 2023) are broken object level authorization (accessing another study's data by changing an id), broken authentication, broken object property level authorization (over-posting, excessive data exposure), unrestricted resource consumption, broken function level authorization, SSRF, security misconfiguration and unsafe consumption of third-party APIs. I prevent them with per-object authorization checks, DTOs, rate limits, validation and hardened configuration.
i: BOLA: every query filtered by what the caller may access (resource-based authorization), never trusting ids from the client.
Input validation and parameterised queries for injection.
Limits: payload size, page size, rate limits, timeouts.
Security headers, HTTPS only, no stack traces, least-privilege service accounts.
Inventory and version APIs so old endpoints do not stay exposed.
f: What is BOLA in practice?
GET /api/studies/42/subjects works for a user who has no access to study 42 because the API only checked login.
How do you test for it?
Automated tests calling endpoints as a user without access, expecting 403 or 404.
p2-51.y: For APIs, the biggest one is broken object-level authorization, where a user changes an id and sees someone else's data, so I check access to each object, not just the endpoint. Then broken authentication, injection, excessive data exposure and missing rate limits. I prevent them with per-resource checks, parameterized queries, response DTOs instead of entities, rate limiting and security tests.
p2-51.k: owasp, api security, bola, idor, injection, authorization
x: For APIs, the OWASP API Security Top 10 is the most relevant list, and a few risks matter most in practice.

Broken access control is the number one risk, especially broken object-level authorization: a user changes an id in the URL and gets someone else's data. Prevention is checking authorization for every specific resource, not just at the endpoint level. In our clinical system, that means checking study assignment on every request. Next, broken authentication: weak token validation, long-lived tokens, or no logout. We validate tokens fully, keep them short, and have a denylist. Injection: prevented with parameterised queries through EF Core, and input validation. Excessive data exposure and mass assignment: prevented with DTOs for input and output. Lack of rate limiting: prevented with rate limiting middleware and gateway throttling. Security misconfiguration: verbose errors, open CORS, default settings, prevented with secure defaults and reviews. And vulnerable components: dependency scanning and SonarQube in the pipeline.
Plus logging and monitoring, so attacks are actually noticed, without logging sensitive data.
These are part of our code review checklist for every new endpoint, which catches most problems before they ship. I can go deeper into access control.

p2-52.q: XSS (cross-site scripting) injects malicious script into your pages so it runs in other users' browsers with their session; CSRF (cross-site request forgery) tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request to your site, using their cookies. XSS abuses the user's trust in the site; CSRF abuses the site's trust in the user's browser.
i: XSS defences: output encoding (React does it), sanitising HTML (DOMPurify), CSP, HttpOnly cookies.
CSRF defences: SameSite cookies (Lax default in modern browsers), anti-forgery tokens for cookie-authenticated forms, checking Origin headers.
Bearer tokens in Authorization headers are not sent automatically, so token APIs are not CSRF-prone, but tokens in JS are XSS-prone.
ASP.NET Core: [ValidateAntiForgeryToken] and AddAntiforgery for cookie-auth endpoints.
f: Can XSS bypass CSRF protection?
Yes; script running on your origin can read tokens and send requests.
What does SameSite=Lax allow?
Cookies on top-level GET navigations from other sites, but not on cross-site POSTs or iframes.
p2-52.y: XSS is when an attacker gets their script to run in our page, for example through unescaped user input, so it can steal data from the user's session. CSRF is when another site tricks the user's browser into sending a request to our site with their cookies. For XSS, I encode output and use a Content Security Policy. For CSRF, I use SameSite cookies and anti-forgery tokens.
p2-52.k: xss, csrf, cross-site scripting, cross-site request forgery, security
x: XSS and CSRF are both browser-based attacks, but they work in opposite directions.

XSS, cross-site scripting, is when an attacker manages to run their own JavaScript inside your site, usually by injecting it through user input that's displayed without proper encoding, like a comment or a name field. That script runs with your site's privileges, so it can read data on the page, steal tokens from localStorage, or act as the user. Prevention: encode output, which React does by default; sanitise any HTML you must render, with DOMPurify; use a Content Security Policy to block inline and unknown scripts; and keep session cookies HttpOnly, so scripts can't read them.

CSRF, cross-site request forgery, is when an attacker's website makes the user's browser send a request to your site, and the browser automatically includes the user's cookies, so the request looks legitimate. For example, a hidden form that submits a change. Prevention: SameSite cookies, which stop cookies being sent on cross-site requests, anti-forgery tokens in forms, which ASP.NET Core supports built in, and checking the Origin header.
APIs using bearer tokens in headers, not cookies, aren't vulnerable to CSRF, but they are to XSS if tokens sit in localStorage. I can explain how we store tokens.

p2-53.q: Secrets live in a managed store (AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store SecureString, Azure Key Vault, Azure DevOps secret variables), are loaded at runtime by the service's IAM role, never committed to Git or baked into images, rotated regularly, scoped per environment with least-privilege access, masked in logs, and audited.
i: Local development: user secrets or a local .env excluded from Git.
Rotation: Secrets Manager rotates RDS credentials automatically; apps re-read on failure.
Detection: secret scanning in CI (GitHub secret scanning, gitleaks) and pre-commit hooks.
Avoid environment variables for very sensitive values where possible (visible in process listings and task definitions); fetch at runtime.
In the MCP server each user's PAT comes from their environment, never from files in the repo.
f: What if a secret is committed?
Rotate it immediately, then remove it from history; assume it is compromised.
Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store?
Secrets Manager adds rotation and cross-account sharing at a cost; Parameter Store is cheaper for config and simple secrets.
p2-53.y: Secrets never go in code, config files in Git or logs. We store them in AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, encrypted with KMS, and services read them at runtime using their IAM role, so no keys are hard-coded. Access is limited to the services that need each secret, and we rotate them. Locally, developers use user secrets.
p2-53.k: secrets management, secrets manager, parameter store, kms, rotation, credentials
x: My rule for secrets is simple: they never appear in source code, configuration files in git, container images or logs.

Secrets live in a managed store. On AWS, that's Secrets Manager for credentials that should rotate, and Parameter Store SecureString for others, encrypted with KMS. In Azure, Key Vault, and in pipelines, secret variables. Services read them at runtime using their IAM role, so there are no keys to bootstrap the keys. Access follows least privilege: each service can read only its own secrets, per environment, and access is audited through CloudTrail. Secrets are rotated regularly. For RDS, Secrets Manager does it automatically, and apps re-read the secret if a connection fails. For local development, developers use .NET user secrets or a local file that's excluded from git.
Detection matters too: secret scanning in CI and pre-commit hooks, like gitleaks, so if someone accidentally commits a key, it's caught and rotated immediately. And logs mask sensitive values.

The same principle applies to tools I've built. In our CIRT MCP server, each user's Azure DevOps personal access token comes from their own environment, never from a file in the repository, and the server acts with that user's own permissions. I can explain how rotation works without downtime.

p2-54.q: The Model Context Protocol is an open standard (introduced by Anthropic in late 2024, now widely adopted) that lets AI applications connect to external tools and data in a uniform way. An MCP server exposes tools (actions), resources (readable data) and prompts over JSON-RPC 2.0; any MCP host such as Cursor, Claude, VS Code Copilot or ChatGPT can discover and call them, so one integration works with many AI clients.
i: Transports: stdio for local servers launched by the host, and Streamable HTTP for remote servers (it replaced the older HTTP+SSE transport).
Lifecycle: initialize handshake with capability negotiation, then tools/list and tools/call.
Tools have a name, description and JSON Schema input; results are content blocks, optionally structured output.
Remote servers use OAuth 2.1 based authorization in the spec.
Official SDKs exist for C#/.NET (ModelContextProtocol package), TypeScript, Python and more.
Analogy: "USB-C for AI tools": the host is the laptop, servers are peripherals.
f: MCP vs function calling?
Function calling is a model feature inside one app; MCP standardises how tools are packaged and discovered across apps.
Tools vs resources?
Tools perform actions with side effects; resources are data the host can read into context.
p2-54.y: MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard for connecting AI assistants to tools and data. An MCP server exposes tools with names, descriptions and input schemas, and any MCP client, like Cursor, Claude or VS Code, can discover and call them. So I build the integration once and it works in many AI tools. I built an MCP server with about 77 tools for our deployments.
p2-54.k: mcp, model context protocol, ai tools, agent, tools
x: The Model Context Protocol, MCP, is an open protocol that standardises how AI applications connect to external tools and data. A good way to think of it is like USB-C for AI: one standard connector instead of a custom integration for every pair of tools.

There are three roles. The host is the AI application, like Claude, Cursor or GitHub Copilot. Inside it, an MCP client connects to MCP servers. An MCP server exposes capabilities: tools, which are actions the model can call, like "queue a build"; resources, which are data the model can read; and prompts, which are reusable templates. The client discovers what the server offers, including each tool's name, description and input schema, and the model decides when to call a tool based on the user's request. Communication uses JSON-RPC, over stdio for local servers, or HTTP for remote ones.
The benefit is that you build an integration once, and it works with any MCP-compatible host. Before MCP, every AI tool needed its own plugin format.

I built the CIRT MCP server, with about 77 tools, which lets AI agents run builds, releases and multi-node deployments on our on-premise Azure DevOps Server. It cut deployments from 6 hours to 2, and from 6 people to 1. I can walk through its design.

p2-55.q: The CIRT MCP server lets AI agents run build, release and multi-node deployment operations on our on-prem Azure DevOps Server. About 77 tools are grouped by domain (builds, releases, approvals, multi-node deployments, artifacts, environment checks, logs), each with a precise name, description and typed schema, wrapping the Azure DevOps REST APIs with the caller's own permissions; it cut deployment time from 6 hours to 2 and people per deployment from 6 to 1.
i: Naming convention verb_noun by domain (queue_build, get_release_status, deploy_release_stage) so the model picks correctly.
Descriptions say when to use the tool and what it returns; parameters have enums and examples [for environments FV, TechOps, UAT, Prod].
Outputs are short structured summaries (status, failing step, link), not raw JSON dumps, to save context.
Long operations return an id and a status tool to poll, avoiding timeouts.
Composite tools [for "deploy to environment and verify versions on all nodes"] reduce many-step mistakes.
Built in [C# with the official MCP SDK over stdio], packaged so teammates install with one command.
f: Why so many tools instead of a few generic ones?
Specific tools with tight schemas are easier for the model to use correctly and easier to secure than one "run any API call" tool.
How did you test it?
Unit tests for each tool's validation and mapping, plus dry runs against non-production environments before UAT.
w: I spot a manual, error-prone process and automate it end to end.
I design tools for both the AI and the humans who must trust it.
p2-55.y: The CIRT MCP server lets AI agents run builds, releases and multi-node deployments on our on-premise Azure DevOps Server. The about 77 tools are grouped by area, like builds, releases, deployments and diagnostics, and each has a clear name, description and typed inputs. It calls the Azure DevOps APIs with the user's own permissions. It cut deployment time from 6 hours to 2, and people needed from 6 to 1.
p2-55.k: mcp server, cirt mcp, 77 tools, azure devops, deployment automation
x: The CIRT MCP server lets AI agents run build, release and multi-node deployment operations on our on-premise Azure DevOps Server. I designed it around one idea: the model should always be able to pick the right tool and use it correctly.

The about 77 tools are grouped by domain: [roughly 15] for builds, [20] for releases and approvals, [25] for multi-node deployments, and [17] for information, like logs, artifacts and environment checks. Names follow a verb-noun convention, like queue_build, get_release_status and deploy_release_stage, so the model chooses correctly. Each description says when to use the tool and what it returns, and parameters are typed with enums and examples, like the environment names [FV, TechOps, UAT and Prod]. Outputs are short, structured summaries, like status, failing step and a link, not raw JSON dumps, to save the model's context. Long operations return an id, and a separate status tool polls, so nothing blocks for hours. A few composite tools, like deploying to an environment and verifying versions on all nodes, reduce multi-step mistakes.
It's built in C# on .NET 8 with the official MCP SDK, runs locally over stdio, and calls Azure DevOps with each user's own permissions.
The result: deployments went from 6 hours to 2, and from 6 people to 1. I can explain the safety design.

p2-56.q: I make it safe through least privilege (each user's own Azure DevOps credentials, no shared admin token), separating read-only from write tools, requiring explicit confirmation and keeping human approval gates for production, validating every input against schemas and allow-lists, adding timeouts and idempotency, logging every tool call, and never returning secrets.
i: Prompt injection risk: logs or work items can contain text that tries to instruct the agent, so tools treat outputs as data and sensitive actions always need confirmation.
Allow-lists for environments, pipelines and nodes; reject anything else.
Dry-run modes show what would happen first.
Rate limits and concurrency limits avoid accidental floods (one deployment per environment at a time).
Audit log: who, which tool, which parameters, result, timestamp; supports GxP traceability.
MCP hosts also ask the user to approve tool calls; we do not rely on that alone.
f: What is the confused deputy problem here?
A server with broad rights doing things on behalf of a user who should not have them; using the caller's own token avoids it.
Could the agent deploy to production by mistake?
No; production stages still require Azure DevOps approvals by authorised people.
p2-56.y: I made it safe in layers. It uses each user's own Azure DevOps token, so the agent can't do more than that person can. Most tools are read-only, write actions need confirmation, and environment names are checked against an allow-list. Approvals for controlled environments stay with humans in Azure DevOps. Every tool call is logged, and secrets never appear in outputs.
p2-56.k: mcp security, permissions, approvals, allow-list, audit log, safety
x: An MCP server lets an AI model take real actions, so safety has to be designed in, not added later. I think about it in a few layers.

First, identity and least privilege. The server acts with the calling user's own credentials and permissions, never a shared admin token. So the AI can never do more than that user could do manually. Second, separating risk. Read-only tools, like getting status or logs, are separate from write tools, like queuing a build or deploying. Destructive or production-affecting actions require explicit confirmation, and our existing human approval gates in Azure DevOps stay in place. The AI doesn't bypass the GxP process. Third, input validation. Every input is validated against a schema, with allow-lists for things like environment names, so a model can't pass something unexpected. Fourth, auditability. Every tool call is logged with who, what, parameters and result. Fifth, protection against prompt injection. Content returned from tools, like logs, is treated as data, not instructions, and tools never execute arbitrary commands.
And clear errors, so the model reports a failure instead of guessing.
In our CIRT MCP server, these choices were what made teammates comfortable using it on real UAT deployments. I can explain how we rolled it out safely.

p2-57.q: A good tool definition has a clear, unique, action-oriented name; a description saying what it does, when to use it (and when not), and what it returns; a small, strongly typed input schema with enums, defaults and examples; concise, structured output with actionable error messages; and predictable, safe behaviour (idempotent where possible).
i: Fewer, well-scoped tools beat many overlapping ones; overlapping tools confuse models.
Errors should tell the agent what to do next ("Release 123 is waiting for approval by QA").
Keep outputs small: summaries and ids, with separate tools for details.
Annotations like readOnlyHint and destructiveHint in MCP help hosts decide on confirmation.
Test with real prompts and watch which tool the model chooses.
f: What is the most common mistake?
Vague descriptions and huge raw outputs that waste context and lead to wrong tool choices.
How do you version tools?
Add new tools or optional parameters rather than changing behaviour of existing ones.
p2-57.y: A good tool has a clear name and a description that says what it does and when to use it, because that is what the model reads to choose. The inputs should be few, typed and validated, with allowed values listed. The output should be short and structured, with next steps. Errors should explain how to fix the problem. Small focused tools work better than one tool that does everything.
p2-57.k: tool definition, mcp, agent tools, function calling, tool design
x: A good tool definition makes it easy for the model to choose the right tool and call it correctly the first time. It's really API design, but the consumer is an AI model.

The name should be specific and verb-first, like queue_build or get_release_status, not something vague like "build" or "helper". The description is the most important part: it should say what the tool does, when to use it, and when not to, what it returns, and maybe a short example. The model reads it to decide. The input schema should be small and typed, with enums for fixed choices, like environment names, sensible defaults, and only truly required fields marked as required. Fewer, clearer parameters mean fewer mistakes. The output should be compact and structured, like a status, the key fields and a link, instead of huge raw responses that waste the model's context. And errors should be clear and actionable, like "environment UAT2 doesn't exist; valid values are FV, TechOps, UAT, Prod", so the model can correct itself.
Also, avoid overlapping tools that do almost the same thing, because the model will pick the wrong one.
These rules came directly from building our CIRT MCP server with about 77 tools. I can share examples of descriptions that improved tool selection.

p2-58.q: I use Copilot inline completions for boilerplate, mappings and tests, and Cursor chat and agent mode for explaining unfamiliar code, multi-file refactors, upgrade chores and drafting SQL, YAML and scripts, guided by project rules for our conventions. I always review, build and test the output, because I own every line I commit.
i: Cursor rules files hold our coding standards and architecture notes so suggestions match the codebase.
MCP servers (including ours) let the agent check builds and deployments from the editor.
Good uses: test generation, regex and LINQ drafts, log summarisation, migration scaffolding, PR descriptions.
Avoid pasting secrets or patient data; use company-approved tools and settings.
Example: the [.NET 10 upgrade] used agent mode for repetitive package and API changes, reviewed file by file.
f: Has AI ever produced wrong code for you?
Yes, for example plausible but non-existent APIs or missing null checks; tests and review caught them.
Does it make you less skilled?
No, I use it for speed on known work and still reason through design and correctness myself.
p2-58.y: I use Copilot completions for boilerplate, mappings and test cases. I use Cursor chat and agent mode to explain unfamiliar code, do multi-file refactors and upgrade chores, and draft SQL, YAML and scripts, with project rules so it follows our conventions. But I always review, build and test the output, because I own every line I commit.
p2-58.k: github copilot, cursor, ai coding, developer productivity
x: I use GitHub Copilot and Cursor every day as a productivity tool, but I treat their output like code from a new teammate: useful, but always reviewed.

Inline completions handle repetitive code very well: DTO mappings, boilerplate, simple tests and LINQ queries. Chat helps me understand unfamiliar code quickly, like an older module or a library I haven't used before. In Cursor, agent mode is great for multi-file changes, refactors and upgrade chores, like updating packages or replacing an API across a solution. We use project rules, so it follows our conventions, like our logging and error handling patterns. And through a RAG service I built in Python, exposed as MCP tools, Copilot and Cursor pull our existing code and coding standards as context, so implementations fit the project and hallucinate less. I also use it to generate unit tests and test data, to draft SQL and pipeline YAML, and to write documentation and pull request descriptions.

What I don't do is accept large changes without reading them, or let it touch security-sensitive code without careful review. Everything still goes through compilation, tests, SonarQube and code review.

The biggest impact for me was in building the CIRT MCP server, where the AI tools sped up writing the tool wrappers, and the server itself now lets those same tools run our deployments. I can explain how I review AI-generated code.

p2-59.q: I treat AI code like code from a new teammate: read every line, check it compiles and passes tests (and write tests for edge cases), verify APIs and packages exist and are current, run static analysis and security scans (SonarQube, dependency checks), and look for the common AI mistakes: injection, missing authorization, hardcoded secrets, swallowed exceptions and outdated patterns.
i: Hallucinated packages are a supply-chain risk ("slopsquatting"); confirm every new dependency.
Check licences of suggested code and packages.
Compare with official documentation for version-specific behaviour (.NET 8 vs 10).
Same pull request review and quality gates as all code; no special path for AI code.
f: How do you check accuracy for business logic?
Against requirements and with tests built from real scenarios, not just the AI's own tests.
Who is responsible for AI-written bugs?
The developer who committed it.
p2-59.y: I treat AI code like code from a new team member: I read every line. I check it builds and passes tests, verify any APIs or packages it uses really exist, and look for security problems like string-built SQL, missing authorization or secrets. Our pipeline runs SonarQube and dependency scans on it like any other code. If I can't explain it, I don't commit it.
p2-59.k: ai generated code, code review, security, hallucination, sonarqube
x: I review AI-generated code with the same standards as any pull request, and in some areas, more strictly, because it can look very confident while being wrong.

For accuracy, I read the logic carefully: edge cases, null handling, error handling, and async correctness, like missing awaits or blocking calls. I check that it actually does what I asked, not something similar. I check APIs and packages against official documentation, because models sometimes invent methods, use outdated APIs, or suggest packages that don't exist, which can even be a supply-chain risk if someone registers that name. For security, I look for injection risks, missing authorization checks, hard-coded secrets, unsafe deserialisation, and sensitive data in logs.

Then I verify, not trust. It must compile without warnings, pass unit tests, which I often write or review myself, pass SonarQube and security scans, and actually run. For important logic, I ask for or write tests for the edge cases first.

And the final rule: I only commit code I understand well enough to explain in a code review, and maintain later. If I can't explain it, it doesn't go in. I can give an example of a subtle bug I caught in generated code.

p2-60.q: I give clear context and a specific goal, constraints and the expected output format; provide examples (few-shot); break big tasks into steps and ask for a plan first; give the model the relevant code, docs or errors; ask it to state assumptions and to verify its own output; and iterate based on results.
i: Role and audience: "You are reviewing a .NET 10 API for security issues".
Structured outputs (JSON schema) for anything parsed by code.
Ground answers in provided documents; ask it to say "unknown" when unsure.
Project rule files and reusable prompt templates for the team (the MCP README has [10] example prompts).
For agents: clear stopping criteria and limits.
f: Chain-of-thought?
Asking the model to reason step by step improves complex answers; modern reasoning models do this internally.
Zero-shot vs few-shot?
Zero-shot gives only instructions; few-shot adds examples of input and desired output.
p2-60.y: I give clear context and a role, describe the exact task and the output format I want, and include examples when format matters. For complex work I ask it to plan first and go step by step. I give constraints, like use .NET 8 and our logging style. Then I iterate on the result instead of expecting perfection in one prompt.
p2-60.k: prompt engineering, prompts, few-shot, context, llm
x: Good prompting is mostly about giving the model the same context and clarity you'd give a new colleague.

First, context and goal: the role, the relevant code or files, the exact outcome I want, and constraints, like ".NET 10, use our existing logging pattern, don't add new packages". Vague prompts get generic answers. Second, examples: if I want a particular format or style, I show one or two examples of input and output, which is called few-shot prompting. Third, decomposition: for complex tasks, I ask for a plan first, review it, and then ask for the implementation step by step, instead of one huge request. Fourth, an explicit output format, like JSON with given fields, or "only the changed method". Fifth, iteration with real feedback: I paste the actual compiler error or failing test output back to the model, which is much more effective than saying "it doesn't work".
For tools and agents, the same ideas apply to system prompts and tool descriptions: be specific about when to do something and when not to.
When I introduced our MCP server to the team, I wrote [10] example prompts in the README, and good examples were one of the biggest factors in people succeeding on their first try. I can share a few.

p2-61.q: RAG retrieves relevant pieces of your own documents at question time and gives them to the LLM as context, so answers are grounded in current, private data without retraining. The pipeline: split documents into chunks, create embeddings, store them in a vector index; at query time embed the question, retrieve the most similar chunks (often hybrid with keyword search and re-ranking), and prompt the model to answer from them with citations.
i: Chunking size and overlap strongly affect quality.
Hybrid search (BM25 plus vectors) and a re-ranker improve relevance.
Access control must apply at retrieval so users only see documents they may see.
Evaluate with test questions: retrieval recall, answer faithfulness, citations.
Vector stores: Azure AI Search, OpenSearch, pgvector, Qdrant.
Example idea: [a RAG assistant over IRT SOPs and release runbooks].
f: RAG vs fine-tuning?
RAG adds knowledge that changes; fine-tuning changes behaviour or style; they can be combined.
Why do RAG systems still hallucinate?
Poor retrieval or the model ignoring context; fix retrieval and instruct it to answer only from sources.
p2-61.y: RAG means retrieval-augmented generation. Instead of relying only on what the model learned, we first search our own documents for the relevant parts, using embeddings and a vector search, and give those parts to the model with the question. So answers are based on current, private information, and can cite their sources. We built a [runbook assistant] this way.
p2-61.k: rag, retrieval augmented generation, embeddings, vector search, llm
x: RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, is a way to make a language model answer questions using your own, up-to-date documents, instead of relying only on what it learned during training.

It has two phases. Ingestion: you take your documents, like wikis, runbooks or specifications, split them into chunks, create an embedding for each chunk, which is a vector that represents its meaning, and store them in a vector index. Querying: when a user asks a question, you embed the question, search the index for the most similar chunks, often combined with keyword search, and put those chunks into the prompt with instructions like "answer using only this context and cite sources". The model then answers grounded in that content.

The benefits are that answers use current and private information, without retraining the model, and they can cite sources, so users can verify them, which reduces hallucinations. The quality depends heavily on retrieval: chunk size, good metadata, hybrid search, and re-ranking. And access control matters: users must only retrieve documents they're allowed to see.

In my work, I built a RAG service in Python that gives GitHub Copilot and Cursor the context of our codebase and coding standards, through MCP tools like search_codebase, so their code fits our project and hallucinations drop. I can explain how to evaluate retrieval quality.

p2-62.q: An agent is an LLM running in a loop: it plans, calls tools, observes the results and repeats until the goal is met. Agentic orchestration coordinates one or more agents (planner, executor, reviewer) with their tools, memory, step limits and permissions. AutoGen (Microsoft) provides multi-agent conversation patterns; Claude Code is a terminal coding agent that can use MCP servers; I apply these to engineering workflows such as deployments and code tasks.
i: Patterns: single agent with tools, planner-executor, supervisor with specialists, reviewer loops.
Guardrails: step and cost limits, allow-listed tools, human-in-the-loop for risky actions.
Observability: log every step and tool call for debugging and audit.
Microsoft Agent Framework (2025) brings together AutoGen and Semantic Kernel concepts for .NET and Python.
Our deployment agent flow: [plan the release, queue builds, deploy stage by stage, verify versions, report].
f: When not to use agents?
When a fixed script works reliably; agents add value when steps vary or need judgement.
Biggest risk?
Loops and unintended actions, controlled with limits, confirmations and least privilege.
p2-62.y: Agentic orchestration means an AI agent works toward a goal in a loop: it plans, calls tools, looks at the results and decides the next step, instead of just answering once. Claude Code and Cursor agents do this with coding tools, and AutoGen lets several agents work together. Our deployment agent does this with our MCP tools, with humans approving controlled steps.
p2-62.k: agentic ai, agents, orchestration, autogen, claude code, agent loop
x: An AI agent is a language model running in a loop: it plans what to do, calls a tool, observes the result, and decides the next step, repeating until the goal is reached. Agentic orchestration is how you coordinate that loop, or several agents, safely and reliably.

Orchestration covers a few things. Which agents exist and their roles, for example a planner that breaks down the task, an executor that calls tools, and a reviewer that checks the result. Which tools each agent can use. And the limits: a maximum number of steps, cost or time budgets, permissions, and points where a human must approve. AutoGen, from Microsoft, is a framework for building multi-agent conversations, where agents with different roles talk to each other to solve a task. Claude Code is an agentic coding tool that works in your repository and terminal: it reads files, runs commands, edits code and runs tests, in that same plan-act-observe loop.
The key engineering concerns are reliability and safety: clear tool definitions, good error messages so agents can recover, logging every step, and human approval for risky actions.
Our CIRT MCP server is the tool layer that agents like Claude and Cursor use for deployments, with approvals kept for production. I can explain how agents use it end to end.

p2-63.q: Azure OpenAI (now part of Azure AI Foundry) runs OpenAI models inside the company's Azure tenant with enterprise controls: Entra ID auth, private endpoints, regional data residency, content filtering, and data not used for training. Direct provider APIs may get new models first and are simpler for prototypes. For a regulated healthcare company the enterprise controls usually decide.
i: Compare: model availability and versions, quotas and rate limits, pricing (provisioned throughput vs pay-as-you-go), compliance certifications, network isolation.
Abstraction layers (Microsoft.Extensions.AI IChatClient) make it easy to switch providers in .NET.
Monitor cost, latency and token usage either way.
Patient data rules (HIPAA, GDPR) and company policy decide what can be sent.
f: What is provisioned throughput?
Reserved model capacity with predictable latency, billed per unit instead of per token.
Can you use Claude in Azure?
Azure AI Foundry hosts many models; AWS Bedrock offers Claude and others in AWS.
p2-63.y: Azure OpenAI runs the models inside our company's Azure tenant, with enterprise security, private networking, compliance and the promise that our data isn't used for training. Going to a provider directly can give the newest models sooner and sometimes more features. For company products with sensitive data, we use the enterprise route, like Azure OpenAI.
p2-63.k: azure openai, openai, llm provider, enterprise ai, data privacy
x: Both give you access to powerful language models, but Azure OpenAI wraps them in enterprise controls.

With Azure OpenAI, the models run inside the company's own Azure tenant. You get enterprise security and identity, with Microsoft Entra ID authentication and role-based access, private networking through private endpoints, so traffic doesn't cross the public internet, data residency in chosen regions for compliance, and contractual commitments that your prompts and data aren't used to train models. It also integrates with Azure monitoring, content filtering and governance. Using a model provider's API directly is simpler to start with, may get the newest models and features sooner, and is great for prototypes, but the security, compliance and data agreements depend on that provider's terms and need separate review.

For a regulated healthcare company, the enterprise controls usually decide it. Clinical and personal data must be protected, so private networking, data residency and clear data-use terms are often requirements, not preferences.

My approach would be to prototype quickly, but build production features on the enterprise-approved platform, and design the code behind an abstraction, so we can switch models without rewriting the application. I can explain how I'd keep sensitive data out of prompts.

p2-64.q: I ground the model in trusted data (RAG, tool calls for facts), give clear instructions with permission to say "I don't know", use structured outputs validated by code, keep temperature low for factual tasks, check outputs with rules or a second pass, show sources, keep humans approving important actions, and measure quality with evaluation sets over time.
i: Tools for anything factual or current: let the model call an API rather than remember.
Validate: JSON schema, business rules, allow-lists before acting.
Evals: golden question sets, regression checks when prompts or models change.
Narrow tasks are more reliable than open-ended ones.
Monitor production: feedback buttons, logs of prompts and outputs (without sensitive data).
f: Can hallucinations be eliminated?
No, only reduced and contained by validation and human review.
Example in your MCP server?
Build and release status always come from tool calls to Azure DevOps, never from the model's guess.
p2-64.y: I ground the model with retrieved facts, and tell it to answer only from that context and say I don't know otherwise. I ask for citations so answers can be checked, use structured outputs and validate them in code, and keep humans in the loop for important actions. I also run an evaluation set of real questions whenever the prompt or model changes.
p2-64.k: hallucinations, llm, grounding, evaluation, citations, guardrails
x: Hallucinations can't be eliminated completely, so I reduce them at every layer and design the feature so that mistakes are caught.

First, ground the model in facts. Use RAG to supply relevant documents, and tool calls to fetch real data, like a release status, instead of letting the model guess. Instruct it clearly to say "I don't know" when the context doesn't contain the answer, and to cite sources. Second, constrain the output. Use structured outputs or function calling with a schema, and validate the result in code, like checking that an environment name or id actually exists, before acting on it. Third, evaluate systematically. Keep a test set of realistic questions with expected answers, run it whenever the prompt or model changes, and review samples by hand. Log prompts and outputs, with sensitive data protected, to find failure patterns. Fourth, keep a human in the loop for high-impact actions, like production deployments, and show users the sources so they can verify.
Lower temperature and smaller, focused tasks also help.
In our CIRT MCP server, the model never invents a status. It always calls a tool for real data, and production steps still need human approval. I can explain how we test prompts.

p2-65.q: Teammates kept the manual, multi-person process out of habit and caution, so I made adoption easy and safe instead of mandatory: a [30-minute] live demo on a real UAT deployment, a README with [10] example prompts, pairing with the first [4] engineers, a chat thread for questions, and adding the tools people asked for. Within [about two months] most release deployments used it: 6 hours to 2, 6 people to 1.
i: Addressed fear directly: own permissions, confirmations before risky steps, existing approvals unchanged, everything logged.
Started with low-risk environments (FV, TechOps) before UAT and production.
Measured results to show value (time and people per deployment).
Feedback loop: the "fetch logs for a failed step" tool came from a teammate's request.
Champions: the first users helped others.
