Involve QA and TechOps earlier so their concerns shaped the design from day one.
How do you measure adoption?
Share of release deployments run through the tool and time per deployment.
w: I lead change by example and by removing friction, not by authority.
I take people's concerns seriously and design safety in.
p2-65.y: People kept the old manual process out of habit and caution, so I made adoption easy and safe instead of forcing it. I did a [30-minute] live demo on a real UAT deployment, wrote a README with [10] example prompts, paired with the first [4] engineers, and added the tools they asked for. Within [about two months] most release deployments used it: 6 hours down to 2, and 6 people down to 1.

x: Situation: After I built the CIRT MCP server in .NET 8, it could clearly save time, but teammates kept using the old manual, multi-person deployment process. It wasn't resistance to the idea. It was habit, and caution, because deployments to validated environments are serious in a GxP product.
Task: I wanted the team to adopt it because it genuinely helped, not because it was mandated.

Action: I started with their concerns. The server uses each person's own permissions, risky steps need confirmation, existing approval gates are unchanged, and every action is logged. Then I made it easy to try. I ran a [30-minute] live demo on a real UAT deployment, wrote a README with [10] example prompts, and paired with the first [4] engineers on their first real runs. We started in lower-risk environments, FV and TechOps, before UAT and production. I set up a chat thread for questions and added the tools people asked for. For example, the tool to fetch logs for a failed step came from a teammate's request. And I measured the results, comparing [8 deployments with it and 8 without], so the value was visible, not just my opinion.

Result: Within [about two months], most release deployments used it. Deployment time went from 6 hours to 2, and people needed from 6 to 1. The first users became champions who helped others. I can explain what I'd do differently.

p2-66.q: A monolith is one deployable unit: simple to build, test, deploy and debug, with in-process calls and one database. Microservices split the system into independently deployable services around business capabilities, each owning its data, enabling independent scaling and team autonomy at the cost of distributed-system complexity (network failures, eventual consistency, observability, many pipelines).
i: A modular monolith (clear modules, enforced boundaries) is often the best start.
Split when teams block each other, parts need different scaling or release cadence.
Microservices need automation, monitoring, tracing and contracts before they pay off.
Avoid the distributed monolith: services that must deploy together or share a database.
IRT has [about a dozen] services such as randomization, supply and shipments, notifications.
f: What is Conway's law?
Systems mirror the communication structure of the organisation that builds them.
How do you split a monolith?
Strangler fig: route one capability at a time to a new service.
p2-66.y: A monolith is one application deployed as a single unit, which is simpler to build, test and run, especially early on. Microservices split the system into small services that own their data and deploy independently, which helps big teams and scaling, but adds network failures, data consistency and operations work. I'd start with a well-structured modular monolith and split only where there's a clear need.
p2-66.k: monolith, microservices, architecture, modular monolith, comparison
x: The main difference is how the application is built and deployed: as one unit, or as many independent services.

A monolith is a single deployable application. All features share one codebase, one process and usually one database. It's simple to develop, test and debug, calls between parts are fast in-process calls, transactions are easy, and there's one thing to deploy and monitor. The downsides appear at scale: the codebase can become tangled, one team's change requires redeploying everything, you can only scale the whole application, and one bug can take everything down. Microservices split the application into independent services, each owning one business capability and its own data. Teams can deploy and scale their services independently, failures can be isolated, and each service can use the best technology. But you pay for that with network calls and their failures, distributed data and eventual consistency, and much more DevOps and observability work.
My view is that a well-structured modular monolith is often the right start, and microservices make sense when teams and parts of the system really need independence.
Our IRT platform is microservices, because many teams, [about 5] per release, work on clearly separate areas like randomisation, supply and shipments. I can explain how we keep it manageable.

p2-67.q: The core is POST /studies/{studyId}/subjects/{subjectId}/randomize with an idempotency key, allowed only for authorised site users. In one database transaction it loads the study's randomization scheme (blocked or stratified lists), allocates the next free slot with locking so two sites never get the same slot, assigns a drug kit from site inventory, writes an immutable audit record and stores a SubjectRandomized event in the outbox. Non-functionals: blinding, high availability, validation and full audit.
i: Concurrency: SELECT ... WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK) on the next slot, or a unique constraint on (StudyId, SlotNumber) with retry.
Stratification: separate lists per stratum (site, age group); dynamic methods like minimisation need careful algorithms.
Blinding: treatment arm hidden from most roles; only unblinded roles or emergency unblinding with reason and audit.
Idempotency key stored with the result so retries return the same allocation.
Downstream via outbox: resupply checks, notifications, EDC integration.
Availability: multi-AZ database, no single points of failure; randomization is the most critical path.
c:
SELECT TOP (1) SlotId, Arm FROM dbo.RandomizationSlots WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK, READPAST)
WHERE ListId = @ListId AND SubjectId IS NULL ORDER BY SlotNumber;
f: Why READPAST?
Concurrent requests skip slots locked by others instead of waiting, while order is preserved per list.
What if no kit is available at the site?
Fail the randomization cleanly or follow the study's rule, and trigger urgent resupply alerts.
p2-67.y: Randomization must be correct, consistent and always available, because a patient is waiting at the site. I'd build a service that takes a randomization request with an idempotency key, uses a pre-generated, blinded randomization list per study, and assigns the next slot in a strongly consistent transaction. Every assignment is audited, treatment arms are hidden by access control, and it runs in multiple availability zones.
p2-67.k: randomization, system design, clinical trial, irt, consistency, blinding
x: I'd design randomisation around one absolute rule: every subject must get exactly one correct assignment, and two sites can never get the same slot, because errors here affect the trial's validity and patient safety.

The API would be a POST to studies, subject id, randomise, callable only by authorised users at that subject's site, with an idempotency key, so a retry after a timeout returns the same result instead of randomising twice. A study here means one clinical trial set up in our IRT system, with its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and user roles. The service checks eligibility, then loads the study's randomisation scheme, which might be a pre-generated blocked list, or stratified by factors like age group or country. It allocates the next available slot for that stratum inside a database transaction, with locking, so concurrent requests from different sites can't take the same slot. In the same transaction, it records the assignment, writes a full audit record, and adds an outbox event. Then events trigger the rest asynchronously: kit assignment, supply checks and notifications.

Blinding is critical: the treatment arm is never returned to blinded users, and access to unblinded data is strictly separated and audited. Strong consistency matters more than availability here, so I'd choose SQL Server with proper transactions.
This reflects how IRT systems work, which is my domain. I can go deeper into stratification or emergency unblinding.

p2-68.q: I model shipments from depots to sites with kits, quantities and statuses (Requested, Shipped, In Transit, Delivered, Received, Quarantined); resupply rules (trigger and resupply levels per site, forecast from enrolment) create shipment requests; vendor and courier status updates arrive via SFTP files and APIs, are processed idempotently through events, and the site confirms receipt with temperature data; dashboards and alerts flag delays and low stock.
i: State machine with allowed transitions; reject invalid ones.
Integration: [SFTP poller every 5 minutes] for depot files, Kafka events for status updates to several services.
Expiry dating and temperature excursions: quarantine kits pending review.
Indexes for site and study shipment lists (the [9 s to under 300 ms] fix).
Audit every status change with source (vendor file, user).
f: How do you handle duplicate vendor status files?
File hash dedup and idempotent upserts by shipment id and timestamp.
What triggers resupply?
Site inventory dropping below the trigger level, considering kits in transit and expected enrolment.
p2-68.y: I'd have a supply service that tracks kit inventory at depots and sites and triggers resupply when stock is low. A shipment service creates shipments and sends them to depots and couriers through APIs or SFTP files. Vendors send back status updates, which we validate, deduplicate and process idempotently, then publish events to update stock and notify sites. Reconciliation reports catch any missed updates.
p2-68.k: drug supply, shipment tracking, system design, irt, inventory, vendors
x: I'd split this into a few services around clear responsibilities, connected by events.

An inventory service tracks stock at depots and sites, by kit type, lot and expiry date. A resupply service applies rules, like "when a site has fewer than five kits of a type, or kits are about to expire, create a shipment request", and it's triggered by events rather than polling. A shipment service owns the shipment lifecycle: requested, approved, dispatched, in transit, delivered, received, with every status change recorded. A vendor integration service exchanges data with depot vendors, which in practice is often SFTP files or partner APIs. The services communicate through events over RabbitMQ or Kafka, like KitAssigned, StockLow, ShipmentCreated and ShipmentDelivered, using the outbox pattern, and consumers are idempotent.

Key concerns: strong consistency when allocating scarce stock, cold-chain and temperature excursion handling, full audit trails for GxP, and reconciliation jobs that compare our data with vendor data. Dashboards show shipments stuck in a status too long.

This is close to what I work on. Our vendor exchange uses an ISftpClient abstraction over three libraries, and after our [mid-2024] RabbitMQ incident, publishing uses confirms, so status updates can't be lost silently. I can go deeper into the vendor integration.

p2-69.q: The client uploads the file to S3 with a presigned URL (or to the API for small files), the API creates an import job and returns 202 with a job id; a worker streams and parses rows (CsvHelper), validates schema and business rules collecting per-row errors, then writes valid data in batches inside a transaction (we chose all-or-nothing with the business), reports status and an error file, audits who imported what, and uses a file hash for idempotency.
i: Streaming parse keeps memory flat even for large files; our typical file is [5 MB, ~10,000 rows].
Bulk insert with SqlBulkCopy into a staging table, then validate and merge set-based.
Concurrency limit [2 per user] and a global worker limit protect the database.
Progress endpoint or SignalR for status; error report as CSV with row numbers.
Security: size limits, content checks, CSV injection protection in exported files (prefix =, +, -, @).
f: All-or-nothing vs partial?
All-or-nothing keeps clinical data consistent; partial suits independent rows, with clear reporting.
How do you scale to very large files?
Split into chunks processed in parallel into staging, then one final merge.
p2-69.y: The client uploads the file to S3 with a presigned URL, and the API creates an import job and returns 202 with a job id. A worker streams the rows, validates format and business rules, and collects errors per row. Valid data is written in batches inside a transaction, all or nothing. The user sees progress and an error report, every import is audited, and a file hash stops duplicate imports.
p2-69.k: csv import, bulk import, system design, s3, background job, 202
x: I'd design the CSV import as an asynchronous job, so large files don't block the API, and users get clear, complete feedback.

The upload goes to S3 through a presigned URL, or directly to the API for small files, with a size limit, like [5 MB, about 10,000 rows]. The API creates an import job and immediately returns 202 Accepted with a job id. A background worker picks up the job, streams the file row by row, so memory stays flat, and validates in two passes: the structure, like headers, types and required fields, and then business rules, like "this site exists and is active in this study". A study here means one clinical trial set up in our IRT system, with its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and user roles. It collects every error with its row number, instead of stopping at the first one. Then, depending on the requirement, it either rejects the whole file if anything fails, which is usually right for clinical data, or imports valid rows. Valid rows are written in batches inside transactions. The client polls a status endpoint, or gets a notification, and can download an error report.
Safeguards: a file hash to block importing the same file twice, a limit of [2] concurrent imports per user, and a full audit record.
This is basically the CSV bulk import I designed and mostly built for IRT. I can explain the decisions we made.

p2-70.q: The API gateway pattern puts one entry point in front of many services to handle routing, authentication, rate limiting, TLS and cross-cutting policies. Backend-for-frontend (BFF) gives each client type (web SPA, mobile, partner) its own tailored gateway that aggregates calls and shapes responses for that client, and for SPAs keeps tokens on the server.
i: Tools: AWS API Gateway, YARP (.NET reverse proxy), Azure API Management, Kong, Envoy.
Gateway should stay thin: no business logic, or it becomes a bottleneck.
BFF reduces chatty calls and over-fetching from mobile clients.
BFF security pattern: SPA uses an HttpOnly cookie session; BFF holds OAuth tokens and calls APIs.
c:
builder.Services.AddReverseProxy().LoadFromConfig(builder.Configuration.GetSection("ReverseProxy"));
app.MapReverseProxy();   // YARP routes /api/shipments/** to the shipments cluster
f: Gateway vs service mesh?
Gateway handles north-south (client to service) traffic; mesh handles east-west traffic between services.
One BFF per team or per client?
Per client experience, usually owned by the team building that client.
p2-70.y: An API gateway is a single entry point in front of many services. It handles routing, authentication, rate limiting and logging, so each service doesn't repeat that. Backend-for-frontend means a separate small gateway for each type of client, like web or mobile, shaped exactly for what that client needs, so the front end makes fewer calls.
p2-70.k: api gateway, backend for frontend, bff, microservices, routing
x: The API gateway pattern puts a single entry point in front of a set of microservices, so clients don't need to know about each individual service.

The gateway handles cross-cutting concerns in one place: routing requests to the right service, authentication and token validation, rate limiting and throttling, TLS termination, CORS, logging, and sometimes caching and request aggregation, where it combines several service calls into one response for the client. Backend-for-frontend, or BFF, takes that further: instead of one general gateway, each type of client gets its own thin backend. For example, the web app's BFF returns exactly what the web screens need, and the mobile BFF returns smaller payloads optimised for mobile. The front-end team often owns its BFF, so they can change it without affecting other clients. A BFF is also a good place to keep tokens server-side, instead of in the browser.
The important rule is to keep business logic out of the gateway. It should route and protect, not make business decisions, or it becomes a new monolith.

On AWS, that's API Gateway or an ALB. In the newer IQVIA services on AWS, the ALB routes to our services by path, and API Gateway provides per-partner throttling for external APIs. I can explain when a BFF is worth it.

p2-71.q: The CAP theorem says that during a network partition a distributed data store must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write) and availability (every request gets a non-error response); partition tolerance is unavoidable in real networks. So the real choice is CP or AP behaviour when partitions happen.
i: PACELC extends it: Else (no partition) you trade Latency vs Consistency.
CP examples: traditional relational with synchronous replication, ZooKeeper, etcd; AP examples: Cassandra, DynamoDB default eventually consistent reads.
Many systems are tunable (DynamoDB strongly consistent reads, Cassandra quorum).
In IRT, randomization and kit assignment need consistency (CP behaviour); dashboards and notifications tolerate eventual consistency.
f: Is CAP about all consistency models?
It uses linearizability; weaker models allow different trade-offs.
Why is "CA" not realistic?
Networks do partition, so a distributed system must decide what to do when they do.
p2-71.y: The CAP theorem says that when the network splits, a distributed system has to choose between consistency, meaning everyone sees the latest data, and availability, meaning every request gets an answer. You can't have both during a partition. So for things like randomization I choose consistency, and for things like notifications or reports I accept eventual consistency to stay available.
p2-71.k: cap theorem, consistency, availability, partition tolerance, distributed systems
x: The CAP theorem says that in a distributed system, when there's a network partition, meaning parts of the system can't talk to each other, you have to choose between consistency and availability. You can't fully have both.

Consistency means every read gets the most recent write, or an error. Availability means every request gets a response, even if it might be stale. Partition tolerance isn't really optional, because networks do fail. So the real choice is how the system behaves during a partition. A CP system refuses or delays some requests to stay correct. An AP system keeps answering, possibly with stale data, and reconciles later. When there's no partition, you can have both, and the trade-off becomes latency versus consistency, which is the PACELC extension.

The useful insight is that you choose per feature, not for the whole system. In clinical trials, allocating limited drug kits or a randomisation slot must be consistent, so it's CP: better to fail and retry than to promise the same kit to two sites. But dashboards, notifications and reports can be AP: slightly stale data is fine, and availability matters more.
That's exactly how our IRT platform is designed: transactional SQL for allocation, eventually consistent events for everything around it. I can explain how we handle the stale data in the UI.

p2-72.q: A saga manages a business transaction across several services as a sequence of local transactions, each publishing an event or message that triggers the next; if a step fails, compensating actions undo the earlier steps. It replaces distributed transactions (2PC) in microservices. Sagas are either choreographed (services react to events) or orchestrated (a central coordinator tells each service what to do).
i: Choreography: simple for few steps, but flow is hard to see; orchestration: explicit state, easier to monitor.
Compensations are semantic undos (cancel shipment), not database rollbacks, and must be idempotent.
Use outbox for reliable messaging and correlation ids per saga.
Tools: MassTransit state machines, NServiceBus sagas, AWS Step Functions, Temporal.
Example: [randomize subject, reserve kit, create shipment request, notify site]; if kit reservation fails, mark randomization pending and alert.
f: Saga vs 2PC?
2PC locks resources across systems and is fragile; sagas accept eventual consistency with compensation.
What about isolation?
Sagas lack it; use semantic locks (status Pending) and design for intermediate states.
p2-72.y: A saga handles a business process that spans several services, where one database transaction isn't possible. It is a sequence of local transactions, each publishing an event that triggers the next step. If a step fails, compensating actions undo the earlier steps, like cancelling a reservation. It can be choreographed through events, or orchestrated by one coordinator service.
p2-72.k: saga pattern, distributed transactions, compensation, orchestration, choreography
x: The saga pattern handles business transactions that span several microservices, where a single database transaction isn't possible.

The long transaction is split into a sequence of local transactions. Each service does its part in its own database, and then publishes an event or triggers the next step. If a step fails, the saga runs compensating actions to undo the earlier steps. For example: reserve kits, create a shipment, notify the vendor. If the vendor rejects the shipment, compensations cancel the shipment and release the reserved kits. Compensations are business actions, not database rollbacks, and they must be idempotent too.

There are two styles. Choreography: there's no central coordinator; each service listens for events and reacts, publishing its own events. It's simple for short flows, but the overall process becomes hard to see and change. Orchestration: a central orchestrator tells each service what to do next and tracks the state of the saga. It's easier to understand, monitor and change for complex flows, but the orchestrator is an extra component. AWS Step Functions or a durable workflow engine can play that role.
Sagas need the outbox for reliable events, idempotent consumers, and clear statuses so users see "pending" rather than inconsistent data. I can sketch the shipment saga.

p2-73.q: Every create, update and delete records who, what (old and new values), when (synchronised UTC time), where (source system, IP) and why (reason for change when required), in an append-only, tamper-evident store that users cannot edit or delete, captured automatically (EF Core SaveChanges interceptor, temporal tables or triggers) plus business events, searchable for inspections and retained as regulation requires (21 CFR Part 11, EU Annex 11).
i: Electronic signatures: re-authentication, meaning of signature, linked to the record.
Tamper evidence: hash chaining of records, WORM storage (S3 Object Lock) for archives, restricted database permissions.
Include correlation id so audit entries link to logs and traces.
Audit failures should block the change (same transaction), not silently skip.
SQL Server temporal tables give automatic history for row versions; combine with user context.
f: Audit log vs application log?
Audit logs are regulated business records with retention and integrity rules; application logs are for operations.
How do you show it is tamper-evident?
Hash chain verification and restricted permissions shown in validation evidence.
p2-73.y: In GxP, the audit trail must record who did what, when and why, with old and new values, for every change to regulated data. I'd write audit records in the same transaction as the change, make them append-only so nobody can edit or delete them, use server time in UTC, and record the reason for change. It must be easy to report on for auditors.
p2-73.k: audit trail, gxp, 21 cfr part 11, system design, compliance
x: In a GxP system, the audit trail is a regulatory requirement, under rules like FDA 21 CFR Part 11, so it must be complete, trustworthy and easy to review.

For every create, update and delete of regulated data, I'd record who did it, their user id and name; what changed, with the entity, old values and new values; when, with a synchronised UTC timestamp; where, like the source system or IP; and why, a reason for change where the process requires it. The audit store is append-only and tamper-evident: no user, not even admins through the application, can edit or delete audit records, and techniques like hash chaining or write-once storage can prove nothing was altered.

To capture changes consistently, I'd use an EF Core SaveChanges interceptor that inspects the change tracker and writes audit entries in the same transaction, so a change can't be saved without its audit. Business events, like "subject randomised", are audited explicitly too. Bulk operations that bypass the change tracker need their own auditing. The audit data is stored separately, with retention matching regulatory requirements, and there's a search UI for auditors.
Our correlation id is also stored in audit records, which links an audit entry to the exact request and logs. I can explain the interceptor design.

p2-74.q: I decide the key (user, client, IP, tenant), the limit and algorithm (token bucket for bursts, sliding window for smoothness, concurrency limit for expensive work), where to enforce (gateway for coarse limits, service for business limits), and shared state for multiple instances (Redis with atomic scripts). Rejected requests get 429 with Retry-After, and limits are monitored and tuned.
i: Algorithms: fixed window (simple, bursty at edges), sliding window, token bucket, leaky bucket.
Distributed: Redis INCR with expiry or Lua scripts; or accept per-instance approximate limits.
ASP.NET Core built-in limiter is per instance (Part 10 shows code).
Different tiers for different clients; exempt health checks and internal calls.
Example: [concurrency limit 2 per user on CSV import].
f: Fail open or closed if Redis is down?
Usually fail open for availability, with alerts, unless the limit protects something critical.
Why Retry-After?
Well-behaved clients back off correctly instead of hammering.
p2-74.y: I'd first decide the key, like per user, per API key or per IP, and the limit for each. Then pick an algorithm: token bucket allows short bursts, sliding window is smoother. For one server, ASP.NET Core's built-in rate limiter is enough. Across many servers I'd keep counters in Redis or use the API gateway. Rejected calls return 429 with a Retry-After header.
p2-74.k: rate limiting, system design, token bucket, sliding window, redis, 429
x: I'd design rate limiting by deciding what to protect, who to limit, and where to enforce it.

First, the algorithm. Fixed window is the simplest, like 100 requests per minute, but allows bursts at window edges. Sliding window smooths that out. Token bucket allows short bursts, while enforcing an average rate, which suits most APIs. And concurrency limits cap how many requests run at the same time, which is good for expensive operations. Second, the key: per user, per API key or client, per IP address for anonymous traffic, or per tenant. Third, where. At the edge, API Gateway throttling and WAF rate rules stop abuse before it reaches services. In the application, ASP.NET Core's rate limiting middleware applies finer, per-endpoint policies. With multiple instances, in-app limits are per instance, so for a true global limit, I'd use a shared store, like Redis, with atomic counters.
And the response: return 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header, and well-behaved clients back off. Monitor rejections, so limits are tuned rather than guessed.
In the newer IQVIA services on AWS, partners get per-key limits at API Gateway, and in CIRT, our CSV import has a concurrency limit of [2] imports per user. I can explain the token bucket in detail.

p2-76.q: High availability means removing single points of failure and recovering automatically: multiple instances across availability zones behind load balancers with health checks, Multi-AZ databases with automatic failover, stateless services, retries with backoff and circuit breakers, queues to absorb spikes, graceful degradation, and tested backups and disaster recovery with defined RTO and RPO.
i: Availability targets: 99.9 percent is about 8.8 hours downtime a year; 99.99 percent about 53 minutes.
Redundancy at every layer: DNS, load balancer, compute, data, messaging (quorum queues, Kafka replication).
Deployments without downtime: rolling or blue-green with readiness checks.
Bulkheads isolate failures; timeouts everywhere.
Test it: failover drills, chaos experiments, game days.
f: RTO vs RPO?
RTO is how long you can be down; RPO is how much data (time) you can lose.
Multi-AZ vs multi-region?
Multi-AZ covers data-centre failures; multi-region covers regional outages at much higher cost and complexity.
p2-76.y: High availability means removing single points of failure. I run at least two instances of every service across availability zones behind a load balancer with health checks, use a database with Multi-AZ failover, and keep services stateless. Then I add timeouts, retries and circuit breakers for dependencies, graceful degradation, and good monitoring. And I test failover, not just assume it works.
p2-76.k: high availability, multi-az, redundancy, failover, resilience
x: High availability means the system keeps working when individual components fail. The core idea is removing single points of failure at every layer.

For compute: run multiple instances of every service, spread across at least two availability zones, behind a load balancer that health-checks them and stops sending traffic to unhealthy ones. The orchestrator, like ECS, automatically replaces failed tasks. Services are stateless, so any instance can handle any request. For data: managed databases with Multi-AZ, where a synchronous standby takes over automatically if the primary fails, plus automated backups and point-in-time recovery. Caches and brokers are clustered too. For the application: timeouts, retries and circuit breakers between services, queues to absorb failures, and graceful degradation, so non-critical features can fail without taking down core ones. For deployments: rolling or blue-green, with health checks and automatic rollback, because many outages come from changes.
And then test it: failover drills, chaos experiments like killing instances, and monitoring with alerts, so you know availability is real, not assumed.

In [the newer IQVIA services on AWS], every service runs at least two tasks across two availability zones, and RDS SQL Server is Multi-AZ, because sites in many countries need the system around the clock. I can explain how failover affects connections.

x: Let me explain it with a simple picture. When a new medicine is tested, thousands of patients in hospitals around the world take part. Each patient is randomly given either the new medicine or a comparison treatment, and nobody, not the doctor and not the patient, should know which one. That's what keeps the trial fair.

IRT is the system that makes that random choice fairly and secretly. When a site enrols a patient, IRT decides the treatment group and tells the site which numbered drug kit to give, so the kit number hides what's inside. It also acts like an automatic stock manager: it watches the stock at every hospital, sends shipments from depots before they run out, and tracks those shipments. It also supports electronic consent, and it tracks every kit that patients return, which we call drug accountability. Each trial is set up in IRT as a study, by our internal study build team using our Admin console tooling, a desktop study designer and a newer web-based study builder: the hospitals, the treatment groups, the visit plan and the medicine kits.

Because mistakes here can affect patient safety and the trial results, it's a regulated, GxP system. Every change we make is tested, validated and approved, and every action is recorded in an audit trail.
So in one line: a fair, secret lottery plus a global pharmacy stock manager. I can explain the technical side too if that's useful.

That server is a legacy of CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, which IQVIA acquired: the CIRT application and its validated builds and releases stayed on-premise, while IQVIA's newer services run on AWS, where AI assistants like Copilot and Cursor couldn't reach. A typical deployment took about 6 hours and needed about 6 people on a call, following steps, checking each node and copying logs around. It was slow, expensive and error-prone.

What: I built the CIRT MCP server. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, lets AI tools like Cursor, Claude Code and Copilot call external tools. My server exposes about 77 typed tools for builds, releases, approvals and multi-node deployments, wrapping the Azure DevOps APIs and our install scripts. So an engineer can say "deploy release 4.2 to UAT and verify all nodes", and the agent runs the right steps.

How: it's written in C# on .NET 8 with the official MCP SDK, runs locally over stdio, and is packaged as a .NET global tool. Tools are grouped by domain with clear names and schemas, long operations return an id with a status tool to poll, and outputs are short structured summaries. For safety, it uses each user's own token, separates read and write tools, asks for confirmation on risky steps, keeps the existing approval gates, and logs every call.
Impact: measured on [8 vs 8] comparable deployments, time went from 6 hours to 2, and people from 6 to 1. I can go into any part.

x: Honestly, the hardest part wasn't the code. It was designing the tools so the AI reliably picked the right one out of about 77.

Early on, the model sometimes chose the wrong tool, or passed slightly wrong parameters, because some tools overlapped or had vague descriptions. I fixed that with a strict verb-noun naming convention, like queue_build and get_release_status, descriptions that say "use this when", enums for environment names instead of free text, and by removing overlapping tools. Outputs also mattered: returning raw JSON logs filled up the model's context, so I switched to short structured summaries with a link to the full details.

The second challenge was long-running deployments. A deployment can take an hour, and a tool call can't block that long. So start tools return an id, and status tools poll. The third was the on-premise Azure DevOps Server API. It differs from the cloud documentation in versions and authentication details, so I tested every call against our actual server. And throughout, I had to keep humans in control: read-only tools first, write tools with confirmation, and production only through existing approvals.
The lesson is that for AI tools, interface design matters more than implementation. I can show a before and after tool description.

p3-12.q: IRT exchanges data files with external vendors over SFTP. Integration tests against [a containerised OpenSSH server] in CI.

x: IRT exchanges data files with external vendors, like depot and logistics partners, over SFTP. Things like shipment requests, status updates and inventory files. I owned the component that handles those transfers.

Its key design is one abstraction over three libraries. The ISftpClient interface defines connect, upload, download, list and delete. Behind it, there are three providers: ComponentPro, SSH.NET and Rebex. A factory reads each vendor's configuration and returns the right provider, using keyed services in DI. So the calling code, like the vendor exchange service, never changes, whichever library is used. A base class holds the shared behaviour: retry with backoff for transient network errors, consistent logging with the vendor and file name, and mapping every library's exceptions into our own SftpTransferException, so callers handle errors the same way.

Each provider passes the same set of contract tests, for things like overwriting existing files, timeouts and error behaviour, so they're truly interchangeable. That's Liskov substitution in practice.

I added the Rebex provider and released it to production, moving vendors over one at a time by configuration. It's a good example of how a small abstraction made a risky change routine. I can explain why we needed three libraries.

p3-13.q: ComponentPro was the original library, but its updates had slowed and in [2024] a depot vendor disabled older algorithms like ssh-rsa with SHA-1, breaking our connection; SSH.NET was free but we wanted commercial support for a regulated product. I compared all three on modern algorithm support, support and patching, licence cost and behaviour against each vendor's test server, built a Rebex provider behind the existing interface, and we moved vendors to it one at a time by configuration.

Evaluation matrix made the decision objective and reviewable.
Keeping other providers as fallback reduced risk during migration.
Lesson: abstraction paid off; no caller code changed.

w: I make technical decisions with clear criteria and evidence.

x: Situation: ComponentPro was our original SFTP library, but its updates had slowed. In [2024], a depot vendor hardened their server and disabled older algorithms, like ssh-rsa with SHA-1. Our connection to them broke, and shipment files stopped flowing. SSH.NET, which we also supported, is free and good, but for a regulated product we wanted a library with commercial support and guaranteed patching.
Task: I was asked to restore the connection quickly, and choose a sustainable long-term option.

Action: I compared all three libraries in an evaluation matrix: support for modern algorithms, like rsa-sha2-256 and 512 host keys, curve25519 key exchange and AES-GCM ciphers; the vendor's support and patch history; licence cost; and, most importantly, actual behaviour against each vendor's test server. Rebex came out best. Because we already had the ISftpClient abstraction, I could build a Rebex provider behind the same interface, without changing any caller code. We kept the other providers as fallbacks, and moved vendors over one at a time, purely through configuration.

Result: The broken vendor connection was restored, and other vendors were migrated safely without a single code change in the business logic. The matrix also made the decision objective and easy for others to review. The lesson for me was that the abstraction paid for itself. I can explain how we released it safely.

p3-16.q: In [2024] a manual check caught a study transfer about to overwrite a target study that already had randomized subjects. I replaced the checklist with a backend guard that runs five checks before any transfer: target study status (block if live with subjects or dispensed kits), version compatibility, allowed direction, no transfer already in progress (lock), and user role plus a change request reference; each failure returns a clear reason and every attempt is audited.
i: Fail-closed: if any check can't be evaluated, block.
Lock with sp_getapplock or a unique "transfer in progress" row to prevent races.
Specific error codes help users fix the issue instead of raising tickets.
Released in [2025]; blocked [a handful of] unsafe attempts in its first months.

The UI can be bypassed; the API is the real boundary.

[Only with a documented emergency process and dual approval], audited.
w: I turn near-misses into system-enforced safeguards.

x: Situation: In [2024], a manual pre-check caught a study transfer, moving study configuration between environments, that was about to overwrite a target study that already had randomised subjects. A study here means one clinical trial set up in our IRT system, with its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and user roles. It was caught by a person following a checklist. If it hadn't been, it could have affected live trial data.
Task: I proposed and built a guard in the backend, so this kind of mistake becomes impossible, rather than relying on someone remembering a checklist.

Action: Before any transfer runs, the guard performs five checks. One, the target study's status: block if it's live with subjects or dispensed kits. Two, version compatibility between source and target. Three, the transfer direction is allowed, for example never from a lower environment into production data. Four, no other transfer is already in progress for that study, enforced with a database lock, so two transfers can't race. And five, the user has the right role and has supplied a change request reference. It fails closed: if any check can't be evaluated, the transfer is blocked. Each failure returns a specific reason, so users can fix it themselves, and every attempt, allowed or blocked, is audited.
Result: It was released in [2025], and in its first months it blocked [a handful of] unsafe attempts that would previously have depended on a manual check. I can explain the locking design.

p3-18.q: In [mid-2024] a RabbitMQ node hit its memory high watermark during a [large vendor shipment-status file], blocked publishers and dropped connections, and for [about 40 minutes] status updates silently never reached the shipment service. i: Root cause vs trigger: the file was the trigger; publishing without confirms was the root cause.

Blameless post-mortem shared with the team.
Code for confirms is in Part 2, Q40.
f: Why didn't anyone notice sooner?
There were no errors to alert on; we added a rate-drop alert.

No; randomization and dispensing were unaffected, only shipment status display was delayed.
w: I stay calm under pressure and restore service first.
I fix causes, not just symptoms, and share lessons.

x: Situation: In [mid-2024], one RabbitMQ node hit its memory high watermark while processing a [large vendor shipment-status file]. RabbitMQ blocked publishers and dropped connections. Because our services published without confirms, for [about 40 minutes] shipment status updates silently never reached the shipment service. There were no errors in our logs. Study teams noticed shipments stuck in the wrong status.
Task: I was on support duty, so I owned restoring the data and finding the root cause.

Action: I confirmed what happened using Splunk, Grafana and the RabbitMQ management UI: the memory alarm, blocked connections, and a gap in delivered messages. I drained the backlog, then replayed the missed window from the vendor files. That was safe because our consumers upsert, so reprocessing couldn't create duplicates. Then I separated the trigger from the root cause. The big file was the trigger, but publishing without confirms was the real problem. So I enabled publisher confirms with async tracking and retries, tuned memory, added consumer scaling on queue depth, and added alarms on memory, blocked connections, and the incoming rate dropping to zero during business hours. I shared a blameless post-mortem with the team.
Result: All [about 1,200] updates were recovered that evening. Confirms cost about [5 percent] throughput, and since then there's been no silent message loss. I can show the confirms code.

p3-19.y: In [2024] I delivered three security fixes. First, real logout with tokens: shorter access tokens, refresh token revocation and a denylist in ElastiCache. Second, the SSO "request header too long" error, by moving the auth ticket to the server so the cookie went from [about 13 KB to under 1 KB]. Third, reverse tabnabbing on [about 40] links. x: In [2024], I delivered three security fixes, each from a real finding, and each with a guard so it couldn't come back.

The first was token-based logout. A security review found that tokens in one module kept working for up to [60 minutes] after logout. I shortened access tokens to [15 minutes], revoked refresh tokens on the server at logout, and added a denylist of token ids in Redis, checked on every request in about [1 ms]. A Playwright test replays an old token and expects a 401. The second was the SSO "request header too long" error. Users in many studies had huge SSO cookies, over the server's header limit. I moved the authentication ticket to the server side with ITicketStore, so the cookie went from [about 13 KB to under 1 KB], and [about 30] support tickets stopped. The third was reverse tabnabbing. A scan flagged links opening new tabs without rel noopener. I fixed [about 40] links, created a shared link component with safe defaults, and added an ESLint rule.
These map to OWASP risks: broken authentication and session management, security misconfiguration, and client-side risks.

p3-23.q: I check scope and timing on dashboards (one endpoint or all, since when, release or traffic change), then latency by dependency, then traces and logs by correlation id to find the slow step, mitigate, fix the cause and add an alert. In [March 2025] the shipments API p95 jumped from [about 200 ms to about 3 s] with no release; Query Store showed a plan change after a statistics update (parameter sniffing). I forced the good plan to restore service, then fixed the query and index permanently.
i: Immediate mitigation: Query Store plan forcing or sp_recompile, then a durable fix (OPTION (RECOMPILE) or OPTIMIZE FOR, better index, or .NET-side query shape).
Check thread pool starvation (sync over async), connection pool exhaustion and GC as other causes.
Tools: Grafana, CloudWatch Logs Insights, X-Ray/OpenTelemetry traces, dotnet-counters.
Add a p95 latency alert per endpoint and a Query Store regression review.
f: What is parameter sniffing?
SQL Server compiles a plan for the first parameter values and reuses it, which can be bad for very different values.
How do you spot thread pool starvation?
dotnet-counters shows thread pool queue length growing and thread count climbing slowly.
w: I diagnose systematically from symptoms to cause instead of guessing.
p3-23.y: First I check the dashboards: is it one endpoint or all, since when, and was there a release or a traffic change. Then I look at which dependency is slow, using traces and logs by correlation id. In [March 2025], our shipments API p95 jumped from [about 200 milliseconds to about 3 seconds] with no release. Query Store showed a plan change after a statistics update. I forced the good plan to restore service, then fixed the query and index properly.
p3-23.k: slow api, performance issue, troubleshooting, parameter sniffing, story
x: When an API suddenly gets slow in production, I work in a fixed order: understand the scope, find the slow step, restore service, and then fix the root cause properly.

First, scope and timing. On the dashboards I check whether it's one endpoint or all of them, since when, and whether anything changed, like a release, a configuration change or a jump in traffic. Then I look at latency by dependency, database, downstream APIs and queues, and use traces and logs filtered by correlation id to find exactly which step got slow. I also rule out the usual .NET suspects: thread pool starvation from sync-over-async code, connection pool exhaustion, and garbage collection pressure.

A real example: in [March 2025], our shipments API p95 jumped from [about 200 milliseconds to about 3 seconds], with no release at all. The traces pointed to one SQL query. Query Store showed its execution plan had changed after a statistics update. It was parameter sniffing: the new plan was built for a small study and was terrible for big ones. To restore service quickly, I forced the previous good plan in Query Store. Then I fixed it permanently by improving the index and the query shape, so it no longer depended on a lucky plan.
Afterwards, I added a p95 latency alert per endpoint and a Query Store regression review to our routine, so the next time we'd know within minutes, not from users.

p3-24.q: An ECS worker grew [about 150 MB a day] and was OOM-killed every [about 3 days]. I took dotnet-gcdump snapshots hours apart, found a static ConcurrentDictionary caching study configuration per version with no eviction, replaced it with a size-limited IMemoryCache with a [30-minute] sliding expiry, and load tested overnight; memory now stays flat.
i: Tools: dotnet-counters (GC heap size, gen 2 count), dotnet-gcdump for managed heap diff, dotnet-dump for full analysis with SOS (gcroot to find what holds objects).
Common leaks: unbounded static caches, event handlers not unsubscribed, timers, captured closures, singletons holding scoped services, new HttpClient per call (socket exhaustion).
IMemoryCache with SizeLimit requires Size on every entry.
Alert on memory trend, not just the limit.
c:
services.AddMemoryCache(o => o.SizeLimit = 1_000);
cache.Set(key, config, new MemoryCacheEntryOptions { Size = 1, SlidingExpiration = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(30) });
f: Server GC vs workstation GC?
Server GC uses more memory per core for throughput; containers with limits may prefer DOTNET_GCHeapHardLimit or workstation/DATAS settings.
What is DATAS?
Dynamic adaptation to application sizes, on by default for Server GC since .NET 9, adjusting heap count to reduce memory.
w: I use the right diagnostic tools instead of guessing.
p3-24.y: One of our ECS workers grew [about 150 MB a day] and was killed every [three days] or so. I took memory snapshots with dotnet-gcdump a few hours apart and compared them. The cause was a static dictionary caching study configuration for every version, with nothing ever removed. I replaced it with IMemoryCache with a size limit and a [30-minute] sliding expiry, and load tested overnight. Memory has stayed flat since.
p3-24.k: memory leak, troubleshooting, gcdump, imemorycache, story
x: When memory keeps growing in a .NET service until it restarts, it's almost always something holding references to objects so the garbage collector can't free them. So I measure first, then find what's holding the memory.

I start with dotnet-counters to watch the GC heap size and gen 2 collections, to confirm it's managed memory growing steadily, not just a spike. Then I take two heap snapshots with dotnet-gcdump a few hours apart and compare them, to see which object types keep growing. If needed, dotnet-dump with the SOS gcroot command shows exactly what's keeping those objects alive. The usual suspects are unbounded static caches, event handlers that are never unsubscribed, timers, closures capturing large objects, singletons holding scoped services, and creating a new HttpClient per call.

I had exactly this case. One of our .NET worker services grew by [about 150 MB a day] and crashed with an out-of-memory error every [about 3 days]. The heap comparison showed a static ConcurrentDictionary caching study configuration per version, with no eviction at all, so it just kept growing. I replaced it with a size-limited IMemoryCache with a [30-minute] sliding expiry, and ran an overnight load test to prove it.
Memory now stays flat. I also added an alert on the memory trend, not just on hitting the limit, so slow leaks are caught early.

p3-25.q: Decide fast: if impact is high, roll back to the previous tagged release, then find the cause from logs and the change list and fix forward. After a [UAT] release, 5xx rose to [about 8 percent] because a new required setting was missing from UAT parameters; I rolled back in [15 minutes], added the setting, and switched the options to ValidateOnStart so missing config now fails at startup and stops the deployment instead of failing live requests.
i: Rollback first, investigate second, when users are affected.
ValidateDataAnnotations plus ValidateOnStart (IOptions validation) turns config errors into deploy-time failures.
Readiness checks stop traffic to an instance that fails to start.
Added a configuration item to the release checklist.
f: Why not fix forward immediately?
Rollback is faster and safer when the cause isn't yet certain.
How would canary deploys help?
A small share of traffic would show the errors before full rollout.
w: I reduce impact first, then make the failure impossible next time.
p3-25.y: I decide fast: if the impact is high, I roll back to the previous tagged release first, then find the cause and fix forward. Once, after a [UAT] release, errors went up to [about 8 percent] because a new required setting was missing in UAT. I rolled back in [15 minutes], added the setting, and made our options validate on startup. Now missing configuration fails the deployment instead of failing live requests.
p3-25.k: 500 errors, release issue, rollback, validateonstart, story
x: If 500 errors spike right after a release, my first priority is the users, not the investigation. So I decide quickly: if the impact is high, I roll back to the previous tagged release first, and investigate second. Because we build once and keep every release artifact, rolling back is fast and safe.

Then I find the cause, using the logs filtered for errors, the exception details, and the list of changes in that release, code, configuration and database scripts. Once I understand it, I fix forward with a proper change.

A real example: after a [UAT] release, 5xx errors rose to [about 8 percent]. The logs showed a null configuration value. The release had added a new required setting, but it had been missed in the UAT parameter store. I rolled back within [15 minutes], added the setting, and redeployed. But the more important fix was preventing it from happening again. I switched those options to use ValidateDataAnnotations with ValidateOnStart. Now if a required setting is missing, the service fails at startup, the readiness check fails, and the deployment stops, instead of the service starting happily and failing live requests.

I also added a configuration item to our release checklist, so every new setting is checked in each environment before deployment. That turned a runtime failure into a deploy-time failure, which is exactly where you want it.

p3-26.q: I trace one message by id through each hop: published, confirmed, queued, delivered, acked, processed. In [validation], kit-assignment notifications occasionally vanished; they were delivered, but the consumer used autoAck=true, so when processing hit a transient database timeout the message was already gone. I switched to manual ack after commit, added [3] retries with backoff and a DLQ with an alert.
i: Ack after the side effect commits, never before.
Prefetch (BasicQos) limits unacked messages per consumer.
DLQ alert and replay tool for poison or exhausted messages.
Idempotent handler because redelivery can now happen.
f: Why requeue false?
Requeue true can loop forever; dead-lettering to a retry queue with delay is controlled.
What does prefetch do?
Limits how many unacked messages the broker pushes to a consumer.
w: I follow evidence hop by hop rather than assuming where data is lost.
p3-26.y: I trace one message by its id through every step: published, confirmed, queued, delivered, acknowledged and processed. During [validation], some kit-assignment notifications were vanishing. They were delivered, but the consumer used auto-acknowledge, so when the database had a temporary timeout, the message was already gone. I switched to manual acknowledge after the commit, added [3] retries with backoff, and a dead-letter queue with an alert.
p3-26.k: missing messages, debugging, rabbitmq, ack, dead letter queue, story
x: When messages seem to go missing between two services, I trace one specific message, by its message id, through every hop: was it published, did the broker confirm it, did it land in the queue, was it delivered to the consumer, was it acknowledged, and was it actually processed. Somewhere in that chain, the evidence stops, and that's where the bug is.
I use the publisher's logs, the RabbitMQ management UI for queue and delivery rates, the consumer's logs by correlation id, and the dead-letter queue.

A real example: in our [validation] environment, kit-assignment notifications occasionally vanished. Tracing showed they were published and delivered to the consumer, but never processed. The consumer was using autoAck set to true. That means RabbitMQ deletes the message as soon as it's delivered. So when processing hit a transient database timeout, the message was already gone, and nothing retried it. I switched the consumer to manual acknowledgement, sending the ack only after the database transaction commits. I added [3] retries with exponential backoff, and then a dead-letter queue with an alert for messages that still fail. Because redelivery can now happen, I made sure the handler was idempotent.
The rule I took from it: acknowledge only after the side effect is safely committed, never before. Since that change, we haven't lost a notification.

p3-27.q: Stop the rollout so nodes don't drift, compare the failing node (logs, disk, permissions, service state, config), fix, rerun the idempotent step on that node and verify all nodes report the same version. A UAT deployment failed on node [3 of 5] because the disk was [98 percent] full from old releases and logs; I cleaned up (keeping the last [2] releases), reran, verified versions and added a prerequisite-check tool to the CIRT MCP server (disk space, service account, ports) that runs before every deployment.
i: Idempotent steps make reruns safe.
Log rotation and release retention added to the playbook.
Pre-checks shift failures left, before any node changes.
f: Why stop the rollout?
Mixed versions across nodes can break behaviour and complicate rollback.
How do you verify versions?
A version endpoint or file on each node, checked by a tool.
w: I fix the incident and then automate the check that would have caught it.
p3-27.y: First I stop the rollout so the nodes don't end up on different versions. Then I compare the failing node with the others: logs, disk, permissions, services and config. Once, a UAT deployment failed on node [3 of 5] because the disk was [98 percent] full of old releases and logs. I cleaned it up, reran the step on that node, verified all nodes had the same version, and added a pre-check tool to the MCP server that checks disk, accounts and ports before every deployment.
x: When a multi-node deployment fails on only one node, the first thing I do is stop the rollout, so the nodes don't drift onto different versions. Then I compare the failing node with a healthy one: the deployment logs, disk space, file permissions, the service account, the service state and configuration. Usually the difference jumps out.

Once I find it, I fix the node, rerun the deployment step for just that node, and then verify that every node reports the same version and passes health checks. Because our deployment steps are idempotent, rerunning them is safe.

A real example: a UAT deployment failed on node [3 of 5]. The logs showed a write failure, and checking the node, the disk was [98 percent] full, filled with old release folders and logs that were never cleaned up. I cleaned up, keeping the last [2] releases for rollback, reran the step, and verified all five nodes were on the same version.

Then I prevented it from recurring in two ways. I added log rotation and release retention to the deployment playbook. And I added a prerequisite check tool to our CIRT MCP server that runs before every deployment, checking disk space, the service account and required ports on every node. So now this kind of problem is caught before any node is changed, not halfway through a deployment.

p3-28.q: I capture deadlock graphs from the system_health Extended Events session, find the queries and resources, and fix access order, missing indexes and long transactions. After a release, kit assignment updated Inventory then Shipment while the resupply job did Shipment then Inventory, and a missing index on Inventory (SiteId, Status) caused scans; I aligned the order, added the index, shortened transactions and added retry for error 1205. Deadlocks fell from [about 20 a day] to [about one a week or fewer].
i: Deadlock = cycle of locks; SQL Server kills the cheapest victim (error 1205).
Fixes: consistent access order, covering indexes to reduce lock footprint, short transactions, RCSI to stop readers blocking writers.
EF Core EnableRetryOnFailure retries transient errors including deadlocks; needs execution strategy for user transactions.
c:
SELECT XEvent.query('(event/data/value/deadlock)[1]') AS DeadlockGraph
FROM (SELECT CAST(target_data AS XML) td FROM sys.dm_xe_session_targets t
      JOIN sys.dm_xe_sessions s ON s.address = t.event_session_address
      WHERE s.name = 'system_health' AND t.target_name = 'ring_buffer') d
CROSS APPLY td.nodes('RingBufferTarget/event[@name="xml_deadlock_report"]') AS x(XEvent);
f: Deadlock vs blocking?
Blocking waits until the lock is released; a deadlock is a cycle that never resolves without a victim.
What is RCSI?
Read Committed Snapshot Isolation: readers see the last committed version instead of waiting on writers.
w: I read the evidence (deadlock graphs) and fix design causes, not just add retries.
p3-28.y: I capture the deadlock graphs from SQL Server's system health session to see exactly which queries and tables are involved. After one release, kit assignment updated Inventory then Shipment, while the resupply job did it the other way round, and a missing index caused scans. I aligned the order, added the index, shortened the transactions and added a retry for deadlock errors. Deadlocks went from [about 20 a day] to [about one a week or fewer].
x: When deadlocks suddenly increase, I first get evidence of exactly which queries are involved. SQL Server captures deadlock graphs automatically in the system_health Extended Events session, and each graph shows the two transactions, the statements, and the resources each one held and wanted. A deadlock is just a cycle of locks, and SQL Server picks one victim and kills it with error 1205.

The usual fixes are: access tables in a consistent order, add indexes so queries lock fewer rows, keep transactions short, consider read committed snapshot so readers don't block writers, and retry the victim safely.

A real example: after one release, deadlocks jumped to [about 20 a day]. The graphs showed two code paths. Kit assignment updated the Inventory table and then Shipment, while the resupply job updated Shipment and then Inventory, the opposite order. On top of that, a missing index on Inventory by SiteId and Status meant the update scanned and locked far more rows than it needed. I aligned both paths to the same order, added the index, shortened the transactions by moving non-database work out of them, and enabled retry for deadlock errors through EF Core's retrying execution strategy.
Deadlocks fell from [about 20 a day] to [about one a week or fewer], and the retry handles those rare ones without users noticing.

i: Evidence first: our logs proved the upload, avoiding blame.
Idempotent naming makes re-sends safe.
Post-upload verification closes the loop.
Communication fix as important as the technical one.
f: What if the logs showed a failure?
Check credentials, host key changes and network, fix, re-send and alert.
How do vendors confirm receipt?
[Some send acknowledgement files, which we now monitor].
w: I solve the people-and-process part, not just the code.
p3-29.y: I check our job logs and the server: the file, size, path and permissions, then re-send safely and confirm with the vendor. [One Monday], a depot vendor said our order file hadn't arrived. Our logs showed a successful upload, but the vendor had moved their pickup folder and told a different team. I re-sent to the new path with the same name, then added a check that lists the remote folder after upload, alerts for failed transfers, and a [shared contact list] for vendor changes.
p3-29.k: sftp issue, vendor file, troubleshooting, story
x: When a vendor says they didn't receive a file, I start with evidence rather than assumptions. I check our job logs for that transfer, then verify on the SFTP server itself: the file name, size, path, timestamps and permissions. Then I re-send safely, and confirm with the vendor that it's arrived.

A real example: [one Monday], a depot vendor told us our order file hadn't arrived. Our logs clearly showed a successful upload, with the file name and size, so the transfer itself had worked. When I listed the remote server, the file was sitting in the old folder. It turned out the vendor had moved their pickup folder to [/inbound/irt], and they had announced it to a different team, so it never reached us. Having the logs meant we could resolve it quickly without any blame either way.

I re-sent the file to the new path with the same file name. That was safe, because the vendor deduplicates files by name, so there was no risk of processing an order twice. Then I fixed the gaps. I added a check after every upload that lists the remote folder to confirm the file is really there, alerts on failed transfers, and [a shared integration contact list] so vendor changes reach the right people.
The communication fix was just as important as the technical one, and we haven't had a missed file like that since.

p3-30.q: I run kubectl describe pod for events (image pull, OOMKilled, probe failures) and kubectl logs --previous for the crash, then check config, secrets, limits and probes. A new Node.js tooling service in [dev] crash-looped because warm-up took [about 40 seconds] while liveness started after [10 seconds] and killed it; I added a startupProbe allowing [60 seconds], made part of the warm-up lazy and updated the service template so all services get a startup probe.
i: CrashLoopBackOff = container keeps exiting; Kubernetes backs off restarts up to 5 minutes.
Exit code 137 = killed (often OOM); 1 = app error; check `lastState.terminated.reason`.
Ephemeral debug containers (kubectl debug) help with minimal images.
c:
startupProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /health/live, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 12      # up to 60 s to start
f: What does --previous show?
Logs of the last terminated container instance, where the crash happened.
ImagePullBackOff?
The image or tag is wrong or registry credentials are missing.
w: I fix the template so the whole team benefits.
p3-30.y: I run kubectl describe pod to see the events, like image pull errors, out of memory or probe failures, and kubectl logs with previous to see why it crashed. Then I check config, secrets, limits and probes. Once, a new Node service in [dev] kept crashing because it needed [about 40 seconds] to warm up, but the liveness probe killed it after [10]. I added a startup probe and updated our template so every service gets one.
p3-30.k: crashloopbackoff, kubernetes, pod crash, troubleshooting, story
x: CrashLoopBackOff means the container keeps starting and exiting, and Kubernetes waits longer and longer before each restart, up to five minutes. So I need to find out why it's exiting.

First, kubectl describe pod, which shows the events: image pull errors, OOMKilled, or failing probes. Then kubectl logs with the previous flag, which shows the logs from the crashed container, not the new one. The exit code helps too: 137 means it was killed, often out of memory, and 1 usually means the application itself failed, like missing configuration. Then I check the configuration, secrets, resource limits and probe settings.

A real example: a new Node.js tooling service in our [dev] cluster kept crash-looping, but the logs showed no error at all. The events showed liveness probe failures. The service needed [about 40 seconds] to warm up, loading data at startup, but the liveness probe started checking after [10 seconds]. So Kubernetes decided it was stuck and killed it, over and over, before it could ever finish starting.

I added a startup probe allowing [60 seconds], which pauses liveness checks until the app has started, and I made part of the warm-up lazy, so it starts faster anyway. Then I updated our service template so every new service gets a startup probe by default. The lesson is that a crash loop isn't always a crash; sometimes the platform is killing a healthy but slow app.

p3-31.q: I check whether timeouts happen always or on cold starts and find the slow call. A DynamoDB-stream Lambda for [shipment notifications] timed out at [30 s] as volume grew: an HttpClient was created per invocation and a slow downstream API had no timeout. I moved the client outside the handler, set a [5-second] timeout with retry, cut batch size from [100 to 25], enabled ReportBatchItemFailures so only failed records retry, and raised memory from [512 MB to 1 GB].
i: Partial batch responses avoid reprocessing whole batches and endless retries.
Bisect on error and maximum retry attempts plus an on-failure destination prevent stuck shards.
More memory also gives more CPU.
Long work belongs in queues or ECS, not one Lambda call.
f: Why is a per-invocation HttpClient bad?
Each creates new connections and TLS handshakes, slowing calls and exhausting sockets.
What happens on a stream batch failure without partial responses?
The whole batch is retried, blocking the shard until success or expiry.

p3-31.y: I first check whether it times out always or only on cold starts, and find the slow call. A Lambda for [shipment notifications] started timing out as volume grew. It created a new HttpClient on every run, and a slow downstream API had no timeout. I moved the client outside the handler, set a [5-second] timeout with retry, reduced the batch size, made only failed records retry, and gave it more memory. The timeouts stopped.
p3-31.k: lambda timeout, aws lambda, troubleshooting, story
x: When a Lambda function times out, I first check the pattern: does it time out on every call, only on cold starts, or only under load? Then I find the slow step, using logs, timings, and traces in X-Ray.

A real example: in one of IQVIA's newer AWS services, we had a Lambda triggered by a DynamoDB stream that sent [shipment notifications]. As volume grew, it started hitting its [30-second] timeout. I found two problems. First, it created a new HttpClient on every invocation, which is slow and wastes connections. Second, it called a downstream API that was sometimes slow, with no timeout at all, so one slow call used up the whole Lambda budget. And because it processed batches of [100] records, one failure meant retrying the entire batch.

The fixes: I moved the HttpClient outside the handler, so it's reused across invocations. I set a [5-second] timeout on the downstream call, with a retry. I reduced the batch size from [100 to 25]. I enabled ReportBatchItemFailures, so only the failed records are retried, not the whole batch. And I increased memory from [512 MB to 1 GB], which in Lambda also gives more CPU. I also made sure failed records eventually go to an on-failure destination, so the stream can never get stuck.
The timeouts stopped. And as a general rule, if work genuinely needs a long time, it belongs in a queue with a worker on ECS, not in a single Lambda call.

Moving the ticket to a server-side ITicketStore with cached per-request permissions shrank it to under 1 KB and stopped the tickets.

Other causes of random logout: clock skew on token validation, cookies scoped to the wrong domain, data protection keys not shared across instances.
Data protection keys must be persisted and shared (e.g. Redis or S3) when running several instances, or cookies fail to decrypt.
f: Why would logins fail after scaling out?
Each instance had its own data protection keys, so cookies from one couldn't be read by another.
How do you handle clock skew?
Sync clocks and allow a small ClockSkew in token validation (default 5 minutes).
w: I find patterns in messy support data.

Then I inspect the technical suspects: cookie sizes and header sizes, token expiry, clock skew between servers, cookie domain conflicts, and whether data protection keys are shared across instances, because if they aren't, a cookie created on one instance can't be read by another.

A real example: in [2024], we got [about 30] tickets in [two weeks] from users getting a 400 error after logging in through SSO. The pattern was that they were mostly study managers assigned to many studies. A test user with many groups reproduced it. Our authentication cookie stored every role and group claim, so for these users it was split into several chunked cookies totalling [about 13 KB]. Together with other cookies on the domain, that went over the server's [16 KB] header limit, and the server rejected the request.

Raising the limit would only postpone it. So I moved the authentication ticket to the server side with ITicketStore, backed by Redis, so the cookie only holds a small key, and loaded study permissions per request through a cached claims transformation. The cookie dropped to [under 1 KB], and the tickets stopped, with no visible change for users.

x: When a test passes on my machine but fails in CI, I assume an environment difference until proven otherwise. The usual suspects are culture and time zone, file paths and case sensitivity, the operating system, environment variables, test execution order and shared static state, and timing assumptions.

A real example: a date-formatting test passed on my Windows laptop but failed on our Linux build agent. The code formatted a date using the current culture implicitly. On my machine, the culture produced one format, and on the Linux agent, running with a different culture and invariant globalisation settings, it produced another. So the test was really testing my machine's settings, not the code.

I fixed the code to format with an explicit culture, set the culture explicitly in the test, and then verified it by running the tests inside the same .NET SDK container image the agent uses. That last step is very useful: reproducing CI locally usually finds the cause in minutes.

Other common causes I check: Linux paths are case-sensitive, so use Path.Combine and correct casing. xUnit runs test classes in parallel, so shared static state makes tests flaky. And code that calls DateTime.Now directly depends on time, so injecting TimeProvider makes it deterministic. The goal is tests that give the same result on every machine, every time.

p3-35.q: I read it critically, check APIs against docs, build, test and add tests, run scans, and never merge code I can't explain. A real example: while building our deployment tooling, Copilot suggested an HTTP retry policy. It looked clean and professional, but it retried every failure, on every request. One of those requests was the POST that creates a release in Azure DevOps. If that POST times out, it may actually have succeeded on the server, so retrying it could create duplicate releases. That's a subtle bug, and it would only appear under real network problems.

I changed the policy to retry only idempotent requests, like GETs, and only transient failures, like 408, 429 and 5xx responses, with exponential backoff. In .NET 8 the standard resilience handler even has an option to disable retries for unsafe HTTP methods. Then I added a unit test proving that POSTs are never retried, so the rule can't be lost later.
I shared the example with the team as a reminder for reviews. AI tools make me much faster, but responsibility for correctness and security stays with me.

Task: I took ownership of all three, with the goal of fixing each root cause and adding a guardrail so it stayed fixed.

Action: I prioritised by risk, so logout came first. I shortened access tokens to [15 minutes], revoked refresh tokens on the server at logout, and added a denylist of token ids in Redis that every API checks, which costs only about [1 ms] per request. For the header problem, the SSO cookie held every claim and was [about 13 KB], so I moved the authentication ticket to the server side with ITicketStore, and the cookie dropped to [under 1 KB]. For tabnabbing, I fixed [about 40] links with rel noopener noreferrer, built a shared link component with safe defaults, and added an ESLint rule. Each fix had tests, including a Playwright test that replays an old token after logout and expects a 401, and each went through code review, the SonarQube quality gate and our regulated release process.
Result: All three passed security retest with no regressions, and the SSO tickets stopped. What I took from it is that a fix isn't complete until there's a test or rule that stops it coming back.

x: Situation: In [2024], during a study transfer, which copies study configuration between environments, a person following a manual checklist noticed that the transfer was about to overwrite a target study that already had randomised subjects. A study here means one clinical trial set up in our IRT system, with its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and user roles. It was caught, but only because someone remembered to check. If it had gone through, it could have affected live trial data.
Task: I wanted to make that mistake impossible, so safety didn't depend on someone's memory.

Action: I proposed and built a guard in the backend that runs five checks before any transfer is allowed. First, the target study's status: it blocks the transfer if the study is live with subjects or dispensed kits. Second, version compatibility between source and target. Third, the transfer direction must be allowed. Fourth, no other transfer can be in progress for that study, enforced with a database lock so two transfers can't race. And fifth, the user must have the right role and provide a change request reference. It fails closed: if any check can't be evaluated, the transfer is blocked. Every failure returns a clear reason, so users know what to fix, and every attempt, allowed or blocked, is audited for GxP.

Result: It was released in [2025], and in its first months it blocked [a handful of] unsafe attempts. The lesson for me is to turn important checklists into code, so the system prevents the risk, rather than just hoping people catch it.

p3-50.q: In SAFe PI planning, teams plan the next program increment (several sprints), align objectives and map dependencies; refinement (grooming) clarifies stories, acceptance criteria and estimates; and each sprint has planning, daily stand-ups, a review/demo and a retrospective.
