x: Primary and foreign keys are the basic tools for identity and integrity in a relational database.

A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table. It can't be null, and there's only one per table, though it can span multiple columns. In SQL Server, the primary key creates a clustered index by default, so it often also defines the physical order of the data. A good primary key is small, stable and never changes, like an integer identity or a GUID. A foreign key is a column, or columns, in one table that refers to the primary key of another table. It enforces referential integrity: you can't create a shipment for a site that doesn't exist, and you can't delete a site that still has shipments, unless you've defined cascade rules, like cascade delete or set null.
In practice, I always index foreign key columns, because SQL Server doesn't do it automatically, and joins and deletes depend on them.
In a clinical system, foreign keys are a cheap but very strong guarantee of data integrity, so we never skip them for convenience. I can explain how to choose between integer and GUID keys.

p5-19.q: A unique constraint forbids duplicate values and is backed by a unique index. A table has one primary key but can have many unique keys; the PK can't be null, while a unique key in SQL Server allows one NULL (use a filtered unique index to allow many).
i: Unique constraints enforce business rules regardless of app bugs or races.
Composite unique keys (StudyId, KitNumber).
A unique constraint allows one NULL in SQL Server; use a filtered unique index (WHERE col IS NOT NULL) to allow many NULLs.
c: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX UX_Users_Email ON dbo.Users(Email) WHERE Email IS NOT NULL;
f: Why enforce uniqueness in the database too?
Concurrent requests can both pass an app check.
Can a FK reference a unique key?
Yes, not only primary keys.
p5-19.y: A unique constraint makes sure no two rows have the same value in a column or set of columns. Compared with a primary key, a table can have many unique keys but only one primary key, and a unique key allows a null in SQL Server. I use unique constraints for business rules, like no duplicate site numbers in a study.
p5-19.k: unique constraint, unique key, primary key, constraints
x: A unique constraint guarantees that no two rows have the same value in a column, or a combination of columns. SQL Server enforces it with a unique index behind the scenes.

A primary key is also unique, but there are differences. A table has only one primary key, but can have many unique constraints. A primary key can't contain nulls, while a unique constraint in SQL Server allows one null, or with a filtered unique index you can allow many. The primary key is the row's main identity, used by foreign keys, while unique constraints protect alternate keys, which are natural business identifiers. And by default, the primary key is clustered, while unique constraints are non-clustered.
A typical design is a surrogate primary key, like an integer Id, plus unique constraints on natural keys that must never duplicate.

In our IRT database, kits have an integer Id as the primary key, but KitNumber has a unique constraint, because two physical kits with the same number would be a serious problem in a trial. The database enforces it even if two requests race each other. I can explain how we surface that as a 409 in the API.

p5-20.q: A composite index covers several columns, such as (StudyId, Status, ShipmentDate). Column order matters: it supports seeks on the leading column(s), so put equality-filtered columns first and range or sort columns after. It can serve queries on StudyId alone or StudyId plus Status, but not Status alone.
i: Leftmost prefix rule.
INCLUDE columns make it covering without widening the key.
Our shipment fix used exactly (StudyId, Status, ShipmentDate) INCLUDE, cutting reads from [400,000 to 2,000].
Our shipment index (StudyId, Status, ShipmentDate) INCLUDE (...) served the main list query: equality columns first, the range/sort column last.
f: Why equality before range?
After a range column, later key columns can't be used for seeking.
Can SQL Server use a skip scan?
Not generally; it would scan instead.
p5-20.y: A composite index covers more than one column. The order of columns matters: SQL Server can seek on the first column, or the first and second, but not the second alone. I put equality filters first and range or sort columns last. Our shipment list used an index on StudyId, Status, then ShipmentDate, with display columns included.
p5-20.k: composite index, multi-column index, column order, sql server
x: A composite index is an index on more than one column, for example StudyId, Status and ShipmentDate together.

The order of columns matters a lot. The index is sorted by the first column, then by the second within that, and so on, like a phone book sorted by surname then first name. So it can support seeks on the leading columns: StudyId alone, or StudyId and Status, or all three. But it can't efficiently seek on Status alone, because Status isn't the leading column. That's called the leftmost prefix rule.

My rule for column order is: put equality columns first, the ones compared with equals, and range columns last, like dates with greater than or less than, because once you hit a range, the following columns can't be used for seeking. Then add INCLUDE columns for anything the query selects, to avoid key lookups.

Our shipment list index followed exactly that: StudyId and Status for equality, then ShipmentDate for the range, with the displayed columns included. That's what let the query seek directly to a study's pending shipments in a date range. I can show the execution plan difference.

p5-21.q: A filtered index is a non-clustered index with a WHERE clause (e.g. only Pending shipments): smaller, cheaper to maintain and faster for queries on a hot subset. The query predicate must match the filter, and parameterised queries may not use it unless the optimizer can prove the match.
i: Great for status columns where few rows are "active".
Filtered unique indexes allow uniqueness only among non-null or active rows.
Requires specific SET options (QUOTED_IDENTIFIER, ANSI_NULLS).
Parameterized queries may not use a filtered index if the plan can't prove the filter matches; use literals or OPTION(RECOMPILE) when needed.
f: Why might a parameterised query ignore it?
The plan must be valid for any parameter value, so it can't rely on the filter.
Fix?
Use a literal for the filtered value or OPTION (RECOMPILE).
p5-21.y: A filtered index only covers rows that match a condition, like only active shipments. It's smaller, faster to maintain, and great when most queries look at a small part of the table. A common use is a unique index that ignores nulls. The query needs to match the filter, otherwise SQL Server can't use it.
p5-21.k: filtered index, partial index, sql server
x: A filtered index is a non-clustered index with a WHERE clause, so it only contains a subset of the table's rows.

For example, an index on ShipmentDate, WHERE Status equals Pending. If only a small percentage of shipments are pending at any time, this index is much smaller than a full one. That means less storage, faster seeks, cheaper maintenance on writes, and more accurate statistics for that subset. It's ideal for queries that always target a "hot" subset of the data. Another classic use is a filtered unique index, like enforcing that a kit number is unique only where it's not null, or only among active records.

The catch is that the query's predicate has to match the filter, so SQL Server knows the index covers it. Parameterised queries can make that tricky, because the optimizer can't always prove a parameter matches the filter. It works best with literal values, like Status equals Pending in the query text.

In our IRT system, dashboards repeatedly query pending and in-transit shipments, which are a small fraction of all shipments. A filtered index on those statuses made those dashboard queries much faster. I can explain how to check whether the index is used.

p5-22.q: Indexes help because the B-tree lets SQL Server seek rows in logarithmic time instead of scanning, cover queries without lookups, and avoid sorts. They hurt when there are too many: every insert, update and delete must maintain them, they use storage and memory, and unused or duplicate indexes add cost without benefit.
i: Check sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats for unused indexes.
Key lookups on many rows can make a seek slower than a scan.
Fragmentation matters less on SSDs; statistics freshness matters more.
Monitor with sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats: indexes with many updates and no seeks are candidates to drop.
f: How many indexes are too many?
There's no fixed number; judge by write workload and usage stats.
What is a key lookup?
Fetching extra columns from the clustered index for each row found in a non-clustered index.
p5-22.y: An index is like a book's index: SQL Server finds rows directly instead of scanning the whole table, which makes reads much faster. But every insert, update and delete must also update the indexes, and they take storage. So too many or unused indexes slow down writes. I add indexes for the main queries and remove ones that are never used.
p5-22.k: indexes, performance, write overhead, sql server
x: Indexes improve performance by letting SQL Server find rows without reading the whole table.

An index is a B-tree, sorted by its key. Instead of scanning millions of rows, SQL Server navigates the tree in a few page reads, which is logarithmic, and seeks straight to the matching rows. A covering index, with included columns, can answer the whole query without touching the table. Indexes also help with sorting and joins, because data is already ordered.

But they have costs. Every insert, update and delete must also update every relevant index, so write-heavy tables slow down with too many indexes. They use disk and memory. Random keys can cause page splits and fragmentation. And indexes on low-selectivity columns, like a true or false flag, or indexes no query uses, are pure cost with no benefit.

So I add indexes based on real queries and execution plans, and periodically check the index usage DMVs to find unused or duplicate indexes to remove. When we added the covering index for our shipment list, we also tested the write impact in validation, because shipments are updated frequently. I can explain how to find missing index suggestions.

p5-23.q: An execution plan is the optimizer's recipe for a query: operators (seeks, scans, join types, sorts), estimated vs actual row counts and costs. I read the actual plan to find scans, key lookups, bad estimates, spills and implicit conversions, and use Query Store to see plan history and regressions.
i: Read right to left, top to bottom; thick arrows mean many rows.
Warnings: implicit conversion, missing index, tempdb spills.
Join types: nested loops (small inputs), hash (large unsorted), merge (sorted inputs).
Query Store can force a known good plan.
f: Estimated vs actual plan?
Estimated shows the plan without running; actual adds real row counts.
What does a big estimate vs actual gap mean?
Stale statistics or parameter sniffing; investigate cardinality.
p5-23.y: An execution plan shows how SQL Server will run, or actually ran, a query: which indexes it uses, the join types, and the estimated versus actual row counts. It's the main tool for tuning. I look for scans on large tables, key lookups, and big gaps between estimated and actual rows. That's how I found the problems in our slow shipment query.
p5-23.k: execution plan, query plan, sql server, tuning
x: An execution plan is the optimizer's recipe for running a query: which indexes to use, in what order to access tables, which join algorithms to use, and where to sort or aggregate.

SQL Server's optimizer creates the plan based on statistics about the data, and then caches it for reuse. The plan is a tree of operators, like index seeks and scans, key lookups, nested loops, hash and merge joins, and sorts. Each shows estimated rows and cost, and in the actual plan, the actual rows too. There are two versions: the estimated plan, which doesn't run the query, and the actual plan, which runs it and shows what really happened.

When I read a plan, I look for a few red flags: scans on large tables where I expected a seek, expensive key lookups, sorts or hash operations spilling to tempdb, and big differences between estimated and actual rows, which point to stale statistics or parameter sniffing. I use SSMS for single queries, and Query Store to see plans over time and spot regressions.
In our shipment list fix, the plan showed a clustered index scan and key lookups, and that directly told me what to fix. I can walk through that plan.

p5-24.q: A table scan reads every row of a heap; an index scan reads all or a large range of an index (clustered index scan reads the whole table); an index seek navigates the B-tree directly to matching rows. Seeks are best for selective queries; scans can be fine for large portions of data.
i: Non-SARGable predicates (functions on columns, leading wildcards, implicit conversions) force scans.
Range scans are seeks with a range predicate.
Key lookups after a nonclustered seek can dominate cost; covering indexes with INCLUDE remove them.
c:
-- Non-SARGable: WHERE YEAR(ShipmentDate) = 2025
-- SARGable:    WHERE ShipmentDate >= '2025-01-01' AND ShipmentDate < '2026-01-01'
f: Is a scan always bad?
No, reading most of a small table is cheaper by scan.
What is SARGable?
A predicate that can use an index seek (Search ARGument able).
p5-24.y: A table scan reads every row of a table with no clustered index. An index scan reads the whole index, which is still a lot. An index seek jumps directly to the matching rows using the index, which is what we want for selective queries. When I see a scan on a big table, I check for a missing index or a non-SARGable condition.
p5-24.k: table scan, index scan, index seek, sql server, performance
x: These are three ways SQL Server can read data, and they differ hugely in cost.

A table scan reads every row of a heap, which is a table without a clustered index. An index scan reads all, or a large range, of an index, either the clustered index, which is effectively the whole table, or a non-clustered one. Both scale with the size of the table, so they get slower as data grows. An index seek uses the B-tree structure to navigate directly to the matching rows, reading only a few pages to find them. That scales with the number of matching rows, not the table size.

Seeks aren't always better, though. If a query needs a large percentage of the table, a scan can genuinely be cheaper than thousands of seeks plus lookups, and the optimizer chooses that on purpose. The problem is an unexpected scan for a selective query, usually caused by a missing index, a non-SARGable predicate, or a data type mismatch.

In our slow shipment list, the plan showed a clustered index scan for a query that needed a few hundred rows. Fixing the predicate and adding the right index turned it into a seek, and reads dropped from [about 400,000 to 2,000]. I can explain how to spot that in a plan.

p5-25.q: A cardinality estimate is how many rows the optimizer expects at each plan step; statistics are histograms of column value distributions (up to 200 steps) used to make those estimates. Bad estimates from stale or missing statistics lead to bad plans, like nested loops over millions of rows.
i: Auto update statistics triggers after a threshold of changes (dynamic threshold since SQL Server 2016).
UPDATE STATISTICS ... WITH FULLSCAN for skewed data.
Table variables historically estimated 1 row (improved with deferred compilation in SQL 2019).
Auto-update statistics triggers after a percentage of changes; large tables may need manual UPDATE STATISTICS after bulk loads.
f: Why did a plan change overnight in your incident?
A statistics update caused recompilation with an unrepresentative parameter value.
What is the cardinality estimator version?
The model tied to compatibility level; changes can shift plans after upgrades.
p5-25.y: Cardinality is the number of rows SQL Server expects at each step of a query. Statistics are the data distribution information it uses to make that estimate. If statistics are outdated, the estimate is wrong, and SQL Server may choose a bad plan. So after big data loads, I make sure statistics are updated.
p5-25.k: cardinality, statistics, query optimizer, sql server
x: Cardinality is the number of rows the optimizer expects at each step of a query plan. Statistics are what it uses to make those estimates.

Statistics are objects that describe how values are distributed in a column or index, mainly through a histogram of up to 200 steps, plus density information. When the optimizer sees a filter like StudyId equals 42, it uses the histogram to estimate how many rows will match. That estimate drives every decision: which index to use, which join type, and how much memory to grant. If the estimate is badly wrong, the plan can be terrible, for example a nested loop over a million rows, or a sort that spills to tempdb.

Statistics go stale when data changes a lot, for example after a big data load. SQL Server updates them automatically after enough changes, but on large tables that threshold can be reached late. Then I update them manually, or schedule maintenance.

The symptom to look for is a big gap between estimated and actual rows in the actual plan. In our IRT system, after a large data import, [one query became slow until we updated statistics], which is why we now update stats after big imports. I can explain how this relates to parameter sniffing.

p5-26.q: UNION removes duplicates, which costs a sort or hash; UNION ALL keeps every row and is faster. Use UNION ALL unless you truly need de-duplication.
i: Column count and types must match; names come from the first query.
ORDER BY applies to the whole result, at the end.
UNION adds a sort or hash distinct, which costs CPU and memory on large sets.
Use UNION ALL by default when sets can't overlap or duplicates are fine.
f: When is UNION needed?
When overlapping sources may return the same row and duplicates are wrong.
UNION vs JOIN?
UNION stacks rows vertically; JOIN combines columns horizontally.
p5-26.y: Both combine the results of two queries. UNION removes duplicate rows, which needs extra sorting work. UNION ALL keeps all rows, including duplicates, so it's faster. I use UNION ALL by default, unless I actually need duplicates removed.
x: Both combine the results of two or more queries into one result set, with the same columns. The difference is how they treat duplicates.

UNION removes duplicate rows from the combined result. To do that, SQL Server has to compare all rows, which means an extra sort or hash operation, and that costs CPU and memory, and can spill to tempdb on large results. UNION ALL simply appends the results and keeps every row, including duplicates. It's faster, because there's no deduplication step, and it can stream results without waiting for all of them.

So my default is UNION ALL. I only use UNION when I actually need distinct rows, and the inputs can genuinely overlap. Very often the two queries can't produce the same row anyway, for example combining "shipments from depot A" with "shipments from depot B", and then UNION is just wasted work.

It's one of those small things I look for in code reviews of SQL, because people often write UNION out of habit. On a large reporting query, switching to UNION ALL removed an expensive sort from the plan. I can explain how to read that in the execution plan.

p5-27.q: EXISTS stops at the first match; IN compares against a list or subquery. Modern optimizers often produce the same semi-join plan for both, but NOT IN with NULLs in the subquery returns no rows, so I prefer NOT EXISTS for anti-joins.
i: Large IN lists from apps create plan cache bloat; use table-valued parameters or JSON (OPENJSON).
EF Core 8+ translates Contains on lists using OPENJSON parameters.
NOT IN with a NULL in the subquery returns no rows; NOT EXISTS behaves as expected, so prefer it.
c: SELECT s.* FROM Sites s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Shipments sh WHERE sh.SiteId = s.Id);
f: Why does NOT IN fail with NULL?
Comparison with NULL is unknown, so the whole predicate isn't true.
How did EF Core 8 change Contains?
It sends the list as a JSON parameter, keeping one cached plan.
p5-27.y: IN checks if a value is in a list or subquery, and EXISTS checks if a subquery returns any row. For most queries, SQL Server builds the same plan. The big difference is NOT IN: if the subquery contains a null, it returns nothing, which surprises people. So I use NOT EXISTS for that case.
p5-27.k: exists, in, not exists, not in, sql
x: EXISTS and IN both check whether a value has a match in another set, and modern SQL Server often produces the same plan for both. But there are differences worth knowing.

EXISTS checks whether a subquery returns any row, and stops at the first match, so it's naturally efficient for existence checks. It's also correlated, meaning it can compare several columns. IN compares a value against a list of values, or the result of a subquery. For a short fixed list, like status IN Pending and Shipped, IN is the clearest. For subqueries, the optimizer usually converts both into the same semi-join.

The important difference is with negation and NULLs. NOT IN returns no rows at all if the subquery returns even one NULL, because comparing with NULL is unknown. That's a classic, silent bug. NOT EXISTS doesn't have that problem. So I always prefer NOT EXISTS for "find rows with no match".

For example, "sites with no shipments" in our system is written with NOT EXISTS against the shipments table, which is correct and uses the foreign key index efficiently. In EF Core, a negated Any translates to exactly that. I can show an example of the NOT IN bug.

p5-28.q: A CTE is a named query for one statement: not materialised, readable, and supports recursion. A temp table (#t) is materialised in tempdb, can be indexed, has statistics and can be reused across statements in the session. Use CTEs for readability, temp tables for large intermediate results reused or needing indexes.
i: Table variables (@t) have limited statistics; good for small sets.
CTE referenced twice is evaluated twice.
Recursive CTEs for hierarchies (MAXRECURSION default 100).
Table variables have limited statistics (improved by deferred compilation in SQL Server 2019+); temp tables have full stats.
f: Is a CTE faster than a subquery?
No, it's the same; it's about readability.
Temp table vs table variable?
Temp tables have statistics and are better for larger data.
p5-28.y: A CTE is a named query that exists only for one statement, which makes complex queries readable, and it can be recursive. A temporary table is stored in tempdb, lasts for the session, can have indexes and statistics, and can be reused across several statements. For large intermediate results used more than once, I use a temp table.
p5-28.k: cte, temporary table, temp table, sql
x: Both hold an intermediate result inside a larger query, but they behave very differently.

A CTE, defined with WITH, is a named query that exists only for the single statement that follows it. It's not stored anywhere; the optimizer simply expands it into the main query, like a view. So it's mainly about readability, breaking a complex query into named steps. It's also the only way to write recursive queries, like walking a depot hierarchy. But if you reference a CTE twice, it may be computed twice. A temporary table, with a hash prefix, is actually materialised in tempdb. It can have indexes, it gets its own statistics, and it can be reused across several statements in the same session or procedure.

So my rule: CTE for readability and recursion in a single query. Temp table when the intermediate result is large, reused multiple times, or when the optimizer is making bad estimates on a complex query, because materialising it with real statistics often gives a much better plan.

In our IRT reporting, a heavy monthly report became much faster when I moved a large intermediate step from a CTE into an indexed temp table. Table variables are another option, for small sets. I can explain the difference.

p5-29.q: ROW_NUMBER gives a unique sequence even for ties; RANK gives ties the same rank and leaves gaps (1,1,3); DENSE_RANK gives ties the same rank without gaps (1,1,2). All need OVER (ORDER BY ...), optionally PARTITION BY.
i: Deterministic ROW_NUMBER needs a unique ORDER BY (add a tie-breaker).
NTILE splits into buckets; LAG/LEAD access neighbouring rows.
Use ROW_NUMBER for pagination and dedup; DENSE_RANK for "nth highest" when ties count once.
c:
SELECT SiteId, KitCount,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY KitCount DESC) rn,
  RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY KitCount DESC) rnk,
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY KitCount DESC) drnk
FROM SiteStock;
f: Which for nth-highest distinct value?
DENSE_RANK.
Can you filter on a window function in WHERE?
No, wrap it in a CTE or subquery first.
p5-29.y: All three number rows in order. ROW_NUMBER gives unique numbers, 1, 2, 3, even for ties. RANK gives ties the same number and then skips, like 1, 1, 3. DENSE_RANK gives ties the same number without gaps, like 1, 1, 2. I use ROW_NUMBER for paging and removing duplicates, and DENSE_RANK for nth highest.
p5-29.k: row_number, rank, dense_rank, window functions, sql
x: All three are window functions that number rows within a partition, based on an ORDER BY. The difference is how they handle ties, rows with the same ordering value.

ROW_NUMBER gives every row a unique sequential number, 1, 2, 3, 4, even if values tie. The order among tied rows is arbitrary, unless you add a tie-breaker column. RANK gives tied rows the same rank, and then leaves a gap. So if two rows tie for second place, you get 1, 2, 2, 4. DENSE_RANK also gives ties the same rank, but without gaps: 1, 2, 2, 3.

The use cases follow from that. ROW_NUMBER is for picking exactly one row per group, like the latest status per shipment, or for deduplication, or paging. RANK is for competition-style rankings, where gaps make sense. DENSE_RANK is for questions like "the top 3 distinct values", for example the sites with the three highest dispensing counts, including ties.
In our IRT database, I use ROW_NUMBER partitioned by shipment, ordered by status date descending, to get each shipment's current status from the history table. I can write that query out.

p5-30.q: Group and count: SELECT KitNumber, COUNT(*) FROM Kits GROUP BY KitNumber HAVING COUNT(*) > 1. To see or delete the duplicate rows themselves, use ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY KitNumber ORDER BY Id) and keep rn = 1.
i: Delete duplicates via a CTE where rn > 1, then add a unique constraint to prevent recurrence.
Delete duplicates keeping one: WITH d AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY Email ORDER BY Id) rn FROM Users) DELETE FROM d WHERE rn > 1.
Prevent recurrence with a unique index after cleanup.
c:
WITH d AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY StudyId, KitNumber ORDER BY Id) rn FROM Kits)
DELETE FROM d WHERE rn > 1;
f: Why can you delete from a CTE?
SQL Server allows DML through a CTE over a single base table.
What prevents new duplicates?
A unique constraint or index.
p5-30.y: I group by the columns that should be unique and use HAVING COUNT greater than one, which lists the duplicate values. To see or delete the extra rows, I use ROW_NUMBER partitioned by those columns and keep only row number one. After cleaning up, I add a unique constraint so it can't happen again.
p5-30.k: duplicate records, group by, having, row_number, sql
x: There are two common ways to find duplicates in SQL, and the second also helps you clean them up.

The first is GROUP BY with HAVING. For example, select KitNumber and COUNT star from Kits, group by KitNumber, having COUNT star greater than 1. That lists every value that appears more than once, and how many times. If duplicates are defined by several columns, I group by all of them.

The second uses ROW_NUMBER. Over PARTITION BY KitNumber ORDER BY Id, each row in a group of duplicates gets a number, 1, 2, 3. Rows with number 1 are the ones to keep, usually the oldest, and rows with a number greater than 1 are the extras. Wrapped in a CTE, I can review them, and if appropriate, delete or merge them.
Then, most importantly, I prevent it from happening again with a unique constraint, and fix the code path that allowed it.

In a regulated system, I wouldn't just delete duplicates. We'd investigate the root cause, document it, and apply a reviewed data fix with an audit trail. I've done that for a duplicate import issue, which is also why our CSV import now uses a file hash. I can walk through that.

p5-31.q: SELECT DISTINCT Salary FROM Emp ORDER BY Salary DESC OFFSET N-1 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROWS ONLY; or DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) in a CTE and filter on rank = N, which handles ties correctly.
i: The classic MAX with subquery works for second highest only.
Return NULL when there's no nth value if required.
OFFSET/FETCH alternative: SELECT DISTINCT Salary ... ORDER BY Salary DESC OFFSET n-1 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROW ONLY.
c:
WITH r AS (SELECT Salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) dr FROM Emp)
SELECT DISTINCT Salary FROM r WHERE dr = @N;
f: Why DENSE_RANK not ROW_NUMBER?
Ties would otherwise count as separate positions.
Per department?
Add PARTITION BY DepartmentId.
p5-31.y: The cleanest way is DENSE_RANK ordered by salary descending, then pick the rows where the rank equals N, which also handles ties correctly. Another option is OFFSET N minus 1 rows and fetch next one row on distinct salaries. For the second highest only, a simple MAX of salaries less than the overall max also works.
p5-31.k: nth highest salary, second highest, dense_rank, sql
x: There are a few ways to find the nth-highest value, and the main thing to get right is how ties are handled.

The cleanest general approach uses DENSE_RANK. Rank the salaries with DENSE_RANK over ORDER BY Salary descending, in a CTE, and then select the rows where the rank equals N. Because DENSE_RANK gives equal salaries the same rank, with no gaps, "second highest" really means the second distinct salary, and it returns every employee who earns it. Another approach is SELECT DISTINCT Salary ORDER BY Salary descending, then OFFSET N minus 1 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROW ONLY. And for just the second highest, a classic answer is SELECT MAX Salary WHERE Salary is less than the overall MAX.
The trap is using ROW_NUMBER or TOP without DISTINCT. If two people share the highest salary, "second row" gives you the highest salary again, which is wrong.
I also mention what happens if there's no Nth value, for example fewer than N distinct salaries: these queries return nothing, or null with MAX, and the caller should handle that.
In my day-to-day work, the same pattern answers questions like "the second most recent shipment per site". I can write the full query if you like.

p5-32.q: Use ROW_NUMBER with PARTITION BY: WITH r AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY SiteId ORDER BY ShipDate DESC) rn FROM Shipments) SELECT * FROM r WHERE rn <= 3. CROSS APPLY with TOP is an alternative that can be faster with a good index.
i: Index (SiteId, ShipDate DESC) supports both.
CROSS APPLY with TOP (N) ... ORDER BY can be faster than ROW_NUMBER when an index supports the per-group ordering.
Ties: use RANK or WITH TIES if equal values should all appear.
c:
SELECT s.Id, x.* FROM Sites s
CROSS APPLY (SELECT TOP (3) Id, ShipDate FROM Shipments sh WHERE sh.SiteId = s.Id ORDER BY ShipDate DESC) x;
f: When is CROSS APPLY better?
When there are few groups and an index allows a seek per group.
Ties?
Use RANK or DENSE_RANK if ties should all be included.
p5-32.y: I use ROW_NUMBER partitioned by the group and ordered by the ranking column, inside a CTE, then keep rows where the number is less than or equal to N. For example, the latest three shipments per site. If an index supports it, CROSS APPLY with TOP N can be even faster.
p5-32.k: top n per group, row_number, partition by, cross apply, sql
x: "Top N per group" is one of the most common SQL patterns, for example the three most recent shipments for each site.

The standard solution uses ROW_NUMBER in a CTE. Select from Shipments, adding ROW_NUMBER OVER PARTITION BY SiteId ORDER BY ShipDate descending, as rn. PARTITION BY restarts the numbering for each site, and ORDER BY decides which rows come first. Then, in the outer query, select where rn is less than or equal to 3. If ties should be included, I use RANK or DENSE_RANK instead. An alternative is CROSS APPLY: for each site, apply a subquery that selects TOP 3 shipments for that site ordered by date. With a good index on SiteId and ShipDate, CROSS APPLY can be very efficient when there are few groups and many rows per group, because it seeks per group.
Either way, an index on the partition column and the order column, like SiteId and ShipDate, is what makes it fast.

In EF Core, the same thing can be written with GroupBy and Take inside a Select, and recent versions translate it into a ROW_NUMBER query. In our IRT dashboards, we use this pattern to show each site's latest shipments. I can write it out.

p5-33.q: A dirty read reads uncommitted data that may be rolled back; a non-repeatable read gets different values for the same row within a transaction because another transaction updated it; a phantom read finds new rows on re-running a range query because another transaction inserted them.
i: Read Uncommitted (NOLOCK) allows dirty reads; Read Committed prevents them; Repeatable Read prevents non-repeatable reads; Serializable prevents phantoms; Snapshot gives a consistent versioned view.
NOLOCK can also skip or double-read rows, not just read dirty data.
READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT (RCSI) avoids readers blocking writers by reading row versions from tempdb.
Isolation levels: Read Uncommitted allows all three; Repeatable Read stops non-repeatable reads; Serializable stops phantoms.
f: Why avoid NOLOCK?
It can return wrong results, including missing or duplicated rows.
Which isolation does RCSI give?
Read Committed using row versions, so readers don't block writers.
p5-33.y: A dirty read is reading data another transaction hasn't committed yet, which might be rolled back. A non-repeatable read is reading the same row twice in a transaction and getting different values, because someone updated it. A phantom read is running the same query twice and getting new rows. Higher isolation levels prevent each of these.
p5-33.k: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read, isolation levels
x: These are three concurrency problems that can happen when transactions run at the same time, and isolation levels exist to prevent them.

A dirty read is reading data that another transaction has changed but not yet committed. If that transaction rolls back, you've read data that never really existed. A non-repeatable read is when you read the same row twice in one transaction and get different values, because another transaction updated and committed it in between. A phantom read is when you run the same range query twice, like all pending shipments for a site, and the second time new rows appear, because another transaction inserted them.

Isolation levels map to these. Read Uncommitted allows all three. Read Committed, SQL Server's default, prevents dirty reads. Repeatable Read also prevents non-repeatable reads. Serializable prevents phantoms too. Snapshot isolation gives a consistent view of the data as of the start of the transaction, without blocking writers.

In practice, I pick the level per use case. For example, when allocating kits to a site, a phantom could mean promising the same stock twice, so that short transaction uses stricter isolation. I can explain how snapshot isolation works.

p5-34.q: ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules and constraints hold after each transaction), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere beyond the isolation level) and Durability (committed data survives crashes, via the transaction log).
i: Write-ahead logging gives durability and rollback.
Distributed systems trade some ACID across services (sagas, eventual consistency).
Durability in SQL Server comes from write-ahead logging: the log record is hardened before commit returns.
Distributed services can't have ACID across databases cheaply, so we used outbox plus eventual consistency.
f: How does SQL Server guarantee durability?
Log records are hardened to disk before commit returns.
ACID vs BASE?
BASE (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent) describes many NoSQL systems.
p5-34.y: ACID describes reliable transactions. Atomicity means all or nothing. Consistency means the data always follows the rules and constraints. Isolation means concurrent transactions don't interfere with each other. Durability means once committed, the data survives a crash. Our CSV import relies on atomicity: everything saves, or nothing does.
p5-34.k: acid, atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability, transactions
x: ACID is the set of four guarantees that a reliable database transaction provides.

Atomicity means all or nothing. If a transaction has five steps and the fourth fails, the first three are rolled back, so you never end up halfway. Consistency means a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another, so all rules, like constraints, foreign keys and checks, still hold after it commits. Isolation means concurrent transactions don't interfere with each other, and each behaves as if it were running alone, to the degree set by the isolation level. Durability means once a transaction is committed, it stays committed, even if the server crashes a second later, because SQL Server writes changes to the transaction log on disk before confirming the commit.
These guarantees are why relational databases are the backbone of systems where correctness really matters.

In clinical trials, that's critical. When a subject is randomised, recording the assignment and allocating the kit must happen together or not at all. With a single ACID transaction, we never get a subject randomised without a kit. Across services, where we can't have one transaction, we use outbox and sagas instead. I can explain those.

p5-35.q: Optimistic locking takes no locks; it detects conflicts at write time with a rowversion and fails the second writer, best for low contention (EF Core concurrency tokens). Pessimistic locking locks the row while working (SELECT ... WITH (UPDLOCK)), best for high contention like allocating the next randomization slot.
i: EF Core throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException; reload and retry or show a conflict.
APIs expose the version as an ETag with If-Match.
EF Core: a rowversion column marked IsRowVersion() gives optimistic concurrency; catch DbUpdateConcurrencyException and return 409.
c: public class Shipment { public int Id { get; set; } [Timestamp] public byte[] RowVersion { get; set; } = []; }
f: What does EF do with [Timestamp]?
Adds the version to the UPDATE WHERE clause and checks rows affected.
Risk of pessimistic locking?
Blocking and deadlocks if transactions are long.
p5-35.y: Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare: there's no lock, but a version column is checked when saving, and if someone else changed the row, the save fails. Pessimistic locking locks the row while working on it, so others wait. I use optimistic locking with a rowversion column for user edits, and pessimistic locks only for short critical sections.
p5-35.k: optimistic locking, pessimistic locking, concurrency, rowversion
x: These are two strategies for handling two users or processes trying to change the same data at the same time.

Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare. It doesn't lock anything while the user works. Instead, each row has a version, like a SQL Server rowversion column. When saving, the update includes WHERE version equals the original version. If someone else changed the row in the meantime, no row is updated, and the application detects the conflict and handles it, by retrying, merging, or returning 409 to the user. In EF Core, that's a concurrency token and DbUpdateConcurrencyException. It's scalable, because no locks are held.

Pessimistic locking assumes conflicts are likely, so it locks the rows up front, for example with an UPDLOCK hint inside a transaction, and others must wait. It guarantees no conflicts, but reduces concurrency, and long locks cause blocking and deadlocks.

So my rule: optimistic by default, pessimistic only for short, high-contention critical sections. In our IRT system, editing shipments and sites is optimistic. But allocating the last available drug kits at a depot uses a short pessimistic lock, because two sites must never get the same kit. I can explain that design.

p5-36.q: Measure first (Query Store, wait stats, slow query logs), then fix the top queries (indexes, SARGable predicates, less data fetched, better joins), keep statistics fresh, shorten transactions, consider RCSI, cache hot reads, and scale hardware only after.
i: Wait stats tell where time goes (PAGEIOLATCH = I/O, LCK = blocking, CXPACKET = parallelism).
Batch and set-based operations instead of row by row.
Archive old data, partition very large tables.
Measure first: Query Store top resource consumers, wait stats, and actual execution plans before changing anything.
f: What do you check first?
Top queries by total CPU and duration in Query Store.
When would you partition?
Very large tables where sliding windows or maintenance per partition help.
p5-36.y: First I measure, using Query Store to find the most expensive queries, wait statistics, and execution plans. Then I fix the biggest problems: missing or wrong indexes, non-SARGable queries, N+1 calls from the app, and loading too much data. I also keep transactions short and statistics updated. Measuring before and after proves the fix worked.
p5-36.k: database performance, optimization, query store, indexes, tuning
x: My approach to database performance is always to measure first, fix the biggest problems, and then measure again.

First, find what's actually slow. Query Store shows the most expensive queries by CPU, duration and reads, wait statistics show what the server is waiting on, and application metrics show which endpoints suffer. Second, fix the top queries. That usually means proper indexes, SARGable predicates, avoiding SELECT star, removing N+1 patterns from the application, and checking execution plans. Third, the schema and maintenance: correct data types, sensible normalisation, up-to-date statistics, and index maintenance. Fourth, reduce load: cache reference data in the application or Redis, use read replicas for reporting, and archive or partition old data. And keep transactions short, to reduce blocking and deadlocks.
Only after that do I consider scaling up the server, because hardware hides problems rather than fixing them.

My best example is our shipment list, which went from [about 9 seconds to under 300 ms], and logical reads from [about 400,000 to 2,000], with a predicate rewrite, a covering index and paging, no hardware changes at all. I can walk through that.

p5-37.q: Start from real query patterns. The clustered key should be narrow, unique, static and ever-increasing; add non-clustered indexes on foreign keys and frequent filters with equality columns first, INCLUDE columns to cover hot queries, filtered indexes for hot subsets, and remove unused or duplicate indexes. Verify with execution plans.
i: Avoid wide clustered keys: they're copied into every non-clustered index.
Consider write cost on busy tables.
Review missing index DMVs critically; they often over-suggest.
Design from queries: list the top queries' WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY columns, then build the fewest indexes covering most of them.
f: Why ever-increasing clustered keys?
Inserts go to the end, reducing page splits and fragmentation.
Are missing index suggestions reliable?
They're hints; combine and validate them.
p5-37.y: I design indexes from the real queries. I list the main queries' WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY columns, and build composite indexes with equality columns first and range columns last, adding INCLUDE columns to avoid lookups. I aim for the fewest indexes that cover the most important queries, then check the plans and usage over time.
p5-37.k: index design, composite index, covering index, sql server
x: I design indexes from real query patterns, not by guessing, and I always weigh the read benefit against the write cost.

The clustered index should usually be narrow, unique, static and ever-increasing, like an integer identity, because every non-clustered index carries the clustered key, and random keys cause page splits. Then non-clustered indexes. I index foreign key columns, since SQL Server doesn't do it automatically, and the columns used in frequent filters and joins. For composite indexes, I put equality columns first and range columns last, and add INCLUDE columns for what the query selects, so it's covered without key lookups. For hot subsets, like only pending records, a filtered index can be much smaller.

Then I verify. I check the execution plan to confirm the index is actually used, and over time I look at the index usage DMVs to find indexes that are never read but are constantly updated, and remove unused or duplicate ones.

The covering index from our shipment list fix is a good example: StudyId and Status for equality, ShipmentDate for the range, plus the displayed columns. We also tested its write impact in validation. I can explain how I'd find missing indexes.

p5-38.q: Microservices are small, independently deployable services, each owning one business capability and its data, communicating over APIs or messages. Teams can build, deploy and scale them separately.
i: Characteristics: database per service, decentralised governance, automated deployment, design for failure.
Size by business capability, not lines of code.
IRT services: randomization, supply, shipments, notifications.
Each service owns its data; sharing a database between services recreates a monolith.
f: Must each service have its own database?
Logically its own data, at least separate schemas with no cross-service access.
Microservices vs SOA?
Microservices are finer-grained, with smart endpoints and dumb pipes rather than an ESB.
p5-38.y: Microservices is an architecture where the system is split into small, independent services, each owning one business area and its own data, deployed on its own and talking over APIs or messages. In IRT, we have separate services for things like randomization, supply and shipments.
x: Microservices is an architectural style where an application is built as a set of small, independently deployable services. Each service owns one business capability and its own data, and they communicate over APIs or messages.

The key word is independent. Each service can be developed, deployed, scaled and even written in a different technology, without coordinating a big release with everyone else. A service owns its database, so no other service reaches into its tables; it shares data only through its API or events. That gives teams autonomy, and a failure in one service can be isolated instead of taking down everything.

But it's a trade-off. You exchange the simplicity of one process for the complexity of a distributed system: network failures, eventual consistency, distributed tracing, and a lot more DevOps work. So it pays off for large systems and multiple teams, not for every project.

In my work, our IRT platform combines a legacy .NET Framework core with newer domain microservices, for example the IRT API, notifications, reports, supply management and integrations, as ASP.NET Core services communicating via REST and RabbitMQ, hosted on-premise, while [IQVIA's newer services run on AWS ECS]. I coordinate releases across [about 5] scrum teams. I can explain how we drew the service boundaries.

p5-39.q: Advantages: independent deploys and scaling, fault isolation, team autonomy and technology choice per service. Disadvantages: distributed-system complexity (network failures, eventual consistency), harder testing and debugging, operational overhead (many pipelines, monitoring, tracing) and data consistency challenges.
i: Needs mature DevOps and observability.
Latency from network hops.
Advantages: independent deploys, scaling per service, fault isolation, team autonomy.
Disadvantages: network failures, distributed data consistency, more ops (observability, CI/CD per service).
f: Biggest hidden cost?
Operational complexity and data consistency across services.
How do you mitigate it?
Platform automation, templates, tracing and clear contracts.
p5-39.y: The advantages are independent deployments, scaling each service separately, fault isolation, and teams owning their own services. The disadvantages are the complexity of a distributed system: network failures, keeping data consistent across services, and much more work on monitoring, testing and deployment. So the benefits must be worth that cost.
x: Microservices bring real benefits, but every benefit comes with a cost.

The advantages: independent deployment, so one team can release without waiting for others. Independent scaling, so only the busy service gets more instances. Fault isolation, so a failure in notifications doesn't stop randomisation. Team autonomy, with clear ownership of each service. And freedom to choose the best technology per service.

The disadvantages: everything becomes a network call, which adds latency and new failure modes, so you need timeouts, retries and circuit breakers. Data is distributed, so you lose simple transactions and must handle eventual consistency, with patterns like outbox and sagas. Testing and debugging across services is harder, so you need contract tests, correlation ids and distributed tracing. And there's much more DevOps work: a pipeline per service, container orchestration, monitoring and alerting for many moving parts.

My summary is that microservices trade code complexity for operational complexity. It's worth it when you have several teams and parts of the system that genuinely change and scale differently. In our IRT platform, correlation ids and the outbox pattern were exactly the kind of investments this required. I can explain when I'd avoid them.

p5-40.q: I wouldn't use microservices for a small team or early product, unclear domain boundaries, low scale, no DevOps maturity (CI/CD, monitoring), or when strong transactional consistency across the whole domain matters. A modular monolith is the better default.
i: Premature splitting creates a distributed monolith.
Extract services later along proven boundaries.
Small teams, unclear domains, or early products: start with a modular monolith and split on proven boundaries.
If services must always deploy together, they are a distributed monolith.
f: What is a modular monolith?
One deployable with strongly separated modules and boundaries.
Signal it's time to split?
Teams blocking each other or different scaling needs.
p5-40.y: I wouldn't use microservices for a small team, an early product, or a domain that isn't well understood yet, because the overhead is high and the boundaries will likely be wrong. If services always have to be deployed together, it's just a distributed monolith. In those cases, a well-structured modular monolith is better, and you split later where needed.
p5-40.k: when not to use microservices, monolith, modular monolith
x: I wouldn't use microservices when the costs clearly outweigh the benefits, which is more often than people think.

Some clear signals. A small team, because one team managing ten services spends more time on infrastructure than features. An early-stage product, where the domain isn't well understood yet, because wrong service boundaries are very expensive to fix later, and you end up with a distributed monolith, where every change touches several services. Low scale, where there's no need to scale parts independently. Low DevOps maturity, without solid CI/CD, monitoring and on-call, because microservices depend on all of that. And a domain that needs strong transactional consistency across most of its data, where splitting the data creates more problems than it solves.

In those cases, I'd start with a modular monolith: one deployable application, but with clear internal module boundaries, separate schemas or at least separate DbContexts per module, and communication through interfaces or in-process events. If a module later needs independent scaling or a separate team, it can be extracted into a service with much less risk.
I'd rather earn microservices than start with them. I can describe how I'd extract a module from a monolith.

p5-41.q: I use Domain-Driven Design: split by business capability and bounded context, the area where one model and its language are consistent (Randomization, Supply, Shipments). Signals include different data ownership, change frequency, team ownership and scaling needs; Event Storming workshops help find them.
i: A "Kit" means different things in Supply vs Dispensing: separate models.
Context maps describe relationships (customer-supplier, anti-corruption layer).
Avoid splitting by technical layer (a "data service").
Event storming with domain experts finds boundaries where language and data ownership change.
f: What is an anti-corruption layer?
A translation layer protecting your model from another system's model.
What is ubiquitous language?
Shared terms between developers and domain experts within a context.
p5-41.y: I find service boundaries around business capabilities, not technical layers. A bounded context, from domain-driven design, is an area where terms have one clear meaning and one team owns the data. For example, a shipment means something specific in the shipment context. Talking with domain experts, through event storming, helps find where these boundaries are.
p5-41.k: service boundaries, bounded context, ddd, domain driven design
x: Service boundaries are the hardest part of microservices, and I use Domain-Driven Design, specifically bounded contexts, to find them.

A bounded context is an area of the business where one model and one language stay consistent. The same word can mean different things in different contexts. For example, in clinical trials, a "kit" in the supply context is stock with a lot number and expiry date, while in the dispensing context, it's something assigned to a subject at a visit. Each bounded context is a natural candidate for a service, with its own model and its own data.

To find them, I look at business capabilities, like randomisation, supply management, shipments, consent and notifications. Then I check some signals: Does each area own its own data? Do they change at different rates, or belong to different teams? And how chatty would they be? If two candidate services constantly need synchronous calls to each other to do anything, the boundary is probably wrong, and they belong together.

In our IRT platform, randomisation, supply and shipments are separate contexts that communicate mainly through events, which keeps them loosely coupled. I can explain how event storming helps discover these boundaries.

p5-42.q: Synchronous REST or gRPC when the caller needs an immediate answer; asynchronous events or commands (Kafka, RabbitMQ) when it doesn't, to decouple services and absorb load. Prefer async for state changes others react to, and keep synchronous chains short.
i: gRPC for internal high-performance calls with contracts (Protobuf).
Events carry facts ("ShipmentDelivered"); commands request actions.
Always with timeouts, retries and idempotency.
Rule of thumb: sync for queries needing an immediate answer, async events for state changes others react to.
f: Why avoid long synchronous chains?
Latency adds up and one failure breaks the whole chain.
Events vs commands?
Events notify many about something that happened; commands tell one handler to do something.
p5-42.y: They should use synchronous calls, like REST or gRPC, when the caller needs an immediate answer, like fetching data for a screen. They should use asynchronous messaging, like Kafka or RabbitMQ, when other services just need to react to something that happened, like a shipment status change. Async messaging keeps services more independent and resilient.
p5-42.k: microservices communication, rest, grpc, messaging, async
x: Microservices communicate in two main ways, and choosing between them depends on whether the caller needs an immediate answer.

Synchronous communication, with REST or gRPC, is request and response. The caller waits for the result. It's simple and intuitive, and it's the right choice when the caller genuinely needs the answer now, like the UI loading a study, or checking whether a subject is eligible. gRPC is useful for high-performance internal calls. The downside is temporal coupling: if the callee is slow or down, the caller is too.

Asynchronous communication uses messages through a broker, like RabbitMQ or Kafka. Commands ask another service to do something, and events announce that something happened, like "shipment dispatched". The producer doesn't wait, and doesn't even need to know who's listening. That decouples services, absorbs traffic spikes and survives temporary outages, but it brings eventual consistency and harder tracing.

Whatever the style, every contract, API or message, is versioned and kept backward compatible. In our IRT platform, the UI and partners use REST, and workflows between services use RabbitMQ events, with an outbox for reliability. I can explain when we chose Kafka instead.

p5-43.q: Synchronous (REST/gRPC) is simple with an immediate result but creates temporal coupling: a slow or down callee affects the caller. Asynchronous messaging decouples in time and absorbs spikes, enabling independent scaling, but adds eventual consistency, duplicate handling and harder debugging.
i: Request/reply over messaging exists but adds complexity.
Choose per interaction, not per system.
Sync chains multiply latency and failure probability: three services at 99.9% each give about 99.7% combined.
Async decouples availability but needs idempotency, ordering decisions and monitoring of lag.
f: Example of each in IRT?
REST to randomize a subject (needs an answer); Kafka events for shipment status changes.
How do you debug async flows?
Correlation ids, tracing and message logs.
p5-43.y: With REST, which is synchronous, the caller waits for the answer, which is simple but couples availability: if the other service is down, the call fails. With messaging, which is asynchronous, the sender publishes and moves on, so services stay independent and can absorb spikes. But then we need idempotency and must accept eventual consistency.
p5-43.k: rest vs messaging, synchronous, asynchronous, communication
x: The core difference is whether the caller waits.

With synchronous communication, like REST or gRPC, the caller sends a request and waits for the response. It's simple to build and debug, and the caller gets an immediate, definite result. But it creates temporal coupling: both services must be up at the same time. If the callee is slow, the caller is slow too, and long chains of synchronous calls multiply latency and failure risk.

With asynchronous messaging, through queues or event streams, the sender publishes a message and moves on. The receiver processes it when it can. That decouples services: if the receiver is down, messages wait safely in the queue. It absorbs load spikes, and new consumers can subscribe without changing the producer. The costs are eventual consistency, because the result isn't immediate, more complex error handling with retries, dead-letter queues and idempotency, and harder end-to-end tracing.

My rule is: use synchronous when the user or caller needs the answer now, and asynchronous for everything that can happen in the background. In our platform, creating a shipment is a REST call, but notifying the vendor and updating inventory happen through RabbitMQ events. I can explain how we trace those flows.

p5-44.q: Service discovery is how services find each other's current addresses: DNS-based (Kubernetes Services, ECS Service Connect / Cloud Map) or registry-based (Consul, Eureka), often behind load balancers. Clients call a stable name instead of IPs that change with scaling.
i: Client-side vs server-side discovery.
.NET Aspire provides service discovery for HttpClient (Microsoft.Extensions.ServiceDiscovery).
On ECS: Cloud Map or Service Connect; on Kubernetes: Services and DNS; behind an ALB, the ALB is the stable endpoint.
Client-side vs server-side discovery: client picks an instance from a registry vs a load balancer picks.
f: Why not hardcode IPs?
Containers come and go with changing IPs.
ECS Service Connect?
Managed service discovery and proxy for ECS services with metrics.
p5-44.y: Service discovery is how a service finds the network address of another service, since instances come and go. On Kubernetes, services get DNS names. On ECS, we use Cloud Map, Service Connect, or a load balancer as a stable address. That way services call a name, and the platform routes to healthy instances.
p5-44.k: service discovery, dns, cloud map, service connect, kubernetes
x: Service discovery is how services find each other's current network address, when instances are constantly starting, stopping and moving.

In a cloud or container environment, you can't hard-code IP addresses. Containers are replaced on every deployment, scaled up and down automatically, and restarted on failure, and each time they may get a new IP. Service discovery solves this with a registry that tracks healthy instances, and a stable name that callers use.

There are two common approaches. Server-side discovery through a load balancer: callers use a stable DNS name for the load balancer, which knows the healthy targets. In AWS, that's an internal Application Load Balancer in front of ECS services. And DNS-based discovery built into the platform: in Kubernetes, a Service gives a stable DNS name, and in ECS, Service Connect or Cloud Map registers tasks automatically. There's also client-side discovery, where the client asks a registry and picks an instance itself, which was common with tools like Consul or Eureka.

In CIRT, services find each other through stable DNS names in configuration, backed by internal load balancers, and on AWS through ECS service registration, with health checks removing unhealthy instances. I can explain how health checks feed into it.

p5-45.q: Retrying non-idempotent operations duplicates side effects; retrying permanent errors (400, 401, validation) wastes resources; and retry storms from many clients amplify an outage. So I retry only transient errors (timeouts, 408, 429, 5xx), with exponential backoff and jitter, limited attempts, idempotency keys, and a circuit breaker.
i: Retry budgets limit total retries.
Respect Retry-After headers.
Retries at multiple layers multiply (3 × 3 × 3 = 27).
Retry only transient errors (timeouts, 5xx, 429 with Retry-After) and idempotent operations; use exponential backoff with jitter.
f: Why jitter?
To spread retries so clients don't retry in sync.
Example?
The Copilot retry suggestion that would have duplicated release creation (Part 3 Q35).
p5-45.y: Retrying everything can make things worse. Retrying a non-idempotent call, like creating a payment, can create duplicates. Retrying permanent errors, like a 400 or a bad password, never helps. And many clients retrying at once can overload a struggling service. So I retry only temporary errors on safe operations, with backoff, jitter and a limit.
p5-45.k: retries, retry storm, idempotency, backoff, resilience
x: Retries are useful, but retrying everything can turn a small problem into a big one.

There are three main dangers. First, non-idempotent operations. If a POST to create a shipment timed out, it may have actually succeeded. Retrying it blindly can create a duplicate. So I only retry operations that are idempotent, or made idempotent with an idempotency key. Second, permanent errors. A 400 validation error, a 401 or a 404 won't succeed the second time, so retrying just wastes time and resources and delays the real error. Third, retry storms. If a service is struggling and every client retries aggressively, the load multiplies, and the struggling service can never recover. With several layers each retrying three times, one request can become dozens.

So I retry only transient errors, like timeouts, 503s, 429s and network failures. I use exponential backoff with jitter, so clients don't retry in sync, a small maximum number of attempts, and a circuit breaker to stop retrying a service that's clearly down. And I retry at one layer only, not at every level.
That's how our vendor API calls are configured with the standard resilience handler. I can explain how jitter helps.

p5-46.q: Bulkhead isolation uses separate resource pools per dependency (connection pools, concurrency limits, queues) so one slow dependency can't exhaust all threads or connections and take the whole service down. The name comes from ship compartments that contain flooding.
i: Polly concurrency limiter or ASP.NET Core rate limiting per dependency.
Separate HttpClients with their own handlers per downstream.
Separate worker pools or queues per workload type.
Polly v8 / Microsoft.Extensions.Resilience: the concurrency limiter strategy acts as a bulkhead.
f: Bulkhead vs circuit breaker?
Bulkhead limits resources used; circuit breaker stops calling a failing dependency.
Example in IRT?
[Separate consumer pools for vendor file processing and notifications].
p5-46.y: Bulkhead isolation is like the compartments in a ship: if one floods, the ship still floats. In software, I limit the resources, like concurrent calls or threads, given to each dependency, so one slow dependency can't use up everything and bring down the whole service. Polly has a concurrency limiter for this.
x: Bulkhead isolation is a resilience pattern that stops one failing dependency from taking down everything else. The name comes from ships, which are divided into watertight compartments, so a leak in one doesn't sink the whole ship.

In software, the problem is shared resources. If a service calls three dependencies, and one becomes very slow, requests to it pile up and hold threads, connections or memory. Eventually the whole service runs out, and even requests that don't need the slow dependency start failing. A bulkhead gives each dependency its own limited pool of resources: a maximum number of concurrent calls, a separate connection pool, or a separate queue. When one dependency's pool is full, extra calls to it fail fast, or queue briefly, but other dependencies keep working normally.
In .NET, Polly's concurrency limiter, or the rate limiter strategy, implements this per HttpClient. At the infrastructure level, running separate worker services per queue is also a bulkhead.

In our platform, slow vendor SFTP transfers run in their own worker service with their own limits, so a slow vendor never affects randomisation or the main API. I can explain how it combines with circuit breakers.

p5-47.q: Distributed tracing follows one request across services with a trace id and spans (timing per hop), using OpenTelemetry and W3C traceparent headers, visualised in X-Ray, Jaeger or Grafana Tempo. It shows where latency and errors occur in a multi-service flow.
i: .NET has built-in Activity/ActivitySource; HttpClient and ASP.NET Core propagate context automatically.
Propagate through messages by putting traceparent in headers.
Sampling controls cost.
f: Trace id vs correlation id?
Similar purpose; trace ids are standardised and include parent-child spans.
How do you trace through RabbitMQ?
Inject traceparent into message headers and start a consumer span from it.
p5-47.y: Distributed tracing follows one request as it moves through many services. Each service adds a span with its timing, and they're linked by a trace id passed in headers. So I can see the whole journey and exactly where it was slow or failed. We use OpenTelemetry for this, together with our correlation ids in logs.
p5-47.k: distributed tracing, opentelemetry, trace id, spans, observability
x: Distributed tracing is the ability to follow a single request as it travels through multiple services, and see where time is spent and where errors happen.

Each incoming request gets a trace id. Every service that handles part of it records a span, a timed unit of work, like "handle HTTP request", "query database" or "publish message", with the trace id and a parent span id. The trace context is passed along between services in headers, using the W3C traceparent standard, and in message headers for queues. The spans are sent to a tracing backend, like AWS X-Ray, Jaeger or Grafana Tempo, which reassembles them into a timeline, a waterfall view showing every hop and how long it took.

In .NET, OpenTelemetry is the standard way to do this. ASP.NET Core, HttpClient and many libraries already create spans automatically through Activity, so you mostly add the exporter and a few custom spans.

Before full tracing, we solved the most painful part with our correlation-id middleware in [2024], which links logs across our [4] services. Tracing adds timing on top of that, so you can see, for example, that a slow request was waiting on one database query in one service. I can explain how logs and traces connect.

p5-48.q: Eventual consistency means data across services becomes consistent after a short delay rather than instantly, accepted for availability and decoupling. Design for it with idempotent consumers, clear UI states (Pending), versioning and reconciliation jobs.
i: Read-your-writes can be provided for the user who made the change.
Monitoring lag between services.
Users must see something sensible meanwhile, e.g. "Processing" status, not stale success.
Reconciliation jobs catch messages that went missing despite the outbox.
f: Where is it unacceptable in IRT?
Randomization slot allocation and kit assignment within a transaction.
How do you show it in a UI?
Status like "Processing" and refresh or push updates.
p5-48.y: Eventual consistency means that after a change, different services may briefly show different data, but they all catch up after a short time. It's the trade-off for decoupled services that talk through events. The user interface should show something sensible meanwhile, like a processing status, and we use reconciliation to catch anything missed.
x: Eventual consistency means that when data changes in one service, other services will see the change, but not instantly. After a short delay, everything becomes consistent.

In a microservices system, each service owns its data, and they share changes through events. When the shipment service marks a shipment as dispatched, it publishes an event, and the inventory and notification services update their own data when they process it, maybe a few hundred milliseconds later. During that window, different services can show slightly different states. We accept that in exchange for availability and loose coupling, because the alternative, distributed transactions across services, is slow and fragile.

The important part is designing for it. Use clear intermediate states, like Pending or Processing, so users understand that something is in progress. Make consumers idempotent, because events can arrive twice. Handle out-of-order events, for example with version numbers. And monitor for messages that fail, so nothing stays inconsistent forever.

In our IRT platform, the UI shows a shipment as "Requested" until the vendor confirms it, rather than pretending it's instant. And dead-letter queue alarms make sure stuck events are investigated. I can explain where we still need strong consistency.

p5-49.q: Timeouts, retries with backoff, circuit breakers and fallbacks for synchronous calls; asynchronous messaging with durable queues and DLQs; idempotent handlers; sagas with compensation for multi-step workflows; and health checks with alerts.
i: Graceful degradation: show cached data when a dependency is down.
.NET 8 standard resilience handler bundles these for HttpClient.
Timeouts on every call, retries with backoff, circuit breakers, fallbacks, and DLQs for async work.
Idempotent consumers so retries don't double-apply.
f: What is a fallback?
An alternative response when the call fails, like cached or default data.
What timeout values?
Based on the dependency's p99 plus margin, always less than the caller's own timeout.
p5-49.y: I assume calls will fail. Every call has a timeout, temporary errors are retried with backoff, and a circuit breaker stops calling a service that's down. I provide fallbacks where possible. For async work, messages that keep failing go to a dead-letter queue, and consumers are idempotent so retries are safe.
p5-49.k: failure handling, resilience, timeout, retry, circuit breaker, dlq
x: Failures between services are normal in a distributed system, so I design for them at several levels.

For synchronous calls: a timeout on every call, so nothing hangs forever. Retries with exponential backoff and jitter, only for transient errors and idempotent operations. A circuit breaker, so we stop calling a service that's clearly down and fail fast instead. And a fallback where it makes sense, like serving cached reference data.

For workflows that don't need an immediate answer, I prefer asynchronous messaging with durable queues. If the consumer is down, messages wait. Failed messages are retried a limited number of times and then moved to a dead-letter queue, so they're not lost and don't block the queue. Consumers are idempotent, so redelivered messages are safe. For multi-step business processes across services, a saga coordinates the steps, and compensating actions undo earlier steps if a later one fails.
And all of this needs monitoring: alerts on error rates, circuit breaker state, queue depth and dead-letter queues.

I learned this the hard way. In [mid-2024], RabbitMQ hit a memory alarm, and because we published without confirms, [about 1,200] shipment status updates were lost silently over [about 40 minutes]. We recovered by replaying the vendor files, and fixed it for good with publisher confirms, retries and alerts. I can walk through that story.

p5-50.q: Version APIs (URL segment or header) and message contracts (additive changes, a schema version field), stay backward compatible, use consumer-driven contract tests, and deprecate old versions with notice. Prefer additive, non-breaking changes so versions rarely change.
i: Tolerant reader: consumers ignore unknown fields.
Asp.Versioning library for ASP.NET Core.
Schema registry for Kafka (Avro/Protobuf compatibility rules).
Prefer backward-compatible changes (additive fields); version URLs (/v2) only for breaking changes, with a deprecation window.
f: What's a breaking change?
Removing or renaming fields, changing types or meanings, new required inputs.
How long do you keep old versions?
Per agreement with consumers, with monitoring of usage.
p5-50.y: I version the contracts, both APIs and events. I prefer backward-compatible changes, like adding optional fields, so consumers don't break. For breaking changes, I add a new version, like v2 in the URL or a new event version, run both for a while, and remove the old one after consumers move. Each service is deployed independently with its own version.
p5-50.k: microservices versioning, api versioning, backward compatibility
x: Versioning microservices is about letting each service evolve without breaking the others, because they're deployed independently.

For APIs, I version in the URL or a header, like /api/v2, and stay backward compatible within a version. Additive changes, like new optional fields or new endpoints, are fine. Removing or renaming fields, or changing their meaning, is breaking, and needs a new version. The old version stays available, is marked deprecated, and is removed only after consumers have moved, which we confirm in the logs. For messages and events, the same rules apply: additive changes only, a schema version field in the message, and consumers that tolerate unknown fields. For a breaking change, we publish a new event type or version, sometimes both in parallel during the transition.
Consumers should also be tolerant readers: ignore fields they don't understand, and don't fail on them.

The deployable artifacts are versioned too: container images use semantic versions and the git commit, so we always know exactly what's running. In our pipelines, we compare OpenAPI documents between versions to catch accidental breaking changes. I can explain consumer-driven contract tests, which help here too.

p5-51.q: Each service has its own pipeline: build, test, image, IaC; deployments are independent to ECS or Kubernetes with rolling or blue-green strategies, health checks and automatic rollback, with configuration per environment and the same image promoted everywhere.
i: Shared pipeline templates for consistency.
Feature flags decouple release from deploy.
Contract tests prevent breaking consumers.
Each service has its own pipeline and artifact; rolling or blue/green deployments with health checks gate traffic.
f: How do you deploy a change spanning two services?
Make it backward compatible and deploy in order (provider first).
ECS deployment circuit breaker?
Stops and rolls back a deployment when tasks fail to become healthy.
p5-51.y: Each service has its own pipeline that builds, tests and produces a versioned Docker image. We deploy it to ECS with rolling updates and health checks, so traffic only goes to healthy tasks, and a deployment circuit breaker rolls back automatically if it fails. The same image is promoted through all environments.
p5-51.k: microservices deployment, ci/cd, ecs, rolling deployment
x: The key principle is that every microservice can be built, tested and deployed independently.

Each service has its own CI/CD pipeline. It builds the code, runs unit and integration tests, runs quality and security scans like a SonarQube gate and container image scanning, builds a Docker image tagged with the version and commit, and pushes it to a registry like Amazon ECR. Infrastructure is defined as code, with Terraform or CloudFormation, so environments are reproducible. Then the pipeline deploys to the orchestrator, ECS or Kubernetes, environment by environment.

For the deployment itself, I use rolling updates by default: new tasks start, pass health checks, and only then are old tasks drained and stopped, so there's no downtime. For riskier changes, blue-green or canary deployments let us shift traffic gradually and switch back instantly. Automated rollback triggers if health checks or alarms fail. Database changes are backward compatible, so old and new versions can run side by side during the rollout.

In our regulated environment, deployments to validated environments go through approval gates, with release evidence attached. I coordinate those releases across [about 5] scrum teams. I can explain how we handle a rollback.
