p5-52.q: Golden signals per service, centralised structured logs with correlation ids, distributed tracing, Grafana or CloudWatch dashboards, SLOs with alerts, and business metrics such as shipments processed.
i: Same telemetry conventions across services (OpenTelemetry semantic conventions).
Dependency maps from traces.
Synthetic checks for critical flows.
Correlation ids across services (our [2024] middleware) let you follow one request through logs and traces.
f: What's an SLO?
A target like 99.9 percent of requests under 500 ms over 30 days.
Synthetic monitoring?
Scripted checks simulating user flows on a schedule (CloudWatch Synthetics).
p5-52.y: I monitor each service with metrics for the golden signals, structured logs with correlation ids, and distributed traces. Dashboards in Grafana show health in one place, and alerts fire on user impact, like error rate or latency. The correlation id lets me follow one request through all services.
p5-52.k: microservices monitoring, observability, metrics, logs, tracing
x: Monitoring microservices means being able to answer, quickly, "is anything broken, where, and why" across many services.

I think of three pillars. Metrics: for each service, the golden signals, which are latency, traffic, errors and saturation, plus business metrics like shipments processed. For message-driven services, queue depth, consumer lag and dead-letter queue counts are essential. Logs: structured JSON logs from every service, centralised in one place, with a correlation id so one search shows a request across services. Traces: distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry, to see the path and timing of a request through every hop.

On top of that, dashboards in Grafana or CloudWatch per service and per business flow, and alerts based on service level objectives, like "p95 latency above 500 ms for 5 minutes", or "any message in a dead-letter queue". Alerts must be actionable, or people start ignoring them.

In our platform, Splunk and Grafana dashboards show each service's health, and our correlation-id work from [2024] means support can trace a failed request across [4] services in [a few minutes] instead of [about an hour]. We also have AlertWatchDog, our Quartz-scheduled alert engine, which emails study teams about events like low stock or shipments through RabbitMQ, and our RabbitMQ consumers alert on dead-letter queues.

p5-53.q: Private networking (VPC, security groups) plus mTLS where required; service identities (OAuth client credentials tokens or IAM roles) with authorization per call; secrets from a vault; and zero trust: never assume the internal network is safe.
i: Validate tokens audience-scoped per service.
Service mesh can provide mTLS automatically.
Least-privilege security group rules.
On AWS: IAM roles per task, security groups allowing only required ports, and TLS; JWT client-credentials for app-level identity.
f: Client credentials flow?
A service authenticates with its own credentials to get an access token for another API.
Why not trust internal traffic?
A compromised service could otherwise reach everything.
p5-53.y: All traffic is encrypted with TLS. Each service has its own identity, using IAM roles on AWS or OAuth client credentials tokens for app-level calls, and the receiving service checks permissions. Network rules, like security groups, only allow the traffic that's needed. Secrets are kept in Secrets Manager, never in code.
p5-53.k: service-to-service security, mtls, client credentials, iam, zero trust
x: I secure service-to-service communication on the principle of zero trust: a request isn't trusted just because it comes from inside our network.

There are several layers. Network: services run in private subnets inside a VPC, with security groups allowing only the expected traffic, so most services aren't reachable from the internet at all. Encryption: TLS between services, and mutual TLS where policy requires, so both sides prove their identity. Identity: each service has its own identity, either OAuth client-credentials tokens from the identity provider, with specific scopes, or IAM roles when calling AWS services. The receiving service validates the token and its scopes on every call, just as it would for a user. Least privilege: each service gets only the permissions it needs. And secrets, like client secrets or keys, live in AWS Secrets Manager, never in code or images, and are rotated.
The point is that if one service is compromised, the attacker shouldn't automatically be able to call everything else.

In our platform, internal services call each other with client-credential tokens and scopes, and our AWS services use IAM roles for AWS resources, with no long-lived keys. I can explain how token caching works for service calls.

p5-54.q: Timeouts everywhere, circuit breakers, bulkheads, rate limiting and load shedding, async queues to absorb spikes, graceful degradation and fallbacks, and avoiding deep synchronous call chains.
i: Retry with backoff and budgets to avoid amplification.
Health checks shouldn't call dependencies deeply (avoid cascading restarts).
Timeouts shorter than the caller's, circuit breakers, bulkheads, load shedding (429) and caches for read paths.
Avoid retry storms: retry budgets and jitter.
f: What is load shedding?
Rejecting excess requests early (503/429) to protect the system.
How do circuit breakers help?
They stop calls to a failing dependency, giving it time to recover and failing fast.
p5-54.y: A cascading failure is when one slow service makes its callers slow, and it spreads. I prevent it with timeouts that are shorter than the caller's, circuit breakers, bulkheads to limit resources per dependency, and rejecting extra load early with a 429. I also avoid retry storms with backoff and jitter.
p5-54.k: cascading failure, circuit breaker, timeout, bulkhead, resilience
x: A cascading failure is when one slow or failing service causes its callers to fail, and then their callers, until the whole system is down. Preventing it is about containing failure.

The main techniques work together. Timeouts on every call, so a slow dependency can't hold threads forever. Circuit breakers, so after repeated failures we stop calling and fail fast, giving the dependency time to recover. Bulkheads, so each dependency has its own limited resources and can't exhaust the whole service. Rate limiting and load shedding, so when overloaded, a service rejects some requests quickly rather than slowing down for everyone. Asynchronous queues, which absorb spikes and decouple services. Caching and graceful degradation, so non-essential features can be switched off while core features keep working. And careful retries with backoff and jitter, because aggressive retries are often what turns a slowdown into an outage.
Architecturally, the biggest factor is avoiding long chains of synchronous calls, because each hop multiplies the risk.

In our IRT platform, vendor integrations run asynchronously in separate workers. So when a vendor's system was slow, only vendor transfers were delayed. Randomisation and the main UI weren't affected. I can explain how we tested that.

p5-55.q: Unit tests; integration tests with a real database and broker in containers (Testcontainers); consumer-driven contract tests (Pact) between services; a few end-to-end tests on critical flows; plus performance and resilience tests.
i: Test pyramid: many unit, fewer integration, few E2E.
WebApplicationFactory for in-memory API tests.
.NET Aspire testing for distributed app tests.
Consumer-driven contract tests (e.g. Pact) catch breaking API changes before deploy.
f: Why contract tests?
They catch breaking API changes without full end-to-end environments.
Why not EF Core InMemory provider?
It behaves differently from real databases; use SQLite or Testcontainers.
p5-55.y: I test at several levels: unit tests for logic, integration tests for each service with real dependencies in containers, and contract tests so a service doesn't break its consumers. Then a few end-to-end tests for the critical journeys. Monitoring after release is part of testing too.
p5-55.k: microservices testing, contract testing, integration tests
x: Testing microservices needs several layers, because a lot of the risk is in how services interact, not just inside each one.

Unit tests cover the business logic of each service, quickly and in isolation. Integration tests check each service with its real dependencies, like a real SQL Server and RabbitMQ in containers with Testcontainers, so queries, serialisation and messaging configuration are tested. Contract tests check the agreements between services. With consumer-driven contracts, using a tool like Pact, each consumer defines what it expects from a provider, and the provider's pipeline verifies it still meets those expectations. That catches breaking changes before deployment, without needing every service running together. A small number of end-to-end tests then cover the critical business journeys across the whole system.
For resilience, load tests and chaos tests, like killing an instance or adding latency, verify that timeouts, retries and circuit breakers really work.

In our IRT work, integration tests with WebApplicationFactory and real databases caught the most bugs per effort, and Playwright and Cucumber tests cover critical flows like randomisation for validation evidence. I can explain how contract tests fit into the pipeline.

p5-56.q: Environment variables plus central stores (AWS Parameter Store / Secrets Manager, Azure App Configuration), per-environment values, validation at startup (ValidateOnStart), no secrets in code, and feature flags for runtime toggles.
i: Configuration providers layered in .NET: appsettings, environment, secrets, command line.
IOptionsMonitor for reload without restart.
Version and review config changes like code.
Parameter Store/Secrets Manager plus appsettings per environment; options validated on start.
f: How do you change config without redeploying?
Central store with reload (IOptionsMonitor) or feature flags.
Why validate at startup?
Missing config fails the deployment, not live requests (the UAT lesson).
p5-56.y: Each service reads configuration from appsettings files plus environment-specific values from Parameter Store, and secrets from Secrets Manager. The values are injected into the containers at startup and bound with the Options pattern. Options are validated on start, so a missing value stops the deployment instead of breaking at runtime.
p5-56.k: configuration management, parameter store, secrets manager, options pattern
x: Configuration across many services needs to be consistent, secure and traceable, without rebuilding images for each environment.

The principle is "build once, configure per environment". The same container image runs everywhere, and only configuration changes. Non-secret settings come from environment variables and a central store, like AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store, organised by path, like /irt/production/shipments. Secrets, like database passwords, API keys and certificates, live in AWS Secrets Manager, with encryption, access controlled by IAM, and automatic rotation. They're never in code, images or appsettings files committed to git. The values for each environment are managed through infrastructure as code, so changes are reviewed and versioned. Each service loads its configuration at startup, binds it to typed Options classes, and validates it with ValidateOnStart, so a missing or invalid setting fails the deployment immediately.
For settings that must change without a redeploy, like feature flags, a dynamic source with IOptionsMonitor or a feature flag service works well.
In our services, Secrets Manager and Parameter Store feed ASP.NET Core configuration, and per-vendor SFTP settings are named options. I can explain how we rotate secrets without downtime.

p5-57.q: Structured JSON logs with correlation ids shipped to one place (CloudWatch Logs, OpenSearch, Loki), common fields (service, environment, version, trace id), retention policies, no PHI or secrets, and queries and alerts on top.
i: Serilog or built-in JSON console logger.
Log levels set per category; avoid noisy debug in production.
Source-generated logging ([LoggerMessage]) for performance.
Structured JSON logs with correlation id, service name and environment fields make cross-service queries possible.
f: Why structured logs?
Fields can be queried and aggregated instead of parsing text.
How do you avoid logging PHI?
Redaction (Microsoft.Extensions.Compliance), reviewed log templates, and tests.
p5-57.y: All services write structured JSON logs with the same fields: service name, environment and correlation id. They're shipped to CloudWatch Logs, and we query them with Logs Insights. Because the fields are consistent, one query can follow a request across all services. We never log sensitive data.
p5-57.k: centralized logging, cloudwatch, structured logging, correlation id
x: Centralised logging means all services send their logs to one place, in a consistent format, so you can search across the whole system instead of logging into individual servers or containers.

Each service writes structured JSON logs, with message templates, not free text. Every log line carries common fields: service name, environment, version, and most importantly a correlation id, plus business identifiers like ShipmentId where relevant. Containers write logs to standard output, and the platform ships them to the central store, like CloudWatch Logs, OpenSearch, or Grafana Loki. Then one query can show everything that happened for one request, across every service. Log levels are controlled in configuration, so we can increase detail temporarily without redeploying.

Two rules are critical. Retention policies, so we keep logs as long as needed for support and compliance, but not forever. And never logging secrets or personal or clinical data, which in our domain is a regulatory issue.

In our platform, logs go to Splunk, and since our correlation-id rollout in [2024], a saved Splunk search by correlation id shows a request's full journey across [4] services. That cut support triage from [about an hour to a few minutes]. I can show a sample query.

p5-58.q: An API gateway in front of stateless services on ECS or Kubernetes with autoscaling; database per service with Redis caching; async messaging for events; observability (logs, metrics, traces); CI/CD per service; resilience patterns; and multi-AZ deployment.
i: Start with clear bounded contexts.
Platform templates for new services.
Security: identity provider, mTLS or tokens between services.
Stateless services behind load balancers, autoscaling on CPU or queue depth, caching, and async processing for spikes.
f: What's the first bottleneck usually?
The database; plan indexing, caching and read replicas.
How do you handle cross-service queries?
API composition or read models built from events (CQRS).
p5-58.y: I'd keep services stateless behind load balancers so they can scale out, with autoscaling on CPU or queue depth. Each service owns its database, with caching for hot reads, and heavy or spiky work goes through queues. I'd add resilience patterns, observability from day one, and an API gateway in front.
p5-58.k: scalable architecture, microservices design, system design
x: I'd design it in layers, with scalability and resilience built into each one.

At the edge, an API gateway or load balancer handles routing, TLS, authentication and rate limiting. Behind it, stateless services, so any instance can handle any request, running in containers on ECS or Kubernetes with autoscaling on CPU, requests or queue depth. For data, each service owns its database, so they scale and change independently. A Redis cache takes repeated reads off the database, read replicas serve reporting, and very high-volume, simple access patterns can use DynamoDB.

Between services, I prefer asynchronous events through Kafka or RabbitMQ for workflows. That absorbs traffic spikes and decouples services. The outbox pattern makes publishing reliable, and consumers are idempotent so retries are safe. Synchronous calls are kept for cases that need an immediate answer, with timeouts, retries and circuit breakers.
Across everything: observability with metrics, logs and tracing, CI/CD per service with infrastructure as code, and security with service identities and secrets management.

That's broadly how [the newer IQVIA services I've worked on] run on AWS: ASP.NET Core services on ECS behind an ALB, SQL Server on RDS, ElastiCache, and RabbitMQ with an outbox. Our CIRT platform follows the same ideas on-premise, with IIS, SQL Server, Redis and RabbitMQ. I can draw it on a whiteboard.

p5-59.q: For synchronous request/response needs: UI and partner calls that need an immediate answer (get a study, randomize a subject). REST is simple, widely understood, works with gateways, caches and tools, and has standard semantics for status codes.
i: gRPC considered for internal high-throughput calls, but browser support and tooling favoured REST.
OpenAPI contracts for clients.
REST suits request/response queries from the React UI; HTTP caching and tooling (OpenAPI) are mature.
Messaging was used where the caller didn't need an immediate answer (shipment status updates).
f: Why not GraphQL?
Our clients have stable, known needs; GraphQL adds complexity for little gain.
When would you pick gRPC?
Internal, high-volume service-to-service calls with streaming.
p5-59.y: We chose REST for the React UI and for queries that need an immediate answer, because it's simple, well understood, and has great tooling like OpenAPI. For things like shipment status changes, where the caller doesn't need to wait, we used messaging instead. So REST for request and response, events for reacting to changes.
p5-59.k: why rest, api choice, design decision
x: I chose REST where the caller needs an immediate, definite answer, as part of a request and response interaction.

Typical cases are the UI and partner systems. When a site user opens a study, randomises a subject, or requests a shipment, they need to know the result right now: did it succeed, and what was assigned? That's a natural request-response interaction, and REST over HTTP is the simplest way to model it. It's also universally understood. Front-end developers, external partners and testers all know it, tools like Swagger and Postman make it easy to explore and test, and responses can be cached where appropriate. Errors map cleanly to HTTP status codes and ProblemDetails, and it works through every proxy and firewall.

I didn't choose REST for everything, though. For things that can happen in the background, like updating inventory after a shipment, notifying vendors or sending emails, we use messaging, because the caller shouldn't wait for or depend on those services.
So the decision is really about coupling and timing: REST for "I need the answer now", events for "something happened, whoever cares can react". I can explain why we used Kafka in some cases.

p5-60.q: Kafka fits when producers shouldn't wait for or know their consumers, several consumers need the same events, replay and retention matter, and throughput is high, as with shipment status events consumed by several services.
i: Decoupling: new consumers added without changing producers.
Ordering per key (ShipmentId).
Replay for rebuilding read models or recovering.
Kafka keeps events for replay and multiple independent consumers; REST is point-to-point and immediate.
f: Downside?
Eventual consistency and operational complexity.
Why not RabbitMQ for that?
RabbitMQ deletes messages after consumption; Kafka keeps them for replay by multiple groups.
p5-60.y: For shipment status events, several services needed the same events: supply, notifications and reporting. With REST, the sender would have to call each one and handle each failure. With Kafka, the sender publishes once, each service reads at its own pace, events are kept so we can replay them, and order per shipment is preserved by the key.
p5-60.k: kafka vs rest, event streaming, design decision
x: I'd choose Kafka over REST when the communication is really "something happened" rather than "please give me an answer".

With REST, the producer calls each consumer directly, waits for each one, and needs to know who they are. If a consumer is down, the producer must handle it. With Kafka, the producer publishes an event to a topic once, and doesn't know or care who consumes it. Several consumers can read the same events independently, each at its own pace. Kafka also retains events for a configured period, so a consumer that was down catches up from where it left off, a new consumer can replay history, and you can reprocess events after fixing a bug. And it handles very high throughput.

So Kafka fits when producers shouldn't wait for consumers, multiple services need the same events, replay and retention matter, or volume is high. REST stays the right choice when the caller needs an immediate answer.

For example, shipment status events are needed by inventory, notifications, reporting and audit. Publishing them once to a topic, instead of the shipment service calling four other APIs, removed coupling and made adding a new consumer a non-event for the producer. I can compare Kafka with RabbitMQ too.

p5-61.q: Producers buffer and retry (idempotent producer, delivery timeout) and then fail, so I write events to an outbox in the same transaction as the data and a relay publishes when Kafka is back; consumers resume from committed offsets; alerts fire on producer errors and consumer lag.
i: MSK multi-AZ with replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas 2 reduces outages.
acks=all for durability.
Producers buffer and retry (delivery.timeout.ms); after that, the app must persist to an outbox and resend.
Consumers simply pause and resume from committed offsets when the cluster returns.
f: What does acks=all mean?
The leader waits for all in-sync replicas before acknowledging.
How do you avoid losing events?
Outbox pattern plus idempotent consumers.
p5-61.y: Producers buffer and retry for a while, but if Kafka stays down, the app must not lose events. That's why we use the outbox pattern: events are saved in the database with the business change, and published when Kafka is back. Consumers simply pause and continue from their last committed offset when Kafka recovers.
p5-61.k: kafka unavailable, outbox, resilience, failure handling
x: If Kafka is unavailable, the goal is that nothing is lost, and the system recovers on its own when Kafka comes back.

On the producer side, the Kafka client already buffers messages in memory and retries, up to the delivery timeout. With the idempotent producer enabled, those retries don't create duplicates. But if the outage lasts longer, the produce calls eventually fail. That's why I don't rely on publishing directly in the business transaction. I use the outbox pattern: the event is saved in an outbox table in the same database transaction as the business change, and a background publisher sends it to Kafka. If Kafka is down, events simply wait in the outbox and are published when it recovers. On the consumer side, consumers can't fetch, so they pause, and when Kafka is back, they resume from their last committed offsets, so nothing is skipped.

To avoid outages in the first place, Kafka runs as a multi-broker cluster with topic replication, a replication factor of 3, across availability zones, so losing one broker doesn't stop anything. Managed services like Amazon MSK help here.

And we alert on broker health, consumer lag and outbox size. I care about this because of our RabbitMQ outage in [mid-2024], where publishing without confirms silently lost [about 1,200] updates. The lesson applies to any broker: the producer must know whether the broker really accepted the message. I can explain that story.

p5-62.q: True end-to-end exactly-once across systems is rarely possible; I achieve effectively-once with at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers (inbox table or upserts), the outbox pattern on the producer side, and Kafka transactions for read-process-write within Kafka.
i: Store offsets with data in the same transaction for Kafka-to-DB.
Deduplicate by message id with a unique constraint.
Kafka transactions plus idempotent producers give exactly-once within Kafka (read-process-write).
With external side effects (database, email), use at-least-once plus idempotent consumers (processed-message table).
f: What is Kafka EOS?
Exactly-once semantics using idempotent producers and transactions within Kafka.
Why isn't it end-to-end?
External side effects (DB writes, emails) aren't part of Kafka's transaction.
p5-62.y: True exactly-once across systems is very hard. Kafka has transactions and idempotent producers for exactly-once inside Kafka. But when the consumer writes to a database or sends an email, I use at-least-once delivery with an idempotent consumer: a processed-messages table with a unique message id, so duplicates are skipped. That gives an exactly-once effect.
p5-62.k: exactly-once, idempotent consumer, kafka transactions, deduplication
x: Honestly, true end-to-end exactly-once processing across different systems is rarely achievable. What we build in practice is "effectively once": at-least-once delivery combined with idempotent processing.

At-least-once means a message may be delivered more than once, for example if a consumer processes it but crashes before acknowledging. So the consumer must be idempotent, meaning processing the same message twice has the same effect as processing it once. Common techniques are storing processed message ids in a table, in the same transaction as the business change, and skipping ids already seen; using upserts instead of inserts; and natural unique constraints. On the producer side, the outbox pattern ensures an event is published if and only if the business transaction committed.

Inside Kafka itself, there is exactly-once semantics: idempotent producers prevent duplicates from retries, and Kafka transactions let a consumer read, process and write to another topic, and commit the offset, atomically. But that only applies within Kafka. As soon as you write to a database or call an external API, you need idempotency again.
In our IRT consumers, every message carries an id, and an inbox table makes redelivered messages a no-op. I can show how that table works.

p5-63.q: Requests come through API Gateway or an ALB to .NET services in Docker on ECS, in private subnets across availability zones; data lives in RDS SQL Server and DynamoDB, with ElastiCache for caching; events go through Kafka (MSK) and RabbitMQ; Lambda handles event-driven tasks; S3 stores files; secrets come from Secrets Manager; CloudWatch and Grafana monitor; and IaC plus Azure DevOps pipelines deploy it.
i: Draw layers: edge (Route 53, WAF, ALB/API Gateway), compute (ECS Fargate), data, messaging, observability.
Security: task roles, security groups, VPC endpoints, KMS encryption.
HA: multi-AZ for ALB, ECS, RDS and MSK.
Only describe what you can defend; say which parts you worked on most.
f: Why both RDS and DynamoDB?
Relational data with transactions in RDS; high-scale key-value access patterns (idempotency, sessions) in DynamoDB.
How do vendors connect?
SFTP integrations and APIs through the gateway.
p5-63.y: Our services run as Docker containers on ECS Fargate in private subnets across two availability zones, behind an Application Load Balancer, with API Gateway and SSO in front. Data is in SQL Server on RDS with Multi-AZ, plus DynamoDB for some cases and ElastiCache Redis for caching. Secrets are in Secrets Manager, and we monitor with CloudWatch and Grafana. Deployments go through Azure DevOps.
p5-63.k: aws architecture, ecs, rds, alb, system overview
x: Our CIRT platform itself, the legacy core and the newer .NET APIs, still runs on-premise on IIS with SQL Server, a legacy from before IQVIA acquired Cenduit, while [the newer IQVIA services I've worked on run on AWS]. I'll walk through the AWS side from the request inwards.

Requests from the UI and partners come in through Route 53 DNS to an Application Load Balancer, and API Gateway for some partner-facing APIs, with TLS terminated using ACM certificates and AWS WAF in front. Behind that, our .NET services run as Docker containers on ECS, in private subnets spread across two availability zones, with autoscaling. For data, the core relational data is in RDS SQL Server with Multi-AZ failover, DynamoDB handles some high-volume, simple-access data, and ElastiCache Redis is used for caching. Messaging between services uses RabbitMQ, with an outbox pattern. Lambda handles some event-driven pieces, and S3 stores files, like imports and vendor exchanges.

For operations, logs and metrics go to CloudWatch, with dashboards in Grafana. Secrets are in Secrets Manager, configuration in Parameter Store, services use IAM task roles, and infrastructure is defined as code, deployed through our CI/CD pipelines.
My part is mostly the .NET services, their integration with these components, and the release and monitoring side across [about 5] teams. I can draw it out or go deeper into any part.

p5-64.q: AWS was the company's chosen cloud for IRT; its managed services (ECS, RDS, Lambda, DynamoDB) reduce operational work, it has strong compliance programmes for life sciences, global regions for data residency, and mature IaC and security tooling.
i: Managed services let small teams focus on features.
Compliance: HIPAA eligibility, GxP guidance from AWS.
Honest answer: it was an organisational decision; I can explain the benefits.
Company standard plus managed services (RDS, ECS Fargate, ElastiCache) reduce ops for a small team.
f: Would you pick Azure instead?
Either works; choose by company skills, existing contracts and services.
What's the biggest AWS benefit for you?
Managed infrastructure with fine-grained IAM.
p5-64.y: AWS was the company standard, and its managed services fit a small team: ECS Fargate means no servers to patch, RDS handles database backups and failover, and ElastiCache, Secrets Manager and CloudWatch cover caching, secrets and monitoring. That let us focus on building the product.
p5-64.k: why aws, cloud choice, managed services
x: AWS is IQVIA's standard cloud. Our product started as CIRT at Cenduit, with on-premise servers and an on-premise Azure DevOps Server, and after IQVIA acquired Cenduit, AWS became the standard for IQVIA's newer services, while CIRT itself is still on-premise. So the decision was made at an organisational level, and it fits our product well for a few reasons.

First, managed services reduce operations work. ECS runs our containers, RDS handles SQL Server backups, patching and failover, and Lambda and DynamoDB need almost no infrastructure management. That lets a product team focus on features, not servers. Second, compliance. Clinical trial systems are regulated, and AWS provides the certifications, encryption, audit logging with CloudTrail, and controls that help us meet GxP and data protection requirements. Third, global reach. Trials run in many countries, and AWS regions let us host where the data needs to be. Fourth, mature tooling: infrastructure as code, monitoring with CloudWatch, and solid security services like IAM, KMS and Secrets Manager.
That said, the design principles I use, containers, managed databases, messaging, infrastructure as code and observability, transfer directly to Azure or GCP. I've worked with Azure concepts too.
In my day-to-day work, I use ECS, RDS, ElastiCache, S3, CloudWatch, Secrets Manager and Lambda, mainly around our .NET services. I can go deeper into any of these.

p5-65.q: ECS is AWS-native, simpler, with deep IAM and ALB integration and no control-plane fee; EKS is managed Kubernetes, portable across clouds with a large ecosystem, but more complex and with a control-plane fee. Both can run on Fargate or EC2.
i: ECS fits AWS-only teams wanting less operational load.
EKS fits Kubernetes skills, multi-cloud, or ecosystem needs (Helm, operators, service mesh).
EKS Auto Mode (2024) reduces node management.
ECS is simpler and AWS-native; EKS gives Kubernetes portability and ecosystem at higher operational cost.
f: Which does IRT use?
ECS for production services.
Can you move from ECS to EKS later?
Yes; containers are portable, but deployment definitions change.
p5-65.y: ECS is AWS's own container service. It's simpler, tightly integrated with AWS, and has no control plane cost. EKS is managed Kubernetes. It's more powerful and portable, with a huge ecosystem, but more complex to run. For a team focused on AWS, ECS is often enough, and that's what we use.
p5-65.k: ecs, eks, kubernetes, container orchestration, comparison
x: Both run containers on AWS, but they're different in philosophy and complexity.

ECS, Elastic Container Service, is AWS's own container orchestrator. It's simpler to learn and run, deeply integrated with AWS: IAM task roles, ALB target groups, CloudWatch and Cloud Map work out of the box, and there's no fee for the control plane. The trade-off is that it's AWS-specific. EKS, Elastic Kubernetes Service, is managed Kubernetes. It gives you the standard Kubernetes API and its huge ecosystem, like Helm, operators and service meshes, and your workloads are portable across clouds and on-premises. But Kubernetes is complex to operate well, needs more expertise, and EKS charges per cluster.
Both can run on EC2 instances or on Fargate, without managing servers.

So my rule: if the organisation is all-in on AWS and wants simplicity, ECS. If it's standardising on Kubernetes across clouds, has the skills, or needs that ecosystem, EKS. For [the newer IQVIA services I worked on], ECS was the right choice. A product team can operate it without a dedicated platform team, and it integrates cleanly with the rest of our AWS setup. I can compare it with how we'd model the same services in Kubernetes.

p5-66.q: Fargate is serverless compute for containers on ECS or EKS: you set CPU and memory per task and AWS runs it, with no EC2 instances to patch, scale or secure. You pay per vCPU and GB per second.
i: Each task gets its own isolated kernel boundary and ENI.
Fargate Spot for interruptible workloads at a discount.
Limits: no privileged containers or daemon sets; ephemeral storage up to 200 GB.
You pay per vCPU and memory per second; no EC2 patching, but less control (no daemonsets, GPU limited).
f: Fargate vs EC2 launch type cost?
Fargate costs more per unit but saves operations; EC2 is cheaper at steady high utilisation.
Can you SSH into Fargate?
Use ECS Exec for a shell instead.
p5-66.y: Fargate is the serverless way to run containers on ECS or EKS. I just define the CPU and memory for a task, and AWS runs it without me managing any EC2 servers or patching. I pay per second for what the task uses. All our ECS services run on Fargate.
x: Fargate is AWS's serverless compute engine for containers. It works with both ECS and EKS, and it means you run containers without managing any servers.

Normally, to run containers on ECS, you need a cluster of EC2 instances: you choose instance types, patch the operating system, scale the instances, and pack containers onto them efficiently. With Fargate, you just define the task: the container image, and how much CPU and memory it needs. AWS finds the capacity, runs it in its own isolated environment, and you pay for the CPU and memory the task uses while it's running. There are no instances to patch, scale or right-size.

The trade-offs: it can be more expensive per unit of compute than well-utilised EC2 instances, especially at large steady scale, and you have less control, for example no GPU support and limited host-level access. Fargate Spot can reduce cost for interruptible work.

For most product teams, the reduction in operational work is worth it. It's a big part of why a team our size can run several services without a dedicated infrastructure team, and patching the host is AWS's responsibility. I can explain how we size tasks.

p5-67.q: API Gateway provides API management: auth (JWT, Lambda authorizers), throttling, usage plans, request validation, transformations and direct Lambda integration, priced per request. ALB is a layer 7 load balancer for containers and instances: cheaper at high steady traffic, path and host routing, WebSockets and long connections, priced per hour and LCU.
i: Use both: API Gateway for external APIs, ALB for internal services.
API Gateway has a default 29-second integration timeout; ALB idle timeout is configurable up to 4000 seconds.
API Gateway: auth, throttling, usage plans, request validation; ALB: cheaper at high request volume, path/host routing to containers.
HTTP API (API Gateway v2) is cheaper and faster than REST API when advanced features aren't needed.
f: Which for high-volume internal traffic?
ALB, for cost and simplicity.
Can ALB authenticate users?
Yes, with OIDC or Cognito authentication actions.
p5-67.y: API Gateway is a managed API front door with features like authentication, throttling, request validation, usage plans and API keys, and it's great with Lambda. An ALB is a load balancer that routes HTTP traffic by path or host to containers or servers, and is cheaper at high volumes. Often we use API Gateway for public APIs, and an ALB in front of ECS services.
p5-67.k: api gateway, alb, application load balancer, comparison
x: Both can sit in front of your services and route HTTP requests, but they're built for different jobs.

API Gateway is an API management service. Beyond routing, it gives you authentication, with JWT authorisers or Lambda authorisers, throttling and usage plans with API keys per client, request validation, transformations, caching, and direct integration with Lambda and other AWS services. It's priced per request, and it has limits, like a default 29-second integration timeout and payload size limits. The Application Load Balancer is a layer 7 load balancer. It distributes HTTP and HTTPS traffic across targets like ECS tasks or EC2 instances, with path- and host-based routing, health checks, and WebSocket support. It has fewer API management features, but it's simpler and much cheaper at high, steady traffic, because it's priced by capacity, not per request.
So I use API Gateway when I need API management features, like external partners with keys and quotas, or serverless backends. And ALB for high-volume traffic to containers.
In the newer IQVIA services on AWS, the ALB fronts our ECS services, and API Gateway is used for some partner-facing APIs where we need per-client throttling. I can explain how they can be combined.

p5-68.q: Lambda runs functions on events (API Gateway, S3, SQS, DynamoDB Streams, EventBridge schedules); you pay per request and duration, and AWS manages servers and scaling. It supports managed .NET LTS runtimes (.NET 8 and newer as AWS adds them), plus custom runtimes or container images, up to 15 minutes per invocation and 10 GB memory.
i: Event source mappings poll SQS, Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams.
Cold starts; mitigate with SnapStart, provisioned concurrency, AOT.
Lambda Powertools for .NET for logging, metrics, tracing and idempotency.
Cold starts for .NET can be reduced with Native AOT or SnapStart (supported for .NET managed runtimes since late 2024).
f: Is Lambda good for APIs?
For spiky or low traffic, yes; for steady high traffic, containers are often cheaper.
What runs your Lambda .NET code?
The managed .NET runtime or a container image with the Lambda runtime interface.
p5-68.y: Lambda is AWS's serverless compute. I upload a function, and AWS runs it in response to events, like an HTTP request, a file in S3, or a message in a queue, scaling automatically. I pay only for the time it runs. It's best for short, event-driven tasks. We used one for [shipment notifications].
x: AWS Lambda is serverless compute for running code in response to events, without managing any servers.

You upload a function, in .NET, Node, Python and others, and configure what triggers it: an API Gateway request, a file uploaded to S3, messages in an SQS queue, changes in a DynamoDB stream, or a schedule. AWS runs the function when an event occurs, scales automatically from zero to thousands of concurrent executions, and you pay only for the number of requests and the execution time. Each invocation can run for up to 15 minutes, and you configure memory, which also scales the CPU.

The trade-offs: cold starts, the delay when a new execution environment starts, which matters for latency-sensitive APIs, although SnapStart and provisioned concurrency help. The 15-minute limit. And it's stateless, so state must live elsewhere. For constant high traffic, containers can be cheaper.

So Lambda is great for event-driven glue, scheduled jobs and spiky workloads. In the newer IQVIA services on AWS, Lambda handles some event-driven pieces, like reacting to files landing in S3 and lightweight scheduled tasks, while the core services run on ECS. I can explain how we handle errors with dead-letter queues.

p5-69.q: Lambda concurrency is the number of executions running at the same time. Accounts have a regional limit (1,000 by default, raisable); reserved concurrency guarantees and caps a function's share; provisioned concurrency keeps environments initialised to avoid cold starts.
i: Throttling returns 429 for sync calls; async events retry.
Reserved concurrency of 0 disables a function (an emergency stop).
Protect downstream databases by capping concurrency.
Reserved concurrency caps a function to protect downstream databases; provisioned concurrency keeps instances warm.
f: How do you protect RDS from Lambda scaling?
Reserved concurrency plus RDS Proxy for connection pooling.
Reserved vs provisioned?
Reserved limits and guarantees capacity; provisioned pre-warms environments for latency.
p5-69.y: Concurrency is the number of Lambda instances running at the same time, and each one handles one request at a time. Accounts have a regional limit. Reserved concurrency guarantees and also caps the number for one function, which protects downstream things like databases. Provisioned concurrency keeps instances warm to avoid cold starts.
p5-69.k: lambda concurrency, reserved concurrency, provisioned concurrency
x: Lambda concurrency is the number of executions of your functions running at the same time.

Each concurrent execution needs its own execution environment. If a function takes one second and receives 100 requests per second, it needs about 100 concurrent executions. By default, an AWS account has a regional limit, usually 1,000 concurrent executions shared by all functions. If that's reached, extra requests are throttled. For synchronous callers, they get a 429 error, and for async sources like SQS, the event is retried later.

There are two controls. Reserved concurrency sets aside a portion of the account limit for one function. It guarantees that function capacity, and also caps it, which is useful to protect a downstream database from being overwhelmed by thousands of parallel connections. Provisioned concurrency keeps a number of execution environments initialised and warm, which removes cold starts for latency-sensitive functions, at an extra cost.

Concurrency matters a lot when a Lambda talks to a relational database. Without a cap, a burst of events can open too many connections. So I set reserved concurrency, or use RDS Proxy for connection pooling. I can explain how SQS batch processing interacts with this.

p5-70.q: The timeout is the maximum run time per invocation, configurable up to 15 minutes. Set it a little above the expected duration, set downstream timeouts below it, and move long work to queues, Step Functions or ECS.
i: SQS visibility timeout should be at least 6x the function timeout (AWS guidance).
API Gateway caps synchronous calls at its integration timeout.
Monitor Duration p99 against the timeout.
Max timeout is 15 minutes; API Gateway has its own integration timeout (29 s by default) that can cut off earlier.
f: What happens on timeout?
The invocation is stopped; async events retry; stream batches retry.
Why set downstream timeouts lower?
So the function can handle failures cleanly instead of being killed.
p5-70.y: A Lambda timeout is the maximum time a function can run, from 3 seconds by default up to 15 minutes. If it runs longer, it's stopped. I set it a bit above the normal run time, put timeouts on downstream calls, and remember that API Gateway has its own, shorter timeout. For long jobs, I use a different service, like ECS.
x: The Lambda timeout is the maximum time a single invocation is allowed to run before AWS stops it. It's configurable from 1 second up to 15 minutes, and the default is only 3 seconds.

When the timeout is reached, the function is stopped, and the invocation fails. For synchronous callers, that's an error. For asynchronous events, Lambda retries, and with SQS the message becomes visible again and may be retried. So any work it did before the timeout must be safe to repeat, which means idempotency.

How I set it: a little above the realistic maximum duration, not the maximum allowed, so a stuck call fails fast instead of burning money. It also has to fit with the surrounding timeouts. For example, API Gateway has a 29-second integration timeout by default, so a Lambda behind it doesn't benefit from a 10-minute timeout. And for SQS, the queue's visibility timeout should be longer than the Lambda timeout, or messages get processed twice.

For work that genuinely takes longer than 15 minutes, Lambda is the wrong tool. I'd use Step Functions to split it into steps, or a container task on ECS. I can explain how we handle a timeout mid-process.

p5-71.q: DynamoDB is a fully managed NoSQL key-value and document database with single-digit millisecond latency at any scale, on-demand or provisioned capacity, global tables, streams, TTL and transactions. You design tables around access patterns.
i: Partition key plus optional sort key; GSIs and LSIs for other access patterns.
Strongly consistent reads optional (not on GSIs).
On-demand pricing cut significantly in late 2024, making it the default choice for many.
Design access patterns first; partition key choice determines scalability (avoid hot partitions).
f: When not to use DynamoDB?
Ad-hoc queries, complex joins and reporting; use relational or analytics stores.
Does it support transactions?
Yes, TransactWriteItems across up to 100 items.
p5-71.y: DynamoDB is AWS's fully managed NoSQL key-value and document database. It gives very fast, predictable performance at any scale, with no servers to manage. I design it around access patterns, using partition and sort keys. It's great for simple, high-volume lookups, but not for complex joins or ad-hoc queries.
x: DynamoDB is AWS's fully managed NoSQL database. It stores data as key-value items and documents, and delivers consistent single-digit millisecond latency at practically any scale.

Each table has a primary key, either just a partition key or a partition key plus a sort key. The partition key decides which partition stores the item, so data spreads across many servers automatically, and the sort key orders items within a partition, which allows efficient range queries, like all events for a shipment in time order. You can add secondary indexes for other access patterns. It's serverless: there are no servers to manage, you choose on-demand capacity, paying per request, or provisioned capacity. It also has Streams for change events, TTL to expire items automatically, transactions, and global tables for multi-region replication.
The key difference from SQL is design. You design the table around your access patterns, up front. It's very fast for known lookups, but poor at ad-hoc queries and joins.

In the newer IQVIA services on AWS, the core relational data stays in SQL Server, and DynamoDB is used for simpler, high-volume data like status and event lookups. I can explain partition key design and hot partitions.

p5-72.q: A GSI (global secondary index) has a different partition and sort key, its own capacity, can be created any time and is eventually consistent; an LSI (local secondary index) keeps the same partition key with a different sort key, must be created with the table, supports strong consistency and limits each partition key's item collection to 10 GB.
i: Project only needed attributes to save cost.
Sparse indexes: only items with the attribute appear.
GSI throttling can back-pressure writes to the base table.
GSIs are eventually consistent and can be added anytime; LSIs must be created with the table and share its partition key.
f: When use an LSI?
Rarely; when you need strongly consistent alternate sort orders within a partition.
What is a sparse index?
A GSI on an attribute that only some items have, giving a cheap filtered view.
p5-72.y: A GSI, global secondary index, lets me query by a completely different partition key, and I can add it any time. It's eventually consistent. An LSI, local secondary index, keeps the same partition key with a different sort key, must be created with the table, and can be strongly consistent. I use GSIs for most extra access patterns.
x: Both are secondary indexes in DynamoDB that let you query data by something other than the table's primary key, but they work differently.

A Global Secondary Index, or GSI, can have a completely different partition key and sort key from the table. For example, the table is keyed by ShipmentId, and a GSI is keyed by SiteId and ShipDate, so you can query all shipments for a site. It can be created or deleted at any time, it has its own capacity settings, and it's updated asynchronously, so reads from it are eventually consistent. A Local Secondary Index, or LSI, keeps the same partition key as the table, but uses a different sort key. For example, the same ShipmentId partition, but sorted by status instead of date. It must be created when the table is created, it supports strongly consistent reads, and it shares the table's capacity. It also limits each partition key's data to 10 GB.

In practice, GSIs are much more common, because they're flexible and can be added later as new access patterns appear. LSIs are niche, used when you need strong consistency on an alternative sort order.
When designing, I list the access patterns first, then decide which are served by the table and which need a GSI. I can explain GSI overloading.

p5-73.q: RDS is a managed relational database (SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, plus Aurora) with automated backups, patching, Multi-AZ failover, read replicas and monitoring. An EC2-hosted database gives full control (OS, unsupported features, custom agents) but you own backups, HA, patching and scaling.
i: RDS Custom for SQL Server when you need OS-level access.
Point-in-time restore from automated backups.
Performance Insights for query analysis.
RDS handles backups, patching and Multi-AZ failover; EC2 gives OS control at the cost of running it yourself.
f: When choose EC2?
Features RDS doesn't support or special licensing needs.
What does Multi-AZ do?
Maintains a synchronous standby in another AZ with automatic failover.
p5-73.y: RDS is AWS's managed relational database service for engines like SQL Server and PostgreSQL. AWS handles backups, patching, Multi-AZ failover and monitoring. Running a database on EC2 gives full control of the operating system and settings, but then we do all that work ourselves. For most cases, RDS is the better choice, and we use it for SQL Server.
p5-73.k: rds, ec2 database, managed database, aws
x: RDS, Relational Database Service, is AWS's managed service for relational databases. It supports SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, and Aurora.

With RDS, AWS takes care of the undifferentiated work: provisioning, operating system and database patching, automated backups with point-in-time recovery, monitoring, and high availability. Multi-AZ deployments keep a standby in another availability zone, with automatic failover if the primary fails. Read replicas offload read traffic, and storage can scale. The alternative is installing the database yourself on an EC2 instance. That gives you full control: any version, any configuration, OS-level access, and features RDS doesn't support. But you own everything: patching, backups, monitoring, replication and failover, which takes real database administration effort and is easy to get wrong.
So my default is RDS, unless there's a specific need RDS can't meet, like a feature or setting it doesn't allow, or certain licensing situations.

In [the newer IQVIA services on AWS], SQL Server runs on RDS with Multi-AZ, while the CIRT study databases are on-premise SQL Server. For a regulated system, automated backups and tested failover are a big part of our compliance story, and the team spends its time on query performance and schema, not on patching. I can explain how failover affects the application.

p5-74.q: Redis is in-memory with sub-millisecond reads, rich data structures and TTLs, ideal for caches, sessions, rate limits, locks and leaderboards; a database is the durable system of record with queries, transactions and constraints. Redis complements a database rather than replacing it.
i: Redis persistence (RDB/AOF) exists but isn't a substitute for a primary DB in most designs.
Valkey is the open-source fork after Redis licence changes in 2024; ElastiCache supports it.
Cache invalidation and consistency need design.
Our logout denylist used ElastiCache Redis keyed by jti with TTL equal to token expiry: [~1 ms] lookups.
f: Can Redis lose data?
Yes, on failover or eviction, so cache data must be rebuildable.
Why Valkey?
An open-source, Linux Foundation fork, cheaper on ElastiCache.
p5-74.y: Redis keeps data in memory, so it's extremely fast, often under a millisecond, but it's best for temporary data like caches, sessions and counters. A database stores data durably and supports complex queries and transactions, but is slower. So the database is the source of truth, and Redis speeds up hot reads. Our logout denylist uses Redis with an expiry.
x: Redis and a database serve different purposes, and they usually work together rather than replacing each other.

Redis is an in-memory data store. Because data lives in memory, reads and writes take well under a millisecond. It has rich data structures, like strings, hashes, lists, sets and sorted sets, and built-in expiry with TTL. That makes it ideal for caching, session data, rate limiting counters, distributed locks, leaderboards and short-lived tokens. But it's not designed to be the system of record. Persistence is optional, memory is expensive, and it doesn't support relational queries or rich transactions. A database, like SQL Server, is the durable source of truth. It stores data safely on disk, supports complex queries, joins, constraints and ACID transactions. It's slower per operation, but correct and complete.
The common pattern is cache-aside: check Redis first, and on a miss, read from the database and store the result in Redis with an expiry. The hard part is invalidation when data changes.

In the newer IQVIA services on AWS, ElastiCache Redis caches reference data, and in CIRT, our on-premise Redis holds the token denylist, which our APIs check in about [1 ms] on every request. The real data stays in SQL Server. I can explain the token denylist design.

p5-75.q: Block Public Access, least-privilege bucket policies and IAM, encryption at rest (SSE-KMS) and in transit (HTTPS-only policy with aws:SecureTransport), versioning and Object Lock where needed, short-lived presigned URLs, access logging or CloudTrail data events, and VPC endpoint policies.
i: Disable ACLs (Object Ownership: bucket owner enforced, default since 2023).
New objects are encrypted with SSE-S3 by default since 2023.
Macie to find sensitive data.
f: SSE-S3 vs SSE-KMS?
KMS adds key policies, audit and rotation control.
What is Object Lock?
WORM retention that prevents deletion or overwrite for a period.
p5-75.y: I keep buckets private with Block Public Access, and grant access through IAM roles and bucket policies with least privilege. Data is encrypted at rest with KMS and in transit with HTTPS only. I use presigned URLs for temporary access, turn on versioning for important data, and log access with CloudTrail.
p5-75.k: s3 security, bucket policy, encryption, block public access
x: I secure S3 in layers, starting from "nothing is public unless explicitly needed".

First, access. Block Public Access is turned on at the account and bucket level. Bucket policies and IAM policies follow least privilege: each service's role can access only the specific bucket and prefix it needs, and only the actions it needs. Second, encryption. At rest with SSE-KMS, using a customer-managed key when we need control over key access, and in transit by adding a bucket policy that denies any request not using HTTPS. Third, data protection: versioning, so overwritten or deleted objects can be recovered, and Object Lock for data that must be immutable for compliance. Fourth, temporary access: presigned URLs that expire after a few minutes, for uploads or downloads by clients, instead of opening the bucket. Fifth, network: VPC gateway endpoints, so traffic from our services doesn't go over the internet. And finally, auditing with server access logs, CloudTrail data events, and AWS Config rules that flag misconfigured buckets.
In our platform, CSV imports and vendor files go through S3 with exactly this setup, and uploads use presigned URLs. I can explain how the presigned upload flow works.

p5-76.q: IAM controls who can do what on which AWS resources through users, groups, roles and policies. A user is a long-term identity with credentials (password, access keys); a role is assumed temporarily by services, apps or people and gives short-lived credentials, the preferred approach.
i: Workloads use roles (ECS task role, Lambda execution role, EC2 instance profile).
People use IAM Identity Center (SSO) instead of IAM users.
STS AssumeRole for cross-account access.
Prefer roles with temporary credentials everywhere; users with long-lived keys are a common breach source.
f: Why avoid access keys?
They're long-lived and leak easily; roles rotate credentials automatically.
What is a trust policy?
The part of a role defining who can assume it.
p5-76.y: IAM is AWS's identity and access management: it controls who can do what on which resources. A user is a long-term identity, a person or app with permanent credentials. A role is an identity that's assumed temporarily, with short-lived credentials. I prefer roles everywhere, like ECS task roles, because there are no long-lived keys to leak.
p5-76.k: iam, iam role, iam user, aws security
x: IAM, Identity and Access Management, controls who can do what on which AWS resources. It's made of identities, like users, groups and roles, and policies, which are JSON documents that allow or deny specific actions on specific resources.

An IAM user is a long-term identity, with permanent credentials like a password or access keys. Historically used for people, but today, for humans, we prefer single sign-on through IAM Identity Center, so there are no long-lived keys to leak. An IAM role is an identity without permanent credentials. It's assumed by someone or something, and AWS issues temporary credentials that expire automatically. Roles are used by services, like an ECS task role or a Lambda execution role, for cross-account access, and for federated users.
So roles are almost always preferred. Temporary credentials rotate automatically and can't be accidentally committed to git. Long-term access keys are a common cause of security incidents.

In the newer IQVIA services on AWS, every ECS service has its own task role, with least-privilege policies, like read access to one S3 prefix and one secret. No service has access keys in its configuration. I can explain how the SDK finds those credentials.

p5-77.q: CloudWatch Logs holds detailed event records, searchable with Logs Insights; CloudWatch Metrics are numeric time series (CPU, latency, errors) for graphs and alarms. Logs explain what happened; metrics show trends and trigger alerts cheaply.
i: Metric filters derive metrics from logs.
Embedded Metric Format: emit metrics inside structured logs.
Logs cost per GB ingested; metrics per metric and API call.
Metric filters can turn log patterns into metrics, which alarms can then watch.
f: How long are metrics kept?
Up to 15 months with decreasing resolution.
How do you search logs across services?
Logs Insights queries across multiple log groups.
p5-77.y: CloudWatch Logs stores the detailed text or JSON log events from our services, which I search with Logs Insights to see what exactly happened. CloudWatch Metrics are numbers over time, like CPU, request count or errors, which are cheap to keep and great for dashboards and alarms. I can also turn log patterns into metrics with metric filters.
p5-77.k: cloudwatch logs, cloudwatch metrics, monitoring, aws
x: CloudWatch Logs and CloudWatch Metrics are both part of AWS's monitoring service, but they answer different questions.

Logs are detailed records of individual events: each request, error or business action, with all its context. They're great for investigating what happened, especially with structured JSON logs. CloudWatch Logs Insights lets you query them, for example filtering by correlation id, or counting errors by type. Metrics are numeric time series: CPU usage, request count, latency, error rate, queue depth, measured over time. They're cheap to store, fast to graph, and they're what alarms and autoscaling work on. AWS services publish many metrics automatically, and you can publish custom ones, like shipments processed.

They connect through metric filters, which turn patterns in logs into metrics. For example, counting log lines with level Error, so you can alarm on them. The embedded metric format lets you write metrics inside log lines.

In practice: metrics and alarms tell me that something is wrong, and logs tell me why. In our services, alarms on ALB 5xx rates and latency point us to a problem, and then a Logs Insights query by correlation id shows exactly which request failed and where. I can show a sample query.

p5-78.q: CloudWatch alarms watch a metric against a threshold over periods (e.g. 5xx over 1 percent for 5 minutes) and move between OK, ALARM and INSUFFICIENT_DATA, triggering actions like SNS notifications, autoscaling or EC2 actions.
i: Composite alarms combine conditions to reduce noise.
Anomaly detection bands for seasonal metrics.
"M out of N" datapoints to avoid flapping.
Treat missing data deliberately (notBreaching, breaching).
f: How do you avoid alert noise?
Composite alarms, sensible periods and alerting on symptoms.
Missing data setting for a heartbeat metric?
Treat as breaching so silence triggers the alarm.
p5-78.y: A CloudWatch alarm watches a metric and changes state when it crosses a threshold for a set time, like error rate above two percent for five minutes. It can send a notification through SNS to email or chat, or trigger actions like autoscaling. We have alarms on errors, latency and queue depth for our services.
x: A CloudWatch alarm watches a metric and takes action when it crosses a threshold for a certain period.

You define the metric, the statistic, like average or p95, the threshold, and how many evaluation periods must breach. For example, "ALB 5xx errors above 1 percent of requests, for 5 consecutive minutes". The alarm has three states: OK, ALARM and INSUFFICIENT_DATA. When it changes state, it can trigger actions: send a notification through SNS to email, Slack or a paging tool, trigger autoscaling, or run automation. Composite alarms combine several alarms with AND and OR logic, which reduces noise, for example only paging when both errors are high and traffic is normal. Anomaly detection alarms learn a metric's normal pattern instead of a fixed threshold.

The skill is in making alarms actionable. Too sensitive, and people start ignoring them. Too loose, and you find out from users. I prefer alarms on symptoms users feel, like errors and latency, and a few critical ones like dead-letter queue depth.

In the newer IQVIA services on AWS, we have alarms on 5xx rates, p95 latency, RDS CPU and connections, and any message in a dead-letter queue. After the SQL fix, we added a latency alarm on that endpoint too. For things a metric can't show, like a scheduled job that failed, we record it in a failed-jobs table and alert on it, and AlertWatchDog, our alert engine, emails business alerts like low stock.

p5-79.q: Check scope and recent changes; CloudWatch dashboards and alarms (ALB 5xx, target health, ECS task restarts, RDS CPU and connections, queue depth); Logs Insights by correlation id; traces; then mitigate (rollback, scale) and fix the root cause.
i: Check AWS Health Dashboard for service issues.
CloudTrail for configuration changes.
ECS stopped task reasons (OOM, health check failures).
Start from the dashboard (errors, latency), correlate with recent deploys, then dig into Logs Insights and traces.
f: Where do you see why an ECS task stopped?
The stopped reason in the ECS console or DescribeTasks.
How do you find who changed a security group?
CloudTrail events.
p5-79.y: I start with the dashboards to see what's affected and since when, and check if it matches a recent deployment or a change. Then I look at CloudWatch Logs Insights and traces with the correlation id, and check the health of dependencies like RDS or the message broker. I mitigate first, often with a rollback, then fix the root cause.
p5-79.k: aws troubleshooting, production issue, cloudwatch, incident
x: I troubleshoot production issues in a structured way: understand the impact, stabilise, then find the root cause.

First, scope and timing. Which users or features are affected, since when, and what changed recently, like a deployment, a configuration change or a traffic spike. Then dashboards and alarms: ALB 5xx rates and target health, ECS task restarts and CPU or memory, RDS CPU, connections and slow queries, and queue depth. Next, logs: Logs Insights filtered by errors, or by the correlation id from a failing request, to see exactly where it breaks. ECS service events show things like out-of-memory kills or failing health checks. CloudTrail shows configuration changes, and the AWS Health Dashboard shows if it's an AWS-side problem.

Mitigation comes before the perfect fix. If a deployment caused it, roll back. If it's load, scale out. Then find and fix the root cause, and write a blameless post-incident review with actions, like a new alarm or test.

In our RabbitMQ outage in [mid-2024], shipment status updates stopped arriving for [about 40 minutes]. The broker logs showed a memory alarm blocking publishers, and because we published without confirms, [about 1,200] updates were lost silently. We recovered by replaying the vendor files, then added publisher confirms and alerts so it can't happen silently again. I can walk through that incident.

p5-80.q: Agree RTO and RPO with the business, then pick a strategy: backup and restore (cheapest, slowest), pilot light, warm standby or active-active (fastest, most expensive). Automate infrastructure with IaC, replicate data cross-region, and test restores and failovers regularly.
i: AWS Backup for centralised, cross-region, cross-account copies.
RDS cross-region read replicas or snapshots; S3 cross-region replication; DynamoDB global tables.
Runbooks and game days.
Define RPO/RTO first; strategies range from backup/restore to pilot light, warm standby and multi-site active-active.
f: What's the most common DR failure?
Untested backups that don't restore.
Why cross-account backups?
Protection against account compromise or ransomware.
p5-80.y: First I agree two numbers with the business: RPO, how much data we can lose, and RTO, how fast we must recover. Then I pick a strategy: backup and restore for relaxed targets, pilot light or warm standby for faster recovery, or active-active across regions for near zero. Infrastructure as code helps rebuild quickly, and we regularly test the recovery.
p5-80.k: disaster recovery, rpo, rto, backup, multi-region
x: Disaster recovery design starts with the business, not the technology, by agreeing two numbers.

RTO, the Recovery Time Objective, is how long the system can be down. RPO, the Recovery Point Objective, is how much data loss is acceptable, measured in time. Those decide the strategy and the cost. There are four standard strategies. Backup and restore is the cheapest, with hours of recovery. Pilot light keeps core data replicated and minimal infrastructure ready in another region. Warm standby runs a scaled-down copy of the full system that can scale up quickly. And active-active runs in multiple regions at once, with near-zero RTO, at the highest cost.

The building blocks: automated backups with cross-region copies, data replication, like RDS cross-region read replicas, DynamoDB global tables and S3 cross-region replication, and infrastructure as code, so we can rebuild an entire environment in another region quickly. Then runbooks, and most importantly, regular DR drills, because an untested DR plan is just a hope.
For a clinical trial system, sites must be able to randomise and dispense around the clock, so RTO and RPO are strict and DR is part of our validation. I can explain how a DR drill is run.

p5-81.q: Autoscaling adjusts capacity to load automatically: EC2 Auto Scaling groups, ECS service scaling, DynamoDB capacity, Lambda concurrency. Target tracking (keep CPU near a target) is simplest; step scaling reacts to alarm thresholds; scheduled scaling handles known peaks; predictive scaling uses forecasts.
i: Scale on the right metric (requests per target, queue depth).
Warm-up and cooldown settings matter.
ECS service autoscaling with target tracking on CPU or ALB requests per target.
Scale-in cooldowns and graceful shutdown avoid dropping in-flight work.
f: Why scale in slowly?
To avoid flapping and keep capacity for returning load.
What is predictive scaling?
Using ML forecasts of traffic to add capacity ahead of time.
p5-81.y: Autoscaling adds or removes capacity automatically based on demand. In ECS, I use target tracking, for example keep average CPU around 60 percent or a set number of requests per task. It scales out quickly when load rises and scales in slowly to avoid flapping. The service must be stateless and shut down gracefully.
x: Autoscaling means automatically adjusting capacity to match the load: adding instances when demand goes up, and removing them when it goes down. You get performance during peaks and save cost during quiet times.

In AWS, it applies at several levels: EC2 Auto Scaling groups for instances, ECS service autoscaling for the number of tasks, Lambda, which scales automatically, and DynamoDB capacity. There are a few policy types. Target tracking is the most common: you set a target, like keeping average CPU at 60 percent, or a number of requests per task, and AWS adds or removes capacity to stay near it. Step scaling reacts to alarm thresholds with defined steps. Scheduled scaling handles predictable patterns, like scaling up before business hours. For message consumers, scaling on queue depth works better than CPU.

A good rule is to scale out quickly and scale in slowly, with cooldowns, to avoid flapping. And the application must be ready for it: stateless services, fast startup, health checks, and graceful shutdown.
Our ECS services use target tracking on CPU and request count, with a minimum of two tasks across availability zones for resilience. I can explain how graceful shutdown makes scale-in safe.

p5-82.q: A security group is stateful, attached to instances or ENIs, and has allow rules only; a NACL is stateless, attached to subnets, with allow and deny rules evaluated in number order, so return traffic needs explicit rules. Security groups are the main control; NACLs add a coarse subnet-level guard.
i: Security groups can reference other security groups.
NACLs need ephemeral port ranges for return traffic.
Security groups are stateful and attached to ENIs; NACLs are stateless and apply to subnets.
NACLs need explicit ephemeral-port rules for return traffic.
f: Which to use to block a specific IP?
A NACL deny rule (or WAF).
Stateful meaning?
Return traffic for allowed connections is automatically allowed.
p5-82.y: A security group is a firewall on each resource, like an ECS task or a database. It's stateful, so return traffic is allowed automatically, and it has only allow rules. A NACL is a firewall on the whole subnet. It's stateless, so I need rules both ways, and it supports deny rules. We mostly rely on security groups.
p5-82.k: security group, nacl, network acl, aws networking
x: Both are virtual firewalls in an AWS VPC, but they work at different levels and in different ways.

A security group is attached to individual resources, like an EC2 instance, an ECS task or an RDS database, through their network interfaces. It's stateful: if you allow inbound traffic, the response is automatically allowed back out. It only has allow rules; anything not allowed is denied. And rules can reference other security groups, for example "the database accepts port 1433 only from the API's security group", which is very clean. A network ACL is attached to a subnet and applies to all traffic entering or leaving that subnet. It's stateless, so you must explicitly allow return traffic, usually on ephemeral ports. It has both allow and deny rules, evaluated in numbered order, and the first match wins.
In practice, security groups do most of the work, because they're simpler and more precise. NACLs are a coarse extra layer, for example to explicitly block a known bad IP range for a whole subnet.
In the newer IQVIA services on AWS, the ALB, ECS services and RDS each have their own security group, chained by references, so only the expected path is open. I can draw that out.

p5-83.q: A NAT Gateway lets resources in private subnets make outbound internet calls (package downloads, external APIs) without being reachable inbound. It's managed and highly available within an AZ, so deploy one per AZ, and watch data processing costs.
i: VPC endpoints avoid NAT costs for AWS services (S3 gateway endpoint is free).
IPv6 uses an egress-only internet gateway instead.
Lets private subnets reach the internet outbound; charged per hour and per GB processed.
VPC endpoints for S3/DynamoDB avoid NAT data charges.
f: Why one per AZ?
An AZ failure would otherwise cut outbound access for other AZs, plus cross-AZ charges.
How do you reduce NAT cost?
VPC endpoints for AWS services and caching dependencies.
p5-83.y: A NAT Gateway lets resources in private subnets reach the internet for outbound calls, like downloading packages or calling external APIs, while nothing from the internet can connect in. It's charged per hour and per gigabyte, so for AWS services like S3, I use VPC endpoints instead to save cost.
p5-83.k: nat gateway, private subnet, vpc, aws networking
x: A NAT Gateway lets resources in a private subnet make outbound connections to the internet, while staying unreachable from the internet.

Our ECS tasks and databases run in private subnets, with no public IP addresses, which is good for security. But they still sometimes need to call out, for example to download packages, call an external vendor API, or reach AWS services. The NAT Gateway sits in a public subnet. Private subnets route their internet-bound traffic to it, and it translates the private addresses to its own public IP. Responses come back through it, but nobody on the internet can start a connection inward. It's fully managed and scales automatically. For high availability, you need one per availability zone.

The catch is cost. You pay per hour and per gigabyte processed. A common mistake is sending all traffic to AWS services, like S3, ECR and CloudWatch, through the NAT, which can be expensive. VPC endpoints solve that: gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free, and interface endpoints for other services keep traffic private and often cheaper.
In our VPC, we use NAT Gateways for vendor calls, and VPC endpoints for S3, ECR and Secrets Manager. I can explain how that reduced data transfer costs.

p5-84.q: With an ECS task role (or EKS Pod Identity/IRSA): the SDK credential chain gets temporary credentials automatically, with no access keys in code or images; least-privilege policies scope access, and VPC endpoints keep traffic private.
i: Credentials are served by the container credentials endpoint and rotated automatically.
Separate execution role (ECS agent) from task role (your code).
ECS task roles give each task its own IAM credentials via the container metadata endpoint; the SDK picks them up automatically.
c: var s3 = new AmazonS3Client();   // picks up task role credentials automatically
f: What is IRSA?
IAM Roles for Service Accounts: Kubernetes service accounts mapped to IAM roles via OIDC.
How do you test locally?
Use an SSO profile or assumed role with the same permissions.
p5-84.y: Each ECS task gets an IAM task role. The AWS SDK inside the container automatically picks up temporary credentials for that role, so there are no keys in code or config. The role allows only what that service needs, like reading one secret or one bucket. Traffic to AWS services can go through VPC endpoints.
p5-84.k: ecs task role, iam role, container security, aws credentials
x: Containers should access AWS services using IAM roles, never with access keys baked into images or configuration.

On ECS, each task definition has a task role. When the container runs, ECS provides temporary credentials for that role through a local endpoint, and the AWS SDK's default credential chain picks them up automatically. So in code I just create the S3 or Secrets Manager client with no credentials at all. Those credentials expire and rotate automatically. On EKS, the same idea uses EKS Pod Identity or IRSA, IAM roles for service accounts. Each service gets its own role with least-privilege policies, for example read access to one secret and write access to one S3 prefix. There's also the separate task execution role, which ECS itself uses to pull the image from ECR and fetch secrets at startup.
For network security, VPC endpoints keep traffic to AWS services private, and resource policies, like bucket policies, can require requests to come from our VPC endpoint.

In our platform, no service has an access key anywhere. If a container were compromised, the attacker would only get short-lived credentials limited to that service's permissions. I can show what a task role policy looks like.

p5-85.q: Secrets Manager is built for secrets: automatic rotation (RDS integration), cross-account sharing, versioning, priced per secret per month. Parameter Store holds config and secrets (SecureString with KMS) cheaply with hierarchy, but rotation is manual. I use Secrets Manager for credentials and Parameter Store for configuration.
i: Both integrate with ECS task definitions and .NET configuration providers.
Cache secrets in the app to reduce API calls and cost.
Secrets Manager: rotation, cross-account sharing, per-secret cost; Parameter Store: free standard tier, SecureString with KMS.
We used Secrets Manager for database credentials and Parameter Store for config.
f: Can ECS inject Parameter Store values?
