So it's usually the first choice for AI features built into company products, or anything that touches company or patient data, because it fits the existing governance and security model.

Claude is especially strong at coding and long-context reasoning, and it has excellent agentic tooling, like Claude Code, plus first-class support for MCP, since Anthropic created the protocol. So it's a great choice for developer productivity: working across a codebase, refactoring, writing tests, and driving tools like our deployment server. It's also available through enterprise channels, like AWS Bedrock, when governance requires it.

So why both? Because no single model is best at everything, and different use cases have different requirements. Product features with sensitive data go through the approved enterprise platform, and engineering productivity uses whichever approved tool works best for the task.
The key is designing code behind an abstraction, so we can switch models. My CIRT MCP server already works across Claude Code, Cursor and Copilot unchanged.

p8-33.q: Risks include subtle bugs, insecure patterns (SQL built from strings, missing auth), invented packages or APIs, licence issues, and code nobody understands. I prevent them with review of every line, tests, SonarQube and dependency scanning, verifying packages and APIs exist, secure coding rules in project instructions, and never merging what I can't explain.
i: AI-specific: package hallucination ("slopsquatting").
Example: rejected retry-all suggestion that would duplicate releases.
Risks: insecure patterns (SQL string concatenation, missing auth checks), hallucinated packages, licence issues, and subtle logic bugs.
Controls: same code review and tests as human code, SAST and dependency scanning in CI, and developers accountable for every line.
f: Do you trust AI tests?
I check they assert meaningful behaviour, not just mirror the code.
How do team rules help?
Rules files steer AI toward our secure patterns.
p8-33.y: AI code can contain insecure patterns, like SQL built from strings or missing authorization, made-up packages, licence issues, and subtle bugs. I prevent it by reviewing AI code exactly like human code, running tests, SonarQube and dependency scans in the pipeline, and making each developer responsible for every line they commit.
p8-33.k: ai generated code risks, security, code review
x: AI-generated code has real risks. It can contain subtle logic bugs that look correct. It can use insecure patterns, like building SQL from strings or forgetting an authorization check. It can invent packages or APIs that don't exist, and an invented package name can even be registered by an attacker. It can bring in licensing issues. And maybe the biggest risk is code that gets merged but nobody on the team really understands.

To prevent those problems, I treat AI-generated code like a pull request from a new junior developer. I review every line, I don't accept large changes I can't explain, and I check APIs and packages against official documentation. Tests are required, and for important logic, I write or review tests for the edge cases myself. Then the normal pipeline protects us: compilation with warnings as errors, unit and integration tests, the SonarQube quality gate, dependency vulnerability scanning, and code review by a colleague. For security-sensitive code, like authentication or data access, I'm extra careful.

A real example: Copilot once suggested a retry policy that retried every HTTP call, including the POST that creates a release. A retry after a timeout could have created duplicate releases. I limited retries to safe, idempotent calls and added a test to prove POSTs aren't retried. That's why review matters.

p8-34.q: Separate credentials per environment, with production tools disabled or requiring a different, approval-gated identity; production requires a change request reference and human approval in the release system; the environment is an explicit, validated parameter; confirmations show exactly what will happen; and change windows and audit apply.
i: Default to non-production; production must be opted into explicitly.
Dry-run previews before execution.
Production tools need separate permission and explicit confirmation, and the user's own PAT limits what the agent can do.
Environment allow-lists and dry-run modes; approvals for controlled environments stay in Azure DevOps with humans.
f: What stops a typo deploying to prod?
Allow-listed environment names, confirmation and approval gates.
Should the agent ever hold prod credentials?
Only delegated, short-lived and approval-gated.
p8-34.y: I'd give the agent only the user's own permissions, keep production tools separate with explicit confirmation, and validate the environment against an allow-list, never guessing it. Production approvals stay with humans in Azure DevOps. A dry-run mode shows what would happen first. And every action is logged.
p8-34.k: ai deployment agent security, production safety, approvals
x: To secure an AI deployment agent, I start from one principle: the agent should never be more powerful than the person using it, and it should never be able to deploy to production by accident.

First, identity. The agent acts with the user's own credentials, so it inherits their permissions; there's no shared admin account. Second, environment controls. Environments are an allow-list validated on the server, and production is treated differently: it can require a separate tool, a stronger confirmation, or simply be excluded from the agent. Third, confirmations. Every write action returns a dry-run summary, like "deploy version 4.2.1 to UAT on 5 nodes", and the user must confirm before it runs. Fourth, the platform's own gates stay in place. Production deployments in Azure DevOps require pre-deployment approval from named approvers, and the agent cannot approve anything. Fifth, no destructive tools at all. Sixth, tool outputs are treated as data, not instructions, to resist prompt injection. And everything is logged with the user and a correlation id.

That's exactly how I built the CIRT MCP server. In practice, an accidental production deploy would need the user to confirm the wrong summary, and then a named approver to approve it in Azure DevOps. Those controls are why our quality team was comfortable with it, and why we could go from 6 people to 1.

p8-35.q: The agent creates a request (what, where, version, change request), the system notifies approvers, approval happens in the release tool (Azure DevOps environments) by named people, and the agent polls for the decision and continues or stops, with everything recorded.
i: Timeouts for pending approvals.
Approvers see the agent's summary and evidence.
Use the platform's approval gates (Azure DevOps release approvals) rather than building a parallel system; the agent can only request.
Record approver, time and change request reference.
f: Can the requester approve their own deployment?
Not in production; separation of duties.
How are approvers notified?
Azure DevOps notifications, email or Teams.
p8-35.y: I'd use the platform's existing approval gates, like Azure DevOps release approvals, rather than building a separate system. The agent can only request a deployment and check approval status, never approve. Each approval records the approver, the time and the change request reference.
x: For approval workflows, my principle is to reuse the approval system the organisation already trusts, rather than inventing a new one inside the AI.

In our case, that's Azure DevOps pre-deployment approvals. Controlled environments like production have named approvers configured on the release stage. When a deployment is started, whether by a person or by an agent, Azure DevOps holds it at the gate until an approver approves it there, and it records who approved, when and with what comment. That gives a single, auditable approval trail, which is essential in a GxP environment.

On the agent side, I add a second layer. Write tools in my CIRT MCP server require explicit confirmation from the user, showing a summary of exactly what will happen. A tool can list pending approvals, so the engineer knows who to ask, but there is deliberately no tool that can approve. That separation of duties means the agent can't approve its own work.

If I had to build approvals from scratch, I'd model them as a state machine: requested, approved or rejected, and expired. With role checks, a rule that the requester can't approve their own request, time limits, notifications, and an immutable audit log.
The result is that the AI makes the mechanics faster, but humans remain accountable for decisions.

p8-36.q: An append-only log of every prompt-to-action step: user, agent, tool, arguments (masked), approval reference, result, timestamps and correlation id, stored centrally with retention, and linked to the release system's own audit.
i: Tamper-evident storage (WORM) for regulated contexts.
Include model and tool version for reproducibility.
Log every tool call: user, tool, parameters (secrets redacted), result, duration and correlation id, as structured logs.
Azure DevOps keeps its own history of builds, releases and approvals as the system of record.
f: Why log the prompt?
To understand why the agent acted, with sensitive data masked.
Who reviews audits?
QA, security and release managers as needed.
p8-36.y: I'd log every tool call as structured data: the user, tool, parameters with secrets removed, result, duration and a correlation id, in a central, append-only store. The platform, like Azure DevOps, remains the official record of builds, releases and approvals. Together they show exactly what the agent did and who asked.
x: An audit trail needs to answer four questions for every action: who did it, what exactly they did, when, and what the result was. And the records must be complete and tamper-resistant.

For an AI agent, I log every tool call as a structured event: the user's identity, the tool name, the arguments with secrets masked, whether it was confirmed, the result, the duration, and a correlation id. For deployments, I also record the release id and the related change request. These logs go to a central store, like CloudWatch or a log platform, with retention policies that match our compliance needs, and with no delete rights for normal users, so they can't be quietly changed.

The target system keeps its own audit trail too. Because my CIRT MCP server calls Azure DevOps with the user's own identity, every release, deployment and approval appears under that person's name there. Using ids and timestamps, the two trails can be matched, from the request in the chat, to the API call, to the deployment and its approval.

In a GxP environment, this traceability isn't optional; every change to a validated system must be explainable during an audit. And practically, the logs also help improve the tools, because they show which tools fail and where the agent gets confused.

p8-37.q: Return structured errors, stop rather than guess on write operations, retry only idempotent transient steps, surface the failure and options to the human, keep state so work can resume from the failed step, and record the incident.
i: Never auto-escalate to more powerful actions after failure.
Summarise the relevant log lines.
Tools return clear, structured errors with next steps so the agent can report instead of guessing.
Retries only for idempotent steps (status polls, single-node retry), never blind re-deploys of everything.
f: Should the agent try alternatives automatically?
Only for read-only diagnostics, not writes.
How do you resume?
Per-step state and idempotent steps let you rerun only the failed part.
p8-37.y: Tools return clear, structured errors with suggested next steps, so the agent reports the problem instead of guessing. Only safe steps, like status checks or retrying a single node, are retried, and never a blind redeploy of everything. The user decides what to do next, and the failure is logged.
p8-37.k: failed agent actions, error handling, retries
x: Failed agent actions are normal, so I design for them from the start: the failure should be clear, the system should stay consistent, and a human should decide anything risky.

First, clear errors. A failed tool returns a structured error with what failed, why, and what to try, never a stack trace or secret. For example, "Deployment failed on node 3 at the service install step: disk full." Second, safe retries. Transient errors, like timeouts, are retried automatically with backoff, but only for idempotent operations, and only a limited number of times. Non-idempotent actions are never retried blindly. Third, the agent asks the user. For anything beyond a simple retry, it reports the failure and options, like retry one node or roll back, and waits for the user to confirm. Fourth, a known recovery path. Steps are idempotent, so rerunning is safe, and rollback means redeploying the previous version through the normal approval process. And fifth, everything is logged with a correlation id.

In my CIRT MCP server, when a UAT deployment failed on one node because its disk was full, the status tool pointed straight to the node and step. We cleaned up, used retry_node for just that node, and verified versions. Then I added a pre-check tool, so that failure is now caught before deployment.

p8-38.q: Environment is an explicit, validated parameter (never inferred); per-environment config and credentials; stricter policies as you go up (dev free, UAT confirmed, production approved); consistent tools across environments; and visibility of what's deployed where.
i: Policy table maps environment to required checks.
Version checks prevent deploying untested versions upward.
Environment is an explicit parameter validated against an allow-list, never inferred.
Per-environment configuration and stricter rules (confirmations, approvals) as you move toward production.
f: Why not infer environment from context?
Inference errors are dangerous; explicit is safer.
How do you prevent skipping environments?
Promotion rules: only versions validated in the previous stage.
p8-38.y: The environment is always an explicit parameter, checked against an allow-list, never guessed by the AI. Each environment has its own settings, and the rules get stricter as we move toward production, with more confirmations and human approvals for controlled environments.
x: To design an agent for multiple environments, I make the environment an explicit, validated input, and I let each environment have its own rules, because dev and production carry very different risks.

First, the environment is a required parameter, defined as an enum, like FV, TechOps, UAT and Prod, so the model can't invent a value, and the server checks it against an allow-list. There's no default environment, so the agent never deploys somewhere by assumption. Second, per-environment configuration: each environment maps to its own release stage, node list and settings, kept in configuration, not hard-coded. Third, rules increase with risk. Lower environments can be deployed with a simple confirmation. UAT needs a clear summary and confirmation. Production also needs approval from named approvers in Azure DevOps, and could even be restricted to a separate tool or role. Fourth, permissions come from the user's own identity, so people can only deploy where they're already allowed to. And every summary and log entry states the environment clearly.

That's how my CIRT MCP server works across our environments, each with [4 to 6] nodes. One engineer can safely move a release from FV through TechOps and UAT, and the controls get stricter at each step, without anyone remembering the rules by hand.

p8-39.q: The agent acts with the calling user's identity and roles (delegated, not a super-user); roles map to allowed tools and environments; tools check permissions server-side; tokens are short-lived and scoped; and the agent can never grant itself rights or call admin APIs.
i: On-behalf-of token flows for delegated access.
Audit escalation attempts.
Agent acts with the user's identity and permissions, never a shared super-user.
No tool can change permissions or approvals, preventing escalation via the agent.
f: What is privilege escalation for agents?
Gaining more rights than the user, e.g. via a shared service account.
How does OBO help?
The downstream API sees the real user's identity and permissions.
p8-39.y: The agent acts with the user's own identity and permissions, never a shared super-user account. Tools are grouped by risk and checked against the user's role. And no tool can change permissions or approvals, so the agent can't be used to escalate privileges.
p8-39.k: rbac, ai agents, privilege escalation, permissions
x: RBAC, role-based access control, means permissions are given to roles, and users get roles. For AI agents, the key rule is that the agent must never have more access than the human it's acting for. Privilege escalation happens when the agent runs with a powerful service account, so any user can do more through the agent than they could directly.

So first, I avoid shared high-privilege identities. The agent acts with the user's own delegated credentials, like a personal access token or an OAuth token for that user. The target system, like Azure DevOps, then enforces that user's permissions on every call. Second, I map roles to tools. For example, a viewer can only use read tools, a developer can deploy to lower environments, and production deployment needs a release manager role plus a separate approval. The server checks the role before running a tool. Third, least privilege for tokens: only the scopes needed, with expiry. Fourth, no tools for things nobody should do through the agent, like deleting pipelines or changing permissions. And fifth, approval can't be done by the requester.
In my CIRT MCP server, using each engineer's own token meant Azure DevOps enforced RBAC for us. The agent made people faster, not more powerful, which was key to getting it approved.

p8-40.q: Secrets stay server-side in a vault; tools use them but never return them; the model never sees credentials; tokens are short-lived; secrets are masked in logs and outputs; and access is audited and rotated.
i: Output filters detect secret patterns.
Separate secrets per environment.
Secrets live in the OS credential store or a vault, never in prompts, tool outputs or logs.
Short-lived, least-privilege tokens with rotation.
f: What if the model asks for a secret?
Tools refuse; there's no tool that returns secrets.
Why short-lived tokens?
Leaks expire quickly.
p8-40.y: Secrets stay in the operating system's credential store or a vault, never in prompts, tool outputs or logs. I use short-lived, least-privilege tokens with expiry and rotation. The agent never sees the secret value, only the server uses it to call the API.
x: For an AI agent, the most important rule about secrets is that the model should never see them. The tools use secrets; the model only sees the results.

First, storage. Secrets never go in code, prompts, the repository or configuration files that get committed. For a local agent, like my CIRT MCP server, the user's personal access token comes from an environment variable in their own MCP configuration. For a hosted agent, secrets live in a secrets manager, like AWS Secrets Manager or Azure Key Vault, and are loaded at runtime using a managed identity or IAM role, so there's no secret needed to get the secret. Second, keep them out of the model's context. Tool outputs never include tokens or connection strings, and logs mask sensitive values, so nothing leaks into chat history or log files. Third, least privilege and short lifetimes. Each token has only the scopes it needs and an expiry date, and gets rotated. Where possible, I use delegated OAuth tokens for each user instead of long-lived keys. Fourth, monitoring: unusual usage of a credential triggers an alert, and any leak means immediate revocation.
In the CIRT MCP server, these rules meant that even if a conversation or log was shared, it contained no credentials, and each token only had that one engineer's limited permissions.

p8-41.q: Classify actions by risk (read, reversible write, irreversible or production); run policy checks before execution (environment, permissions, change window, versions); require confirmation or approval by risk level; prefer dry runs; and verify the outcome afterwards.
i: Policy engine (OPA or custom rules) for consistent decisions.
Blast radius assessment: how many nodes or users affected.
Classify tools by risk (read, write, destructive) and apply checks per class: read freely, writes with confirmation, destructive with approval.
Validate parameters deterministically (environment, version format, existence) before execution.
f: Example of irreversible?
Deleting data or dropping a database.
Post-action verification?
Health checks, versions and smoke tests.
p8-41.y: I classify tools by risk: read-only, write, and destructive. Read tools run freely, write tools need confirmation, and destructive actions need human approval or aren't offered at all. Before running anything, deterministic checks validate the environment, version and that the target exists.
p8-41.k: ai safety, action safety, risk classification
x: To evaluate whether an AI action is safe, I look at two things: how much damage it could do, and how sure we are that it's correct. Then the controls match the risk.

First, classify the action. Read-only actions, like getting status or logs, are low risk and can run automatically. Write actions in lower environments are medium risk and need user confirmation. Production changes, or anything irreversible, are high risk and need confirmation plus human approval in the platform. Destructive actions, like deleting data or pipelines, simply aren't available to the agent. Second, validate the specific call on the server. Is the environment on the allow-list, does the id exist, is the user allowed to do this, and is it within limits, like one release at a time. Third, preview: show a dry-run summary of exactly what will happen, so a human can catch a misunderstanding. Fourth, check the context. Was this action triggered by the user's request, or by something the agent read in a log or document? Instructions that come from data are a warning sign of prompt injection. And fifth, make it reversible where possible and log everything.
In my CIRT MCP server, every tool falls into one of these risk levels, which made the safety rules simple to explain and easy for our quality team to approve.

p8-42.q: An orchestrator assigns tasks to specialist agents (planner, deployer, verifier), each with only its own tools; shared state lives in a store, not in prompts; there are step and cost limits and human checkpoints; and every handoff is logged.
i: Verifier agent checks results independently.
Fail-safe: any agent can stop the workflow.
Specialised agents (planner, coder, reviewer) with narrow tools and a coordinator; avoid giving every agent every tool.
Add termination conditions and cost limits; our [AutoGen experiment] used coder plus reviewer agents for unit tests.
f: Why separate tools per agent?
Least privilege and clearer behaviour.
How do you debug it?
Traces of each agent step and handoff.
p8-42.y: I'd use a few specialised agents, like a planner, a coder and a reviewer, each with only the tools it needs, and a coordinator that passes work between them. I'd add limits on steps and cost, and clear stopping conditions. Our [AutoGen experiment] used a coder and a reviewer agent to draft unit tests.
x: A multi-agent architecture splits a complex task across several specialised agents, coordinated by an orchestrator, instead of one agent doing everything.

I'd design it like this. First, clear roles. For example, a planner breaks the goal into steps, a worker agent performs the steps using tools, and a reviewer checks the results against rules or tests. Each agent has focused instructions and only the tools it needs, which is least privilege for agents. Second, an orchestrator that controls the flow: who runs next, what information is passed between agents, and when the task is finished. Patterns can be sequential, like a pipeline, or a supervisor that delegates. Third, limits. A maximum number of steps and a budget for tokens and time, so agents don't loop forever. Fourth, shared state that's explicit, like a task record, not hidden in long conversations. Fifth, human checkpoints before any risky action. And sixth, tracing every step and tool call, so you can debug which agent did what.

I tried this pattern in [an internal experiment] with AutoGen, with a coder agent writing unit tests and a reviewer agent checking them, while I approved the final result. My lesson was that multi-agent setups add cost and complexity, so I only use them when separation, like review, adds real value. Otherwise, one agent with good tools is simpler.

p8-43.q: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework where a client gets an access token to call an API on a user's or its own behalf (authorization code with PKCE, client credentials). OpenID Connect is an identity layer on top that adds the ID token and userinfo endpoint so apps know who the user is: OAuth is for access, OIDC for login.
i: Scopes limit what tokens allow.
OAuth 2.1 consolidates best practices (PKCE required, no implicit flow).
OAuth 2.0 is delegated authorization (access tokens for APIs); OIDC adds authentication with an ID token about the user.
Use Authorization Code with PKCE for browser and mobile apps; client credentials for service-to-service.
f: Can you use OAuth for login without OIDC?
Not safely; access tokens aren't meant to prove identity to the client.
Client credentials flow?
Machine-to-machine without a user.
p8-43.y: OAuth 2.0 is about authorization: it lets an app get an access token to call an API on the user's behalf, without the user's password. OpenID Connect is built on top and adds authentication: an ID token that tells the app who the user is. For browser apps, I use the authorization code flow with PKCE.
p8-43.k: oauth, openid connect, oidc, authorization, authentication
x: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework. It lets an application get limited access to an API on behalf of a user, without ever seeing the user's password. The user signs in at an authorization server, approves access, and the application receives an access token, which it sends to the API. The token has scopes, like read only, and an expiry. For web and mobile apps, the recommended flow is the authorization code flow with PKCE. For service-to-service calls, there's the client credentials flow, with no user involved.
The important point is that OAuth is about access, not identity. It tells the API "this app may do these things", but it doesn't define who the user is.

OpenID Connect, OIDC, is an identity layer built on top of OAuth 2.0. It adds an ID token, which is a signed JWT containing information about the user, like their id, name and email, plus a userinfo endpoint and standard scopes like openid and profile. So the application can actually log the user in.
A simple way to say it: OAuth answers "what can this app access?", and OpenID Connect answers "who is the user?".
In my work, our applications use OIDC to sign users in through single sign-on, and then use the OAuth access token to call our ASP.NET Core APIs, which validate the token and check scopes and roles.

p8-44.q: Single sign-on lets you log in once with a central identity provider and access many apps. The app redirects to the IdP; the user authenticates (with MFA); the IdP returns tokens or a SAML assertion; the app creates its own session; other apps reuse the IdP session without asking for credentials again.
i: Protocols: OIDC (modern) and SAML 2.0 (enterprise legacy).
Single logout is harder; requires end-session or front/back-channel logout.
The app redirects to the identity provider; the user signs in once; the IdP issues tokens or SAML assertions trusted by many apps.
Our SSO cookie fix ([~13 KB→<1 KB]) came from storing too many claims in the cookie.
f: SAML vs OIDC?
SAML uses XML assertions; OIDC uses JSON tokens and suits APIs and mobile.
Why is logout hard with SSO?
Each app has its own session; all must be ended.
p8-44.y: SSO, single sign-on, lets a user log in once and access many applications. The app redirects the user to the identity provider, the user signs in there, and the provider sends back a token that the app trusts. Other apps trust the same provider, so no new login is needed. Our SSO cookie fix came from storing too many claims in that cookie.
p8-44.k: sso, single sign-on, identity provider, oidc, saml
x: SSO, single sign-on, lets a user sign in once with a central identity provider and then access many applications without signing in again.

Here's how it works with OpenID Connect, which is the common modern approach. The user opens an application, which sees there's no session and redirects them to the identity provider, like Microsoft Entra ID or Okta. The user signs in there, maybe with multi-factor authentication, and the identity provider creates its own session for them. It then redirects back to the application with an authorization code. The application exchanges that code for tokens, validates the ID token, and creates its own session, usually a secure cookie. When the user opens a second application, it also redirects to the identity provider, but because the user already has a session there, they're sent straight back, logged in, without typing anything. SAML is an older XML-based standard that works in a similar way.
The benefits are fewer passwords, central security policies like MFA, and one place to disable a user's access.

I've worked on SSO problems in our applications. In one case, users were randomly logged out because the session cookie had grown to [about 13 KB], close to the browser's limit, because we stored all the claims in it. We moved the claims to a server-side session, keeping the cookie [under 1 KB], and the issue stopped.

p8-45.q: SQL injection is when untrusted input changes a SQL query's meaning (e.g. ' OR 1=1 --), letting attackers read or change data. Prevent it with parameterised queries (EF Core, Dapper parameters), never string concatenation, least-privilege database accounts, input validation and allow-lists for dynamic identifiers like sort columns.
i: EF Core FromSql with interpolated strings parameterises safely; FromSqlRaw with concatenation doesn't.
Stored procedures are safe only if they don't build dynamic SQL unsafely.
EF Core and Dapper parameterize by default; FromSqlInterpolated is safe, FromSqlRaw with concatenated strings is not.
c: var rows = await db.Shipments.FromSql($"SELECT * FROM Shipments WHERE SiteId = {siteId}").ToListAsync(); // parameterised
f: Is FromSqlRaw unsafe?
Only when you concatenate input; with parameters it's fine.
Can you parameterise column names?
No; use allow-lists.
p8-45.y: SQL injection is when user input is put directly into a SQL query, so an attacker can change the query, for example to read or delete data. I prevent it by always using parameterized queries. EF Core and Dapper do this by default, and with raw SQL I use interpolated or explicit parameters, never string concatenation.
p8-45.k: sql injection, security, parameterized queries, owasp
x: SQL injection is an attack where user input is treated as part of a SQL command, instead of as data. It happens when code builds a query by concatenating strings. For example, a login query built as "select from users where name equals" plus whatever the user typed. If the attacker types a quote followed by "or 1 equals 1", the query's meaning changes, and it can return every user. Worse inputs can read other tables, change data, or delete it.

The main fix is parameterised queries. The SQL text is fixed, with placeholders like @name, and the values are sent separately. The database always treats them as data, never as code, so injection isn't possible. In .NET, that means SqlParameter with ADO.NET, parameters in Dapper, or Entity Framework Core, which parameterises LINQ queries automatically. One trap: in EF Core, FromSqlRaw with string concatenation is still vulnerable, while FromSqlInterpolated or FromSql parameterise the values.
Extra layers help too: validate input, use a database account with least privilege, so the application can't drop tables, and use stored procedures carefully, without dynamic SQL inside them.
In my code reviews, any SQL built with string concatenation is a blocker, and our static analysis in SonarQube flags it automatically as well.

p8-46.q: HttpOnly stops JavaScript reading the cookie, limiting XSS token theft; Secure sends it only over HTTPS; SameSite (Lax or Strict) stops it being sent on cross-site requests, reducing CSRF; plus narrow Domain and Path, sensible expiry, and the __Host- prefix for strict scoping.
i: SameSite=None requires Secure, for legitimate cross-site use.
Browsers default to Lax when SameSite is missing.
Chrome and Edge treat cookies without a SameSite attribute as Lax (other browsers differ, so always set it explicitly); None requires Secure; use the __Host- prefix to lock cookies to the host.
c:
options.Cookie.HttpOnly = true; options.Cookie.SecurePolicy = CookieSecurePolicy.Always;
options.Cookie.SameSite = SameSiteMode.Lax; options.Cookie.Name = "__Host-irt";
f: What does __Host- enforce?
Secure, Path=/ and no Domain attribute, so only the exact host gets it.
Lax vs Strict?
Strict never sends on cross-site navigation; Lax allows top-level GET navigations.
p8-46.y: HttpOnly stops JavaScript from reading the cookie, which protects it from XSS. Secure means it's only sent over HTTPS. SameSite controls whether the cookie is sent with requests from other sites: Lax or Strict help prevent CSRF, and None requires Secure. For auth cookies, I set all three properly.
p8-46.k: secure cookies, httponly, secure, samesite, cookie security
x: Cookies often hold session or authentication data, so how they're configured matters a lot for security. There are three key attributes.

HttpOnly means JavaScript in the page can't read the cookie. So if an attacker manages a cross-site scripting attack, they still can't steal the session cookie. Every authentication cookie should be HttpOnly.
Secure means the browser only sends the cookie over HTTPS, so it can't be intercepted on an unencrypted connection.

SameSite controls whether the cookie is sent with requests that come from other sites, which protects against cross-site request forgery. Strict means it's only sent when the request starts from your own site. Lax, the default in modern browsers, also sends it for top-level navigation, like clicking a link, but not for cross-site form posts or background requests. None sends it everywhere, but must be combined with Secure, and is needed for some cross-site scenarios, like certain single sign-on flows.
Beyond those, I keep cookies small, set a sensible expiry, and use the __Host- prefix where possible to lock a cookie to one domain.
In ASP.NET Core, I configure these in the cookie authentication options. In our applications, I've also fixed a sign-in problem where a SameSite setting blocked the cookie during an SSO redirect.

p8-47.q: HTTPS, OAuth/JWT validation, authorization policies per endpoint and resource, input validation, rate limiting, a CORS allow-list, no sensitive data in logs, secrets in a vault, dependency scanning, private networking with service identities between services, and monitoring for abuse.
i: OWASP API Top 10 as checklist.
Zero trust between services.
Authentication at the gateway and in each service (zero trust), with scopes and policies per endpoint.
Rate limiting (ASP.NET Core's built-in middleware since .NET 7), input validation, and TLS everywhere.
f: First thing you check in a security review?
Authorization on every endpoint, especially object-level.
How do you secure internal APIs?
Tokens with audiences, network policies and mTLS where needed.
p8-47.y: I authenticate every request, at the gateway and in each service, and authorize with policies and per-record checks. Traffic is encrypted with TLS, inputs are validated, and rate limiting protects against abuse. Services talk using their own identities with least privilege, and secrets are in a vault.
p8-47.k: api security, microservices security, zero trust
x: I secure APIs and microservices in layers, so no single mistake exposes everything.

First, authentication. Every API requires a valid token, usually a JWT from our identity provider using OAuth and OpenID Connect. The API validates the signature, issuer, audience and expiry. Service-to-service calls use their own identities, like the client credentials flow, never shared user tokens. Second, authorization. Policies check roles, scopes, and also ownership, so a user can only access their own data. That object-level check is one of the most common API vulnerabilities. Third, input validation on every request, and parameterised queries against injection. Fourth, transport security: HTTPS everywhere, and internal services in private networks, only reachable through a gateway. Fifth, an API gateway for rate limiting, throttling and central policies. Sixth, secrets in a secrets manager, never in code. Seventh, safe errors: no stack traces or internal details in responses, just a problem details response with a correlation id. And finally, monitoring and logging, plus scanning: static analysis, dependency scanning and container image scanning in the pipeline.

In my projects, that means ASP.NET Core APIs with JWT validation and authorization policies, FluentValidation, SonarQube and image scanning in Azure DevOps, and secrets in secret variable groups for CIRT and AWS Secrets Manager for our AWS services.

p8-48.q: IAM least privilege with roles and SSO, no root use, MFA; private subnets and security groups; encryption with KMS; S3 Block Public Access; Secrets Manager; CloudTrail, GuardDuty, Security Hub and AWS Config; patching; and separate accounts per environment with SCP guardrails.
i: IAM Access Analyzer for unused and external access.
WAF for public endpoints.
Least-privilege IAM roles, private subnets, security groups, encryption with KMS, and CloudTrail plus GuardDuty.
Infrastructure as code reviewed through pull requests.
f: What does GuardDuty do?
Detects threats from CloudTrail, VPC flow and DNS logs.
What are SCPs?
Organisation-level policies limiting what accounts can do.
p8-48.y: I use IAM roles with least privilege, keep services and databases in private subnets with tight security groups, and encrypt data at rest with KMS and in transit with TLS. CloudTrail and GuardDuty monitor activity, and all infrastructure changes go through code and review.
p8-48.k: aws security, iam, encryption, cloudtrail, guardduty
x: To secure AWS resources, I follow least privilege and defence in depth.

First, identity. IAM roles with only the permissions each service needs, no long-lived access keys in code, and no use of the root account. Our ECS tasks and Lambda functions each have their own role. Humans sign in through single sign-on with multi-factor authentication. Second, networking. Services and databases run in private subnets of a VPC. Security groups allow only the specific traffic needed, like the load balancer to the service port, and the service to the database port. Only the load balancer is public. Third, encryption. Data is encrypted at rest using KMS, for S3, RDS and EBS, and in transit with TLS. S3 buckets block public access by default. Fourth, secrets in AWS Secrets Manager, with rotation, read at runtime through the task's role. Fifth, monitoring and audit: CloudTrail records every API call, CloudWatch for logs and alarms, and GuardDuty for threat detection. And sixth, everything defined as code, so security settings are reviewed and consistent, not clicked by hand.
In the IQVIA services I've worked on in AWS, on ECS, Lambda, S3 and RDS, this means each service only touches what it needs, and nothing internal is exposed to the internet.

p8-49.q: dotnet list package --vulnerable, npm audit, plus pipeline tools (Dependabot, Mend, Snyk, Trivy for images); fail on critical issues, update regularly, and track exceptions with expiry dates.
i: NuGet audit runs during restore by default since .NET 8 (with transitive packages audited by default in .NET 9+).
SBOMs for inventory.
dotnet list package --vulnerable, npm audit, and Dependabot or similar in CI with a fail threshold.
Track transitive dependencies; central package management made our upgrades consistent.
f: What is NuGet Audit?
Restore-time vulnerability warnings using the GitHub Advisory Database.
Transitive vulnerabilities?
Vulnerable packages pulled in indirectly; update or pin the fixed version.
p8-49.y: The pipeline scans dependencies on every build, using tools like dotnet list package vulnerable, npm audit, or Dependabot, and fails the build on serious issues. I also scan container images. We update packages regularly, and central package management made it easy to update the same package across all projects.
p8-49.k: dependency scanning, vulnerabilities, npm audit, dependabot
x: Dependency vulnerability scanning checks the third-party packages and container images we use against databases of known vulnerabilities, so we find risky versions before attackers do.

I do it at a few stages. In development and in the pipeline, dotnet list package with the vulnerable flag checks NuGet packages, including transitive ones, and npm audit does the same for front-end packages. Tools like Dependabot, Snyk or OWASP Dependency-Check can run these automatically. For containers, image scanners like [Trivy] or Amazon ECR's scanning check the base image and operating system packages. In the pipeline, these scans run on every build, and the build fails if there are high or critical vulnerabilities, so a vulnerable version can't silently reach production.

Then there's the process. Each finding is triaged: is it actually reachable in our code, how severe is it, and is there a fixed version. Critical ones are fixed straight away; others are planned. When we can't upgrade immediately, we document the risk and the mitigation. Keeping dependencies updated regularly, and using minimal base images, reduces the number of findings in the first place.
In my team, we added image scanning in Azure DevOps during the .NET 10 upgrade, which made our container security much more visible.

p8-50.q: Assess severity and exploitability, contain (WAF rule, disable feature, rotate secrets), fix and test, release through an expedited but controlled change, verify, check logs for exploitation, notify as required, and run a post-mortem with actions.
i: Coordinate with security and compliance teams.
Communicate carefully; don't disclose details publicly before fixing.
Assess severity and exploitability, mitigate quickly (WAF rule, config change), then patch via controlled emergency change.
Root cause and a test or scan rule so it doesn't return.
f: How fast should you patch critical issues?
Per policy, often within days, with containment immediately.
What if data was exposed?
Follow incident and breach notification procedures.
p8-50.y: First I assess how serious and exploitable it is. Then I reduce the risk quickly, for example with a configuration change or a WAF rule, and release a proper fix through an emergency change, still documented. Afterwards I find the root cause and add a test or scan rule so it doesn't come back.
x: When a security vulnerability is found in production, I treat it like an incident: contain it quickly, fix it properly, and learn from it.

First, assess. How severe is it, can it actually be exploited, is it already being exploited, and what data or systems are exposed? I check the logs for any signs of abuse. Second, contain. Depending on the risk, that might mean disabling a feature with a flag, blocking a pattern at the gateway or firewall, rotating exposed credentials, or restricting access, while the real fix is prepared. Third, fix. A proper code or configuration fix, with a test that proves the vulnerability is gone. In a validated environment, the change still goes through our change process, but as an urgent or emergency change, with the right approvals. Fourth, communicate: inform the security team, managers, and if data could be affected, follow the company's process for that. And fifth, learn. A blameless post-incident review, then add a check, like a static analysis rule or a scanning gate, so the same type of issue is caught automatically next time.

A smaller real example: we found that a token kept working for [60 minutes] after logout. We moved to [15-minute] tokens and added a denylist in Redis, checked in [about 1 ms], so logout takes effect immediately.

p8-51.q: Stateless services behind a gateway and load balancer, autoscaled; resource-oriented design with paging, filtering and versioning; caching (CDN, Redis, HTTP caching with ETags); async processing for heavy work; database indexing, read replicas and sharding when needed; rate limiting; and observability.
i: Estimate load: requests per second, payload sizes, read/write ratio.
Connection pooling and async I/O.
Stateless services behind load balancers, caching, pagination, async processing, and rate limits.
Database: indexes, read replicas, and partitioning when needed; observability on p95 latency.
f: First bottleneck?
Usually the database.
How do you handle spikes?
Autoscaling, queues and rate limiting.
p8-51.y: I'd keep the API stateless behind a load balancer so I can add instances, with autoscaling. I'd add caching for hot reads, pagination for lists, async processing for heavy work, and rate limits. For the database, indexes first, then read replicas, and partitioning if needed. And I'd monitor p95 latency and errors.
p8-51.k: scalable api, high volume, system design
x: For a scalable, high-volume REST API, I'd start by clarifying the requirements: the expected traffic, the read-to-write ratio, latency targets, and how consistent the data must be. Then I'd design in layers.

At the front, a load balancer or API gateway handles TLS, authentication and rate limiting. Behind it, the API runs as stateless instances, for example ASP.NET Core in containers on ECS, so I can scale horizontally just by adding instances, with autoscaling on CPU or request count. Being stateless is the key; no session data lives in memory on one server.

For data, I'd use a relational database like SQL Server or PostgreSQL, with good indexes, and read replicas for heavy reads. A Redis cache sits in front for hot data, using cache-aside with sensible expiry. Responses use pagination, and async code throughout, so threads aren't blocked waiting on I/O.
Anything slow, like generating reports or sending emails, goes to a message queue and is processed by background workers, and the API returns 202 Accepted with a status link.
For resilience: timeouts, retries with backoff for safe calls, circuit breakers, and health checks. And for observability: structured logs with correlation ids, metrics and tracing.

That's the same pattern I use at work: stateless .NET APIs behind a load balancer, on IIS for CIRT and on ECS for IQVIA's newer services, with SQL Server, Redis caching and RabbitMQ for background work.

p8-52.q: POST creates a short code (base62 of a unique id, or a random 7-character code with collision check); GET /{code} returns a 301/302 redirect. Store code → URL in a key-value store (DynamoDB), cache hot codes in Redis/CDN, and track clicks asynchronously.
i: 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion codes.
301 is cached by browsers (less analytics); 302 keeps every hit visible.
Prevent abuse: rate limits, malware URL checks.
Short codes via base62 of a unique id; redirect with 301 vs 302 (302 if you need click analytics); cache hot codes in Redis.
f: 301 is permanent and cached; 302 is temporary and keeps hits flowing to you.
How do you generate unique ids at scale?
Distributed id generators (Snowflake-style) or pre-allocated ranges.
p8-52.y: The service takes a long URL and returns a short code, like a base62 version of a unique id, and stores the mapping in a database. When someone opens the short link, it looks up the code and redirects, using a cache like Redis for popular links. I'd add expiry, abuse protection, and click analytics if needed.
p8-52.k: url shortener, system design, base62, redis
x: A URL shortener takes a long URL and gives back a short code, and when someone opens the short link, it redirects them to the original. It's very read-heavy: far more redirects than new links.

The API has two main operations: POST to create a short link, which returns the code, and GET on the code, which returns a redirect. I'd use a 302 redirect if we want to count clicks, because 301 is cached by browsers.

For generating codes, a simple and reliable approach is a unique numeric id, from a database sequence or a distributed id generator, encoded in base 62, using letters and digits. Seven characters give over three trillion combinations. That avoids collisions, unlike random codes, which need a uniqueness check. If custom aliases are allowed, they're checked for uniqueness.
For storage, a key-value table mapping code to URL, plus creation date, owner and expiry. That fits well in a database like DynamoDB, or SQL with an index on the code.
For scale, a Redis cache in front, because popular links are read millions of times, and a CDN can even serve redirects at the edge. The application servers are stateless and scale horizontally.
Extras: click analytics sent asynchronously through a queue, so redirects stay fast; rate limiting; and malicious URL checks.

p8-53.q: Producers publish notification events to a queue; a service applies user preferences and templates, then channel workers (email, SMS, push) send through providers (SES, SNS) with retries, rate limits, deduplication and status tracking.
i: Idempotency keys to avoid duplicate sends.
Priority queues for urgent alerts.
Opt-out and quiet hours.
Queue per channel (email, SMS, push) with retries, templates, user preferences and idempotency keys to avoid duplicate sends.
f: How do you avoid duplicate notifications?
Dedup by event id and idempotent sending.
What if a provider is down?
Retry with backoff or fail over to another provider.
p8-53.y: Other services publish a notification request to a queue. Workers for each channel, like email, SMS and push, pick it up, apply templates and the user's preferences, and send through providers. Failed sends are retried with backoff and then go to a dead-letter queue. An idempotency key prevents duplicate messages.
p8-53.k: notification service, system design, queues, email, sms
x: A notification service sends messages, like emails, SMS and push notifications, on behalf of other services, so each service doesn't have to build that itself.

Other services publish a notification request, either through an API or, better, as an event on a message queue like RabbitMQ or SQS, so they aren't slowed down or blocked if a provider is down. The request contains the user, the template, the data, and the priority.

The notification service then looks up the user's preferences and contact details, like which channels they want and whether they've opted out. It renders the right template for the channel and language, and puts a message on a queue for each channel. Separate workers for email, SMS and push send through providers, like Amazon SES or Twilio. Each worker can scale independently.

Reliability matters. Retries with exponential backoff for temporary failures, a dead-letter queue for messages that keep failing, and idempotency keys so a retry never sends the same notification twice. Rate limits per user prevent spamming, and urgent messages, like security alerts, get a higher-priority queue.
Finally, every notification is stored with its status: queued, sent, delivered or failed, for tracking and support.
We used this kind of pattern for vendor and shipment notifications with RabbitMQ, including retries and a dead-letter queue.

p8-54.q: Services for Orders, Inventory, Payments and Shipping, each with its own database; placing an order runs a saga that reserves stock, takes payment and creates a shipment, with compensations on failure; an order state machine; outbox events; and idempotent APIs.
i: Inventory reservation with expiry.
Read models for order history.
Order state machine with explicit transitions; inventory reservation and payment via sagas with compensations.
Outbox for events; idempotent APIs with keys.
f: What if payment fails after reserving stock?
Compensate by releasing the reservation.
Orchestration or choreography?
Orchestration for clear visibility of order state.
p8-54.y: I'd model the order as a state machine with clear allowed transitions, like created, paid, shipped and delivered. Placing an order reserves stock and takes payment through a saga, with compensating actions if a step fails. Events are published through an outbox, and APIs use idempotency keys so retries don't create duplicate orders.
p8-54.k: order management, system design, saga, state machine
x: An order management system takes an order from creation through payment, fulfilment and delivery, and the most important thing is that it stays correct even when parts of the system fail.

I'd split it into services: an order service, inventory, payment, shipping and notifications, each owning its own database. The order is modelled as a state machine: created, payment pending, paid, packed, shipped, delivered, or cancelled, with clear rules about which transitions are allowed.

The creation API is idempotent, using an idempotency key from the client, so a retry after a timeout never creates two orders. When an order is placed, the system reserves inventory, then takes payment. Because those are separate services, I'd use a saga instead of a distributed transaction. Each step publishes an event, and if a later step fails, like payment being declined, compensating actions run, like releasing the reserved stock.

To publish events reliably, I'd use the outbox pattern: the order change and the event are saved in the same database transaction, and a background process publishes the event to the message broker. Consumers are idempotent, because messages can be delivered more than once.
Reads, like order history, can use a separate read model or cache. And every state change is logged for audit.
Our clinical supply orders and shipments at work follow a similar state-driven, event-based design.

p8-55.q: The client asks the API for a presigned S3 URL and uploads directly (multipart for large files); an S3 event triggers virus scanning and validation; metadata goes to a database; processing runs async with status updates; downloads use presigned GET URLs; lifecycle rules manage storage.
i: Size and type limits in presigned POST policies.
Quarantine bucket until scanned.
Pre-signed S3 URLs so clients upload directly; virus scan and metadata processing via S3 events.
Multipart upload for large files and size limits.
f: Why direct-to-S3?
Offloads bandwidth and avoids API timeouts.
How do you resume large uploads?
Multipart upload with part retries.
p8-55.y: The client asks the API for a presigned S3 URL and uploads directly to S3, so large files don't go through our servers. An S3 event then triggers processing, like virus scanning and extracting metadata. I'd use multipart upload for big files, size limits, and store file details in a database with access control.
p8-55.k: file upload service, system design, s3, presigned url
x: For a file upload service, the main design goal is to keep large files away from the application servers, and to treat every uploaded file as untrusted.

For the upload itself, the client asks the API for permission, and the API checks authentication and validates the file type and size. It then returns a pre-signed URL for S3, so the client uploads directly to S3, and the application servers never carry the bytes. For large files, S3 multipart upload allows parallel parts and resuming after a failure.

The file lands in a quarantine area first. An S3 event triggers processing, for example a Lambda function or a worker. It scans the file for malware, checks the real content type rather than trusting the file extension, and for data files like CSV, validates the content. Only after passing does the file move to the clean bucket, and its metadata, like owner, size, status and location, is stored in a database. The user can see the status: uploaded, processing, ready or rejected, with clear error messages.
Security: buckets are private and encrypted, downloads use short-lived pre-signed URLs, and there are per-user size limits and rate limits.

I built something similar for a CSV import feature. Files up to [5 MB, about 10,000 rows] were validated in the background, users got a clear row-by-row error report, and processing that took [2 to 3 days] by hand now took [under an hour].

p8-56.q: The API stores the job and enqueues it (SQS or RabbitMQ); autoscaled workers process with visibility timeouts, retries with backoff and a DLQ; handlers are idempotent; job status and progress are stored and exposed; scheduling uses EventBridge or cron; and priorities use separate queues.
i: Heartbeats extend visibility for long jobs.
Scale on queue depth.
Queue-based workers, idempotent jobs, retries with DLQ, visibility timeouts and job status tracking.
Scale workers on queue depth.
f: What if a worker crashes mid-job?
The message becomes visible again and another worker retries.
How do you report progress?
Status table updated by workers, polled or pushed via SignalR.
p8-56.y: Jobs go into a queue, and a pool of workers picks them up. Each job is idempotent, so retries are safe, failed jobs are retried with backoff and then sent to a dead-letter queue. I track each job's status in a database so users can see progress, and scale the workers based on the queue length.
p8-56.k: job processing, distributed jobs, workers, queues, system design
x: A distributed job-processing system runs background work, like reports, imports and data processing, across many workers, reliably.

Producers submit jobs through an API or by publishing to a queue, like RabbitMQ or SQS. Each job gets an id and a record in a database with its status: queued, running, succeeded or failed, so users can check progress. Workers are separate processes, for example containers on ECS, that take jobs from the queue. Because work is pulled from a queue, I can scale by adding workers, often autoscaled on queue length.

Reliability is the core of the design. A worker acknowledges a message only after the job is finished, so if a worker crashes, the job goes back to the queue. That means a job can run more than once, so jobs must be idempotent, for example by checking the job's status, or using unique keys. Failures are retried with exponential backoff, and after a maximum number of attempts, the job moves to a dead-letter queue for investigation. Long jobs report progress and use heartbeats or visibility timeouts. Different priorities can use separate queues, and scheduled jobs can use a scheduler like Hangfire or EventBridge.
Monitoring covers queue depth, job duration and failure rates, with alerts.
Our import and notification processing works this way, with RabbitMQ, manual acknowledgements and a dead-letter queue.

p8-57.q: Idempotency keys on every request; a double-entry ledger; payment provider integration with webhooks; a state machine (created, authorised, captured, refunded, failed); reconciliation with provider reports; strong consistency for balances; and PCI compliance by tokenising cards through the provider.
i: Never store raw card numbers.
Webhook signature verification and idempotent handling.
Idempotency keys on every payment request; a ledger with double-entry records; reconciliation with the provider.
Never store card data; use a PCI-compliant provider and tokens.
f: Why double-entry?
Every movement balances, making errors detectable.
How do you handle webhook duplicates?
Dedup by event id.
p8-57.y: Every payment request carries an idempotency key, so a retry never charges twice. I'd keep a ledger with double-entry records and reconcile it with the payment provider daily. Card data is never stored by us, we use a PCI-compliant provider with tokens. Payment status updates come through provider webhooks.
p8-57.k: payment system, system design, idempotency, ledger
x: In a payment system, correctness matters more than anything else: never charge twice, never lose a payment, and always be able to explain every movement of money.

Most companies don't process cards directly; they use a payment provider, like Stripe or Adyen, which keeps card data out of our systems and simplifies compliance. Our payment service stores a payment record with a state machine: created, authorised, captured, failed, or refunded.

The key techniques are these. First, idempotency. Every payment request has an idempotency key, so if the client or our service retries after a timeout, the provider and our database recognise it, and the customer is charged once. Second, reliable state updates. The provider confirms results through webhooks, which are verified with signatures and handled idempotently, because they can arrive more than once or out of order. Third, an append-only ledger, using double-entry records, so balances are calculated from entries that are never edited. Fourth, reconciliation: a daily job compares our records with the provider's reports and flags any difference. Fifth, the outbox pattern, so payment events reach other services reliably.
Security includes tokenised cards, encryption, strict access and full audit logs.
The same principles of idempotency and reconciliation apply to our vendor integrations, where duplicate or missing updates have real consequences.

p8-58.q: Clients keep WebSocket connections to gateway servers; messages are persisted (partitioned by conversation id) and fanned out via a pub/sub layer (Redis or Kafka) to the gateways holding recipients' connections; offline users get push notifications; ordering is per conversation; and read receipts are separate events.
i: SignalR with a Redis backplane or Azure SignalR Service in .NET.
Presence tracked with TTL heartbeats.
WebSockets (SignalR) for live delivery, messages stored per conversation with ordering ids, and offline delivery via push.
Scale out with a backplane (Redis or Azure SignalR Service).
f: How do you scale WebSockets?
Many gateway nodes with a pub/sub backplane.
How do you guarantee order?
Sequence numbers per conversation.
p8-58.y: Clients connect with WebSockets, using SignalR in .NET, for live messages. Messages are stored per conversation with an ordering id, and delivered to online users instantly, while offline users get a push notification and fetch messages later. To scale across servers, I'd use a backplane like Redis.
p8-58.k: chat system, messaging, system design, websockets, signalr
x: For a chat system, the main challenges are real-time delivery, ordering, and handling users who are offline.

Clients keep a persistent connection, usually WebSockets, to chat servers. In .NET, I'd use SignalR, which handles WebSockets and fallbacks. Because users connect to different servers, I need a way to route messages between them. SignalR's Redis backplane, or a managed service like Azure SignalR Service, does that, or a pub/sub system that knows which server each user is connected to.

When a user sends a message, the server first stores it in the database, then delivers it. Messages are stored per conversation, with a sequence number, so they can be shown in order, and that store needs to handle a lot of writes, so a partitioned database like Cassandra or DynamoDB fits well, keyed by conversation. The client sends a unique message id, so retries don't create duplicates.

If the recipient is online, the message goes straight to them. If they're offline, it's stored, and a push notification is sent through a notification service. When they reconnect, they fetch everything after the last message they've seen.
Extras include read receipts, typing indicators, presence with heartbeats, and group chats, which fan out to all members.
Security means authenticated connections, authorisation per conversation, and encryption in transit.

p8-59.q: Services own their data and publish domain events through an outbox to Kafka; consumers are idempotent and update their own read models; sagas coordinate workflows; a schema registry manages contracts; DLQs and replay handle failures; and tracing follows events end to end.
i: Event versioning and compatibility rules.
Monitor consumer lag.
Events as contracts with schemas and versioning; outbox for reliable publishing; idempotent consumers.
Choreography for simple flows, orchestration (saga) when you need visibility.
f: Biggest challenge?
Debugging and consistency across asynchronous flows.
How do you rebuild a read model?
Replay events from Kafka retention or a snapshot.
p8-59.y: Services publish events when something important happens, and other services react to them. Events are versioned contracts with schemas, published reliably through an outbox, and consumers are idempotent. For simple flows, services react on their own, and for longer business processes, an orchestrator saga gives better visibility.
p8-59.k: event-driven, microservices, system design, events, outbox
x: In an event-driven microservices system, services communicate mainly by publishing events about things that happened, like OrderPlaced or ShipmentDelivered, and other services react to them. That keeps services loosely coupled: the publisher doesn't need to know who's listening.

I'd design it like this. Each service owns its own database, and nobody else reads it directly. Services publish events to a broker. Kafka suits high-volume event streams that several consumers read and might need to replay; RabbitMQ suits task-style messages and commands with flexible routing and retries.

To publish reliably, I'd use the outbox pattern: the data change and the event are saved in one database transaction, and a background process publishes the event. Consumers must be idempotent, because events can be delivered more than once, for example by storing processed event ids. For business processes across services, I'd use sagas with compensating actions instead of distributed transactions.

Events need clear, versioned contracts, and changes should be backward compatible. I'd also include a correlation id in every event, with distributed tracing, because following one request across services is otherwise very hard. Dead-letter queues catch messages that keep failing, and I'd monitor consumer lag.

At work, our IRT platform uses RabbitMQ for notifications, cache refresh and integration events, [with Kafka in some newer services], and I learned the importance of publisher confirms the hard way when [about 1,200] updates were lost silently in [mid-2024].

p8-60.q: A central identity provider (OIDC) issues short-lived signed JWT access tokens and rotating refresh tokens; APIs validate tokens locally with cached public keys (JWKS); MFA and risk-based checks at login; sessions and revocation handled with refresh token revocation and denylists; and the IdP scales horizontally behind load balancers.
i: Use a managed IdP (Entra ID, Cognito, Okta, Keycloak) rather than building one.
Rate-limit login endpoints; lockout and bot protection.
Use a proven IdP (OIDC) instead of building one; short-lived access tokens, refresh token rotation, and MFA.
Revocation via a jti denylist like our logout fix ([15-min] tokens, ElastiCache, [~1 ms]).
f: Why validate tokens locally?
No call to the IdP per request, so it scales.
How do you revoke immediately?
Short token lifetimes plus a jti denylist.
p8-60.y: I wouldn't build my own, I'd use a proven identity provider with OpenID Connect. Apps use short-lived access tokens with refresh token rotation, and MFA for users. For logout or revocation, a denylist of token ids in Redis works, like our fix with [15-minute] tokens and about [1 millisecond] checks.
p8-60.k: authentication system, system design, oidc, tokens
x: For a scalable authentication system, my first decision would be to use a proven identity provider, like Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, AWS Cognito, or Duende IdentityServer, rather than writing authentication logic from scratch, because security mistakes there are very costly.

The design uses OpenID Connect for sign-in and OAuth 2.0 for API access. Users sign in at the identity provider, with multi-factor authentication and single sign-on, and applications receive tokens. For web and mobile apps, the authorization code flow with PKCE. For service-to-service calls, the client credentials flow.

For scale, the key is that APIs validate JWT access tokens locally, using the provider's public signing keys, which are cached. So there's no call to the identity service on every request, and the APIs stay stateless and scale horizontally. Access tokens are short-lived, like [15 minutes], and refresh tokens are rotated, so a stolen token is only useful briefly. For immediate revocation, like logout, a small denylist of token ids in Redis can be checked very quickly.
Passwords, if stored at all, are hashed with a strong algorithm like bcrypt or Argon2. Add rate limiting and lockout against brute force, and log every sign-in for audit.
I've implemented exactly that denylist pattern after finding that tokens worked for [60 minutes] after logout. The check in ElastiCache takes [about 1 ms].

p8-61.q: Consistent hashing across cache nodes, replication for availability, LRU eviction and TTLs, the cache-aside pattern, invalidation on writes via events, and protection against stampedes (request coalescing, jittered TTLs, early refresh), monitored with hit ratio and latency.
i: Hot key mitigation: local caches or key replication.
Managed: ElastiCache cluster mode.
Cache-aside with TTLs, consistent hashing across nodes, and invalidation on writes.
Protect against stampedes (HybridCache, released alongside .NET 9, coalesces concurrent requests for the same key).
f: Why consistent hashing?
Adding or removing nodes only moves a small share of keys.
What is a cache stampede?
Many requests missing the same key at once and overloading the database.
p8-61.y: I'd use cache-aside with expiry times, spread keys across nodes with consistent hashing, and invalidate entries when data changes. To avoid a stampede, where many requests rebuild the same entry at once, I'd use request coalescing, which HybridCache in .NET does for us. Redis cluster is the usual choice.
p8-61.k: distributed cache, caching, redis, system design
x: A distributed cache stores frequently read data in memory across several nodes, so applications get fast reads and the database gets less load.

I'd use something like Redis, or a managed version like ElastiCache, rather than building one. The data is split across nodes, using consistent hashing or Redis cluster hash slots, so adding nodes only moves a small part of the keys. Each primary node has replicas in other availability zones for failover.

For how the application uses it, the usual pattern is cache-aside: read from the cache first, and on a miss, read from the database, then store the result with a time-to-live. When data changes, the application updates the database and removes the cache key, so the next read gets fresh data.

There are a few problems to design for. Cache stampede, when a popular key expires and many requests hit the database at once; I'd use locking, so only one request reloads it, or refresh it early. Randomised expiry times, so many keys don't expire together. Eviction policies, like least recently used, with memory limits. And treating the cache as optional: if Redis is down, the application should fall back to the database, maybe more slowly, but still working.
At work, we cache reference data and study configuration in Redis, and our token denylist also lives in Redis, which needs very fast lookups.

p8-62.q: A web UI and vendor APIs go through a gateway with SSO; services for Study setup, Randomization, Supply, Shipments and Subjects; SQL Server per service with audit tables; Kafka and RabbitMQ for events and work queues; SFTP and API integrations; ECS across AZs; observability; and GxP controls (validation, audit trail, change control).
i: Randomization path is strongly consistent and highly available.
Blinding enforced by authorization.
Vendor integrations isolated behind adapters so a vendor change doesn't touch core services.
Multi-AZ ECS and RDS for availability; reporting off read replicas.
f: Most critical service?
Randomization and kit assignment.
How do you keep audit consistent?
Audit written in the same transaction as changes.
p8-62.y: Users and vendors come in through a gateway with SSO. Behind it are services for study setup, randomization, supply, shipments and subjects, each with its own SQL Server database and audit tables. Kafka and RabbitMQ carry events and work queues, vendor integrations use SFTP and APIs, everything runs on ECS across availability zones, and GxP controls like validation and audit trails apply throughout.
p8-62.k: clinical trial platform, irt design, system design, architecture
x: Our platform supports clinical trials: setting up studies, randomising patients, and managing the supply of trial medication to sites around the world. A study here means one clinical trial set up in our IRT system, with its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and user roles. At a high level, I'd describe it like this.

Users and vendors come in through an API gateway, with single sign-on for users and secure APIs and SFTP for vendors. Behind that, there are services for each business area: study setup in our Admin console tooling, a transaction engine for screening, randomisation and dispensing, supply, external eConsent status, notifications, and DARM for drug accountability. The UI is component-based, with older screens in Angular and newer modules in React with TypeScript. Each service owns its own SQL Server database, with audit tables that record every change, because in a GxP regulated environment, every change must be traceable.

Services communicate through APIs for things that need an immediate answer, like randomising a patient, and through messaging for everything else. Kafka carries events like shipment status updates that several services consume. RabbitMQ handles work queues, like processing vendor files and sending notifications. Vendor integrations with depots use SFTP and APIs, with validation and retries. Redis caches reference data.

Everything runs in containers on AWS ECS across availability zones, with CloudWatch and Grafana for monitoring. Releases go through Azure DevOps pipelines with FV, TechOps and UAT environments, approvals and change control, and I built the CIRT MCP server to automate those deployments, which cut them from 6 hours to 2.
The key design themes are reliability, auditability and compliance, because real patients depend on the medication arriving.

p8-63.q: Scale stateless services horizontally with autoscaling, cache reads, and move heavy work to queues. For the database: indexes and query tuning first, then read replicas, caching, vertical scaling, archiving old data, partitioning, and finally sharding by study or tenant if needed.
i: CQRS read models for reporting.
Connection pooling and RDS Proxy.
Scale stateless services horizontally; cache reference data; move heavy work to queues.
Database: indexes and query tuning first, then read replicas, then partition by study.
f: Why shard by study?
Most queries are within one study, so shards stay independent.
When add read replicas?
When reads dominate and slight lag is acceptable.
p8-63.y: I'd scale services horizontally since they're stateless, cache reference data, and move heavy work to queues. For the database, first tune queries and indexes, then add read replicas for reporting, and finally partition data, for example by study, if one database can't keep up.
p8-63.k: scaling, database scaling, read replicas, partitioning
x: To scale the architecture, I'd first find the real bottleneck using metrics, rather than guessing. Then I'd scale each layer appropriately.

The application layer is the easy part if services are stateless. No session data in memory, so I can run more instances behind the load balancer, with autoscaling on CPU, request count, or queue length for workers. Slow work moves to background workers through queues, so the API stays fast.

The database is usually the harder part. Step one is optimising: the right indexes, efficient queries, avoiding N plus one problems, and short transactions. That often gives the biggest win. I once took a query from [8 to 12 seconds] to [under 300 milliseconds] just by fixing the query and the index. Step two is caching hot data in Redis. Step three is read replicas, sending read-only queries to replicas while writes go to the primary, accepting slight replication delay. Step four is scaling up the database server, which is simple but has limits. Step five, only if really needed, is partitioning data, for example archiving old data, or sharding by a key like study or tenant, which adds a lot of complexity.
I'd also split data by service, so each service owns its own database and they scale independently. And I'd load test before going live, to know the limits before users find them.

p8-64.q: Caching for reference data (countries, depots, study configuration), sessions and token revocation, and read-heavy lookups. Kafka for high-volume event streams with multiple consumers and replay (shipment status). RabbitMQ for work queues and commands with per-message acks and retries (notifications, file processing). Synchronous APIs where the caller needs an immediate answer (randomize, get study).
i: Choose per interaction based on coupling, latency and delivery needs.
Caching: reference data and permissions (Redis).
Kafka: shipment status events with replay and many consumers; RabbitMQ: task queues (notifications, reports).
Synchronous APIs: user-facing reads and commands needing an immediate answer, such as randomization.
f: Why not Kafka for everything?
Work queues with per-message retry and priorities fit RabbitMQ better.
What shouldn't be cached?
Data needing strict consistency like slot allocation.
p8-64.y: I'd use caching for reference data and permissions, in Redis. Kafka for shipment status events that many services consume and we may need to replay. RabbitMQ for task-style work like notifications and reports, with retries per message. And synchronous APIs for user-facing reads and commands that need an immediate answer, like randomizing a patient.
p8-64.k: caching, kafka, rabbitmq, synchronous apis, design choices
x: I choose between these based on what each interaction needs: an immediate answer, a task to be done, or an event that others care about.

Synchronous APIs are for when the user or caller needs an answer right now. For example, viewing a study, or randomising a patient, where the site staff wait for the result. They're simple, but they couple services together in time, so I keep synchronous chains short and use timeouts and circuit breakers.
