x: The virtual DOM is a lightweight JavaScript description of what the UI should look like. When state or props change, React calls your components again to produce a new description, compares it with the previous one, and then applies only the necessary changes to the real browser DOM. That comparison is called reconciliation. Updating the real DOM is the expensive part, so doing the minimum there keeps apps fast, while you write code as if the whole UI is redrawn each time.

React's diffing uses two simple assumptions to be fast. If an element's type changes, for example from a div to a span, or from one component to another, React throws away the old subtree and builds a new one. And for lists, it uses keys to know which item is which between renders.

That's why keys matter. A key should be a stable, unique id from the data, like a site id. If you use the array index, and items are inserted, removed or sorted, React matches the wrong items, which can cause wrong input values, lost focus, or unnecessary re-rendering. Keys also let you reset a component on purpose, by changing its key.
Modern React does this with its Fiber architecture, which can split rendering work and prioritise urgent updates, like typing.
Angular has the same concern with track in @for loops, so in both parts of our IRT UI, lists are always tracked by a real id.

p12-7.q: Both hooks hold state inside a component, and the choice is about how complex the state and its updates are.
p12-7.k: usestate, usereducer, reducer, dispatch, complex state, react state
x: Both hooks hold state inside a component, and the choice is about how complex the state and its updates are.

useState is the simple one. You get a value and a setter. It's ideal for independent, simple values, like whether a dialog is open, the text in a search box, or a selected tab. When the new value depends on the old one, I use the function form of the setter, so updates are never lost.

useReducer is better when the state has several related fields that change together, or when there are many different kinds of updates. You write a reducer function that takes the current state and an action, like "row added" or "file validated", and returns the new state, and components call dispatch with actions. All the update logic is in one pure function, which is easy to read and easy to unit test without rendering anything, and impossible states are easier to avoid. With TypeScript, I type the actions as a discriminated union, so each action's payload is checked.
A real example: a multi-step import screen, with steps, a selected file, validation results and errors, fits useReducer much better than five separate useState calls that must be kept in sync.
If that state needs to be shared across many components, I move the same reducer pattern into Redux Toolkit, which is on my resume and uses exactly this model.

Dates are sent as ISO strings, and enums as strings, so they're readable on both sides. And contract tests check the important responses.

This mattered a lot in our project, because our React modules call the newer .NET 9 and 10 APIs, while the legacy portal still uses older endpoints. [We type the React API calls from the APIs' OpenAPI documents], so the front end always agrees with the backend.

In React, the built-in way is React.lazy with a dynamic import. You wrap a component, like the reports page, in React.lazy, and the bundler, like Vite or webpack, automatically puts it into its own chunk. You render it inside a Suspense boundary, which shows a fallback, like a spinner, while the chunk downloads.

The most effective place to split is by route: each major page or module loads separately, so a site user never downloads the admin screens. Inside pages, heavy components that aren't immediately visible, like charts, editors or large dialogs, are also good candidates. You can prefetch likely next routes on hover or when the browser is idle, so navigation still feels instant. And I check the result with a bundle analyser, because sometimes one large library is the real problem.
Errors while loading a chunk, for example after a new deployment, should be caught by an error boundary with a reload option.
It's the same idea as lazy-loaded routes in Angular. In our IRT UI, both the older Angular modules and the newer React modules load per feature, so users only download what their role needs.

The setup is simple. configureStore creates the store with good defaults, like the dev tools and checks for accidental mutations. Each feature has a slice, made with createSlice, which defines its initial state and reducers in one place, and generates the action creators automatically. Inside reducers, you can write code that looks like it mutates state, because Immer turns it into immutable updates. createAsyncThunk handles async logic, like calling an API, with pending, fulfilled and rejected actions.

With TypeScript, I define a RootState type from the store, and an AppDispatch type, and then create typed hooks, useAppSelector and useAppDispatch, which every component uses. That way, selectors and dispatched actions are fully checked, and state shapes are defined once with interfaces.

RTK Query is the data-fetching part of Redux Toolkit. You define an API with endpoints, and it generates hooks, like useGetShipmentsQuery, with caching, deduplication and cache invalidation through tags, similar to React Query.

I keep Redux for truly global client state, like the selected study, user preferences or a multi-step workflow, and let a query library handle server data. That keeps the store small, which matters in a large app like our IRT UI.

p13-6.q: A clinical trial, which we also call a clinical study, is a research study in people that tests whether a new medicine or treatment is safe and works. Before a medicine can be approved by regulators, like the FDA in the US or the EMA in Europe, it has to go through these trials.

x: A clinical trial, which we also call a clinical study, is a research study in people that tests whether a new medicine or treatment is safe and works. Before a medicine can be approved by regulators, like the FDA in the US or the EMA in Europe, it has to go through these trials.

There are a few key players. The sponsor is usually the pharmaceutical company that owns the drug and pays for the trial. A CRO, a contract research organisation like IQVIA, runs parts of the trial and provides technology like IRT. Sites are the hospitals and clinics where patients, called subjects, take part, run by investigators and site staff.

Every trial follows a protocol, a detailed plan that defines who can join, what treatments are compared, how patients are assigned to them, what happens at each visit, and what is measured. Trials usually run in phases. Phase one tests safety in a small group, phase two tests whether it works and the right dose, and phase three compares it with standard treatment in thousands of patients across many countries.
To keep results fair, most trials are randomised, meaning a computer decides by chance which treatment each patient gets, and blinded, meaning patients and doctors don't know which one it is.

In IRT, a study is that one trial set up in our system: its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and users. Our software makes sure the randomisation and the drug supply follow the protocol exactly.

p13-7.q: A study is one clinical trial set up in our IRT. It holds everything the system needs to run that trial exactly as the protocol says.

It contains protocol metadata, like the study name, phase and blinding. Countries, sites and depots, with which depot supplies which sites. Treatment arms and cohorts, with cohort caps that limit enrolment per arm. The randomisation design: the method, like permuted blocks or minimisation, the stratification factors, and the pre-generated randomisation lists. The visit schedule, with windows and what's dispensed at each visit. Dynamic forms and call flows, meaning the exact screens and questions a site sees, like screening questions. Kit types and packaging. Supply settings, like buffer levels, resupply triggers, and expiry and do-not-ship rules. Roles and permissions, including who is blinded and unblinded. Alert and notification templates, reports, and integrations, like feeds to EDC or eCOA systems.

Technically, each study gets its own SQL Server database, provisioned from a common model schema of [about 560] tables, while shared master data, like users and global settings, lives in a global master database. That separation keeps every trial's data isolated, which suits a regulated product.

The configuration is built by our internal team using our study-build tooling, which I call the Admin console, then validated and transferred between environments, from build to UAT to production, with a diff review. The site portal and APIs then read the configuration at runtime, so one codebase serves very different trials.

On screen, the site user signs in through Keycloak single sign-on, picks the study and site, and opens the subject flow, either in the legacy ASP.NET MVC portal or the newer React screens. The screens are dynamic: the forms, fields and visit and call flows are designed by our internal study build team in the designer tool, stored as configuration in the study's own database, and rendered at runtime. The site enters the subject's details, and the system runs the eligibility rules, which come from form validations plus configurable rule expressions for study-specific logic. If the subject is ineligible, they're recorded as a screen failure, with the reason. If eligible, they get a subject number and can move on to randomisation. Valid consent matters too: where the study uses eConsent, the consent status received from the external eConsent system must be valid before screening or randomisation can proceed.

Behind the screens, the request goes to our .NET APIs, which call the transaction engine in the legacy core, and everything is written to the study database with full audit history: who did what, when, and the old and new values.

p13-10.q: Randomisation assigns each eligible subject to a treatment arm by chance, following the protocol. In our IRT, a study is one clinical trial set up in the system, with its arms, strata and pre-generated randomisation lists.

x: Randomisation assigns each eligible subject to a treatment arm by chance, following the protocol. In our IRT, a study is one clinical trial set up in the system, with its arms, strata and pre-generated randomisation lists.

The flow goes like this. The site user, signed in through Keycloak single sign-on, opens the subject in the legacy MVC portal or the newer React screens and confirms randomisation. The request goes to our .NET APIs, which call the transaction engine API, a wrapper around the transaction engine in our legacy .NET Framework core. The transaction engine checks the subject's state and eligibility, works out the stratum from the stratification factors, checks cohort caps, and takes the next available slot from the right randomisation list, or uses minimisation if the study is dynamic. The assignment, any kit allocated at that visit, and the audit records are written to the study's own SQL Server database in one transaction.
Blinding is protected throughout: blinded users see only a kit number, never the arm. Only unblinded roles, or an emergency unblinding, reveal treatment.

After randomisation, post-randomisation hooks trigger integration flows, through MuleSoft today, to sync the result to systems like the sponsor's EDC or eCOA, and events on RabbitMQ drive notifications and cache refreshes. [I added idempotency on the API side, so a retried request returns the original result instead of randomising twice.]

p13-11.q: A randomisation list is a pre-generated sequence of treatment assignments, created by a statistician before a clinical trial starts. In our IRT, a study is one trial set up in the system, and its lists are uploaded through our randomisation list management feature, then used slot by slot.

x: A randomisation list is a pre-generated sequence of treatment assignments, created by a statistician before a clinical trial starts. In our IRT, a study is one trial set up in the system, and its lists are uploaded through our randomisation list management feature, then used slot by slot.

Block randomisation, or permuted blocks, keeps the arms balanced as enrolment goes on. For a two-arm study with a one-to-one ratio and a block size of four, each block contains two of each arm, in a random order. So after every four subjects, the arms are perfectly balanced, and the block size is kept hidden from sites so nobody can guess the next assignment.

Stratification makes sure balance also holds within important groups, called strata, like age band, region or disease severity. Each combination of stratification factors gets its own list, or its own blocks, and a subject takes the next slot from their stratum's list. Lists can be central, or blocked by site or stratum.

Dynamic randomisation, or minimisation, is the alternative when there are too many strata for lists. Our system implements the Pocock-Simon method: for each new subject, it calculates which arm would minimise imbalance across all factors, and assigns it with a high probability, keeping some randomness.

On top of that, cohort caps limit how many subjects can enrol per arm or cohort. In our code, permuted block and Pocock-Simon are separate implementations behind one randomisation interface, chosen by the study's configuration.

p13-12.q: Re-randomisation means assigning a subject who is already randomised to a new treatment arm, at a later point in the study, because the protocol says so. In our IRT, a study is one clinical trial set up in the system, and re-randomisation is configured per study.

Common reasons are crossover designs, where subjects switch to another treatment after a period, a second treatment stage, where responders and non-responders are randomised again, or moving into an extension phase.

Technically, it's a follow-up transaction in our transaction engine. It releases the subject's old assignment, according to the study configuration, and draws a new slot or arm, from a separate list or using the study's crossover configuration, which defines which arms a subject can move to. The subject keeps the full history of both assignments, and every re-randomisation is audited with the reason, who did it and when.

The same safeguards as the first randomisation apply. The subject must be in the right state for that stage. A subject can only be re-randomised once per stage, enforced in the database, not just the UI. Blinding is protected, so blinded users never see either arm. And kit dispensing after re-randomisation must match the new arm.
[I worked on making the re-randomisation request idempotent, so a double click or a network retry can't re-randomise a subject twice.]

In our IRT, a study is one clinical trial set up in the system, and the important design point is that our eConsent is integration-based: IRT doesn't capture the signature itself.

x: Informed consent is the patient's documented agreement to take part in a clinical trial, after the risks and procedures are explained. eConsent means doing that electronically. In our IRT, a study is one clinical trial set up in the system, and the important design point is that our eConsent is integration-based: IRT doesn't capture the signature itself.

Consent is taken in an external eConsent system. Our IRT receives the consent status through integration flows, over SFTP files or APIs. These were built in MuleSoft and are being migrated into a .NET data transfer API. IRT stores the status per subject, along with the consent documents, versions and status configuration for the study.

IRT then uses that status to enforce the protocol. Screening and randomisation are gated on valid consent, so a site can't randomise a subject whose consent is missing, withdrawn or out of date. And consent events trigger notification emails, for example when a new consent version requires re-consent after a protocol amendment, or when a subject withdraws consent.
Because it's regulated, every status change received is stored with full audit history, never overwritten, so we can show exactly what consent status applied when a transaction happened.

The integration is where the engineering challenge is: files arrive late or out of order, so processing has to be idempotent, ordered by event time, and monitored, with alerts if an expected file doesn't arrive.

The journey goes like this. The site pharmacist records accountability entries per kit: units used, unused, returned or damaged. The site creates a return shipment back to the depot, entering the courier's air waybill. The depot confirms receipt. A clinical research associate, the monitor, does a reconciliation review and resolves any discrepancies through a discrepancy approval. Finally, kits are marked for destruction, with the destruction location recorded and a final approval.

Kit statuses follow that lifecycle: available, in transit, received at site, dispensed, partially used, returned, in transit to depot, received at depot, reconciled and destroyed, plus damaged, lost, quarantined and blocked.

Technically, DARM was built in the legacy ASP.NET MVC portal, and it's the module we're migrating to React with TypeScript right now, starting with accountability entry and return shipments, on top of new .NET APIs. There's also a mobile path through our MuleSoft layer.
Every step is a validated state change with an audit record, and blinding is protected, so blinded users never see which arm a kit belongs to.

In a double-blind study, neither the subject nor the site staff know. In our IRT, a study is one trial set up in the system, and blinding is enforced at the role and field level.
p13-15.k: blinding, unblinding, emergency unblinding, double blind, unblinded users, code break, blinded roles
x: Blinding means the people in a clinical trial don't know which treatment a subject is receiving, so expectations can't bias the results. In a double-blind study, neither the subject nor the site staff know. In our IRT, a study is one trial set up in the system, and blinding is enforced at the role and field level.

Blinded users never see the arm or kit contents. They see only kit numbers, and kits for different arms look identical. Only specific unblinded roles, like an unblinded pharmacist or a supply manager, can see treatment information, and the APIs and screens are filtered by those roles, not just hidden in the UI. Reports and notifications respect the same rules.

Emergency unblinding is for a medical emergency, when a doctor must know the treatment to treat the patient. In our system, it's a privileged transaction. Only authorised roles can perform it, a reason is mandatory, and depending on the study's configuration, the user must re-authenticate with an electronic signature. The system records who unblinded, when and why, in an unblinding history table, can notify the sponsor, and can exclude the subject from further dosing.
The engineering principles are least privilege, enforcement in the backend, and a complete, tamper-proof audit trail, because unblinding is one of the first things an inspector checks.

p13-16.q: Dispensing and resupply make sure every subject gets the right drug at the right visit, and every site has enough stock without waste. In our IRT, a study is one clinical trial set up in the system, with its kit types, depots and supply settings.

x: Dispensing and resupply make sure every subject gets the right drug at the right visit, and every site has enough stock without waste. In our IRT, a study is one clinical trial set up in the system, with its kit types, depots and supply settings.

Dispensing: at a dispensing visit, the system assigns specific kit numbers that match the subject's arm, without revealing the arm to blinded users. It picks kits that won't expire before the next visit, using the study's expiry and do-not-ship rules. It also supports replacement kits, for example if a kit is damaged, partial dispensing, and dose management, where the dose changes during the trial, which is one of our newer React and .NET 10 modules.

Resupply: each dispensing reduces the site's inventory. Our supply and drug management logic, in the legacy core, applies the study's resupply strategy, either min and max levels, or predictive, which looks at upcoming visits. When stock drops below the trigger, it generates a shipment from the right depot. Sites confirm receipt, which makes the kits available.

Around that, there are depot and site inventory views, shipment tracking, material block and quarantine for problem lots, relabelling to extend expiry, and material forecasting dashboards, which are fed by a scheduled SSIS job. Depots and couriers are connected through integrations, mostly SFTP file exchanges.
The goal is no subject ever missing a dose, while keeping expensive drug waste low.

Before go-live, the study is built by our study build team in our Admin console tooling, in the build environment. They test its behaviour with the simulator, the configuration is reviewed against the protocol, and it goes through user acceptance testing, often with the sponsor, with documented evidence, because it's GxP. Then it's transferred to production with our transfer tool, which shows a diff of every configuration change for review, and the study-transfer safety guard I built checks things like the target study's status and the user's role. Then sites are activated, initial shipments go out, and the first subject can be screened.

A protocol amendment is a change to the trial's plan while it's running, like adding a country, a new arm, an extra visit, or a new consent version. It's handled like a controlled release: configured and tested in the build and UAT environments first, reviewed through the diff, and transferred to production, never edited directly in production. Existing data is never overwritten; history tables keep what applied when. Some changes trigger follow-up actions, like re-consent notifications, or adjusted resupply levels.
The guiding rule is that a live study's existing data must never be damaged by a configuration change, which is exactly why the transfer guard and diff review exist.

A typical schedule has a screening visit, a randomisation visit, which is often day one, and then treatment visits, like week two, week four and so on, until an end-of-treatment and a follow-up visit. For each visit, the configuration says whether drug is dispensed, which kit types and how many, whether returns are collected for drug accountability, and the allowed time window, like plus or minus three days around the target date.

IRT uses it in several ways. It guides the site through the right steps at each visit, using visit flows and call flows designed in our study designer tool and rendered dynamically on screen. It checks windows and warns, or blocks, if a visit is too early or too late. It picks kits that won't expire before the next visit. It forecasts upcoming demand per site, which drives predictive resupply. And unscheduled visits are supported, for example to replace a damaged kit.

Technically, the visit schedule is configuration in the study's own database, built by our study build team and transferred between environments with a diff review, and visit data for each subject is stored with full audit history.

The cost is operational: hundreds of databases to migrate consistently, so deployments must be automated and verified.

Inside a study database there are three groups of tables. Configuration: countries, sites, arms, cohorts, strata, randomisation lists and parameters, visits, kit types, supply settings and forms. Transactional data: subjects, subject visits, randomisation assignments, kits with their status and location, shipments, accountability entries and returns, and consent status received from eConsent. And audit: history tables for changes, an unblinding history, and a data audit log with who, what, when, old and new values, and the reason for change.

Design rules: status changes are validated and recorded, never silently overwritten; allocation uses transactions and locks so a slot can't be used twice; and blinded data is only exposed to unblinded roles. EF Core handles most access in the new APIs, with tuned SQL where performance matters.

ARM templates and Bicep map to CloudFormation and the CDK, while Terraform works on both.

The concepts are the same: store settings and secrets outside code, build once, promote through stages with approvals, use identities instead of keys, and monitor everything. In practice, we still use Azure DevOps to deploy into AWS, and AlertWatchDog, our Quartz-based alert engine, would map to EventBridge Scheduler, SQS, Lambda and SES on AWS.

A variable group in Azure DevOps is a named set of variables, like UAT-Shipments, that pipelines link to. Values are injected into the pipeline at run time, and secret variables are masked in logs. They can also be linked to Azure Key Vault. Access is controlled by Azure DevOps security, and changes are recorded in its history. The key point is that variable groups are a pipeline feature: the values exist at deploy time, and the pipeline has to push them into the application's configuration.

In AWS, Systems Manager Parameter Store holds configuration as a hierarchy of paths, like /irt/uat/shipments/timeout, with versions, and SecureString values encrypted with KMS. Secrets Manager is for real secrets, like database passwords, with automatic rotation. The big difference is that the application reads them at run time, using its IAM role, so the pipeline doesn't need to know secret values at all.

So the mapping is: plain variables to Parameter Store, secret variables and Key Vault to Secrets Manager, and Azure DevOps permissions to IAM policies. During our transition, a setting once existed in a variable group but was missing in UAT Parameter Store, so I added a parity check to the CIRT MCP server that compares both before each deployment.

In Azure DevOps, a build pipeline produces an artifact, and a release pipeline deploys it through stages, one per environment, like FV, TechOps, UAT and production. CodePipeline is the orchestrator: a pipeline with stages, like source, build, and deploy per environment, and actions in each stage. Approvals map to manual approval actions, which pause the pipeline until a person approves, often with an SNS notification. CodeDeploy does the actual deployment, to EC2 instances, on-premise servers with an agent, Lambda, or ECS, with rolling or blue-green strategies and automatic rollback on alarms.

The ideas match one to one: build once, promote the same artifact, approvals before controlled environments, and automated rollback. The differences are mostly about tooling and identity: AWS uses IAM roles instead of service connections. [We haven't moved our releases to CodePipeline], because our release history and approvals in Azure DevOps are part of our validation evidence, so we deploy to AWS from Azure DevOps instead.

x: Our product started as CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, and its code lived in Team Foundation Server, using TFVC, Team Foundation Version Control. [It moved to Git, in Azure DevOps Server, after IQVIA acquired Cenduit,] as part of modernising the CIRT platform.

The core difference is centralised versus distributed. TFVC is centralised: there's one server copy, you check files out and in, branches are heavy server folders, and many operations need the server. Git is distributed: every developer has the full history locally, branches are cheap and fast, and work happens offline, with pull requests to review and merge. Git made pull requests with policies, like required reviewers, a passing build and a SonarQube quality gate, the normal way of working, which fits GxP well, because every change is reviewed and traceable.
A TFVC-to-Git migration needs some care: deciding how much history to bring, mapping branches, handling large binary files, and retraining people on branching and merging.

On the hosting side, Azure Repos is Git inside Azure DevOps. In Azure DevOps, a service connection stores how to connect to an external system, like Azure, a Docker registry, Kubernetes, or AWS. Pipelines reference it by name, and access to it is controlled, so only approved pipelines can use a production connection. The weak version stores long-lived secrets, like a client secret or an access key, inside it. The better version uses workload identity federation, with OpenID Connect, so no secret is stored.

In AWS, the equivalent identity is an IAM role. The pipeline, or the build agent, assumes a role and receives short-lived credentials, valid for maybe an hour. The role's trust policy says who may assume it, like a specific OIDC identity or a specific EC2 instance profile, and its permission policy says exactly what it can do, like pushing to one ECR repository and updating specific ECS services. Every call is recorded in CloudTrail.

So the mapping is: a service connection becomes a role that the pipeline assumes, plus a trust policy. The principles I follow are the same on both sides: no long-lived keys, one identity per environment, least privilege, and production identities usable only by approved pipelines.

Azure Service Bus offers queues, for one consumer processing each message, and topics with subscriptions, for publish and subscribe, all in one service. It has rich features: sessions for ordered processing per key, dead-letter queues, scheduled messages, duplicate detection, and transactions.

In AWS, those are split. SQS provides queues. Standard queues give nearly unlimited throughput with at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering, and FIFO queues give strict ordering per message group and deduplication, which is like Service Bus sessions. Dead-letter queues are built in. SNS provides topics for publish and subscribe, and the common pattern is SNS fanning out to several SQS queues, one per consumer, which matches a Service Bus topic with subscriptions. EventBridge adds event routing with rules, and Amazon MQ runs RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ as a managed broker.

In CIRT, we actually use RabbitMQ, with retry and dead-letter exchanges, and Kafka only in some newer AWS services, rather than SQS or Service Bus. But the same rules apply on any of them: idempotent consumers, because delivery is at least once, dead-letter queues with alerts, and confirmations on publish. I added publisher confirms to RabbitMQ after an outage in [mid-2024].

Its job is to tell the right people when something important happens or needs attention in a study, meaning one clinical trial set up in our system. Each study has its own alert definitions, configured during study build: for example, a shipment dispatched or delivered, low stock at a site, a subject randomised, a cohort cap reached, or a drug accountability action waiting for approval.

On each run, AlertWatchDog evaluates those definitions against the study's data and, for each alert that fires, publishes a message to RabbitMQ through our shared messaging library. Notification consumers pick the messages up, render the right HTML email template, from [about 48] templates managed by our notification API, and send the email through SMTP to the recipients for that study and role.

A few design points matter in a regulated product. Blinding: blinded recipients never get treatment information, so templates and recipient lists respect roles. Reliability: the RabbitMQ consumers use retry and dead-letter exchanges, and failed scheduled runs are recorded in a failed-jobs table, so nothing is silently lost. Audit: what was sent, to whom and when is recorded.
[My work on it was mainly on the notification side: moving sending to a .NET 9 consumer, adding retry and dead-letter handling, and adding new alert types for drug accountability.]

Every function has exactly one trigger, which is what starts it. Common triggers are HTTP, for small APIs and webhooks, timer, for schedules written as CRON expressions, queue triggers, for Azure Storage queues or Service Bus, blob triggers, when a file is uploaded, and Event Grid or Event Hubs triggers, for events and streams. The trigger also passes in the data, like the queue message.

Bindings are a declarative way to connect to other services without writing client code. An input binding reads data, like a blob or a table row, and an output binding writes data, like putting a message on a queue or saving a document, just by returning a value or setting a parameter. They remove boilerplate, though for complex logic I still use the normal SDK clients with dependency injection.

Functions live inside a Function App, which shares configuration, the hosting plan and scaling. In .NET, the isolated worker model is the current approach: functions run in their own process, with normal dependency injection, middleware and logging.
In that proof of concept, a timer trigger replaced the Quartz job, a queue output binding wrote each alert, a queue trigger sent the email, and Durable Functions handled escalation.

Normal functions are short and stateless, but some processes need to run many steps, wait for events, or take hours. Durable Functions lets you write that as an ordinary-looking C# method, and the framework saves its progress, so it survives restarts and doesn't pay for waiting time.

There are three kinds of functions. An orchestrator function describes the workflow: call this activity, then that one, wait for an event, set a timer. Activity functions do the actual work, like calling an API or sending a message. And a client function starts orchestrations, for example from an HTTP or queue trigger. Under the hood, it uses event sourcing: the orchestrator replays its history to rebuild its state, which is why orchestrator code must be deterministic. No direct I/O, no DateTime.Now, and no random numbers inside it; those go in activities, or use the context's own time.

Common patterns are function chaining, fan-out and fan-in to run work in parallel and combine results, async HTTP APIs for long jobs, monitors that poll until a condition is met, and human interaction, waiting for an approval with a timeout. Durable entities hold small pieces of state.

I used the human interaction pattern in [my Azure Functions proof of concept of AlertWatchDog, our alert engine]. When an alert fires, the orchestration notifies the team channel, waits [15 minutes] for someone to acknowledge, and if nobody does, escalates to the on-call person. On AWS, the equivalent is Step Functions.

The hosting plan decides cost, scaling and cold starts. The Consumption plan is pure serverless: you pay per execution, it scales to zero, and it scales out automatically, but it has cold starts, execution time limits, and no private network access. The Flex Consumption plan is the newer version, with faster scaling, virtual network integration, and the option of always-ready instances to avoid cold starts. The Premium plan keeps pre-warmed instances, so there are no cold starts, supports virtual network integration and longer runs, but you pay for the minimum instances all the time. And the Dedicated plan runs functions on an App Service plan, like a normal web app, which suits predictable load or existing spare capacity.
To reduce cold starts in code: keep the package small, avoid heavy work at startup, reuse clients like HttpClient as singletons, and use the isolated worker model with ready-to-run compilation.

For [my AlertWatchDog proof of concept], [I chose the Premium plan], mainly because it needed private network access to reach our on-premise SQL Server, and pre-warmed instances meant alerts were never delayed by a cold start. On AWS, the matching ideas are Lambda's provisioned concurrency and VPC configuration.

For cold starts, Lambda has provisioned concurrency and SnapStart, while Azure has Premium pre-warmed instances or always-ready instances on Flex Consumption. For workflows, Durable Functions is code-first, and Step Functions defines a state machine.
Identity maps cleanly: a managed identity in Azure is the execution role in Lambda. Monitoring is Application Insights versus CloudWatch and X-Ray.
My view: the concepts transfer directly, so I'd pick whichever cloud the rest of the system lives on.

p14-29.q: Both run code on a schedule, without a server running cron. In [my Azure Functions proof of concept of AlertWatchDog], a timer trigger replaced the Quartz job and ran [every five minutes], and on AWS the equivalent is EventBridge Scheduler.

x: Both run code on a schedule, without a server running cron. In [my Azure Functions proof of concept of AlertWatchDog], a timer trigger replaced the Quartz job and ran [every five minutes], and on AWS the equivalent is EventBridge Scheduler.

In Azure Functions, a timer trigger is defined on the function itself, with a CRON expression that includes seconds. It runs in the function app's time zone, UTC by default. The runtime makes sure only one instance runs each scheduled occurrence, even when the app scales out, and there's an option to run on startup, which should stay off in production. If the app was down, it can catch up on a missed run.

In AWS, EventBridge Scheduler is a separate service that invokes a target on a schedule. The target is often a Lambda function, but it can also be an ECS task, an SQS queue, a Step Functions state machine, or many other AWS APIs directly. It supports cron and rate expressions, time zones with daylight saving, one-time schedules, a flexible time window to spread load, retries, and a dead-letter queue for failed invocations. The older way was EventBridge scheduled rules, which still work but have fewer features.
So the main difference is that in Azure the schedule belongs to the function, while in AWS it's a separate resource that can trigger many kinds of targets.
Whichever I use, the job itself must be idempotent and safe to run twice, because any scheduler can occasionally retry.

p14-30.q: Both let a function process messages from a queue automatically, with retries, so the producer and the consumer stay decoupled. In [my Azure Functions proof of concept of AlertWatchDog], every alert went onto a queue, and a queue-triggered function sent the email. On AWS, that would be SQS triggering Lambda.

x: Both let a function process messages from a queue automatically, with retries, so the producer and the consumer stay decoupled. In [my Azure Functions proof of concept of AlertWatchDog], every alert went onto a queue, and a queue-triggered function sent the email. On AWS, that would be SQS triggering Lambda.

In Azure Functions, a queue trigger listens to an Azure Storage queue, or a Service Bus queue. The runtime polls the queue, fetches messages in batches, and calls the function once per message. If it throws, the message becomes visible again and is retried, [five times by default], and then it's moved to a poison queue, which you must monitor.

In AWS, Lambda uses an event source mapping on the SQS queue. Lambda polls the queue for you and invokes the function with a batch of messages, up to a batch size and batching window you configure. If the function fails, the whole batch returns to the queue after the visibility timeout, unless you report partial batch failures, which I always enable, so only the failed messages are retried. After the maximum receive count, SQS moves the message to a dead-letter queue. You can also cap concurrency for the mapping, to protect a downstream database.

The same rules apply on both: handlers must be idempotent, because delivery is at least once, the visibility timeout must be longer than the function's timeout, and the dead-letter or poison queue needs an alarm.

p14-31.q: Both orchestrate multi-step, long-running workflows reliably: they keep state between steps, retry failures, wait for events or people, and survive restarts. I used Durable Functions in [my AlertWatchDog proof of concept] for escalation, and on AWS the equivalent is Step Functions.

The biggest difference is how you define the workflow. Durable Functions is code-first: the orchestrator is a C# method, with normal loops, conditions and try-catch, and the framework replays it from its history to rebuild state. That's natural for developers, but the code must be deterministic. Step Functions is definition-first: you describe a state machine in Amazon States Language, as JSON or with the visual designer, with task, choice, parallel, map and wait states. Each step can call Lambda or, directly, over two hundred AWS service APIs, like DynamoDB, SQS or ECS, often without writing a function at all. Its console shows each execution visually, which is great for support.

For waiting on people, Durable Functions uses external events with a timer, and Step Functions uses a task token with a heartbeat or timeout. Step Functions has two modes: Standard, for long workflows up to a year with exactly-once steps, and Express, for high-volume, short workflows.

In [my AlertWatchDog proof of concept], escalation re-notified if a pending approval wasn't actioned within [a set time], then escalated to a supervisor. In Step Functions, that's an SNS notification, a wait with a task token and timeout, and a choice state.

p14-32.q: Both turn telemetry into notifications when something is wrong. [My Azure Functions proof of concept of AlertWatchDog] used Application Insights for its own health, and our AWS services use CloudWatch alarms, so I use both.

x: Both turn telemetry into notifications when something is wrong. [My Azure Functions proof of concept of AlertWatchDog] used Application Insights for its own health, and our AWS services use CloudWatch alarms, so I use both.

In Azure, alerts are part of Azure Monitor. An alert rule watches a signal: a metric, like failed requests or response time from Application Insights, a log query, written in KQL, that runs on a schedule, or an availability test that pings an endpoint. When the condition is met, the rule calls an action group, which defines who is notified and how: email, SMS, Teams through a webhook, a function, or a logic app. Smart detection can also flag unusual failure rates.

In AWS, a CloudWatch alarm watches a metric, with a statistic like average or p95, a threshold and a number of evaluation periods, and has three states: OK, ALARM and insufficient data. On a state change, it typically publishes to an SNS topic, and SNS fans out to email, chat, a paging tool or a Lambda. Metric filters or Logs Insights turn log patterns into metrics, composite alarms combine conditions to reduce noise, and anomaly detection learns normal patterns.
So an alert rule maps to an alarm, an action group maps to an SNS topic with subscriptions, and KQL log alerts map to metric filters or Logs Insights.
The principle is the same: alert on symptoms users feel, make every alert actionable, and always alert when a monitor goes silent.

If a node fails, it can fetch a summary of the failing step's logs and, with confirmation, retry just that node. Finally, a verification tool checks that every node runs the release version.
Every call is written to an audit log. The result: deployments went from 6 hours to 2, and from 6 people to 1.

p15-2.q: The CIRT MCP server is a .NET 8 console application that lets AI assistants run builds, releases and multi-node deployments on our on-premise Azure DevOps Server. It's built in layers, using the normal .NET hosting model.

At the bottom is a typed Azure DevOps client, built on IHttpClientFactory, with the engineer's personal access token, timeouts, and Polly retries with backoff only for safe, read-only calls. Our install scripts are wrapped the same way. Logging uses Serilog, writing to standard error and a rolling file, never to standard output, because stdout carries the protocol.
It's packaged as a .NET global tool. The result: deployments went from 6 hours to 2, and from 6 people to 1.

p15-6.q: MCP messages are JSON-RPC, and a transport is how they travel between the AI host's client and the server. There are two standard options.
p15-6.k: mcp transports, stdio, streamable http, sse, http transport mcp, local vs remote mcp server
x: MCP messages are JSON-RPC, and a transport is how they travel between the AI host's client and the server. There are two standard options.

With stdio, the host starts the server as a local child process and they exchange messages through standard input and output. It's simple and fast, there's no network port and nothing to host, and the server runs with the local user's identity and environment. The catch is that each user runs their own copy, and anything written to standard output must be protocol messages only.

Streamable HTTP is for remote servers. The client sends JSON-RPC messages as HTTP POST requests to one endpoint, and the server can reply with a single JSON response or stream several messages using server-sent events. It replaced the older HTTP plus SSE transport, which needed two separate endpoints. A remote server can serve many users, so you need proper authentication, which the MCP spec defines with OAuth, plus all the usual concerns: TLS, scaling and monitoring.

For the CIRT MCP server, built in C# on .NET 8, I chose stdio. Each engineer runs it locally inside the company network, with their own Azure DevOps personal access token, so every action happens with their permissions and shows their name, and there was no shared server to secure or operate. That fitted a team tool well.
If we rolled it out across the whole organisation, I'd move to Streamable HTTP with OAuth, for central updates, audit and monitoring.

x: The CIRT MCP server, which I built in C# on .NET 8, spends most of its time calling our on-premise Azure DevOps Server, so resilience and logging were essential.

For HTTP, I built a typed Azure DevOps client registered with IHttpClientFactory, so connections are pooled properly and configuration is in one place. A delegating handler adds the engineer's personal access token and a correlation id to every request. Each call has a timeout, so a slow server can't hang a tool call, and cancellation flows through, so if the user stops the agent, the request stops too.

For resilience, I used Polly through the standard resilience handler: retries with exponential backoff and jitter, but only for safe, idempotent calls, like reading a build status, and only on transient errors, like timeouts and 503s. Write calls, like starting a deployment, are never retried automatically, because a retry could start a second deployment. Instead, the tool reports the problem and the model can check status first. A circuit breaker stops hammering the server if it's down, and the tool returns a clear message.

For logging, I used Serilog with structured logs: the tool, the user, duration, result and correlation id. Crucially, it writes to standard error and a rolling file, never standard output, because over stdio, standard output carries the JSON-RPC protocol. Separately, an audit log records every tool call, with secrets removed.
That combination is why the server stayed reliable enough to cut deployments from 6 hours to 2.

p15-17.q: Our RAG service is written in Python, and its main job is to give AI coding tools, like GitHub Copilot and Cursor, the context of our codebase and our coding standards. It has two halves: ingestion and retrieval.

Ingestion. A pipeline collects content from [about 40] repositories, plus our coding standards, architecture decision records and API contracts. Code is chunked by structure using tree-sitter: one chunk per class or method, with its file path, namespace and signature, rather than cutting at a fixed number of characters. Documents are chunked by headings. Each chunk gets metadata, like the repository, path, language, module and last commit, and an embedding from Azure OpenAI. Everything is stored in PostgreSQL with pgvector, which also gives us full-text search and metadata filters in the same database.

Retrieval. When Copilot or Cursor calls the search tool through our MCP server, the query runs as a hybrid search: vector similarity for meaning, and full-text search for exact names, like a class or an error code, merged with reciprocal rank fusion. Filters narrow it by repository or language. Then a re-ranker reorders the top results, and we return the best few chunks, trimmed to a token budget, each with its file path and line numbers, so the tool can cite them and open the real file.
Freshness is handled by an incremental re-index on every merge to main. And it's evaluated with a golden question set, measuring whether the right chunks come back.

x: Chunking decides what the retriever can find, so for code it's one of the most important choices. In our Python RAG service, which gives GitHub Copilot and Cursor the context of our codebase and standards, I chunk code by its structure, not by character count.

Fixed-size chunking, say a thousand characters with some overlap, is simple and works for prose, but for code it cuts methods in half, separates a method from its class, and mixes unrelated code in one chunk. The retrieved pieces then make little sense to the model.

So I used tree-sitter, a parser that builds a syntax tree for many languages, including C#, TypeScript and SQL. From the tree, each chunk is a complete unit: a method, with its class name, namespace and signature added as a header, or a small class as a whole. Very long methods are split at statement boundaries, keeping the signature in each part. Every chunk carries metadata: repository, file path, line numbers, language, symbol name and the last commit, which helps filtering and lets the AI tool open the exact lines.

Some content needs its own rules. Markdown standards and decision records are split by headings, so each rule stays together with its title. Configuration and pipeline YAML is chunked by top-level sections. And generated code, build output and secrets files are excluded entirely.
[Switching from fixed-size to tree-sitter chunking raised our retrieval hit rate on the golden question set from about 62 percent to about 80 percent], before any other tuning.

An embedding is a list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text, so similar content ends up close together, and we can find relevant code even when the words differ. [I used Azure OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small model.] It's good on both code and English, inexpensive, and it runs in our enterprise Azure OpenAI tenant, where our data isn't used for training, which matters for an internal codebase. The query and the chunks must always use the same model, so changing models means re-embedding everything, which I planned for with a model version on every row.

For storage, I compared Chroma, FAISS and pgvector. FAISS is a fast library, but not a database: no metadata filtering or updates out of the box. Chroma is easy to start with. [I picked pgvector, on PostgreSQL in our AWS account], because one database gives vector search, full-text search for hybrid retrieval, metadata filters like repository and language, transactions for incremental updates, and standard backups and access control. At our scale, [a few hundred thousand chunks], an HNSW index keeps queries in milliseconds, so a specialised vector database wasn't needed.
The lesson I'd share: choose the simplest store that supports hybrid search and filtering, because retrieval quality matters far more than the database brand.

p15-20.q: In our Python RAG service, which gives GitHub Copilot and Cursor the context of our codebase and standards, retrieval quality improved most from two things: hybrid search and re-ranking.
p15-20.k: hybrid search, bm25, keyword search, vector search, reranking, re-ranker, reciprocal rank fusion, cross-encoder
x: In our Python RAG service, which gives GitHub Copilot and Cursor the context of our codebase and standards, retrieval quality improved most from two things: hybrid search and re-ranking.

Vector search finds content by meaning. That's great for questions like "how do we handle vendor file retries?", but weak for exact identifiers, like a class name, an error code or a configuration key, because embeddings blur precise tokens. Keyword search, like BM25, is the opposite: excellent for exact terms, poor at meaning. Code questions mix both, so hybrid search runs both and combines them. I used PostgreSQL full-text search alongside pgvector, and merged the two ranked lists with reciprocal rank fusion, which rewards items that rank well in either list, without having to tune scores against each other.

Re-ranking is a second, more careful pass. The first stage retrieves, say, the top 30 candidates quickly. Then a re-ranker, [a small cross-encoder model], reads the query and each candidate together and scores how well they actually match. It's slower, which is why it only runs on the shortlist. The top few results go to the AI tool.
Then I add metadata filters, like repository, language or module, and boost chunks from shared libraries and standards, because those are what we want reused.
On our golden question set, [hybrid search plus re-ranking lifted recall at five from about 80 percent to about 88 percent], and exact-name lookups, which vector search often missed, became reliable.

Re-indexing happens on every merge to the main branch. A step in our Azure DevOps pipeline calls the indexing job with the repository and the list of changed files. For each changed file, the job re-parses it with tree-sitter, recalculates the chunks, and compares a content hash for each chunk with what's stored. Standards and architecture decision records are indexed the same way when their documents change, so a new rule is available to the AI tools the same day.
If we change the embedding model, that's a full re-index into a new table, switched over only after the golden question set passes, so quality never drops during the change.
[Since moving to merge-triggered indexing, the index is normally within minutes of main], and reports of "the AI suggested a method that doesn't exist" became rare.

x: Modern models accept very large contexts, so it's a fair question: why not just give the model the whole codebase? For our project, RAG was clearly better, for five reasons.

First, size. Our IRT codebase spans [about 40] repositories, far more than any context window, plus standards and design documents. Second, quality. Models get worse at using information buried in the middle of a very long context, so a few highly relevant chunks often beat a huge dump. Third, cost and speed. Every token is paid for and slows the response, on every single request. Retrieval sends only what's needed. Fourth, freshness and control. The index updates on every merge, we can filter by repository or module, and every result has a source, so we know exactly what the model saw. Fifth, access control. Retrieval can respect which repositories a user is allowed to see, which a pasted dump can't.

Fine-tuning is the other alternative, but it changes how a model behaves, not what it knows today, and it goes stale with every merge. So my rule is: RAG for knowledge, fine-tuning for behaviour, and long context for working deeply on the few files you're actually changing.

That's how our setup works: our Python RAG service, through MCP tools in Copilot and Cursor, finds the relevant code and standards, and then the agent opens those few files fully in its context to make the change.

Every document chunk in the index carries metadata: its source, its owning team, and an audience label, like general, study build, support or internal engineering. When a user asks a question, the Teams bot or web page passes their identity from single sign-on, and the Python service reads their Azure AD group memberships. The search query then filters chunks by the audiences those groups allow, before ranking, inside the same PostgreSQL query. So content a user can't access is never retrieved, never sent to the model, and can never leak into an answer. Filtering after generation would be too late.

What goes into the index matters just as much. Only approved reference content is indexed: specs, user guides, release notes, Admin console configuration guides, and support resolutions sanitised to remove any patient, site or study data. No production systems are connected. That keeps it outside GxP scope, as an informational tool, which we stated clearly in the interface.
Every question, user and set of cited sources is logged, so we can audit who saw what. And when a document's permissions change, the next indexing run updates its labels.
The principle I followed: the assistant should never let someone see more than they could already open themselves.

Workflows are predictable, cheaper, easier to test and easier to audit. Agents are flexible and handle open-ended tasks, but they're less predictable, use more tokens, and can go wrong in more ways. My rule: use the simplest thing that works. If the steps are known, build a workflow. Use an agent only when the path really depends on what it finds.

I've used both. Our CIRT MCP server, built in .NET 8 with about 77 tools for Azure DevOps Server, is used by agents in Cursor and GitHub Copilot, because a release question can go many ways: check a build, then the release, then approvals. But the risky parts are fixed. Our deployment pre-check is a deterministic workflow inside one tool, not something the model improvises, and write actions require human approval.

Our RAG indexing, by contrast, is a pure workflow: parse, chunk, embed, store, every time. [I also tried a multi-agent setup with AutoGen, for drafting release notes with a writer and a reviewer agent], and learned that a simple two-step workflow gave the same quality with fewer surprises.

p15-37.q: A token is a small piece of text, roughly three quarters of an English word on average. Code often uses more tokens, because of symbols and names. Models read and write in tokens, and pricing, speed and limits are all counted in tokens.

x: A token is a small piece of text, roughly three quarters of an English word on average. Code often uses more tokens, because of symbols and names. Models read and write in tokens, and pricing, speed and limits are all counted in tokens.

The context window is the maximum number of tokens a model can consider at once: the system prompt, the conversation, tool definitions, retrieved documents, and its own answer. Anything outside the window, the model simply can't see.

It matters in three ways. Cost and speed: every token is paid for and slows the response, on every request. Quality: even with very large windows, models use information less reliably when it's buried in a long, noisy context, so more isn't always better. And limits: long agent sessions fill up, and older details drop out or get summarised.

In my work, this shaped design decisions. In our CIRT MCP server, built in .NET 8 with about 77 tools, every tool's name and description takes tokens in every request, so I kept descriptions short and tool results compact, returning summaries instead of raw Azure DevOps JSON. In our Python RAG service, which gives GitHub Copilot and Cursor the context of our codebase and standards, retrieval returns only the few most relevant chunks, trimmed to a token budget, instead of whole files.
So my approach is: give the model the smallest context that fully answers the task.

p15-38.q: Both control how random a model's output is. At each step, the model has a probability for every possible next token. Temperature reshapes those probabilities: low temperature, near zero, makes it pick the most likely tokens, so output is focused and repeatable; higher temperature flattens them, so output is more varied and creative, but also more likely to drift. Top-p, also called nucleus sampling, limits choices to the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p, like 0.9, cutting off unlikely options. Usually you tune one of them, not both.

How I set them depends on the task. For anything factual or structured, like extracting fields, classifying, generating code, or answering from retrieved documents in our RAG assistant, I use low temperature, [around 0 to 0.2], because I want consistent, grounded answers. For drafting text, like release note summaries or brainstorming test scenarios, I use a moderate value, [around 0.5 to 0.7].

Two cautions. Temperature zero isn't fully deterministic on most hosted models, so tests shouldn't depend on exact text; they should check structure and facts. And low temperature doesn't prevent hallucination. A model can be consistently wrong. Grounding, through RAG with citations, and validation matter far more.
In a GxP environment like ours, predictability is valuable, so my default is low temperature, with creativity only where a human reviews the result.

Input guardrails. Validate what comes in: allowed values, lengths and formats. In the MCP server, every tool parameter is validated, like environment names against a known list. In our end-user RAG assistant, questions are checked for personal or patient data before anything is sent.

Clear boundaries. AI helps engineers and staff work faster, but it doesn't make GxP decisions or touch patient data. First, role and goal: who the assistant is and what success looks like. For our IRT Knowledge Assistant, a RAG tool for business analysts, QA and support, it's: answer questions about IRT features using only the provided sources. Second, context: the audience, the domain terms, like study, randomization or drug accountability, and anything it must know. Third, rules: answer only from the sources; cite every claim; if the sources don't cover it, say you don't know; never give advice on patient data. Fourth, output format: short answer first, then details, then citations, or a JSON schema when code consumes the result. Fifth, examples: one or two good examples, because models follow examples more closely than descriptions.

A few habits make the difference. Be specific: "under 120 words" works better than "be concise". Separate instructions from data with clear tags, so retrieved text isn't mistaken for instructions, which also helps against prompt injection. Explain why a rule exists; models follow reasons better. And keep it as short as possible, because every token is sent on every request.

Most importantly, I treat prompts like code. They're versioned in the repository, and every change runs against a golden question set before release, [the same approach we used in our Python RAG service and our CIRT MCP server tool descriptions].

p15-44.q: When code consumes the model's output, free text isn't good enough. I need valid, predictable structure, and I get it in layers.

First, use the model's built-in structured outputs. Azure OpenAI supports a JSON schema response format, where the output is constrained to match the schema, so required fields and types are always there. Tool calling works the same way: the model fills in arguments against a defined schema. That's exactly how our CIRT MCP server, built in .NET 8, receives tool calls: each tool's parameters are typed, and the SDK turns them into a schema the model must follow.

Second, validate anyway. In Python, I define the schema as a Pydantic model and validate every response; in C#, I deserialise into typed classes. Validation checks business rules too, like an environment name being in our list, not just the format.
Third, handle failure. If validation fails, retry once with the error message included, and if it still fails, return a clear error rather than guessing. Never silently accept a half-parsed result.
Fourth, design simple schemas. Fewer fields, clear names, enums instead of free text, and descriptions on each field. Complex nested schemas fail more often.

[In our release-notes helper, which drafts notes from Azure DevOps work items, moving from prompt-only JSON to schema-constrained output with Pydantic validation took parsing failures from a few percent to practically zero.]

It's database-per-tenant, and it suits clinical trials well. Isolation: one sponsor's trial data can never mix with another's, which helps both security and audits. Lifecycle: when a study closes, its database can be archived on its own. Performance: a heavy study doesn't slow down others, and each database stays a manageable size. The cost is operational. Schema changes must reach hundreds of databases consistently. We manage the schema in SQL Server Data Tools database projects in source control, so every change is reviewed, and deployments compare the model to each study database and apply the changes. Changes are backward-compatible, like adding nullable columns first, so the application works during the rollout, and deployment verifies that every study database ends on the expected version. Data fixes go through reviewed scripts, never manual edits, because it's GxP.
Applications pick the right database per request: the study is resolved from the request, and the connection is built for that study's database, with EF Core in the new APIs.
If I designed it again, I'd keep database per study for regulated data, and invest early in automation and monitoring across all the databases.

The React app signs in with an OIDC client library, using the authorisation code flow with PKCE. Authentication is only half. Authorisation uses our own global security model: roles map to modules, and modules to actions, with site access per user, enforced in API attributes, and the UI trims menus to match.

Part 11 adds requirements: a password policy and lockout, idle session timeout handled consistently with an idle timer in React, and re-authentication as an electronic signature on critical actions, like emergency unblinding.
From my resume work: I fixed token-based logout so logged-out tokens stop working immediately, and an SSO cookie "header too long" failure, by keeping only a small session key in the cookie.

p16-7.q: Our IRT, which runs randomisation and drug supply for clinical trials, has many scheduled jobs: AlertWatchDog, our alert engine, report generation, imports and exports, and housekeeping. In the legacy core, they run on Quartz.NET.
p16-7.k: quartz, quartz.net, scheduled jobs, job scheduler, cron jobs dotnet, background jobs, failed jobs, scheduler database
x: Our IRT, which runs randomisation and drug supply for clinical trials, has many scheduled jobs: AlertWatchDog, our alert engine, report generation, imports and exports, and housekeeping. In the legacy core, they run on Quartz.NET.

Quartz.NET is a job scheduling library. A job is a class with an Execute method, and a trigger says when it runs, either simple intervals or CRON expressions. We use the persistent job store in a dedicated SQL Server scheduler database, which matters for three reasons: schedules survive restarts, several servers can run in a cluster without running the same job twice, because Quartz takes database locks, and missed runs can be handled with misfire rules after downtime.

Some practices we follow. Jobs are idempotent, so a re-run after a failure is safe. Long jobs work in batches and respect cancellation, so a deployment can stop them cleanly. Concurrent execution is disallowed for jobs that must not overlap. Failures are recorded in a custom failed-jobs table, with the error and the study, so support can see and re-run them. And every run logs a start, an end and counts, with a correlation id.

For newer services, we use .NET hosted services and RabbitMQ consumers, and some file processing runs as SSIS packages, like the material forecasting load. If I were building fresh on AWS, EventBridge Scheduler would replace Quartz; on Azure, a Functions timer trigger.
The key lesson: a scheduler must make failures visible, because a job that silently stops is worse than one that fails loudly.

p16-8.q: In our IRT, which runs randomisation and drug supply for clinical trials, RabbitMQ carries the asynchronous work: notifications from AlertWatchDog, our alert engine, study configuration events that refresh caches, and integration events.
p16-8.k: rabbitmq in irt, rabbitmq retry, dead letter exchange, retry exchange, rabbitmq consumers, messaging library, cache refresh events, publisher confirms
x: In our IRT, which runs randomisation and drug supply for clinical trials, RabbitMQ carries the asynchronous work: notifications from AlertWatchDog, our alert engine, study configuration events that refresh caches, and integration events.

Every service uses a shared messaging library, built on .NET Standard, so publishing and consuming work the same way everywhere, with the same connection handling, serialisation and message metadata, including a correlation id for tracing across services.

Consumers run as .NET 9 worker services, with some older .NET Framework consumers still running. Reliability is built into the library. Consumers use manual acknowledgements, so a message is only removed after it's processed. If processing fails, the message goes to a retry exchange, which holds it for a delay and sends it back, a limited number of times. After the last retry, it goes to a dead-letter exchange, where it's kept for investigation, and it raises an alert. Consumers are idempotent, because RabbitMQ delivers at least once.

On the publishing side, I learned the importance of publisher confirms the hard way. [In mid-2024, about 1,200 updates were silently lost during a broker problem], because publishes weren't confirmed. I root-caused it and added publisher confirms, so the publisher knows the broker has safely stored each message, and retries if not.
Study configuration uses events too: when a study's configuration changes, an event tells the study consumer services to refresh their caches, so every server sees the new configuration quickly.

p16-9.q: In our IRT, a study is one clinical trial set up in the system, and its configuration, like sites, arms, visits, kit types, forms and permissions, is read on almost every request. It lives in the study's own SQL Server database, so reading it from the database every time would be slow and wasteful.
p16-9.k: caching study configuration, redis, memcached, cache invalidation, cache refresh, distributed cache, config cache
x: In our IRT, a study is one clinical trial set up in the system, and its configuration, like sites, arms, visits, kit types, forms and permissions, is read on almost every request. It lives in the study's own SQL Server database, so reading it from the database every time would be slow and wasteful.

So configuration is cached. Historically the platform used memcached, and it now uses Redis, which is faster to operate with and supports richer data types. Services use cache-aside: read from the cache, and on a miss, load from the study database and store it, keyed by study and configuration area.

The hard part is invalidation. Study configuration changes rarely, but when it changes, for example after a protocol amendment is transferred to production, every server must see it quickly. We do that with events: the change publishes a study event on RabbitMQ, and the study consumer and cache refresh services clear and reload the affected keys. There's also a time-to-live as a safety net, so even a missed event can't leave stale configuration forever.

Some rules matter in a regulated system. Blinded data is never cached in a way that could be returned to blinded users. Transactional data, like inventory or randomisation slots, is never served from cache, because it must be exact. And caches are warmed after deployments, so the first users don't pay the cost.
The principle: cache what's read often and changes rarely, and make invalidation explicit and event-driven.

p16-10.q: Our newer IRT APIs, on .NET 6 through 10, follow the same structure, so any developer can move between them. Our IRT runs randomisation and drug supply for clinical trials, and these APIs sit around the legacy .NET Framework core.
p16-10.k: clean architecture irt, mediatr, fluentvalidation, cqrs handlers, pipeline behaviour, api structure, domain microservices
x: Our newer IRT APIs, on .NET 6 through 10, follow the same structure, so any developer can move between them. Our IRT runs randomisation and drug supply for clinical trials, and these APIs sit around the legacy .NET Framework core.

They use clean architecture with four layers. The domain layer has entities and business rules, with no dependencies. The application layer has use cases, written as MediatR commands and queries, each with one handler. The infrastructure layer has EF Core, the study database connections, the RabbitMQ messaging library, SFTP and calls to the legacy transaction engine. And the API layer has thin controllers that just send a command or query and return the result.

MediatR pipeline behaviours handle cross-cutting concerns once, for every request. A validation behaviour runs FluentValidation validators before the handler, so bad input never reaches business logic, and returns clear field errors. Other behaviours handle logging with timings and a correlation id, and transactions for commands.

Around that, there's global exception middleware that returns ProblemDetails responses, so clients get a consistent error format, JWT bearer authentication with Keycloak, authorisation attributes based on our role, module and action model, and Serilog with enrichers writing to files and Splunk.

The benefits are testability, because handlers can be unit tested without HTTP, consistency across services, and cheap new features, because adding a use case means adding a command, a validator and a handler.

p16-11.q: Our IRT runs randomisation and drug supply for clinical trials, and because it's a hybrid of a legacy core and newer services, logging has three generations.
p16-11.k: logging irt, serilog splunk, log4net, opentelemetry datadog, correlation id, monitoring irt, observability
x: Our IRT runs randomisation and drug supply for clinical trials, and because it's a hybrid of a legacy core and newer services, logging has three generations.

The legacy .NET Framework core uses log4net and Enterprise Library logging. The newer .NET APIs and workers use Serilog, with enrichers that add the service, environment, study, user and correlation id to every event, writing to rolling files and to Splunk, which is where support and developers search across services. The newest data transfer APIs use OpenTelemetry, sending traces and metrics to Datadog, which gives end-to-end traces across service calls.

Correlation is what ties it together. Every request gets a correlation id, which is passed in HTTP headers and in RabbitMQ message metadata, so one search in Splunk shows a transaction from the React screen, through the API and the queue, to the consumer that sent the email.

For monitoring, we watch error rates and latency on the APIs, dead-letter queues on RabbitMQ, failed scheduled jobs in the Quartz failed-jobs table, and missing integration files, and AlertWatchDog sends business alerts, like low stock, by email. [I also built Grafana dashboards for the services I own.]

Some rules matter in a regulated product: no patient-identifying data or secrets in logs, structured fields rather than free text, and log levels that keep production readable. Audit trails are separate from logs, stored in the database, because logs can be rotated but audit records must be permanent.

p16-12.q: Our IRT is a hybrid of a legacy core and newer services, with APIs, queue consumers, scheduled jobs, integrations and two front ends, so we handle errors in each layer, with one goal: nothing fails silently, and users get a clear message.
p16-12.k: error handling irt, problemdetails, global exception middleware, retry dead letter, quartz failed jobs, axios interceptor errors, mule error flows
x: Our IRT is a hybrid of a legacy core and newer services, with APIs, queue consumers, scheduled jobs, integrations and two front ends, so we handle errors in each layer, with one goal: nothing fails silently, and users get a clear message.

In the new .NET APIs, validation errors are caught early by FluentValidation in the MediatR pipeline and returned as field errors. Anything unexpected is caught by global exception middleware, logged with Serilog including the correlation id, and returned as a ProblemDetails response, with no stack traces exposed. Expected business failures, like a subject not eligible for randomisation, return specific, meaningful errors.
In messaging, RabbitMQ consumers use retry exchanges with delays for temporary failures, then a dead-letter exchange, which raises an alert, and consumers are idempotent, so retries are safe.
In scheduled jobs, Quartz job failures are written to a custom failed-jobs table, with the error and the study, so support can see and re-run them.
In integrations, MuleSoft error flows send email alerts, and the new .NET data transfer jobs record failures per file, so a bad file can be fixed and re-processed.

In the React app, axios interceptors handle errors centrally: an expired session redirects to login, and other errors show a friendly message using the ProblemDetails response, with an idle timer logging users out after inactivity.
The shared principle is fail visibly, retry only what's safe to retry, and always keep a correlation id to trace it.

There are two generations. The older reports were built in SAP BusinessObjects, with a legacy reports API and a copy tool for moving report definitions, and they're being replaced.
