[I tuned a slow shipment report from 8 to 12 seconds down to under 300 milliseconds with a covering index and a rewritten query.]
Every report generated is logged, so we know who saw which data.

p16-14.q: Many study drugs must stay within a temperature range, like two to eight degrees, from the depot to the site. A temperature excursion is when a shipment goes outside that range, and the drug may no longer be safe to give. Our IRT, which runs drug supply for clinical trials, has a module to manage this.
p16-14.k: tems, temperature excursion, cold chain, temperature monitoring, shipment temperature, excursion approval, quarantine kits
x: Many study drugs must stay within a temperature range, like two to eight degrees, from the depot to the site. A temperature excursion is when a shipment goes outside that range, and the drug may no longer be safe to give. Our IRT, which runs drug supply for clinical trials, has a module to manage this.

Shipments carry temperature monitoring devices. Their data arrives through an integration, so when a shipment is received, the system knows whether an excursion happened, for how long, and at what temperature. If there's an excursion, the affected kits are put into quarantine automatically, so they can't be dispensed. Then a reviewer, usually the sponsor or the supply team, assesses it against the drug's stability data and decides whether the kits are acceptable, which releases them, or not acceptable, which marks them damaged for return or destruction.
Because the decision affects patient safety, it's a controlled action: only authorised roles can approve it, it requires an electronic signature by re-authentication, and the full history is audited.

Technically, it's a separate API with an Angular 8 UI, one of the Angular sub-applications in our legacy portal, with its own kit statuses connected to inventory, so quarantined kits are excluded from dispensing and resupply calculations, and replacements can be triggered.
It's a good example of IRT protecting patients: no subject should receive a kit that has been out of range unless it's explicitly approved.

p16-15.q: These features protect subjects from receiving drug that shouldn't be used, in our IRT, which runs drug supply for clinical trials, where each trial is set up as a study.
p16-15.k: material block, quarantine, block lot, relabelling, relabeling, expiry extension, kit replacement
x: These features protect subjects from receiving drug that shouldn't be used, in our IRT, which runs drug supply for clinical trials, where each trial is set up as a study.

Material block lets the supply team block a whole lot, or batch, of drug, or specific kits, for example after a quality issue at manufacturing, or when a lot is close to expiry. Blocked kits immediately become unavailable for dispensing and shipping, at every depot and site, and resupply calculations treat them as missing, so replacements can be sent. When the issue is resolved, the block can be lifted. Quarantine is similar but usually automatic and temporary, like after a temperature excursion, until someone reviews it.

Relabelling is about expiry. Drug is labelled with an expiry date, and when stability data supports a longer shelf life, kits can be relabelled with a new date instead of being destroyed. The system tracks which kits were relabelled, the new expiry, and where they are, and dispensing rules use the new date.
Technically, material block is one of our newer features: a .NET API and a React module, published as an npm package into our new React shell app. Relabelling is in the legacy ASP.NET MVC portal.

All of these are controlled actions, limited to authorised supply roles, with reasons and full audit history, and they respect blinding, because blocking a lot must never reveal which arm it belongs to.

Manual drug assignment is the controlled exception, where an authorised user overrides the automatic choice. Typical reasons are a kit that's physically damaged when the pharmacist opens it, a system or connectivity problem during a visit, or a situation the protocol allows, where a specific kit must be given.

Because it touches treatment, it's heavily controlled. Only specific roles can use it. The system still enforces the important rules: the kit must belong to the subject's arm, be available at that site, and not be expired or blocked, so the override can never give the wrong treatment. A reason is mandatory, blinding is protected, so the user selects from valid kit numbers without seeing the arm, and every manual assignment is fully audited and can be reported to the sponsor.
Technically, it's one of our newer modules: a dedicated .NET API and a React user interface, built as an npm package and embedded into our new React shell app.
It shows a pattern I like in regulated systems: allow flexibility for real-world problems, but keep the safety rules in the backend, so the flexibility can't be misused.

p16-17.q: Running out of drug at a site is one of the worst things that can happen in a clinical trial, but overstocking wastes very expensive drug. Our IRT, which runs drug supply for clinical trials, where each trial is set up as a study, helps with both through resupply and forecasting.
p16-17.k: supply forecasting, material forecasting, forecasting dashboard, demand forecast, ssis, supply planning, mfd
x: Running out of drug at a site is one of the worst things that can happen in a clinical trial, but overstocking wastes very expensive drug. Our IRT, which runs drug supply for clinical trials, where each trial is set up as a study, helps with both through resupply and forecasting.

Day to day, resupply is driven by each study's strategy: min and max levels per site, or predictive resupply, which looks at upcoming visits for enrolled subjects and the kits they'll need. When projected stock drops below the trigger, a shipment is generated from the right depot.

Forecasting looks further ahead. Our material forecasting dashboard projects demand per study, country and depot over the coming weeks and months, from current inventory, enrolment rates, visit schedules and expiry dates. That helps supply managers decide when to manufacture, label and move drug between depots, and spot lots that will expire before they're used.

Technically, the data is loaded by scheduled SSIS packages into a reporting structure, the dashboards are an Angular sub-application in the legacy portal, and [a newer version of the forecasting backend is being built as a .NET API].
The design challenge is accuracy versus simplicity: forecasts use clear, explainable rules, so supply managers trust them, and every assumption, like the enrolment rate, is visible and adjustable.

p16-18.k: study promotion, study transfer, transfer tool, diff review, build uat production, configuration promotion, study-transfer guard
x: In our IRT, a study is one clinical trial set up in the system, and its configuration is built by our study build team in our Admin console tooling, in a build environment. It must reach UAT and production exactly as reviewed, because it's GxP.

We promote it with a transfer tool, backed by a data transfer service. It compares the study's configuration in the source environment with the target, and shows a diff viewer of every change: added visits, changed supply settings, new sites, role changes. Reviewers approve that diff, and only then is it applied, so nobody changes production configuration by hand. The same path is used for the first go-live, from build to UAT to production, and for every protocol amendment later.

Safety was the focus of my work here. I built the study-transfer safety guard, which blocks unsafe transfers. For example, it checks the target study's status, so a live study's data can't be overwritten by a configuration meant for a new study, checks that the user has the right role for that environment, and checks that the source and target really are the same study. If a check fails, the transfer stops with a clear reason.
Every transfer is audited with who, when, what changed and the approval, which is exactly the evidence auditors ask for.
The principle: configuration is treated like code, reviewed as a diff, promoted through environments, and guarded against the mistakes that matter most.

Each module exports its routes, pages and components, and declares React, MUI, IQVIA's React design system and Redux Toolkit as peer dependencies, so the shell provides one copy of each. It's built as a library, with TypeScript type definitions, and published by its own pipeline to our private npm feed in Azure DevOps, with a semantic version.

The shell installs the modules it needs at specific versions, registers their routes and Redux slices, and provides shared services: the Keycloak sign-in, the axios instances with interceptors, environment configuration from Vite variables, and the idle timer for session timeout. So each module focuses on its feature.

The benefits are independent development and testing per team, clear ownership, and controlled upgrades, because the shell decides when to take a new module version, which fits validated releases. The trade-offs are version alignment of shared dependencies, and integration testing in the shell, which we handle with a shared dependency policy and end-to-end tests.
Compared with runtime module federation, build-time packages are simpler and fully reproducible, which matters more to us than independent runtime deployment.

p16-20.q: 21 CFR Part 11 is the FDA regulation for electronic records and signatures, and our IRT, which runs randomisation and drug supply for clinical trials, must comply because its records are part of the trial evidence.
p16-20.k: electronic signature, e-signature, re-authentication, session timeout, idle logout, 21 cfr part 11 implementation, part 11 controls
x: 21 CFR Part 11 is the FDA regulation for electronic records and signatures, and our IRT, which runs randomisation and drug supply for clinical trials, must comply because its records are part of the trial evidence.

For electronic signatures, critical actions, like emergency unblinding, approving a temperature excursion or approving drug destruction, require re-authentication at the moment of the action. The user enters their credentials again, verified against Keycloak through a dedicated e-signature verification endpoint, and the signature is recorded with the action: who signed, when, and the meaning of the signature, like "approved". The signature is linked to that record and can't be copied or reused, and the whole flow is audited. Studies can configure which actions need it.

For sessions, idle timeout logs users out after inactivity. In the React app, an idle timer warns the user before logout, then ends the session and redirects to sign-in, and the legacy portal does the same. That prevents someone using an unattended, logged-in screen.

Around those, there are unique user accounts, a password policy with lockout after failed attempts, role-based access with blinded and unblinded separation, and an immutable audit trail with reasons for change on critical edits.
The validation side matters as much as the code: each control is tested in our automated test suites, and the evidence is part of every release.

p16-21.q: In a GxP system like our IRT, which runs randomisation and drug supply for clinical trials, production data can't just be edited, because every record is part of the trial evidence. But real situations need corrections, like a site entering the wrong visit date.
p16-21.k: data correction, production data fix, gxp data change, support tools, sql script production, housekeeping, data fix process
x: In a GxP system like our IRT, which runs randomisation and drug supply for clinical trials, production data can't just be edited, because every record is part of the trial evidence. But real situations need corrections, like a site entering the wrong visit date.

First choice is always the application: if the system offers a correction transaction, like editing subject data with a reason for change, that's used, because it applies the business rules and writes the audit trail automatically.

When that's not possible, there's a controlled data correction process. A support ticket documents the request, the reason and the sponsor's approval. A developer writes a script, which is peer reviewed and tested on a copy in a lower environment. Then it's run in production by an authorised person through our support tooling, which records exactly what ran, when and by whom, and the change is captured in the history and audit tables, with before and after values. The ticket is closed with that evidence.

There are also routine support tools: housekeeping jobs for study databases, an account clean-up tool that deactivates unused accounts, and an integration with the ticketing system, so issues are tracked end to end.

My rule as a developer: never touch production data without a ticket, a review and an audit trail, even when it seems small, because in a regulated product, an undocumented change is itself a finding.

p16-22.q: In our IRT, which runs randomisation and drug supply for clinical trials, testing isn't just about quality; it's evidence for validation, which regulators can inspect.
p16-22.k: test automation irt, selenium, api tests, validation testing, gxp testing, regression suite, playwright cucumber
x: In our IRT, which runs randomisation and drug supply for clinical trials, testing isn't just about quality; it's evidence for validation, which regulators can inspect.

We test at several levels. Unit tests with xUnit or NUnit and Moq cover business rules in the new .NET services, like randomisation edge cases, kit expiry rules and validation, and run on every build with SonarQube quality gates. API tests check the services end to end with real databases. UI automation, in our test automation suite with Selenium, and Playwright with Cucumber in newer areas, covers critical site journeys, like screening, randomising, dispensing, unblinding and drug accountability. Frontend unit tests use Jest.

Automation matters especially because our IRT is configurable: each study behaves differently, so regression suites run against representative study configurations, and the simulator in our study-build tooling lets teams test a study's behaviour before go-live.

For validation, tests are linked to requirements, results are recorded as evidence for each release, and releases move through FV, TechOps, UAT and production only with that evidence attached and approved.

My part: I write unit and integration tests for my services, add Playwright scenarios for features I build, and as release integrator, I check the test evidence before a release moves on. The principle is that a requirement isn't done until there's a test proving it.
